case_summary.text: IBC: Where advance was paid and there was no document or agreement which showed terms of payment of any interest or consideration against time value for money, same was not a financial debt

IBC: Where alleged loan amount granted by appellant was never treated or acknowledged as a loan in books of Corporate Debtor, no repayment demand was made for 15 years before CIRP and audited balance sheet of corporate debtor classified amount claimed by appellant to be advance and not a borrowing, transaction was not a financial debt and, accordingly, Adjudicating Authority was justified in rejecting claim of appellant

IBC: Where a marketing agency, appellant, paid amount under marketing agreement to TV programme/Serial producer in lieu of rights of 'free commercial time' (FCT), since there was no clause that amount paid by appellant was to be repayable along with interest over a period of time, same would not be give rise to financial debt

IBC: Where financial creditors claimed to have advanced loan to corporate debtor and corporate debtor had defaulted in repayment of loan amount, since loan was provided as unsecured loan and there was no interest and no time fixed to repay same, said loan would not fall under category of financial debt

IBC : Where financial creditor had failed to muster clinching proof and evidence in terms of financial records to show that sum advanced by them to corporate debtor was indisputably interest-bearing and that interest had continued to accrue and was being realized as consideration for time value of money, sum advanced by financial creditor to corporate debtor did not satisfy ingredients of financial debt of disbursal, time value of money and commercial effect of borrowing, and thus, instant
IBC : Where unsecured loan was advanced which did neither bear interest nor was same disbursed against consideration for time value of money, said loan would not be financial debt

IBC : In absence of any loan agreement and relevant Board Resolution, merely on basis of Form 26AS (reflecting credit of interest and deduction of TDS), it could not be presumed that any loan was disbursed by applicant to corporate debtor, which could be treated as financial debt; applicant having failed to demonstrate that debt claimed in its application was arising out of any loan transactions and was a financial debt, application was to be dismissed

IBC: Where there was no element of time value for money and petitioner had given friendly loan to respondent-corporate debtor, transaction would not acquire status of financial debt and petition filed under section 7 was to be dismissed

IBC: Where Adjudicating Authority after considering record found that there was material in form of MOU and agreement which dealt with interest free unsecured loan advanced by financial creditors to corporate debtor and concluded that there was no time value of money and that it was not financial debt, findings recorded by Adjudicating Authority could not have been interfered with

IBC : Where petitioner-financial creditor had made payment with an intention to buy 25 per cent equity stake in corporate debtor's development project, money had been invested with an intention to acquire equity stake or some other interest and, therefore, same could not be classified as a financial debt under section 5(8)

IBC : Where financial creditor claimed to have advanced loan to corporate debtor, since financial creditor could not place on record any documentary evidence to suggest that amount claimed to have transferred by it to corporate debtor were advanced as loan, alleged loan amount could not be termed as 'financial debt'

IBC: Where applicant's claim of financial debt against corporate debtor was based on payments made to individuals without evidence of funds disbursed to corporate debtor, agreement terms indicated profit-sharing rather than a fixed repayment obligation, and no assured or time-linked consideration was demonstrated, transaction did not qualify as financial debt and RP rightly rejected applicant’s claim.

IBC: Where there was no element of time value for money and petitioner had given friendly loan to respondent corporate debtor, transaction would not acquire status of financial debt and petition filed under section 7 was to be dismissed

IBC : Where appellant claimed its financial debt on basis of inter-corporate loans given from time to time to corporate debtor, however, there was no disbursement for time value of money and, there was no financial records of corporate debtor reflected any such transaction with regard to alleged inter-company loan, since essential ingredients to prove a financial debt was missing thus, NCLT did not commit any error in rejecting appellant's claim as a financial creditor

IBC: Where financial creditor, ex-director of corporate debtor, claimed to have advanced loan to corporate debtor since there was nothing on record to show if any decision was taken in Board or Resolution passed to raise above alleged loans from financial creditor, alleged debt could not be termed as 'financial debt'

IBC: Where applicant advanced Rs. 3.36 crores to corporate debtor as loan on interest and no share subscription or related binding documents were produced, payment could not be considered as share application money, thus existence of financial debt over threshold was established, warranting admission of insolvency application

IBC : Where appellant claimed its financial debt on basis of inter-corporate loans given from time to time to corporate debtor, however, there was no disbursement for time value of money and there was no financial record of corporate debtor reflecting any such transaction with regard to alleged inter-company loan, essential ingredients to prove a financial debt were missing and, thus, NCLT did not commit any error in rejecting appellant's claim as a financial creditor

IBC : Where NCLAT held that on consideration of documents and correspondences including balance sheets it was evident that amount paid by respondent to corporate debtor as advance for marketing/financial requirement of development project undertaken by corporate debtor was nothing but a financial debt within meaning of IBC and, therefore,
Loan granted by applicant didn't fall under financial debt in absence of records to prove agreed rate of interest

IBC : Where appellant had disbursed money to corporate debtor only as payment which was to be adjusted in sale of land and same was not in consideration for time value of money, sum disbursed was not financial debt under section 5(8)

IBC : Where loan was disbursed to corporate debtor without applicable rate of interest, loan was not against consideration for time value of money and could not be considered as financial debt and, hence, applicant who had disbursed such loan was not financial creditor to be eligible to file petition under section 7

IBC : Definition of 'Financial Debt' in section 5(8) does not expressly exclude an interest free loan; a person who gives a term loan to a corporate person free of interest on account of its working capital requirements is a financial creditor, and, therefore, is competent to initiate Corporate Insolvency resolution process under section 7

IBC : Where loan agreements between parties clearly showed that loans were interest bearing and were in nature of financial debts, which carried time value of money, NCLT erred in dismissing application filed by appellant-operational creditor under section 7 against respondent-corporate debtor on ground that amounts advanced were not financial debts

IBC : Where appellant filed an application under section 7 against corporate debtor but had failed to establish that he had given any loan to corporate debtor directly and no material was placed on record by appellant, in which corporate debtor had unambiguously admitted debt, in absence of financial debt qua corporate debtor,

IBC : Where appellant/financial creditor advanced interest free loan to corporate debtor to discharge its liabilities towards secured financial creditors and said loan was acknowledged by corporate debtor as it was reflected in its balance sheet as unsecured loan, said amount fell within definition of default on part of corporate debtor and, therefore, NCLT had committed a patent error in dismissing application filed under section 7.

I&B Code: Where applicant had failed to bring on record any evidence to suggest that he disbursed money against consideration for time value of money and there was no information about rate of interest on principal amount, loan did not satisfy requirement of financial debt as contemplated under section 5(8)
IBC : Once MOU executed between parties provided for payments of interest, requirements of time value of money, as per Code, was satisfied to make debt due a financial debt
I&B Code: Where there was no written loan agreement money claimed by financial creditor was not debt and therefore, application filed under section 7 was to be rejected

IBC : Where appellant, a government undertaking had invested an amount in corporate debtor by way of an interest free deposit but, no charge document was created in appellant's favour by corporate debtor, appellant could not be classified as a secured financial creditor in absence of such document
IBC : Time value of money exists in case of interest free loan as well and same will be considered as financial debt for filing CIRP under section 7

IBC : Where financial creditor had granted financial assistance to corporate debtor but there was no agreement of loan, financial creditor had failed to establish that transaction in question was a financial debt and corporate debtor had committed default and, therefore, order of NCLT admitting application filed under section 7 by financial creditor was to be set aside

IBC : Where appellants-shareholders of corporate debtor holding 48 per cent shareholding of corporate debtor made part payment towards loan availed by corporate debtor on understanding that 100 per cent shares of corporate debtor would be transferred to appellants, appellants were related parties and amount paid by them was towards 'equity' and same could not be treated as financial debt

IBC: Payment received for shares duly issued to a third party at request of payee could not be a debt, not to speak of financial debt; a personal Loan to a Promoter or a Director of a company cannot trigger Corporate Resolution Process under IBC
IBC: Money given as advance to be used for purpose of profits and to give back equivalent of money given, would take character of financial debt

IBC : Where interest was to be paid as consideration for time value of money, that was received as long term borrowing, debt including principal and interest would fall within purview of financial debt
Claim against consideration for time value of money couldn't be termed as financial debt under IBC
Unsecured Loan without any interest and no fixed time to repay didn’t fall under category of financial debt

IBC : Where NCLAT held that on consideration of documents and correspondences including balance sheets it was evident that amount paid by respondent to corporate debtor as advance for marketing/financial requirement of development project undertaken by corporate debtor was nothing but a financial debt within meaning of IBC and, therefore, NCLT committed an error in holding that respondent was not a 'financial creditor', there was no infirmity in order of NCLAT

IBC : Where on consideration of documents and correspondences, including balance sheets, it was evident that amount paid to corporate debtor as advance for marketing/financial requirements of development project undertaken by corporate debtor was nothing but a financial debt, Adjudicating Authority committed error in holding that appellant was not a 'financial creditor'

IBC : Where financial creditor had failed to demonstrate with cogent evidence that money which he was claiming was disbursed to corporate debtor for time value of money as per section 5(8), disbursal lacked commercial character necessary to constitute a financial debt under IBC and, therefore, application filed under section 7 for initiating CIRP against corporate debtor was to be dismissed

IBC: Payment received for shares duly issued to a third party at request of payee could not be a debt, not to speak of financial debt; a personal loan to a promoter or a Director of a company cannot trigger Corporate Resolution Process under IBC
Unsecured Loan without any interest and no fixed time to repay didn’t fall under category of financial debt: NCLAT
Money paid by marketing agency to TV serial producer without interest wouldn't give rise to financial debt
Interest-bearing loans carrying time value of money was a financial debt; NCLT erred in rejecting a plea made u/s 7

IBC : Where letter issued by corporate debtor to a financial creditor clearly clearly showed that an advance made beyond a security deposit by financial creditor carried interest, which was compoundable and payable quarterly and, corporate debtor had acknowledged this interest in its financial statements as a long-term borrowing, referring to it as a loan since, financial creditor had proved debt and default, NCLT did not commit any error in admitting section 7 application

IBC : Where appellant-financial creditor filed a section 7 application against corporate debtor on basis of a Deed of Assignment, where sum given to corporate debtor by IIL was transferred to appellant, however, said sum was clearly shown as a trade receivable rather than a loan and there was no contract or agreement between corporate debtor and IIL designating sum given as a loan, NCLT did not commit any error in rejecting section 7 application filed by appellant against corporate debtor
Part-payment by appellant towards loan availed by corporate debtor in exchange of 100% shares wasn’t a financial debt

IBC : Where letter issued by corporate debtor to a financial creditor clearly showed that an advance made beyond a security deposit by financial creditor carried interest, which was compoundable and payable quarterly and, corporate debtor had acknowledged this interest in its financial statements as a long-term borrowing, referring to it as a loan, financial creditor had proved debt and default and, therefore, NCLT did not commit any error in admitting section 7 application
Money given to corporate debtor without any stipulation of returning the same wasn't financial debt
Amount claimed to be transferred to corporate debtor couldn’t be termed as ‘financial debt’ without any evidence

HEADNOTE: Section  5(8), read with section  3(12), of the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016 -  Corporate insolvency resolution process -  Financial debt - Applicant - financial creditor claimed that it had disbursed a loan to corporate debtor - On corporate debtor’s failure to pay, an application under section 7 was filed against corporate debtor - It was noted that there was no credible evidence to establish that alleged disbursal was made against time value of money (an essential element for qualifying a claim as a ‘financial debt’ under Section 5(8)) - Transaction in question neither involved any stipulated interest component nor any contractual arrangement indicating accrual of financial gain, return, or profit to alleged Financial Creditor - Furthermore, there were no agreed terms of repayment, nor was there any contemporaneous communication or correspondence evidencing a request for a loan or acknowledgment of such a financial arrangement - Whether in absence of foundational elements, disbursal lacked commercial character necessary to constitute a financial debt under IBC - Held, yes - Whether application under Section 7 was barred by limitation as purported recall of an alleged loan was made nearly 17 years after its initial disbursal - Held, yes - Whether in absence of a categorical admission, a time-barred claim could not be revived - Held, yes - Whether financial creditor had failed to demonstrate, with cogent evidence, existence of a legally enforceable financial debt as defined under Section 5(8) and correspondingly, had not substantiated occurrence of a default as per Section 3(12), and, therefore, instant application was to be dismissed - Held, yes [Paras 14, 16, 22 and 24]

FACT: ■

The applicant- financial creditor claimed that it had extended a loan to the Corporate Debtor during the period from 13.06.2007 to 27.03.2009. The said loan was extended in his personal capacity and was repayable on demand.

■

Corporate Debtor had consistently acknowledged the said loan in its Audited Financial Statements over the years, classifying it as an “Unsecured Loan”.

■

A loan recall notice was issued by the financial creditor on 04.07.2022 demanding immediate repayment of the full outstanding loan. A reminder for payment was further issued via email on 01.08.2022. In response to the aforementioned notice, the Corporate Debtor, through its Financial Controller acknowledged the communication and expressed an intention to amicably settle the matter. Since no steps were taken by the Corporate Debtor to repay the debt a legal notice was issued by the financial creditor.

■

Thus, financial creditor filed instant petition under section 7 to initiate CIRP against corporate debtor for the alleged default on the part of the corporate debtor in repayment of financial debt.

■

The Corporate Debtor raised a dispute that the application under Section 7 was barred by limitation, as the alleged financial debt was stated to have arisen in the year 2005-06, and the demand was purportedly made for the first time in July 2022- after a lapse of nearly 17 years. The corporate debtor argued that such a stale claim could not be revived by unilateral recall or reliance upon self-serving accounting entries. Further, it was contended that the application failed to satisfy the statutory preconditions of Section 7.

■

The corporate debtor also claimed that financial creditor had failed to produce any loan agreement, repayment schedule, or even a basic acknowledgment of terms such as interest, tenure, or security. No board resolution or authorization was passed by corporate debtor to borrow funds from the financial creditor. The absence of any documentation, along with the lack of demand for repayment for nearly two decades, was said to indicate that the financial creditor never extended any loan capable of forming a financial debt.

HELD: ■

The Financial Creditor has pleaded that the loan advanced by him was a loan recallable on demand and qualifies as a financial debt under Section 5 (8). He has further pleaded that even though the loan was interest-free but qualified as disbursal against time value of money. (Para 11)

■

In order for an interest-free debt to qualify as financial debt, an financial creditor must show that the funds were disbursed with ‘consideration for time value of money’. The question of what constitutes ‘time value of money’ varies depending on the facts and circumstances; nonetheless, the financial creditor must demonstrate that it had an interest in the subject matter for which the loan was disbursed and was profiting from it. The pre-requisite is disbursal of money to the borrower for utilization by the borrower and that the disbursal must be against consideration for time value of money even if it is not interest bearing. (Para 13)

■

HEADNOTE: Section 5(8), read with section 7, of the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016 - Corporate insolvency resolution process - Financial debt - Corporate debtor, being respondent company, was engaged in business of leather processing and finished leather products - Nephew of petitioner was majority shareholder and managing director of corporate debtor - Under an understanding between petitioner, corporate debtor and said nephew, petitioner advanced loan of Rs. 1.29 crore to corporate debtor to meet its funds requirements - Said loan was payable on demand but such an understanding did not include payment of any interest against loan - There was also no material to show that loan amount was disbursed against consideration for time value of money - Whether said loan would not be covered under any of sub-clauses of definition of financial debt - Held, yes [Para 12]  Section 238A, read with section 7, of the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016 - Corporate insolvency resolution process - Limitation period - Petitioner provided loan to respondent in 2007 and 2008 - Understanding between petitioner and respondent did not provide a time limit for repayment of debt - Whether in absence of any contract between parties, amount needed to be repaid within three years from date when loan was advanced; thus, loan amount advanced by cheque dated 15-12-2007, 11-2-2008 and 26-3-2008 would have become due and payable on or before 14-12-2010, 10-2-2011 and 25-3-2011, respectively - Held, yes - Whether since there was no material to show that respondent made any admission of debt within such period or even subsequent thereto, instant CIRP application for non-payment filed in 2018 was grossly time barred and, hence, not maintainable - Held, yes [Para 19]IBC : Where unsecured loan was advanced which did neither bear interest nor was same disbursed against consideration for time value of money, said loan would not be financial debt   IBC : In absence of any contract between parties, loan amount needed to be repaid within 3 year from date when loan was advanced; in absence of any admission of debt by debtor company within such period or subsequent thereto, CIRP petition filed beyond three years was grossly time barred

Section 238A, read with section 7, of the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016 - Corporate insolvency resolution process - Limitation period - Petitioner provided loan to respondent in 2007 and 2008 - Understanding between petitioner and respondent did not provide a time limit for repayment of debt - Whether in absence of any contract between parties, amount needed to be repaid within three years from date when loan was advanced; thus, loan amount advanced by cheque dated 15-12-2007, 11-2-2008 and 26-3-2008 would have become due and payable on or before 14-12-2010, 10-2-2011 and 25-3-2011, respectively - Held, yes - Whether since there was no material to show that respondent made any admission of debt within such period or even subsequent thereto, instant CIRP application for non-payment filed in 2018 was grossly time barred and, hence, not maintainable - Held, yes [Para 19]

FACT: The respondent-company was engaged in the business of leather processing and finished leather products. The nephew of the petitioner was the majority shareholder and managing director of the respondent-company at the relevant time. The petitioner advanced unsecured loan of Rs. 1.30 crore to the respondent-company between 2007 and 2008, which was payable on demand.

It was submitted that the petitioner demanded payment in 2016, but to no avail; that the respondent-company had made a payment of Rs. 5 lakh in 2016; however, it failed to make further payments despite several requests. A demand notice was issued to which the company issued a reply denying its liability.

On instant CIRP petitioner filed by the petitioner:

HELD: Issue of financial debt

The Respondent company has admitted that the petitioner being the maternal uncle of the Managing Director, had given Rs. 1.25 lakh. initially. In addition, he had also given Rs. 1.29 crore under cheques dated 15-12-2007, 11-2-2008, 26-3-2008. [Para 6]

From the materials, it is clear that the petitioner had paid Rs. 1.29 crore to the respondent-company to meet its fund requirements.

The definition of financial debt is inclusive one. It indicates that debt along with interest 'if any' is disbursed against the consideration for time value of money. [Para 11]

had filed an application under section 7 to initiate CIRP against the corporate debtor.

The respondent submitted that petitioner had advanced an unsecured loan to the respondent on 9-1-2007 however, petition filed by the appellant in 2020 i.e., after a lapse of 13 years further, petitioner through letter dated 14-9-2017 himself had claimed that the amount was paid for acquisition of 25 per cent equity interest in the development project of the corporate debtor. HELD: By way of instant petition under section 7, the petitioner claims himself to be a financial creditor having an advance unsecured loan equivalent to Rs. 1.11 crores as on 31-3-2007 and presently Rs. 1.85 crores considering the enhanced value of USD. However, the petitioner has not relied upon any loan document which might have been executed between the petitioner and the corporate debtor with regard to the terms and conditions of the said loan transaction along with any repayment schedule or the rate of interest. However, surprisingly, the petitioner has relied upon the notice dated 14-9-2017, which was served upon a Director of the corporate debtor wherein it was stated that the petitioner wired USD 2,50,000/- and further that the petitioner was entitled to obtain 25 per cent equity interest in the corporate debtor, i.e., U.S. Hospitality Private Limited in exchange for the said sum of money. In response to the notice dated 14-9-2017, reply dated 18-9-2017 was sent on behalf of corporate debtor stating that the payment of USD 2,50,000/- was not towards 25 per cent equity interest but was rather an investment in a specific project of U.S. Co., as the said Company was involved in the Project to lease Real Estate in India with a hope of building a hospital on the said property. The petitioner has further relied upon notice dated 24-7-2020 got served by the petitioner upon the corporate debtor and its directors and in of the notice, it has been reiterated by the petitioner that on 1-9-2007, he wired a sum of USD 2,50,000/- from his Bank Account to the corporate debtor.

If the notices dated 14-9-2017 and 24-7-2020 are taken into account, it emerges that it is the specific and definite case of the petitioner that he transferred the amount of USD 2,50,000/- with an intent to buy a 25 per cent stake in the assets of the corporate debtor. [Para 20]

It is well settled that an investment cannot be equated with a loan. In the commercial word, equity financing and debt financing are altogether different modes of finance which are distinct from each other. Equity financing carries no repayment obligation while debt financing involves borrowing of money which is often repayable along with interest or other charges as may be settled between the parties. Therefore, a sum of money invested with an intent of requiring equity stake in a company or some other interest in some of the properties of the company cannot be dubbed as a financial debt or for that matter a loan transaction. [Para 21]

Besides, one cannot be oblivious of the facts that in the notices dated 14-9-2017 and 24-7-2020, the petitioner himself has claimed that the payment in question was made with intent to buy 25 per cent equity stake in the respondent's Company, on the basis of which, it could be safely concluded that the money was given as a loan. In this regard, a reference can be made to the Remittance Certificate Exhibit whereby the money was wired by the petitioner from Spain to the account of the corporate debtor and in the Bank note, it is specifically mentioned that the purpose of remittance was an investment in purchasing, constructing and operating a hotel business in India. [Para 23]

Therefore, by looking at the instant case, it cannot be said to be a case of money having been borrowed by the corporate debtor from the petitioner nor the transaction can be dubbed as a loan transaction. The so-called admission made by the corporate debtor in the reply dated 18-9-2017 that the transaction was invested is of no consequence. In this context, it is further pertinent to mention that the respondent has claimed in the reply that an amount of Rs. 20 lacs were paid back to the petitioner as on 11-2-2008 as is evident from the statement of account (Exhibit G) attached with the reply. So far as the petitioner is concerned, in the rejoinder filed by him, the transfer of an amount of Rs. 20 lacs as on 11-2-2008 has not been specifically denied and it has only been stated that it was a personal transaction not relating to the transaction which took place in the year 2007. Even this plea raised on behalf of the petitioners seems to be a tentative one and does not really explains the exact position and circumstances under which a sum of Rs. 20 lacs were paid to the petitioner. [Para 24]

, the finding of the Adjudicating Authority that the amount of interest at the rate of 24 per cent claimed by the appellant being exorbitant, it was sufficient ground for rejection of the claim of the appellant could not be subscribed to. The Adjudicating Authority, at best, had a limited jurisdiction to examine the decision of the RP on the rejection on the claim and not on the reasonability of computation of the claim or quantum of the debt. [Para 21]

■ It is a well settled precept that in the judgment of the Supreme Court in Orator Marketing (P.) Ltd. v. Samtex Desinz (P.) Ltd. [2021] 128 taxmann.com 424, it has been clearly held that financial debt does not expressly exclude an interest free loan. Thus, financial debt also includes any sum raised under any other transaction having the commercial effect of borrowing even it does not carry an interest component. Be that as it may, the fact that the appellant in the present case has not demonstrated any efforts made by it to recover the loan amount since 2007 cannot be obliterated. There is no material on record to show that any notice or any demand was raised either for repayment of the purported loan or for payment of interest since 2007. If the loan agreement was a genuine one, then the expected course of action on the part of the appellant would have been to seek refund of the loan given by it when it exited the management of the corporate debtor if not earlier. The inordinate and unexplained delay in raising the demand until the corporate debtor was admitted into rigours of CIRP does cast doubts on the legitimacy and bona fide of the alleged transaction as a whole irrespective of the interest component. [Para 22]

■

The Adjudicating Authority has rightly taken note of the 13 years unusual and stony silence on the part of the appellant to recover their dues. This is clearly a case where the appellant seemed to have woken up from their slumber and suddenly remembered to have raised their claim in respect of loan-cum-interest coinciding with the corporate debtor getting admitted into CIRP. Given this fact situation, there is nothing arbitrary on the part of the Adjudicating Authority to find the conduct on the part of the management for maintaining uninterrupted silence for over 15 years on the recovery of their dues including unclaimed interest amount of Rs. 1.04 crores rather unusual lending credence to the fact that the loan agreement was prepared as an after-thought to tailor the filing of their claims. [Para 23]

■

In result, there is substance in the contention raised by the respondents that the claim filed by the appellant was not bona fide as it was not premised on a genuine loan transaction and was bereft of cogent supporting proof. There is no error on the part of the Adjudicating Authority in passing the impugned order rejecting the claims filed by the appellant. [Para 24]

■

The Notes forming part of the balance sheet of the Corporate Debtor as on 31.03.2017 provides separate categories for "Long Term Borrowings" under Note 3 and "Other Long Term Liabilities" under Note 4. The audited balance sheet of the Corporate Debtor also classifies the amount claimed by the Appellant to be a loan to figure under the head of 'Other Advances' which does not denote any financial liability or loan obligation. Moreover, there being no record of TDS deduction reflected in the financial records in respect of the Corporate Debtor, there is no provision of interest. It is also clear therefrom that Rs 30,95,000/-appearing against the name of the Appellant company appears in the head of 'Other Advances' rather than as an unsecured loan as claimed by the Appellant. However, the sum appears under the sub-category of "Other Advances" under the category of "Other Long Term Liabilities". It is clear from the above categorisation that the sum was provided as an advance and was treated as a liability and not a borrowing in the balance sheet and therefore does not partake the character of financial debt. Hence the transaction was not in the nature of a financial debt and could not have been claimed in Form-C. Thus, there is no infirmity in the finding recorded by the Adjudicating Authority that the claim filed by the Appellant does not find support in the books of the Corporate Debtor as a loan.[Para 34]

While the said bank sanctioned a term loan of Rs.14.2 crores for construction of the building and purchase of plant and machinery, the promoters of corporate debtor were required to meet the condition of investing the margin money. Accordingly, all six promoters, including the financial creditor, had given interest free unsecured loan to the corporate debtor.

The financial creditor alleged that the corporate debtor failed to take any steps to liquidate or reduce the liability qua him despite various reminders. Thus, he issued demand notice under section 8. In response to the said notice, corporate debtor submitted that the amount being claimed was not a loan in terms of financial debt, nor was there any agreement to pay interest thereon. It was not to be repaid on demand as it was the basis of procuring financial assistance from their bank for establishing the corporate debtor for its working capital. The financial creditor was an equity holder and with a view to set up a plant, all shareholders had paid various amounts as the margin money to enable them to get the loan facility from Canara bank.

HELD: All Promoters including the Financial Creditor herein, have confirmed the Subordination Agreement with their Bank, for and on behalf of the Corporate Debtor, and have undertaken that the unsecured creditors had extended or continued to extend interest free unsecured loan on the express understanding that all their claims against the respondent company would be subject to the claims of Canara Bank; that all the claims of the unsecured creditors against the respondent company would at all times be subordinate and be subject to any claims of Canara Bank; that unsecured creditors agree not to sue the respondent company for recovering any money tendered to the respondent company as unsecured loan until all the claims of Canara Bank get settled; that the unsecured creditors agree not to join in any bankruptcy or any assignment.

It is therefore submitted by the respondent that since the unsecured loans were interest-free, no interest was promised. Further, it is stated that the transaction inter se the parties does not fall within the definition of financial debt nor is the financial creditor a person to whom a financial debt is owed. There is not Demand Promissory Note executed, nor is there any agreement for payment of any interest. As submitted by the corporate debtor and not denied by the operational creditor, the amount given by him along with 6 others was for promoting and setting up a business. The terms for raising the bank loan necessitated investment of the margin money. This was done by all the promoters and is reflected as unsecured loans, subordinate to the claim of the bank. The bank agreement corroborating this is on record.

From the materials, it is clear that the petitioner had paid Rs. 1.29 crore to the respondent-company to meet its fund requirements.

The definition of financial debt is inclusive one. It indicates that debt along with interest 'if any' is disbursed against the consideration for time value of money. [Para 11] The petitioner in his petition pleaded that the loan was advanced as an understanding between him and the corporate debtor and its managing director, who happened to be his nephew and that the loan was payable on demand. It is nowhere pleaded that such understanding included the payment of interest against the loan and the rate thereof. There is also no pleading that the payment was made against the issue of shares at a future date. The advancement of the said loan accordingly is not covered under any of the clauses of the definition. There is also no material on record to show that the amount was disbursed against the consideration for the time value of the money. [Para 12]

The Respondent pleaded that it availed an unsecured loan of Rs. 5 lakh from the petitioner. The same is manifest from its annual report of 2013-14. Admittedly, the amount was repaid in 2016, which is apparent from the account statement filed along with the petition. According to the petitioner he did not make any payment during 2013-14, which the audited annual report of the respondent company shows as unsecured loan of Rs. 5 lakh. The report is not in dispute. Therefore, its repayment could not be taken as the payment towards interest of the loan amount of Rs. 1.29 crore. More so when the petitioner has credited this amount against the principal amount of Rs. 1.24 crore and showed a default of Rs. 1.24 crore. Besides the petition is completely silent as indicated before that the loan was advanced against an agreed interest. Taking all these aspects into consideration it is accordingly clear, for the purpose of instant case, that the amount would not come within the definition of a financial debt, though it is admitted that the petitioner had advanced said amount to meet the fund requirements of the company. Issue of limitation

The first of the payments was made by cheque dated 15-12-2007 and was credited to the respondent's account on 18-12-2007. The last payment was made by cheque dated 26-3-2008, and was credited to the respondent's account on 27-3-2008. According to the petitioner, it was an understanding and was payable on demand. The Application under section 7 is not a suit. Suits relating to money needs to be filed within three years when the amount became due. In the instant case admittedly, there was no time limit agreed upon between the parties for repayment of the amount advanced. The amount payable on demand pleaded by the petitioner could not be extended for an uncertain period. In the absence of any contract between parties the amount needed to be repaid within three years from the date when they were respectively advanced. There is no material on record to show that the respondent made any admission of debt respectively within these periods or subsequent thereso. [Para 17]

The Application having been filed only on 13-11-2018, was grossly time barred. The debt accordingly was not due and payable. The question of what constitutes ‘time value of money’ varies depending on the facts and circumstances; nonetheless, the financial creditor must demonstrate that it had an interest in the subject matter for which the loan was disbursed and was profiting from it. The pre-requisite is disbursal of money to the borrower for utilization by the borrower and that the disbursal must be against consideration for time value of money even if it is not interest bearing. ■ It is opined that there is no credible evidence to establish that the alleged disbursal was made against the time value of money- an essential element for qualifying a claim as a “financial debt” under Section 5(8). The transaction in question neither involved any stipulated interest component nor any contractual arrangement indicating the accrual of financial gain, return, or profit to the alleged Financial Creditor. Furthermore, there were no agreed terms of repayment, nor was there any contemporaneous communication or correspondence evidencing a request for a loan or acknowledgment of such a financial arrangement. In the absence of these foundational elements, the disbursal lacks the commercial character necessary to constitute a financial debt under the Code. (Para 14)

■

The purported recall of an alleged loan nearly 17 years after its initial disbursal- without any documented agreement, interest component, or discernible commercial consideration—raises serious doubts about the nature of the transaction and is inconsistent with the conduct ordinarily expected of a prudent financial creditor acting in the ordinary course of business. Furthermore, the email dated 05-08-2022, which the financial creditor has relied upon as an acknowledgment under Section 18 of the Limitation Act, falls short of constituting a clear or unequivocal admission of liability. Rather, it reads as a generalized and non-committal response, devoid of any express acknowledgment of debt or promise to repay. In the absence of a categorical admission, such communication cannot, by itself, revive a time-barred claim (Para 16)

The respondent- corporate debtor has further contended that the applicant- financial creditor exercised significant influence over the accounts and affairs of the Corporate Debtor by virtue of his position as a Key Managerial Personnel (KMP) and Director. It was asserted that the financial statements relied upon by the financial creditor were, in fact, authored and approved under his supervision, and that the relevant entries reflecting long-term borrowings were affected at his instance. ■

Moreover, the underlying transaction in question constitutes a Related Party Transaction. It is trite law that a company is governed by its Board of Directors, who bear primary responsibility for the management and conduct of its affairs. The record clearly establishes that the Applicant, was actively controlling and managing the operations of the Corporate Debtor during the relevant period in his capacity as Director. In view of the foregoing factual position, and considering that the Applicant had substantial control over the management and affairs of the Corporate Debtor, it is opined that the Applicant qualifies as a "related party" within the meaning of Section 5(24). Accordingly, his claim warrants close scrutiny under the heightened standards applicable to related party transactions under the Code. Hence the absence of a Board Resolution authorizing a borrowing from Related Party raises doubts with respect to legitimacy of the claim.(Para 18)

Even if the amount disbursed by the Financial Creditor was to be considered as a Debt, it appears as if intent of the financial creditor in the present case is only to invoke the provisions of the Code so as to enforce recovery against the Corporate Debtor. It is a settled law that the scope of the Code is to bring about a resolution of an insolvent debtor and is definitely not a recovery proceeding. (Para 21)

■

In the light of the above discussion, financial creditor has not been able to make out a clear-cut case in his favor. The application filed by the financial creditor under Section 7 is not maintainable, as the essential conditions of "debt" and "default" prescribed under the provision are not satisfied. As per Section 7(1), a financial creditor may initiate the corporate insolvency resolution process (CIRP) against a corporate debtor only upon establishing the existence of a "financial debt" and a "default" in its repayment. In the present case, the financial creditor has failed to demonstrate, with cogent evidence, the existence of a legally enforceable financial debt as defined under Section 5(8), and correspondingly, has not substantiated the occurrence of a default as per Section 3(12). (Para 22)

Having satisfied that there was a disbursal of Rs. 1 crore to the Corporate Debtor by the Appellant sans any written contract or agreement between them, it is next seen whether there was a disbursal with the consideration of time value of money. ■ It is an admitted fact that there was no written contract or agreement between the Appellant and the Corporate Debtor governing the terms and conditions by which the sum was advanced by the Appellant and disbursed to the account of the Corporate Debtor. Be that as it may the decision of this Tribunal in Agarwal Polysacks (supra) is to be followed wherein it has been held that requirement of written financial contract between parties is not a pre-condition for determining whether any amount disbursed is financial debt or not. When there are no written agreements or financial contract between the parties as in the present case, the real nature of transaction becomes the key to decide as to whether the transaction is in nature of financial debt or not. Thus, even if there is no agreement/contract between the parties, nothing precludes the Adjudicating Authority or this Tribunal from looking into the real nature of transaction to determine whether the transaction in question is in the nature of financial debt in terms of the statutory construct of IBC. [Para 21]

■

Though the expression 'time value of money' finds mention in Section 5(8) of the IBC, the term has not been defined in the said enactment. It is well recognised that the most typical example of 'time value of money' is in the form of interest charged on the principal amount that has been borrowed. In the present case, the Appellant has claimed that there was an oral understanding between the two parties that the loan was interest-bearing at the rate of 18 per cent per annum, and that being so, the sum was disbursed with the intent of extending a financial debt to the Corporate Debtor. [Para 22]

■

To substantiate the fact that the loan was actually interest-bearing, the Appellant has contended that the TDS certificates placed on record corroborate that interest amount had been paid by the Corporate Debtor. Secondly, the Corporate Debtor had acknowledged the receipt of this amount in their balance sheets of 31-3-2010 and 31-3-2011 which is duly reflected as 'Loan from Directors and Shareholders'. [Para 23]

■

Even though it has been held by this Tribunal in Prayag Polytech Pvt. Ltd. v. Gem Batteries Pvt. Ltd. in CA(AT)(Ins) No. 713 of 2019 and in Pawan Kumar v. Utsav Securities Pvt. Ltd. in CA(AT)(Ins) No. 251 of 2020 that TDS deduction does not prove a debt, it does not restrain from noticing that TDS deductions were actually made which have corroborative value in substantiating the element of time value of money. When the material available on record is seen, it is noticed that the Appellant has been able to show TDS certificates on interest payment for only two financial years ending 2010 and 2011. For the subsequent years, the Appellant has not been able to submit any proof or evidence of TDS deductions to substantiate that interest liability was being enforced. There is no proof to show that any reminders were sent to the Corporate Debtor seeking interest payment. For the transaction to have been interest-bearing in the true sense, the interest payment should have been paid annually and by logical corollary corresponding TDS deductions ought to have been reflected. This does not seem to have happened. Thus, it is viewed that deduction of TDS for only two years is insufficient to determinatively conclude that interest liability was a quintessential adjunct of the sum disbursed by the Appellant. [Para 24]

■

Coming to the balance sheets of the Corporate Debtor, it is noticed that for financial years ending 2010 and 2011, the amount of loan of the Corporate Debtor qua the Appellant in both the years is shown as Rs. 1,01,07,836. However, no other balance sheets of subsequent years have been placed on record thereafter to show that the debt and interest amount continued to be reflected in their balance-sheets. Though the Appellant has claimed that the 2021 balance sheet of the Corporate Debtor also mentions unsecured loans from Director and other related parties, on a pointed query made by this Bench, it was admitted that the balance sheet ending 2021 had not been produced before the Adjudicating Authority. Hence, it is viewed that when this document was not placed before the Adjudicating Authority, this contention raised at the appellate stage cannot be relied on. Therefore, the Appellant has failed to muster clinching proof and evidence in terms of financial records to show that the sum advanced by them was indisputably interest-bearing and that interest had continued to accrue and was being realised as consideration for time value of money. [Para 25]

Since payments were still not forthcoming from the corporate debtor, the appellant filed a section 7 petition seeking the admission of the corporate debtor into corporate insolvency resolution proceedings which was rejected by the Adjudicating Authority as non-maintainable.

On appeal:

HELD: ■ For any debt to be treated as financial debt, the pre-requisite is disbursal of money to the borrower for utilization by the borrower and that the disbursal must be against consideration for time value of money even if it is not interest-bearing. As to when a Financial Creditor who has disbursed money to a Corporate Debtor against consideration for time value of money can trigger the insolvency resolution process against the Corporate Debtor, as per the scheme of IBC, that stage arises when a default arises in that a debt which has become due, in fact and in law, but has not been paid in whole or part thereof. [Para 12]

■

Submission has been made by the Appellant that an amount of Rs 1 crore had been disbursed to the Corporate Debtor which is validated by the certificate issued by ICICI Bank on 4-5-2021 which clearly states that Rs 1 crore had been credited to the account of the Corporate Debtor from the current account of the Appellant on 19-2-2010. It was also pressed that the disbursal of the above loan amount to the Corporate Debtor was substantiated by the fact that the Corporate Debtor had acknowledged the receipt of this amount in their balance sheets of 31-3-2010 and 31-3-2011 and is duly reflected as 'Loan from Directors and Shareholders'. It was further added that this sum had been disbursed with time value of money on the understanding with the Corporate Debtor that they would repay the amount with interest at the rate of 18 per cent per annum. That TDS was deducted by the Corporate Debtor on the interest amount payable to the Appellant as is evident from the TDS Certificate for the month of March 2010 shows that disbursal had been made against consideration for time value of money. [Para 13]

■

It was contended that there is no need of a written contract to prove the existence of a financial debt and in support of their contention reliance has been placed on the judgment of this Tribunal in Agarwal Polysacks Ltd. v. K.K. Agro Foods and Storage Ltd. in CA(AT)(Ins) No. 1126 of 2022 and Pradeep Tayal v. Essbert Fashion Pvt. Ltd. in CA(AT)(Ins) No. 950 of 2022 which have held that written contract is not mandatory nor a necessary pre-condition for the purpose of proving existence of financial debt. Submission was pressed that the terms and conditions of the loan including the period of loan and the purpose of the loan was not documented but rested on an oral understanding mutually arrived at between the two parties that the loan amount advanced would be returned by the Corporate Debtor on completion of the Madina Project. Since this project was already completed and yet no payment was forthcoming from the Appellant, a legal notice was served upon them claiming repayment of the amount financed by them. Thus, this was a case where a default had been committed by the Corporate Debtor which the Adjudicating Authority failed to appreciate. It was therefore contended that the Adjudicating Authority had committed a grave error by holding that the Appellant was not a financial creditor and that the amount advanced by the Appellant to the Corporate Debtor did not qualify as financial debt. [Para 14]

■

Per contra, it was contended by the Corporate Debtor that the Appellant has failed to show that any default had occurred on the part of the Corporate Debtor. Even if it is accepted that the right to payment arose on the completion of the Madina Project, the said project was not yet complete as procedural compliances were still in the pipeline. It was also submitted that since it is for the Appellant as Financial Creditor to substantiate that the project stood completed and until such substantiation is done, the claim made by the Appellant under Section 7 was pre-mature. Further as there was no tenure of the loan, it shows that the amount advanced was in the nature of an investment and not a loan. The Adjudicating Authority had therefore correctly held that the Appellant had invested money for speculative purposes and such a speculative investor cannot file a Section 7 petition. [Para 15]

FACT: The applicant/financial creditors provided loan facilities to corporate debtor. It was the case of the applicants that dispite of several requests for repayment of debt the corporate debtor failed and neglected to repay the debt. Thus, the applicants filled instant petition to initiate corporate insolvency resolution process against the corporate debtor.

In instant petition, the corporate debtor raised objection that there was neither any document in respect of loan, nor there were details of any applicable interest agreed between the parties. The corporate debtor further alleged that the applicants were neither financial creditors nor the debts claimed in application came within purview of financial debt.

HELD: In the instant case admittedly, applicants issued notices both in Form 3 as well as in Form 4 under rule 5 of the Rules on 3-1-2018 claiming themselves as financial creditors. Secondly, neither any document has been placed on record pertaining to the loan nor there is any supporting evidence to establish applicable rate of interest to be paid on the said loan. Thirdly, the applicants have failed to prove that the loan was disbursed against consideration for time value of money, particularly when respondent company has affirmed that no interest has been paid nor payable at any point of time. [Para 22]

It is pertinent to refer here that the balance sheets of the respondent company reveal that as on 31-3-2015 loans taken from both the applicants stands at Rs. 13 lakhs and Rs. 12 lakhs respectively. Similarly the balance sheet of the respondent company as on 31-3-2016 reflects the same amount of Rs. 13 lakhs and Rs. 12 lakhs as due to both the applicants. The position as on 31-3-2017 also remains the same as per the balance sheet of the respondent company. The position of the loans for the aforesaid three consecutive year endings shows that the amount of loan remains the same all through and with passage of time there has been no accumulation of interest or any other consideration therein. [Para 23]

It is reiterated that in the instant case, neither any loan agreement has been placed on record nor there is any supporting evidence/document to establish applicable rate of interest to be paid on the said loan. The applicant has failed to prove that the loan was disbursed against consideration for time value of money, particularly, when respondent company has affirmed that no interest has been paid nor payable at any point of time. [Para 27]

In the instant case also, there is no document to show that the respondent company either accepted or undertook to repay the loan with interest. The applicant has failed to justify, how without any provision of interest the debt can be termed as a financial debt. Once the claim made in the application does not pertain to 'disbursement against consideration for time value of money', the present claim will not come within the purview of 'Financial Debt' and consequently the applicants cannot be termed as 'Financial Creditor' in respect of the present claim in question. FACT: The financial creditor granted financial assistance of Rs. 6.10 crores to the corporate debtor.

The corporate debtor paid interest once after deduction of TDS, thereafter, corporate debtor failed to pay further interest. The financial creditor recalled the loan.

The corporate debtor had not liquidated the outstanding liabilities. Hence, the financial creditor filed the application under section 7.

The corporate debtor filed the reply and resisted the application on various grounds inter alia lack of any contractual agreement, an undefined period of loan, absence of any agreement for payment of interest at any specific rate and the said transaction did not fall within the definition of financial debt.

NCLT found no substance in the defence raised by the corporate debtor and held that the transaction does not get vitiated for want of agreement in terms of section 186(ii) of the Companies Act, 2013. NCLT by impugned order admitted the application and initiated CIRP against the corporate debtor.

The appellant, ex-director of corporate debtor, filed instant appeal against the impugned order of NCLT.

The appellant submitted that the Adjudicating Authority failed to appreciate that the financial creditor did not produce any loan agreement or instrument along with its application, and there were no pleadings regarding the basic terms of the alleged financial contract or financial debt including the date of repayment, applicable interest and date of default.

HELD: The only issue arises in the instant appeal is whether the transaction in question is a financial debt. [Para 12]

Certain essential conditions are required to be satisfied by a financial creditor seeking to invoke the provisions of CIRP as against the corporate debtor. Following essential conditions are required to be satisfied by a financial creditor.

(i)

There must be disbursal of loan amount,

(ii)

Such disbursal should be made for a consideration for time value of money, and

(iii)

When the debt (Whole or any part of instalment) become due and payable and is not paid by the corporate debtor means committed default. [Para 13]

The above all conditions are to be satisfied by the financial creditor then the Adjudicating Authority may admit the application under section 7 and initiate the CIRP against the corporate debtor. In the instant case, it is an admitted fact that financial creditor transferred Rs. 6.10 crores to the corporate debtor's bank account. This fact is corroborated by the bank entries filed by the financial creditor and the corporate debtor has not denied that the corporate debtor has not received such amount. Thus, aforesaid amount has been disbursed by the financial creditor to the corporate debtor. However, there is no written agreement between the parties to show that the disbursement of such amount is a loan transaction. [Para 14]

Now, it is to be considered whether such amount is disbursed for a consideration for time value of money. [Para 15]

'S' group. Garnishee Notices were issued by the Income Tax Department under section 226(3) of the Income-tax Act, 1961, against 'S' Realty, one of the entities of the 'S' group. It is strenuously contended that as no amount was payable to the Appellant Company, the 'Corporate Debtor Company' did not pay any amount to the Income Tax Department and have informed the same to the Appellant. [Para 12] The Respondent relies on MOU dated 23-3-2018 filed before the Adjudicating Authority. It is the case of the Respondent that the MOU expressly mentions that the appellant shall not be entitled for interest at all. The said MOU also provides that if the advance amount of loan of Rs. 7 Crores given to two parties between January 2015 to April 2015 is not repaid, then the respondent is not liable to pay any amounts to the appellant. The appellant contended that this MOU is forged and fabricated document and a Complaint has also been lodged with the Police and that the stamp and their signature is also fabricated. [Para 14]

Keeping in view the definition of 'Financial Debt' as defined under section 5(8); the nature of transactions entered into between both the parties; that there are several transactions some executed on the same day, between 'S' realty and 'S' properties together with the admitted fact that the Respondent Company was a part of the 'S' group; that the Directorship is common in all the 'S' Companies; it was only on 9-4-2018 that the name of the Respondent Company was changed to 'C' with the new management stepping in; that the statement of account appended to the petition is signed by 'P', the erstwhile Director of the Respondent Company; the entries of debit and credit dated 7-11-2015, 10-11-2015, 24-11-2015 establish several internal transactions between the 'S' group; the Auditor's Report detailing the Related Party transactions which figures the names of common Directors and the corresponding transactions; it is opined that the appellant has failed to satisfy that the transaction in question is a 'Financial Debt' as defined in the Code and a default has occurred. Therefore, the contention of the appellant that ratio of Innoventive Industries (supra) alone is to be applied, cannot be sustained. The scope and objective of the IBC is to be cautious in admitting an Application and not encourage recovery proceedings. For all these reasons, the ratio of 'Phoenix ARC (P.) Ltd. v. Spade Financial Services Ltd. [2021] 124 taxmann.com 24 (SC)' is squarely applicable to the facts of this case. Having held so, one does not wish to go into the technicalities of the authorization of the petition and also the issue of genuineness and veracity of the MOU. [Para 15]

HEADNOTE: Section  5(8), read with section  7, of the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016 and section  186 of the Companies Act, 2013 -  Corporate insolvency resolution process -  Financial debt - Appellant/financial creditor advanced interest free loan to meet financial requirements of corporate debtor to discharge its liabilities towards secured financial creditors - Corporate debtor failed to repay said loan amount despite repeated demands - Financial creditor filed application under section 7 against corporate debtor - NCLT dismissed said application on ground that amount given by the appellant to the corporate debtor was not a financial debt and that loan was given in violation of section 186 of Companies Act, 2013 and, thus, was void - It was noted that amount in question was continuously reflected in balance sheet of corporate debtor as unsecured loan without any caveat, and, therefore, such entry without any qualification/caveat was acknowledgment of debt by corporate debtor as unsecured loan having commercial effect of borrowing - Whether corporate debtor could not take shelter of section 186 of Companies Act to deny its liability to return amount taken by it being a corporate body, which was due and payable - Held, yes - Whether since financial creditor had already proved on record about amount which was disbursed as it had not been disputed and that said amount was debt fully reflected in its balance sheet continuously as an unsecured loan and had not been paid despite fact that repeated demands were made, it fell within definition of default on part of corporate debtor and, therefore, NCLT had committed a patent error in dismissing application filed under section 7 - Held, yes [Paras 20, 22, 25 and 26]

FACT: ■

The appellant was a financial creditor of the corporate debtor(CD). The appellant had advanced an interest free loan to the corporate debtor to discharge the liabilities of the other secured financial creditors. The loan advanced by the appellant did not bear interest and was to be repaid after the settlement of the secured financial loans of the CD under the one time settlement scheme but when the CD failed to repay the loan after settlement of the secured loans, the appellant issued notice and recalled its loan to be repaid within 15 days. The appellant alleged that the amount of loan was reflected in the financial statement of the Respondent as unsecured loan. The corporate debtor failed to repay the loan after settlement of the secured loans.

■

The appellant filed an application under section 7 for the resolution of an interest free loan. The NCLT dismissed the application on ground that amount given by the appellant to the corporate debtor was not a financial debt and, hence, the corporate debtor was not owed to pay the appellant and that the loan was advanced in violation of section 186(2) of the Companies Act, 2013 and, therefore, was void and unforceable.

■

On appeal:

HELD: ■

There is no dispute to the fact that the amount in question is continuously reflected in the balance sheet of the respondent from 2016-17 to 2020-21 in schedule 3A as unsecured loan without any caveat, therefore, such entry without any qualification/caveat is acknowledgment of debt by the CD as unsecured loan is having commercial effect of borrowing. [Para 20]

■

Much emphasis has been laid by the respondent as well as the Tribunal about non-adherence to the provision of section 186 of the Companies Act. Section 186(2)(a) of the Companies Act says that 'no company can directly or indirectly give any loan exceeding 60 per cent of its paid up share capital free reserves and securities premium account of its free reserves and securities premium account whichever is more'. However, section 186(13) provides for punishment for violation of the provisions of the section. It provides that 'the Company shall be punishable with fine which shall not be less than Rs. 25000 but which may extend to Rs. 5 lakh and officer of the company who is in default shall be punishable with imprisonment for a term which may extend to two years and with fine which shall not be less than Rs. 25000 but which may extend to Rs. 1 lakh.' [Para 21]

■

But in no case the debt advanced by the company to a corporate body can be held to be unrecoverable only because of the reason that there was a irregularity in advancement of the loan which became a debt to a third party or in other words the CD cannot take the shelter of section 186 of the Act to deny its liability to return the amount taken by it being a corporate body which is due and payable. [Para 22]

■

Thus, aforesaid amount has been disbursed by the financial creditor to the corporate debtor. However, there is no written agreement between the parties to show that the disbursement of such amount is a loan transaction. [Para 14]

Now, it is to be considered whether such amount is disbursed for a consideration for time value of money. [Para 15] According to the financial creditor, the corporate debtor has paid interest of Rs. 6.05 lakhs after deduction of TDS and this fact is undisputed. Therefore, it is proved that such disbursal has been made for a consideration for time value of money. However, as per the corporate debtor, on the basis of deduction of TDS such inference cannot be drawn. [Para 16]

Thus, aforesaid amount after deduction of TDS has been paid to the financial creditor on this basis it cannot be concluded that the transaction in question is a financial debt. [Para 18]

According to the financial creditor an oral loan agreement can be enforceable in law in view of section 10 of the Indian Contract Act and section 186(11) of the Act. [Para 19]

On the other hand, as per the corporate debtor in absence of a financial contract defined in rule 3(1)(d) of the Insolvency and Bankruptcy (Application to Adjudicating Authority) Rules, 2016 between the corporate debtor and financial creditor, the transaction cannot be termed as financial debt. RBI on issued guidelines to Non-Banking Finance Companies for fair practices which states that the Non-Banking Finance Company should convey in writing to the borrower in vernacular language as understood by the borrower by means sanctioned letter or otherwise, the amount of loan sanctioned along with the terms and conditions including annualised rate of interest. Thus, it is obligatory on the part of the financial creditor that there should be a loan agreement in writing only. [Para 20]

The financial creditor has not furnished any document to show that the transaction in question is a loan transaction. [Para 21]

The financial contract as per the rule 3(1)(d) of the Insolvency and Bankruptcy (Application to Adjudicating Authority) Rules, 2016 is a must between the corporate debtor and the financial creditor for setting out the terms of a financial debt including the tenure of the debt, interest payable and the date of repayment. In the absence of such financial contract, the financial creditor has failed to satisfy that when the debt and interest became due and payable. [Para 22]

The financial creditor has not filed any writing to show that when the debt become due and payable. As per the financial creditor the debt in question is payable on demand. From the notice and the application, it is not clear that on which date the demand was made and the loan and interest became due and payable. [Para 24]

Section 7(3)(a) provides that the financial creditor shall along with the application is required to furnish, a record of default recorded with the information utility or such other record or evidence of default as may be specified. The financial creditor has not filed any evidence of default along with the application under section 7. [Para 25]

Thus, the financial creditor failed to establish when the debt became due and payable and the corporate debtor has committed default. [Para 26]

Apart from the aforesaid, there is no agreement of loan and interest and no document is to stipulate the period of repayment even from the demand notice and the application under section 7. The terms of the loan agreement and other factors are not clear. The corporate debtor company is having authorized and paid up capital of Rs. 1 lakh whereas the financial creditor advanced loan of Rs. 6.10 crores. From the pleadings it is not clear that at relevant time the corporate debtor was in need of such huge amount and the financial creditor agreed to advance unsecured loan for such a huge amount. It is nowhere disclosed that the corporate debtor is engaged in which business and the loan and finances was required for which business requirement. The financial creditor has not filed copy of their balance sheet for relevant years and also balance sheet of the corporate debtor company. [Para 27]

According to the Supreme Court while admitting the section 7 application, it is the duty of the Adjudicating Authority to investigate the real nature of transaction. [Para 28]

IBC recognizes that for the success of insolvency regime the real nature of transaction has to be unearthed in order to prevent any person from taking undue benefit of its provisions to the detriment of the rights of legitimate creditors. It means, while admitting the application under section 7, it is the duty of the Adjudicating Authority to investigate the real nature of the transaction in order to prevent any person from taking undue benefit of its provisions to the detriment of the rights of legitimate creditors. [Para 29]
