5.2 Inter-Corporate Deposits

Inter-corporate deposits are commonly used as financing mechanisms between companies. Inter-Corporate Deposits (ICDs) are a common financing mechanism in which one company lends money to another, usually for a fixed period and often with interest.

NCLT Principal Bench, New Delhi in the matter of Proplarity Infratech (P.) Ltd. v. Sky High Technobuild (P.) Ltd. [CP (IB) No.607/(PB)/2023] rules that Inter Corporate deposits in balance sheet not sufficient to establish financial debt without documentation.

The CD contended that there was no formal loan agreement, and the amount was recorded as an "Inter-Corporate Deposit" rather than a financial debt. The CD argued that the FC did not meet the requirements of Sections 5(7) and 5(8) of the IBC, and that no default occurred under Section 3(12) of the Code.

The NCLT noted that the mere listing of the amount as an "Inter-Corporate Deposit" without detailed documentation or a formal loan agreement was insufficient to establish financial debt. The absence of a loan agreement and supporting documentation weakened the FC's claim.

FC submits it that alleged transaction of Rs. 2,00,00,000 was given as a loan @18%interest p.a. It is observed from the balance sheet of CD that the amount of Rs. 2,00,00,000 has been shown as Inter Corporate Deposit under the heading "Long Term Borrowing" from the period 2013- 2017 and from the period 2018-2021, the said amount has been shown as "Unsecured Loans" under the heading "Long Term Borrowing."

Mere recording of a transaction in the balance sheet of the CD as "Inter-Corporate Deposit" would not constitute it as Financial Debt unless proved by a supporting document.

Additionally, in the matter ofSeaview Merchants (P.) Ltd. v. Ashish Vincom (P.) Ltd. [C.P (IB) 2011/KB/2019], SRF Ltd. v. Birla Tyres Ltd. [2024] 159 taxmann.com 27 (NCLAT - New Delhi), stated that Inter- Corporate Deposit are not Financial Debt unless the loan advanced is proved by way of documentary evidence.

5.3 Convertible Debentures and Hybrid Financial Instruments as Financial Debt.

In terms of Section 5(8)(c), any amount raised pursuant to Optionally Convertible Debentures (OCDs) comes within the meaning of Financial Debt.MAIF Investments India Pte. Ltd. v. Ind-Barath Energy (Utkal) Ltd. [Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 597 of 2018].

There has been a disbursal of Rs. 102 Crores in favour of the 'Corporate Debtor' by way of 'OCDs'. In terms of Section 5(8)(c), any amount raised pursuant to any note purchase facility or the issue of bonds, notes, debentures, loan stock or any similar instrument comes within the meaning of 'financial debt'. Therefore, from the aforesaid fact. There is a disbursal of Rs. 102 Crores in favour of the 'Corporate Debtor' and the 'OCDs' originally met is against the time value of money and per se, constitutes 'financial debt' in the light of Section 5(8)(c) of the 'I&B Code'.

In the matter of Devarakonda Vikas v. DFI Nirman (P.) Ltd. [CP (IB) No. 71/HDB/2025] NCLT held that Redemption of debenture in accordance with the terms of issue is a mandatory obligation. A company's failure to redeem the debentures and pay interest upon maturity constitutes a clear default.

5.4 Redeemable Preference shareholder not a creditor.

5(8) of the Code referred to the Black's Law Dictionary 10th Edition which provides that "disbursement means money paid for the settlement of a debt or for a particular purpose". At the same time, the Court in the same case interpreted "Time Value of Money" and reference was made to Dictionary of Banking (2nd Edition) by Thomas P. Fitch which means the value of payment at present and payment due and payable in future which is discounted by the compounded interest. INTRODUCTION

Financial Debt has been clearly defined under the provisions of section 5(8) of the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016 (hereinafter referred to as 'IBC'). Also, in various judgements/orders by different NCLT/NCLAT benches, the definition has been well unleashed. Further, in the matter of Nikhil Mehta & Sons v. AMR Infrastructure (P.) Ltd. [2017] 84 taxmann.com 163/143 SCL 278, the Hon'ble NCLAT has very clearly explained the criteria to be checked for ascertaining if debt is a financial debt or not. Also, it is well settled that while dealing with the application under section 7 of the IBC the Hon'ble Adjudicating Authority(NCLT)has to only focus on the nature of debt i.e. if it is financial debt or not and whether it is due and defaulted and not having existence of any dispute.

In the recent matter of Drip Capital Inc. v. Concord Creations (India) P. Ltd. [Company Appeal (AT) (CH) (Ins.) No. 167 of 2021, dated 8-11-2021], the Hon'ble NCLT Bengaluru Bench in reference to and interpreting certain sayings of various courts in several judgements, considered the financial position of the corporate debtor even though the debt was duly acknowledged, and considering it as solvent granted 6 months' time to the Corporate Debtor to pay the sum and didn't admitted the application to initiate Corporate Insolvency Resolution Process (CIRP).

In this article, we will analyze the judgement(s) of NCLT and NCLAT in the matter of Drip Capital Inc. (supra)

PRE-REQUISITE FOR FINANCIAL DEBT UNDER SECTION 5(8) OF IBC-

The Hon'ble Appellate Tribunal in the matter of Nikhil Mehta & Sons (supra) has very precisely put forth the basic criteria for considering a debt as financial debt in the code which are mentioned as below-

1.

There must be disbursal of some money from the financial creditor to the corporate debtor,

2.

The same must has been disbursed keeping in consideration to time value of money, and

3.

It must fall in any of the transaction mentioned in sub-clauses of Section 5(8) of the Code.

CHECKPOINTS FOR ADMITTING APPLICATION UNDER SECTION 7 OF IBC-

In the matter of Innoventive Industries Ltd. v. ICICI Bank Ltd. [2017] 84 taxmann.com 320/143 SCL 625the Hon'ble Supreme Court in Para 30 of the judgement has very clearly worded that-

"In the case of a corporate debtor who commits a default of a financial debt, the adjudicating authority has merely to see the records of the information utility or other evidence produced by the financial creditor to satisfy itself that a default has occurred. It is of no matter that the debt is disputed so long as the debt is "due" i.e., payable unless interdicted by some law or has not yet become due in the sense that it is payable at some future date."

5.1 Whether Share Subscription Agreements Can Constitute Financial Debt under IBC?

Share Application Money in the event of non-allotment of shares can be treated as a loan/debt, and such an amount falls under the definition of Financial Debt as defined under Section 5(8) of the Code.

In the matter of Kushan Mitra v. Amit Goel [2022] 136 taxmann.com 313 (NCL-AT), NCLAT held that if the Shares are not allotted within 60 days of receiving the Share Application Money, and if the refund does not take place within 15 days form the expiry of 60 days' time limit, then this amount will be treated as a Deposit, advanced to the Company, which has to be returned by the Company at the rate of 12 percent per annum from the expiry of the 60th day. Thus, the concerned person would receive compensation for the time value of money given to the Company, which changes the nature and character of the money so given. Although the amount was initially paid towards Shares, the equity did not materialise because the allotment was revoked. Thereafter, by operation of law, Section 42(6) of the Companies Act, 2013, the amount has statutorily been given the character of a loan with interest. The same applies to amounts paid as optionally convertible debentures. Blurring the Lines between Financial Creditor and Operational Creditor In order to qualify as a financial creditor under section 5(8) of the IBC, one should be owed a financial debt6 which includes two conditions, firstly, there should be a debt along with interest, if any, which is disbursed against the consideration for the time value of money,7 and secondly, it should be included in one of the specified categories.8 Moreover, a financial creditor must prove that a default has occurred, which takes place when a debt becomes due and payable as per the proof of claims submitted by the creditor.9 Since a claim/payment is flexible enough to include "recompense",10 an operational creditor who has suffered any harm or has to be compensated will become the stakeholder of the insolvencyprocess.11 With respect to the first requirement, any debt, with or without interest is covered under the scope of Section 5(7) of the code. The time value of money requirement, according to which any money we have right now is worth more than the identical sum in future, due to its potential earning capacity12 is present in any kind of transaction. The Court in the case of DF Deutsche Forfait AG v. Uttam Galva Steel Ltd.13 held that if a party fails to repay within the fixed time, then interest can be claimed over operational debt as well, and it is nowhere said that the operational creditor is barred from claiming interest. Therefore, since the premise of claim is based on whether the "X" has taken something from "Y' with an intention to pay back the value, then the law should be applied in a manner to ensure that it is repaid but not dismissed on the ground of procedural irregularities. We need not stick to the ground that procedural justice is always subservient to substantial justice.14

With respect to the second prong, the authors believe that such an operational creditor is at par with home buyers. It is submitted that since Section 5(8)(f) of the IBC uses the words 'any amount' and 'any other transaction', it means that the amounts that are "raised under transactions and not covered by any of the other clauses", would amount to a financial debt if they had the commercial effect of borrowing, making it a 'catch-all provision'.15 Section 3(33) of the IBC defines a 'transaction' as an agreement or arrangement in writing for the transfer of assets, or funds, goods or services, from or to the corporate debtor. Furthermore, the expression "borrow" means to obtain or receive something, on loan for temporary use, intending to give it, or something equivalent back to the lender.16 A perusal of these definitions shows that the expression borrow is wide enough to include an advance given by operational creditors in the form of their services, workmen/employees in the present case when the payment for the same was neglected by a company to keep its operations afloat. This implies that the same amount was borrowed for 'temporary use' i.e. for honouring their commitments and paying back other creditors as long as they intended to give 'something equivalent' back to the operational creditors. Additionally, the commercial aspect, which means transactions having profit as its main aim is present in such a situation of employees who have not been paid, since the company wants to keep its operations afloat by temporarily borrowing the requisite amount from operational creditors, and the operational creditors demanding interest due to delay in payments.17 Additionally, the proof of claim as per the IBBI (Insolvency Resolution Process for Corporate Persons) Regulations, 2016 can be proved by any contractual document indicating that the amount is due in case of employees or through muster rolls in case of workmen.18 It therefore follows that the employees/workmen in such a situation will be considered as a financial creditor at par with home buyers as per Pioneer since they qualify all the parameters based on which the home buyers have been considered as a financial creditor. Therefore, treating them differently will lead to gross violation of principles of natural justice.19

23. Collusive commercial arrangement between creditors and the corporate debtor wouldn't constitute a financial debt, rules SC

[Phoenix Arc (P.) Ltd. v. Spade Financial Services Ltd. [2021] 124 taxmann.com 24 (SC)]

The Supreme Court in an important ruling in the Phoenix Arc (P.) Ltd. v. Spade Financial Services Ltd. case held that entities having commercial arrangements of collusive nature with the corporate debtor could not be considered financial creditors under the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code (IBC) provisions.

Brief facts

In this case, the operational creditor initiated the corporate insolvency resolution process (CIRP) against AKME Projects Limited under section 9 of the IBC.

As part of the process, the Interim Resolution Professional invited claims. In response to the notice, Spade Financial Services Limited and its subsidiary AAA Landmark Private Limited filed claims as creditors.

Spade filed the claim based on an alleged Memorandum of Understanding executed with the Corporate Debtor, which stated that Inter Corporate Deposits (ICDs) of Rs. 26.55 crore have been granted to the Corporate Debtor by Spade, bearing interest of 24 per cent repayable in terms of the mutual agreement between the parties. AAA filed its claim before the IRP for a sum of Rs. 93.90 crore.

Later, the CoC was constituted on May 22, 2018. On May 25, 2018, the IRP rejected the claim of Spade, inter alia, on the ground that the claim was not in the nature of a financial debt in terms of Section 5(8) of IBC since consideration was absent for the time value of money, i.e., the period of repayment of the claimed ICDs was not stipulated.

The IRP also rejected the claim of AAA on the ground that its claim as a financial creditor in Form C was filed after the expiry of the period for filing such a claim.

Having gone through the National Company Law Tribunal (NCLT) and the National Company Law Appellate Tribunal (NCLAT), the dispute reached the Supreme Court.

Supreme Court

Based on the appeals, the Supreme Court framed three issues for consideration which are as follows:

(a)

Whether Spade and AAA are financial creditors of the Corporate Debtor;

(b)

Whether Spade and AAA are related parties of the Corporate Debtor; and

(c)

Whether Spade and AAA have to be excluded from the CoC.

In the present case, the Court said, there was a finding that AAA and Spade were related parties within the meaning of Section 5(24) at the time when the alleged financial debt based on which they assert a claim to be a part of the CoC was created.

"Further, we have also concluded that the transactions between Spade and AAA on the one hand, and the Corporate Debtor on the other hand, which gave rise to their alleged financial debts were deceitful in nature. Therefore, it is evident that there existed a deeply entangled relationship between Spade, AAA and Corporate Debtor, when the alleged financial debt arose," the Court said, adding, the pervasive influence of the promoter/director of the Corporate Debtor over the concerned entities was evident, and allowing them in the CoC would definitely affect the other independent financial creditors.

"Due to the collusive nature of their transactions alleged to be a financial debt under section 5(8), Spade and AAA cannot be labelled as financial creditors under section 5(7)," it added.

UNDERSTANDING THE COURT'S DECISION AND BACKGROUND

After reviewing the arguments, the following two moot questions have surfaced for deliberation in this appeal which both the NCLT and NCLAT failed to address them:

A. Whether in the exercise of powers under sub-section (5) of Section 60, the Adjudicating Authority (i.e., NCLT) can recall an order of approval passed under sub-section (1) of Section 31 of the IBC?

"Section 60 (5) Notwithstanding anything to the contrary contained in any other law for the time being in force, the National Company Law Tribunal shall have jurisdiction to entertain or dispose of

(a)

any application or proceeding by or against the corporate debtor or corporate person;

(b)

any claim made by or against the corporate debtor or corporate person, including claims by or against any of its subsidiaries situated in India; and

(c)

any question of priorities or any question of law or facts, arising out of or in relation to the insolvency resolution or liquidation proceedings of the corporate debtor or corporate person under this Code."

The Hon'ble SC held that a Court or Tribunal has the inherent power to recall an order to ensure justice is served and to prevent misuse of the legal process. Neither the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code (IBC) nor its related Regulations restrict the exercise of this inherent power.

Section 60(5)(c) of the IBC grants authority to the National Company Law Tribunal (NCLT) to address questions of priorities or legal and factual matters related to insolvency proceedings, regardless of any other provisions. Additionally, Rule 11 of the NCLT Rules, 2016 acknowledges the Tribunal's inherent power.

The Hon'ble Court has analysed various decisions on how the Tribunal, or a Court is invested with ancillary or incidental powers: -

In Manohar Lal Chopra v. Rai Bahadur Rao Raja Seth Hiralal3 while interpreting section 151 CPC it is observed that the inherent power has not been conferred upon the court; it is a power inherent in the Court by virtue of its duty to do justice between the parties before it.

In Grindlays Bank Ltd. v. Central Govt. Industrial Tribunal4 it is a well-known rule of statutory construction that a Tribunal or body should be considered to be endowed with such ancillary or incidental powers as are necessary to discharge its functions effectively for the purpose of doing justice between the parties. In a case of this nature, we are of the view that the Tribunal should be considered as invested with such incidental or ancillary powers unless there is any indication in the statute to the contrary.

In a recent decision (i.e., Union Bank of India v. Dinakar T. Vekatasubramanian & Ors.5), a five-member Full Bench of NCLAT held that though the power to review is not conferred upon the Tribunal but the power to recall its judgment is inherent in the Tribunal and is preserved by Rule 11 of the NCLT Rules, 2016. This decision of NCLAT was upheld by a two-judge Bench of this Court vide order dated 31.07.2023 in Civil Appeal No.4620 of 2023 (Union Bank of India v. Financial Creditors [2023] 154 taxmann.com 203/180 SCL 64 (SC)).

Therefore, even when there's no specific provision allowing the Tribunal to recall its order, it still holds the power to do so. However, this power must be used sparingly and not as a means to re-examine the entire case.

INTRODUCTION

The IBC was introduced to consolidate insolvency laws and provide a time-bound mechanism for the resolution of distressed companies. The Code seeks to maximise asset value, promote entrepreneurship, and balance stakeholders' interests.

A critical feature of the insolvency framework under the IBC is the classification of creditors, primarily into financial creditors and operational creditors. This classification determines the rights and powers of creditors in the Corporate Insolvency Resolution Process (CIRP).

Among these, financial creditors hold a dominant position, as they control the Committee of Creditors (CoC), which decides the corporate debtor's fate. Therefore, determining whether a claim qualifies as "financial debt" under Section 5(8) is central to insolvency jurisprudence.

CHAPTER 1

IMPORTANCE OF FINANCIAL CREDITORS IN THE INSOLVENCY PROCESS

Financial creditors occupy a significant role within the insolvency framework. They possess the right to initiate insolvency proceedings under Section 7 of the IBC and are the primary decision-makers during CIRP.

The Committee of Creditors, which comprises financial creditors, is responsible for evaluating and approving resolution plans. The CoC exercises its commercial wisdom in determining whether the corporate debtor should be revived or liquidated.

Section 5(7) of the IBC defines financial creditors- "means any person to whom a financial debt is owed and includes a person to whom such debt has been legally assigned or transferred to."

Essential criteria for being an FC:

i.

A person to whom a financial debt is owed, and includes a person to whom such debt has been legally assigned or transferred to;

ii.

The debt, along with interest, if any, is disbursed against the consideration for the time value of money and includes any one or more modes of disbursed as mentioned in clause (a) to (i) of sub-section (8) of Section 5. CHAPTER 2

MEANING AND SCOPE OF FINANCIAL DEBT

Section 5(8) of the IBC defines financial debt as: "A debt along with interest, if any, which is disbursed against the consideration for the time value of money."

The provision further provides an inclusive list of transactions that may constitute financial debt. These include:

Money borrowed against payment of interest

Amounts raised through credit facilities

Debentures, bonds, or other similar instruments

Finance or capital leases

Any transaction having the commercial effect of borrowing

In the matter of Agarwal Polysacks Ltd. v. K.K. Agro Foods and Storage Ltd. [2023] 155 taxmann.com 358 (NCLAT – New Delhi) A question which rose before NCLAT was – "Whether to prove a Financial Debt, a Financial Creditor has to enter into a 'written' Financial Contract?".

Hon'ble NCLAT held that - A bare perusal of Part V of Form-1 indicates that particulars of financial debt, several documents, records and evidence of default have been referred to, which documents are contemplated to be particulars of financial debt. Use of the word "or" in Regulation 8(2)(a) indicates that by any of the documents referred to in Sub-regulation (2), the existence of debt can be proved. A financial contract supported by financial statements as evidence of the debt is one of the documents contemplated in Regulation 8(2), but that is not an exclusive requirement for proving the existence of debt. When the statutory scheme as reflected in the Application to Adjudicating Authority Rules, 2016 and CIRP Regulations, 2016 is looked upon, it is clear that financial debt can be proved from other relevant documents, and it is not mandatory that a written financial contract can be the only basis for proving the financial debt."

The Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016 ("Code") was enacted for providing a comprehensive and uniform insolvency legislation by replacing the then prevailing ineffective and inadequate insolvency regime. Recently, the Economic Survey highlighted that, for the first time, India has leaped 30 spots to break into the top 100 in the World Bank's Ease of Doing Business Report, 20181. Also, India jumped 33 places in insolvency indices due to the legislative reforms in insolvency regime2.

For giving more teeth to the Code, certain amendments were made to Code by way of the Insolvency and Bankruptcy (Amendment) Act, 20183. Thereafter, for the purpose of evaluating the law and ascertain the key practical challenges in the implementation of the Code, the Government constituted a formal committee known as the Insolvency Law Committee ("Committee") on 16 November, 2017.

The 'Report of the Insolvency Law Committee'4 ("Report") prepared by the Committee has taken into account the market practices, legal principles, international jurisprudence and the views of various stakeholders to provide the following key recommendations to amend the Code:

I. Home-Buyers as Financial Creditors

While deliberating on this issue, the Committee placed reliance on Nikhil Mehta & Sons v. AMR Infrastructure Ltd.5 in which the home buyers were held to be financial creditors as the arrangement between the home buyers and the seller of the apartments was such that the latter had committed to pay assured returns to the former till the possession of the property was handed over. The Committee noted that significant amount of money is raised from the home buyers and is utilised for financing the construction of assets for a real estate project. On failure of completion of such project, the amount is repaid based on time value of money. Therefore, the amount so raised may be classified as 'financial debt' and the home buyers as 'financial creditors'. The Committee however cautioned that not all forward sale or purchase transactions can be classified as 'financial debt'.

II. Interim Finance

Interim finance is defined as a financial debt raised by Insolvency Resolution Professional ("IRP") for financing the cost of going through the Corporate Insolvency Resolution Process ("CIRP")6. Also, since 'financial debt' means 'debt along with interest'7 therefore interest will be charged on any amount raised as interim finance. As per R. 27 of Insolvency and Bankruptcy Board of India (Liquidation Process) Regulations, 2016, interest on interim finance is only calculated till the liquidation commencement date.

Since Interim finance is one of the most important aspects of CIRP therefore interest on interim finance must be calculated for one year after the liquidation commencement date or until repayment (whichever is earlier). This amount should be distributed in priority in order to encourage early repayment and preferential treatment of interim finance.

III. Regulatory dues vis-à-vis Operational Debts

The Committee noted that in case any claim arises due to non-payment by a corporate debtor in lieu any goods or services provided by a regulatory body then such debt may be categorised as 'operational debt' on case to case basis. Also, the regulators have wide ranging powers to recover their dues, therefore, regulatory dues are not required to be included within the purview of 'operational debt'8.

IV. "Payment" or "Repayment"

With respect to the term 'repayment' as provided in the definition of operational debt, the Committee recommended that such term should be substituted by the term 'payment' as the latter is of much wider import than the former. The term 'payment' means "performance of an obligation by the delivery of money or some other valuable thing accepted in partial or full discharge of the obligation". The term 'repay' means "to pay back" or "refund" and the term 'repayment' means "the act of repaying". Accordingly, appropriate amendments have been proposed in other provisions of the Code where words "repayment", "repaid" or "repay" have been used.

In India, inter-corporate loans are important sources of funds for many companies. Often inter-company loans have no written terms. Many loans to wholly owned subsidiaries often bear no (or a below market) interest rate; and/or do not have a fixed repayment date. Such features may pose real practical challenges when applying the classification and impairment provisions of Ind AS 109 Financial Instruments in separate financial statements.

Classification and measurement under Ind AS 109

Under Ind AS 109, a company is required to assess whether an inter-company loan receivable can be classified and subsequently measured at amortised cost. Ind AS 109 permits classification as amortised cost only if the instrument meets both the:

Business model test; and

'SPPI' contractual cash flow characteristics test.

It must be also noted that intercompany loan receivables don't qualify for the simplified approach to impairment available under Ind AS 109, and so the general approach (generally referred to as the three-bucket approach) must be applied when calculating the expected credit loss ('ECL'). These rules are complex enough to apply, but will prove particularly difficult in the absence of a contractual arrangement, as illustrated in the examples given below. A contractual arrangement may take different forms (written, oral, implied, explicit) but should have the following essential features: Offer and Acceptance; Consideration; Intention to create legal relations; Certainty of terms.

In India, typically, lending scenario considerations include:

-

Written agreement (fixed term or repayable on-demand): Consider whether a demand feature is genuine if the lender does not intend, and the circumstances do not indicate, calling repayment for many years.

-

Oral or implicit terms: Written confirmation of the terms

-

No agreed repayment terms: No documented formal terms

There are no specific issues that should arise when intercompany loans are given on normal commercial terms. There may not be any significant challenge with respect to meeting the first 'business model' test under Ind AS 109. However, issues may arise when considering the second 'SPPI' test when there are no formal terms, the terms are limited, or the terms are off-market.

'SPPI' test requires a loan to give rise to cash flows on 'specified dates' that are solely payments of principal and 'interest on the principal amount outstanding'. In practice, it's not always easy to determine the 'specified date' or what the return is as many group companies lend to other group companies without any written agreement, or if written, are not explicit with respect to a repayment date, or the repayment date is contingent on a future event. For example:

-

On-demand loans are repayable when demanded and so the 'specified date' is 'when demanded'. Where it is assumed, in the absence of this being formally stated, that the loan is repayable on demand, it is better to be documented between the parties.

-

Even when timing of repayment is contingent on a specified event occurring, the repayment date is nevertheless 'specified' as being the contingent event.

-

Where a contingent event only impacts the timing of repayment and not the contractual cash flows, then the SPPI test can still be met where the cash flows are solely principal and interest.

-

Interest-free terms do not fail the SPPI test even though the contractual cash flows are just repayment of the principal. Principal is defined in Ind AS 109 as the 'fair value of the financial asset at initial recognition' rather than the gross paramount. Interest will therefore be imputed for accounting purposes, so that interest-free loans have both a principal and interest for Ind AS 109 purposes

-

Some more unusual terms may not be consistent with a basic lending arrangement; eg interest calculated by reference to the borrower's profits will fail the SPPI test.

ECL provision is determined by taking into account the amount and the timing of payments and by considering both the possibility of a credit loss occurring and the possibility that no credit loss occurs, even if the most likely outcome is no credit loss. For these reasons, an impairment provision will always exist, even for intercompany loans receivables that are repayable on-demand, although it may not be material. However, there are generally some practical challenges arising from the need to consider the timing of payments and the probability of a credit loss occurring when repayment terms are fluid or not explicit. For example:

-

Determining when a default, such as becoming past due, occurs.

-

Lack of comparable default patterns from other intercompany loan receivables to consider, and so greater reliance on current and forecast information.

However, the impairment provisions of Ind AS 109 will be difficult to apply to those without formal repayment terms and so it is recommended that companies shall document their understanding of the lending arrangement to reflect its substance and so better enable the application of the standard. Tax implications and repercussions under Companies Act, 2013 also need consideration.

The NCLT dismissed the application on the grounds that since there is a dispute between the parties, it is not satisfied that a default has occurred. Had NCLT first inquired that whether there exists a financial debt; and whether Kotak is a financial creditor, there would not have been any need for determining the existence of default. As per section 7 of the IBC, an application for initiation of CIRP against a corporate debtor can be filed by a financial creditor. According to section 5(7) of the IBC, financial creditor is a person to whom financial debt is owed. According to section 5(8) of the IBC, there are two essential elements for any transaction to be termed as 'financial debt' i.e. 1) It should be a debt along with interest, which is disbursed against the consideration for the time value of money; and 2) It may include any of the events enumerated in sub clauses (a) to (i). On conjoint reading of section 5(7) and 5(8) of the IBC, it can be said that a person is not entitled to initiate CIRP under section 7 of the IBC unless financial debt is owed to him.

Whether failure to redeem OCRPS would fall within the ambit of financial debt?

According to section 5(8)(c) of the IBC, if the amount is raised by issuance of bonds, debentures, or any similar instrument, then such a transaction falls within the ambit of financial debt. There is a fundamental difference between the amount raised by issuing debentures and the amount raised by issuing OCRPS. The distinction was emphasized by the Calcutta High Court in Hindustan Gas and Industries Ltd. v. CIT, [1979] 1 Taxman 546/117 ITR 549 where it observed that in cases where money is raised by way of issuing redeemable convertible preference shares, such amount goes to the share capital of the company, and where money is raised by issuing debentures, such amount goes to loan capital of the company. Since the amount contributed by preference shareholders goes to the share capital, the company does not become debtor for such payment. In contrast, the amount raised by way of issuance of debentures goes to the loan capital of the company and consequently such debenture holders act as creditors of the company and are entitled to fixed rate of interest whether there are profits or not. In view of the above, it can be argued that there is no element of 'consideration for time value of money' when money is raised by issuing OCRPS as preference shareholders are not entitled to any fixed rate of interest but entitled to get dividends only out of profits. Therefore, it can be concluded that transaction of raising money by way of issuing OCRPS will not fall within the ambit of financial debt under section 5(8) of the IBC.

Whether Kotak can be termed as a financial creditor?

Moreover, the owner of a preference shareholder cannot be termed as a creditor of the company. The above view was fortified by Bombay High Court in Aditya Prakash Entertainment (P.) Ltd. v. Magikwand Media Pvt. Ltd.,[Co. Petition No. 404 of 2016, dated 15-3-2018] wherein the court observed that the shareholders of redeemable preference shares of a company do not become creditors of the company if their shares are not redeemed at appropriate time. Further, Gujarat High Court in Anarkali Sarabhai v. CIT, [1997] 90 Taxman 509/224 ITR 422 (SC) had observed that where the company defaults in redeeming the preference shares, holder of the redeemable preference shares cannot compel the company to redeem the shares by suing in debt for the return of its capital.

In the present case, Kotak has filed an application under section 7 of the IBC on the grounds that Indus has failed to redeem the OCRPS. From the foregoing, it is clear that neither Kotak can be classified as financial creditor of Indus nor failure of Indus to redeem OCRPS would fall within the ambit of financial debt. Therefore, had NCLT first determined whether there exists a financial debt or not, there would not have been any need to ascertain existence of default. Consequently, there would not have been any need to refer parties to arbitration in a petition filed under section 7 of the IBC.

IBC vis a vis Arbitration Act

In the present case, although, NCLT framed the question as to whether the provisions of Arbitration Act will prevail over the provisions of the IBC, it did not give a conclusive finding on the same, and kept the question open for debate in future cases. Despite, section 238 of the IBC provides for overriding effect of the IBC over any other law, the provisions of the IBC will not prevail over the provisions of the Arbitration Act in all the cases, and will vary from case to case.

4. CCD under the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016 ['IBC']

4.1 Debentures are prima facie considered to be financial debt as per the definition of financial debt given in the IBC. As per section 5(8), financial debt means a debt along with interest, if any, which is disbursed against the consideration for the time value of money and includes- (c) "any amount raised pursuant to any note purchase facility or the issue of bonds, notes, debentures, loan stock or any similar instrument";

Thus, it is interesting to know the classification of CCD under the IBC in a case where a Financial Creditor holding debentures of the Corporate Debtors.

4.2 The question was raised before the Hon'ble Supreme Court in IFCI Ltd. v. Sutanu Sinha [2023] 156 taxmann.com 681 (SC) whether CCDs can be treated in essence as a form of debt instead of an equity share. The court, having examined the definition of debt in the Code as a 'liability or obligation in respect of a claim,' concluded that the appellant can be deemed a part-owner (i.e. an equity participant) of the company. This is because (as per the subscription agreement), if the company fails to buy back the shares within a specific period, the debentures can automatically be converted into equity shares.

4.3 As a result, the company does not have the right to claim any dues or debt from the Corporate Debtor ("CD"). Therefore, in case such an instrument is treated as debt, it would go against the agreement terms. The court further went on to hold that the investment is essentially a form of debenture which must be compulsorily converted into equity shares, and thus, not specified to be considered as a financial debt under certain circumstances that means it will be part of equity.

4.4 Therefore, it has become a settled position of law that when an investment is made like debentures which are compulsory convertible into equity it will be treated as equity.

4.5 Whereas, the issue relating to Optionally Convertible Debentures [OCD] is still unclear wherein the judiciary has taken to different contradicting opinions. The Hon'ble NCLAT in MAIF Investments India PTE. Ltd. v. Bharath Energy (Utkal) Ltd. [2019] SCC Online NCLAT 825 held that OCDs are considered as financial debt in view of Section 5(8) of the code.

5. CCD under the Foreign Exchange Management Act [FEMA]

5.1 The investment by a non-resident in an Indian Company, in any form, is regulated by the Foreign Exchange Management Act, 1999 read with Foreign Exchange Management (Transfer or Issue of a Security by a Person Resident outside India) Regulations, 2017 as amended in 2019 ('FEMA Regulations').

5.2 Regulation 2(xviii) defines 'Foreign Investment' to mean any investment made by a person resident outside India on a repatriable basis in 'capital instruments' of an Indian company or to the capital of an LLP.

5.3 Regulation 2(v) 'defines Capital instruments' to mean equity shares, 'debentures', preference shares and share warrants issued by an Indian company. The Explanation further provides that the expression 'Debentures' means fully, compulsorily and mandatorily convertible debentures. Thus, the CCDs which are fully and mandatorily convertible into equity, are considered as 'capital instruments' being at par with equity shares.

5.4 As fully, compulsorily and mandatorily convertible debentures alone are regarded as capital instruments, optionally convertible or partially convertible debentures are treated as debt instruments under the FEMA Regulations. These debentures which do not fall within the ambit of 'capital instruments would have to conform to the guidelines on External Commercial Borrowings, i.e. Foreign Exchange Management (Borrowing and Lending in Foreign Exchange) Regulations, 2000.

6. CCD under Income Tax Law

CCDs are treated as equity rather than debt under FEMA regulations and IBC from the date on which the CCDs are issued. We can analyse from the viewpoint of income tax law whether till the time of conversion can the same be recharacterised as equity.

The re-characterization of CCDs as equity and the disallowance of the interest expenditure claimed thereof, has been an issue for consideration under the IT Act.

This concept was first debated in the landmark GE Canada3 case, wherein the Canadian Tax Court opined that the implicit support of the parent company must be taken into consideration when determining the amount of the guarantee fee. (c) Interest-free loans – This is undoubtedly one of the more debatable issues in the space of intragroup financial transactions. Often intra-group arrangements are designed so that interest on loan or guarantee fees is not charged due to various reasons like the poor credit position of the subsidiary, loan proceeds to be used for acquisition purposes furthering the interests of the lender (parent) etc. While there may be plausible reasons for not charging interest, defending the position before the Revenue can pose significant challenges in the absence of strong commercial reasons and robust documentation. The OECD Guidelines acknowledge that benefit accruing to a borrower on being part of a larger group ('implicit support') should not necessitate a charge and there can be situations where a debt provided by the parent can be construed as a 'shareholder service' or 'quasi-equity'4. Still, it would not be correct to conclude that the provision of loans or guarantees without charging interest or fees can always be defended by this argument. In fact, the Indian Transfer Pricing jurisprudence has more often than not quashed the argument of 'quasi-equity'5 and computed interest rates/guarantee fees based on the arm's length principle6. Hence unless several conditions like the use of funds, presence of relevant clauses in the loan agreement, regulatory restrictions on infusing equity etc. are met, an interest-free loan or zero guarantee fee situation would be considered as non-arm's length.

Internal guarantees: service provided or shareholder transaction?According to the OECD Guidelines: "the question whether an intra group service has been rendered…should depend on whether the [guarantee] provides a group [company] with economic or commercial value… This can be determined by considering whether an independent enterprise in comparable circumstances would have been willing to pay for the [guarantee]…"This basically means that for each intra-group guarantee (i) the underlying reason for the guarantee should be established and (ii) it should be determined whether the guarantee creates a benefit for which the guaranteed group company should pay a fee. As further explained in the OECD Guidelines, the guarantee fee should be established by taking into account the perspective of both the guaranteed group company and the guarantor (i.e. the group company issuing the guarantee). That is, the underlying reason for the guarantee should take both these perspectives into account. In the event that a third party (the creditor) would not under any circumstances have been willing to enter into the transaction with the guaranteed company (the debtor) had the guarantee not been issued, it could be concluded that the guaranteed company would not have been able to enter into the transaction on a standalone basis. In other words, the guaranteed group company is not considered by the third party to be financially strong enough to enter into this transaction on a standalone basis. In this case, the guarantee may have been provided by the guarantor in its capacity as a shareholder, as no third party would appear willing to accept the risk associated with the transaction. Hence, the intra-group guarantee may not qualify as a service being rendered and a guarantee fee would not be appropriate. As a further consequence, in many countries a loss resulting from such a guarantee being invoked may not be deductible. In India, however, the concept of 'shareholder services' has failed to cut ice with the Revenue authorities7, though the taxpayer at times, have obtained limited relief in the way of reversal of guarantee fee chargeable through external bank quotes by the Transfer Pricing Officer etc.

Abstract

The Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code 2016 did away with the requirement of assessing the financial health of a company before initiating the Corporate Insolvency Resolution Process in order to further the aim of timely disposal of cases. The Hon'ble Supreme Court in Vidarbha Industries Power Ltd. v. Axis Bank Ltd [2022] 140 taxmann.com 252, however, has reinstated this requirement in case of admitting the applications filed by the financial creditors under section 7 of the Code.

This judgment may benefit certain sectors but is likely to defeat the very purpose for which the code was brought in. The Court through this judgment made it mandatory to admit the applications filed by the Operational Creditors whereas the applications filed by the Financial Creditors may or may not be admitted depending on the discretion of the Adjudicating Authority. Thus, the judgment is also likely to distort the settled order of preference of Financial Creditors over Operational Creditors under the code and is likely to result in unnecessary delays.

The Supreme Court went with the literal interpretation of the code without taking into context and purpose of the same. This judgment is likely to cause confusion due to lack of proper guidelines and may even turn the clock to pre-IBC period.

Introduction

The Financial Creditors ("FCs") and Operational Creditors ("OCs") of a corporate debtor ("CD") are empowered under S.7 and S. 9 of Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016 ("IBC"/ "Code") respectively to file an application for initiating a Corporate Insolvency Resolution Process ("CIRP") before National Company Law Tribunal ("NCLT"). The Hon'ble Supreme Court("SC") of India in its landmark ruling of Innoventive Industries Ltd. v. ICICI Bank Ltd. [2017] 84 taxmann.com 320/143 SCL 625 (SC) pronounced that according to S.7, if the Adjudicating Authority ("AA") is satisfied with the existence of a debt and a default, and no disciplinary proceedings lie against the proposed interim resolution professional, then the AA is bound to admit the application unless the application is incomplete.

However, the SC in its recent verdict of Vidarbha Industries Power Ltd. (supra) while dealing with the issue concerning the nature of S.7(5)(a) of the IBC, conferred a discretionary power on the NCLT not to admit a CIRP application filed by a FC even if it is satisfied that a debt exists and the CD is in default. The SC observed that the legislature deliberately used the expression "may admit" in S.7(5)(a), whereas the expression "shall admit" has been used in S.9(5) in order to convey a different meaning therefore intending section S.7(5)(a) to be discretionary while S.9(5) to be mandatory.

This post, therefore, seeks to examine the Vidarbha Industries judgment in the light of the objective behind the Code, which is speedy recovery and revival of financially distressed entities. Further, it tries to analyze its impact on the IBC regime and address the legal conundrum resulting therefrom.

Judgment & Analysis: A case of inconsistent precedents

Vidarbha Industries, the CD is a power generation company operating a coal-fired thermal power plant in Maharashtra. Aggrieved with the decision of the Maharashtra Electricity Regulatory Commission ("MERC") with regard to the determination of tariff, Vidarbha industries challenged the MERC's decision before the Appellate Tribunal for Electricity ("APTEL"). The APTEL allowed the appeal and consequently Vidarbha was to receive a sum of INR 1,730 crores in terms of APTEL's order.

Subsequently, Axis Bank Limited ("ABL"), the FC filed an application before the National Company Law Tribunal ("NCLT") u/s 7(2) of the Code to initiate CIRP against Vidarbha for non-payment of its debt amounting to INR 553 crore. Vidarbha challenged the admission of CIRP on the ground that its inability to repay the dues of ABL was directly attributable to the MERC's failure to pay INR 1,730 crore on account of litigation pending before the SC against the APTEL's order. Hence, Vidarbha sought a stay of the CIRP proceedings until the question in the appeal regarding the liability of MERC to pay the said amount is resolved by the SC.

The NCLT as well as the NCLAT citing previous SC judgements rejected Vidarbha's application and held that the only two things that the Adjudicating Authority is required to consider are the 'existence of debt' and 'default in servicing the debt', and the fulfillment of both these conditions will instantly trigger corporate insolvency. Further, it was emphatically held that the reason for non-payment of the debt is immaterial to the scheme of the code.

The recently enacted Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016 ('IBC' or 'Code'), was aimed at restructuring the insolvency laws and regulations pertaining to corporates, partnerships, individuals and other entities in India, and providing an effective and time bound resolution process to the creditors. Multiple laws and adjudicating forums governing the financial failures in India, prior to enactment of IBC, were not able to alleviate the distressed credit market and provide a time bound and effective mechanism to the stakeholders to resolve the issue.

The structure of the Code is laid down with an objective to maximize the value of the stakeholders; to restructure and consolidate the businesses; to balance the interest of all the stakeholders; to support the development of credit market; improving ease of doing business and facilitate more investment, leading to higher economic growth and development.

The objective of the new law is to generate a competitive revival or resolution plan, which benefits and maximizes the value of all the stakeholders. The aim was to restructure the businesses, if viable, rather than liquidation. However, the Code has been considered by the financial institutions and other creditors as a fast recovery channel rather than considering the option of restructuring and revival of the businesses. In last two years of enactment of IBC, over 800 companies1 have been going the liquidation process.

Amid financial institutions and other financial and operational creditors being successful in instituting insolvency resolution process against the corporate debtors, the plea of the home buyers for initiating the insolvency resolution process against the corporate debtors, being real estate developers was struck down by the Hon'ble National Company Law Tribunal ('NCLT'). In terms of the provisions of IBC, financial creditor, operation creditor and the corporate debtor itself can initiate the corporate insolvency resolution process. NCLT adjudicated that the home buyers who have invested their money in purchasing the real estate property are not operational creditors and not even financial creditors, hence their plea for initiation of insolvency resolution process cannot be accepted. Tax implications and repercussions under Companies Act, 2013 also need consideration. Illustration 1: Inter company loan repayable on demand

Parent (P Ltd.) makes an interest free loan of Rs. 10 crores to its subsidiary (S Ltd). There is a written agreement in place which provides that the loan is repayable on-demand. Cash flow forecasts for the next 3 years indicate positive cash inflows in each year.

The loan is initially measured at its fair value. As the loan is repayable on-demand, it's fair value is the transaction price and the effective interest rate (EIR) is zero.

In determining a default event, P should consider a range of factors that would indicate that the loan is in default, and not only when the loan is 90 days past due. The factors considered relevant are the availability of liquid assets when the loan is called.

In assessing whether an increase in credit risk relative to the position at initial recognition is indicated, P decides that the availability of liquid assets at the reporting date together with forward looking information is most relevant. Therefore, P decides to rely on its review of S's management accounts and cash flow forecasts when assessing credit risk. Whether there has been a significant increase in credit risk (which determines whether 12-month or lifetime ECLs apply) is largely irrelevant because the maximum period over which ECLs can be measured is the maximum contractual period (including extension options) over which the lender has a contractual obligation to extend credit. This is the period over which the entity is exposed to credit risk, and not a longer period. Given the loan is repayable on-demand, the maximum contractual period, and hence period of exposure to credit risk, is 1 day. Credit losses arising from the risk of a default that may occur after 1 day are not included.

Whilst tracking credit risk for an on-demand loan may not be relevant when measuring ECLs, whether there has been a significant increase in credit risk will be relevant for disclosure purposes (Ind AS 107 requires qualitative and quantitative disclosures on the entity's credit risk exposure and significant credit risk concentrations)

In measuring the expected loss on default, P considers the expected manner of recovery. P judges that to maximise recovery of the loan it would allow S to continue trading for 2 years to fund repayment of the loan rather than arrange a fire sale of the less liquid assets.

Example 2 – impairment testing of an intercompany term loan with fluid terms

Parent (P Ltd) makes an interest free loan of Rs. 10 crores to its subsidiary (S Ltd). There is no written agreement, but the parties have documented in writing, their understanding of the terms and this is supported by cash flow forecasts. The understanding is that the loan could be repaid in around 3 years, as working capital permits, but may be extended to the end of year 6. S has no other debt obligations or credit facilities and is adequately capitalised. Repayments are forecast to begin slowly during year 2 and increase throughout year 3. The loan is initially measured at its fair value, which is determined to be Rs. 8.4 crores.

In determining a default event, P judges that 'days past due' will not be a relevant indicator due to the fluid terms of repayment. P therefore develops a policy on default that considers qualitative factors such as the expected life of the loan and the level of headroom in the cash flow forecasts of S. P judges based on the documented understanding and initial forecasts, that the period it expects to have credit risk exposure for is 3 years, and that if the loan is not fully repaid within 6 years it will consider the loan to be credit impaired. In assessing whether an increase in credit risk relative to the position at initial recognition is indicated, P decides that forward looking information is most relevant given the repayment terms. This is because the fluid terms and the expectation that repayments will most likely be back-ended make past behavioural patterns less relevant. Therefore, P decides to rely on its review of S's cash flow forecasts when assessing credit risk. P judges that an increase in credit risk is significant if the expected life of the loan is extended by more than 1 year, or that less than 1/3 of the loan can be recovered by the end of year 3. The maximum period to consider when measuring expected credit losses is the maximum contractual period (including extension options) over which the entity is exposed to credit risk and not a longer period. P judges that in substance the loan contains an option for S to extend the contractual period, but not beyond year 6, if working capital does not permit repayment as forecast, and that it would be contractually required to continue extending credit.

The advent of Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016 (Code) brought in new classification of Creditors like Financial and Operational and Financial Creditor has been given primacy among the Creditors.

As per Section 5(7) and 5(8) of the Code, a creditor under the Code can be a financial creditor mainly under two circumstances i.e., (i) when corporate debtor directly avails a debt from the creditor and (ii) if corporate debtor furnishes a guarantee to any person. It is undisputed that where a creditor lends money for time value is indeed a Financial Creditor. Further, in a claim based on Corporate Guarantee also, a Creditor would be a Financial Creditor. The moot question is whether a Creditor who has not advanced any money to the corporate debtor, but only a security interest is created by such Corporate Debtor in favour a Creditor to secure the payment of a third party can be termed as Financial Creditor under the Code? To simply put, whether a third party mortgagor, i.e., a Company which had created a security interest to secure the payment by a third party who had availed loan from a lender, is a Financial Creditor or Operational?.

This issue had arisen in the case of Anuj Jain v. Axis Bank Ltd. [2020] 114 taxmann.com 656 (SC). In this case, Jaypee Infratech Ltd. (JIL) had been referred to Corporate Insolvency Resolution Process (CIRP) by the NCLT, Allahabad. The said company had mortgaged its properties in favour of Axis Bank and ICICI Bank for a loan advanced to its holding Company Jaiprakash Associates Ltd. (JAL). Other than this, JIL did not directly avail any loan or Credit facilities from the said Banks. It was simply a case of third party mortgage created by JIL to secure the advances provided to JAL. Axis Bank and ICICI Bank had filed their claim with Interim Resolution Professional (IRP) claiming to be the Financial Creditors when the said IRP had rejected to treat them as Financial Creditors. The said Banks had moved an application before the NCLT against the order of the IRP when the NCLT rejected the same. However, the NCLAT had allowed their appeal when the said IRP had moved Supreme Court against the order of the NCLAT. After analyzing the nature of transaction involved, Supreme Court had held that the said the debts in question were in the form of a third party security which had been given by the corporate debtor JIL so as to secure the loans/advances/facilities obtained by JAL from the lenders. Such a 'debt' is not and cannot be a 'financial debt' within the meaning of the Code and hence, the said lenders, the mortgagees, are not the 'financial creditors' of the corporate debtor JIL.Supreme Court had further elaborated that for a person to be designated as a financial creditor of the corporate debtor, it has to be shown that the corporate debtor owes a financial debt to such person and it becomes clear that a third party to whom the corporate debtor does not owe a financial debt cannot become its financial creditor for the purpose of the Code.

Supreme Court further held as under:

"Keeping the objectives of the Code in view, the position and role of a person having only security interest over the assets of the corporate debtor could easily be contrasted with the role of a financial creditor because the former shall have only the interest of realising the value of its security while the latter would, apart from looking at safeguards of its own interests, would also and simultaneously be interested in rejuvenation, revival and growth of the corporate debtor. Thus understood, it is clear that if the former i.e., a person having only security interest over the assets of the corporate debtor is also included as a financial creditor and thereby allowed to have its say in the processes contemplated by Part II of the Code, the growth and revival of the corporate debtor may be the casualty. Such result would defeat the very objective and purpose of the Code, particularly of the provisions aimed at corporate insolvency resolution.

5. Regulatory penalties under consumer protection laws do not constitute "debt" under IBC; moratorium u/s 96 doesn't apply: SC

Saranga Anilkumar Aggarwal v. Bhavesh Dhirajlal Sheth [2025] 172 taxmann.com 145 (SC)/[2025] 188 SCL 286 (SC)/[2025] 255 COMP CASE 681 (SC) The Supreme Court held that penalties imposed by the National Consumer Disputes Redressal Commission are regulatory in nature and arise from non-compliance with consumer protection laws, and are therefore distinct from debt recovery proceedings under the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code. The Court clarified that the moratorium under section 96 has a limited scope and applies only to legal actions or proceedings in respect of any "debt".

It was held that the moratorium under section 96 does not extend to regulatory penalties imposed for violations of consumer protection laws. The Court further held that penalties and damages awarded by the NCDRC in consumer disputes are not ordinary contractual debts, but are intended to compensate consumers for losses suffered and to deter unethical business practices. Such liabilities fall within the category of "excluded debts" under section 79(15) of the Code and, therefore, do not enjoy the protection of moratorium under section 96.

Murlidhar Vincom (P.) Ltd. v. Skoda (India) (P.) Ltd. [2025] 172 taxmann.com 182 (NCLAT- New Delhi)

In the instant case, the appellant, claiming to be a financial creditor, had advanced funds to the respondent–corporate debtor as share application money for allotment of equity shares. No shares were allotted by the corporate debtor, and the amount was also not refunded. On account of such non-refund, the appellant filed an application under section 7 of the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code alleging default.

The Adjudicating Authority rejected the application holding that share application money, where shares were not allotted, could not be treated as a financial debt. On appeal, the NCLAT examined the applicability of the Companies (Acceptance of Deposits) Rules, 2014. It held that Rule 2 of the CADR Rules envisages that only where any amount is received pursuant to a private placement offer made in accordance with the provisions of the Companies Act, 2013 and no shares are allotted in respect thereof, the amount can be treated as a deposit.

The Tribunal noted that the appellant had failed to place on record any proof of a private placement offer made in accordance with the Companies Act, 2013. In the absence of any evidence of a valid and concluded agreement between the parties relating to allotment of shares, the amount advanced could not be treated as money received in response to a private placement offer. Since the transaction could not be linked to section 42 of the Companies Act, the appellant could not invoke section 42(6).

Accordingly, the NCLAT held that there was no infirmity in the impugned order passed by the Adjudicating Authority rejecting the application under section 7 and dismissed the appeal.

Arena Superstructures (P.) Ltd. v. State of U.P. [2025] 172 taxmann.com 273 (Allahabad)

The matter concerned a developer, ASPL, which was allotted a plot under the Sports City project in Noida through a sub-lease deed. Under the terms of the lease, ASPL was required to pay land premium in sixteen half-yearly instalments along with interest and other dues. Although ASPL defaulted in payment, the NOIDA Authority did not take steps to recover the outstanding amounts. Thereafter, ASPL developed residential apartments, obtained sanction of the layout map, collected funds from homebuyers, and allegedly siphoned off the money without completing the project. It was further alleged that insolvency proceedings were orchestrated to avoid civil and legal consequences.

The High Court held that the NCLT does not have the power to issue directions to the NOIDA Authority to revalidate a layout map, as such powers vest only with the Supreme Court and the High Courts under Article 226 of the Constitution of India. The Court further held that, in view of the apparent fraud played by the management of ASPL and the misappropriation of homebuyers' funds, it could not blindly put its seal of approval on the order passed by the NCLT approving reverse insolvency.

Considering the facts and the totality of circumstances, the Court held that there was no other recourse but to refer the matter to the Enforcement Directorate for investigation. The ED was directed to conduct a fair investigation in accordance with law, trace the trail of siphoned or laundered money, and make all endeavours to bring such funds back into the company so that the outstanding dues of the NOIDA Authority, the State Government, additional compensation payable to farmers, and other liabilities could be discharged.

Consequently, the High Court disposed of the writ petition.

INTRODUCTION

The Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016 (hereinafter 'the Code') proved to be one of the most innovative and reformative legal amendments. It made a paradigm shift in the very approach to the notion of insolvency and bankruptcy by providing a great scope for reorganisation and insolvency resolution in addition to liquidation. The Code also promised to balance all stakeholders' interest and to ensure the availability of credit. The scheme of this Code came before the judicial lens on various occasions. In Innoventive Industries Ltd. v. ICICI Bank Ltd.1, the Hon'ble Supreme Court underscored the various changes in the policy outlook of the Code and highlighted its overriding effect on other pre-existing laws.

Another such interesting decision of the Hon'ble Supreme Court is Swiss Ribbons (P.) Ltd. v. Union of India2, (hereinafter 'the present case') where the Hon'ble Court upheld various provisions of the Code. In this paper, the author aims at examining the correctness of the decision regarding two specific parameters regarding the differential treatment given to the Operational Creditors and Financial Creditors, in view of changed circumstances and other pertinent factors.

FINANCIAL DEBT AND OPERATIONAL DEBT UNDER THE CODE

As the next move, it is relevant to look into the statutory description of Financial Creditor and Operational Creditor under the Code. Section 5(7)of the Code defines Financial Creditor as a person to whom a financial debt is owed and includes its assignees and transferees. Section 5(8) gives a substantive definition to Financial Debt and also provides for an inclusive list of debts falling within the category. As per the provision, Financial Debt is a debt including interest, if any, disbursed for the time value of money against consideration.

From the definition, it is clear that the phraseology is very broad so as to include all kinds of debts associating with the time value for money. Similarly, Section 5(20) defines Operational Creditor as a person to whom an operational debt is owed and includes its assignees and transferees. Operational Debt, as per Section 5(21), is a claim in respect of provision of goods or services including employment or repayment of dues payable to the Central or State Government under law. Here, the test is whether the debt has a bearing on provision of goods and services.

It is now relevant to look at what is 'Claim', since both the definitions employ the said word. Section 5(6) defines Claim as (i) A Right to Payment or (ii) A Right to Remedy for Breach of Contract under law, whether or not they are reduced to judgment, disputed, matured, secured or fixed. Hence, it is clear that the right must be one legally enforceable.

All these definitions appear to be clear and concrete yet there are several instances where the Courts have taken varying stands depending on the facts and circumstances of each case. Hence, what was Financial Debt in one case can easily become Operational Debt in another. For instance, according to Section 5(8)(e) of the Code, "Receivables sold or discounted other than any receivables sold on non-recourse basis" falls within the meaning of Financial Debt.

However, in the recent decision of the National Company Law Tribunal, Bengaluru in Invoice Discounters of BNH Infra Projects (India) (P.) Ltd. v. BNH Infra Projects (India) (P.) Ltd.3 the Hon'ble Tribunal came to the conclusion that Financiers discounting invoices of the corporate debtor become operational creditors by stepping into their shoes. The Tribunal referred to Supreme Court and NCLAT decisions to observe that since there is no disbursement of money to the corporate debtor by the financiers and it was only put in an escrow account maintained by KredX, the facilitator, the fundamental condition of Section 5(8) is not met.

While taking this decision, the Hon'ble Tribunal relied on the Supreme Court decision in Anuj Jain v. Axis Bank Ltd.4, and NCLAT decision in Minions Ventures (P.) Ltd. v. TDT Copper Ltd.5 where the Hon'ble Appellate Tribunal observed that since there is no disbursement of money happening in a discounting transaction and since the discounter steps into the shoes of the seller, he is an Operational Creditor and a Petition u/s. 7 of the Code.

4.3-6 Instrument The expression used in the Explanation is "any other instru-ment by which the liability to pay is deferred to a future date". The term instrument has not been defined under the Act or the General Clauses Act.

The Indian Stamp Act, 1899 under section 2(14) defines instrument as:

"(14) "Instrument" - "instrument" includes every document by which any right or liability is, or purports to be, created, transferred, limited, extended, extinguished or recorded:"

In general parlance, the instrument is understood as writing of a document which is formal in nature and executed between two parties.

4.3-7 Conversion of interest into equity shares

The Delhi High Court in the case of Rathi Graphics Technologies Ltd. (supra) held that when pursuant to a settlement, creditor agrees to convert a portion of interest into shares, it must be treated as an extinguishment of liability to pay interest to that extent and, thus, said conversion of interest into shares should be taken to be 'actual payment' within the meaning of Section 43B.

The Mumbai ITAT in the case of Garware Chemicals Ltd. v. Dy. CIT [2015] 54 taxmann.com 86/68 SOT 223 (Mum. - Trib.) held that there could be no disallowance under Section 43B(1)(d) by invoking Explanation 3C, where interest payable was converted into equity shares as interest liability stood ceased to exist and not deferred as in case of conversion of interest loan or borrowing. The Ahmedabad ITAT also held the same ratio in the case of Marwar Hotel Ltd. v. Asstt. CIT [2015] 62 taxmann.com 385/155 ITD 655 (Ahd. - Trib.).

Also from clauses (d), (da) and (e) of Section 43B(1) read with Explanation 3C/3CA/3D and Circular No. 7 of 2006, it is evident that the deduction is allowed when the liability is discharged and not merely on deferring the same by conversion. The transaction of conversion of interest payable into loan or borrowing is deferment of payment of the amount. But when the interest payable is converted into equity capital, the liability of interest payable ceases to exist and stands discharged.

Therefore, in case of discharge of liability by converting it into equity shares would not fall under the ambit of Explanations as the liability is no more in existence once it is discharged.

The above cases still hold good after the amendment by the Finance Act, 2022 as the conversion of interest into equity shares does not defer the liability to pay to a future date, and any conversion of interest into equity shares should be deemed as an actual payment for the purpose of Section 43B.

4.3-8 Conversion of interest into preference shares

Section 55(1) of the Companies Act, 2013 provides that no company limited by shares shall issue irredeemable preference shares. Further, Section 55(2) of the Companies Act, 2013 provides that a company limited by shares may, if so authorised by its articles, issue preference shares that are liable to be redeemed within a period not exceeding twenty years from the date of their issue subject to such conditions as may be prescribed. Redeemable preference shares can be convertible or non-convertible. Convertible preference shares are converted into equity shares, and non-convertible preference shares are redeemed by repaying the capital.

Should the conversion of interest into the preference shares be treated at par with the conversion into debentures or equity shares?

There are two schools of thought on the same. The first school of thought says conversion of interest into preference shares could not be brought within ambit of Explanation 3C to Section 43B as holder of such shares could not be treated as lender of the assessee, and in fact, lender became an owner with certain rights2. This is further supported by the fact that conversion of interest into equity shares is considered as a discharge of interest liability.

However, on the other hand, due to the redeemable character of preference shares, it should be prudent to treat them like debentures for Section 43B. A preference share is an instrument, and since, in India, irredeemable preference shares cannot be issued, the liability to pay against the preference shares continues to exist, although it may be deferred. Hence both the conditions in Explanation 3C are satisfied, and consequently, conversion of interest into preference shares should not be regarded as actual payment of interest under Section 43B, till the preference shares are redeemed.

The CBDT should clarify this issue to avoid any litigation on the same.

Rathi Graphics Technologies Ltd. [2015] 64 taxmann.com 65/[2016] 235 Taxman 550 (Delhi)] held that conversion of a portion of interest into shares should be considered as 'actual payment' within the meaning of section 43B. It is so because, pursuant to a settlement, the creditor agrees to convert a portion of interest into shares, it must be treated as an extinguishment of liability to pay interest to that extent. In essence, there will be no further outstanding interest to that extent. 5.11-2 Loan must be taken from another with an obligation to return Loan must be taken with an obligation to return. In a loan, the amount taken is returned or repaid to fulfil the contract. Return or repayment of the loan is the happy ending to the contract desired by both parties at the inception itself. Trade advances taken by the supplier of goods or services or advances taken by the vendor of property or share application money is not a loan. Return/repayment of such advances may happen when the original agreement or contract to supply goods/services/property/allot shares could not be fulfilled. In a loan, the original agreement is to return the money taken with or without interest. In trade advance, the original agreement is to supply goods/services in return. In share application money, the original contract is to allot shares. It is repaid/returned when the original contract cannot be fulfilled. Therefore, trade advances, advances for property and share application money are not loans [See CIT v. Alpex Exports (P.) Ltd. [2014] 49 taxmann.com 389/[2015] 230 Taxman 140 (Delhi), CIT v. I. P.
