5.11-3 Unpaid/deferred purchase price is not a 'loan'

The following judicial decisions are noteworthy:

(a)

An agreement to pay the balance of consideration due by the purchaser does not give rise to a loan. A loan of money undoubtedly results in a debt, but every debt does not involve a loan. Liability to pay a debt may arise from diverse sources, and a loan is only one of such sources. Every creditor who is entitled to receive a debt cannot be regarded as a lender [Bombay Steam Navigation Co. (P.) Ltd. v. CIT [1965] 56 ITR 52 (SC)].

(b)

A loan is defined by the Oxford English Dictionary as 'a thing lent; something the use of which is allowed for a time, on the understanding that it shall be returned or an equivalent given; esp., a sum of money lent on these conditions and usually with interest'. The essential requirement of a loan is the advance of money (or of some article) upon the understanding that it shall be returned, and it may or may not carry interest. The debt here arose not out of an advance but out of the sale of the flat by the company to the seventh petitioner. The company gave to the seventh petitioner time to pay a part of the purchase price. The seventh petitioner was, thus, given financial accommodation by the company in the matter of payment of the debt. Such financial accommodation was not and did not amount to a loan [Dr. Fredie Ardeshir Mehta v. Union of India [1991] 70 Comp. Cas. 210 (Bom.)].

(c)

The legislative has, for reasons of policy, thought it fit not to define the term "loan" in an inelastic or rigid manner, and in every case, we have got to look to the substance or the essential nature of the transaction for the purpose of determining as to whether or not it is a "loan" within the meaning of the Act. If a vendor of property feeling unable to rely on the personal credit of the purchaser merely takes a bond or security from him in respect of unpaid purchase money the transaction by itself cannot rank as a loan because there is no element of advance involved in it [Kunja Behari Pal v. Satyendra Nath, AIR 1941 Cal. 689 cited in Radha Kisen Chamria v. Keshardeo Chamria, AIR 1954 Cal. 105].

(d)

The amount of the unpaid price (of plant & machinery supplied by a non-resident) cannot be said to be a loan advanced by the non-resident to the buyer, nor can be the non-resident be said to be a lender to the buyer so far as that amount was concerned [CIT v. Saurashtra Cement & Chemical Industries Ltd. [1975] 101 ITR 502 (Guj.)].

(e)

Amount payable to electricity company in respect of electricity charges is not a loan from the electricity company [Ashiana Paper Mills Pvt. Ltd. v. Punjab State Electricity Board, AIR 2008 P&H 119].

(f)

In PCIT v. Boeing India (P.) Ltd. [2023] 146 taxmann.com 131 (Del.), since assessee-company was a debt free company and no interest was paid to creditor/supplier nor any interest had been earned from unrelated party, question of receiving any interest on receivables did not arise. Also see, Integra Software Services (P.) Ltd. v. DCIT [2022] 145 taxmann.com 460 (Chennai – Trib.). The inclusion of the expression 'receivables' does not mean that de hors the context every item of 'receivables' appearing in the accounts of an entity, which may have dealings with foreign AEs would automatically be characterised as an 'international transaction'. There may be a delay in collection of monies for supplies made, even beyond the agreed limit, due to a variety of factors which will have to be investigated on a case-to-case basis. Importantly, the impact this would have on the working capital of the assessee will have to be studied. In other words, there has to be a proper inquiry by the TPO by analysing the statistics over a period of time to discern a pattern which would indicate that vis-a-vis the receivables for the supplies made to an AE, the arrangement reflects an international transaction intended to benefit the associated enterprise in some way—PCIT v. Kusum Health Care (P.) Ltd. [2018] 99 taxmann.com 431 (Delhi). When assessee had already factored in impact of receivables on working capital and thereby on its pricing/profitability vis-à-vis that of its comparables, any further adjustment only on basis of outstanding receivables would distort picture and recharacterise transaction which is not permissible.

In Avenue Asia Advisors (P.) Ltd. v. DCIT [2017] 85 taxmann.com 311/250 Taxman 539 (Delhi), it has been held that there are several factors which need to be considered before holding that every 'receivable' is an 'international transaction' and it requires an assessment on working capital of assessee and impact of receivables.

Where TPO had undertaken a study of transactions that assessee entered into with its AE and delay in payment of invoices raised by assessee, and on that basis he had sought to make an addition towards interest on delayed payment but since perusal of transactions undertaken shows that no pattern was discernible which would suggest any arrangement or understanding between assessee and its AE that would qualify said transaction as an 'international transaction', hence, no addition could be made—PCIT v. Amadeus India (P.) Ltd. [2020] 113 taxmann.com 393 (Delhi).

Where TPO made adjustment on account of notional interest related to alleged delay in collecting receivables by assessee from its AEs, since amount received by assessee in advance from its AE for outweighed amount received late, accordingly, there was no outstanding receivable from AEs to assessee, and, hence, impugned adjustment on account of notional interest was to be set aside—PCIT v. McKinsey Knowledge Centre India (P.) Ltd. [2021] 131 taxmann.com 253/[2022] 284 Taxman 484 (Delhi).

Where an Indian AE has entered into an independent contract with Indian customers for installation, commissioning and maintenance of equipment which has been manufactured by its ultimate parent company of USA, in such cases it cannot be said to be falling within the ambit of 'international transaction' since there being no contract between Indian customer and the US company with respect to such maintenance services—CIT v. Stratex Net Works (India) (P.) Ltd. [2013] 33 taxmann.com 168/215 Taxman 533 (Delhi).

Where money was routed through the AE for the purpose of acquiring distribution rights of certain movies, but due to the failure of such business deal, the AE returned back the money and did not keep the money for significant amount of time. Such a transaction would not be in the nature of financing or lending or advancing of money and, hence, not be falling within the scope of 'international transaction'—PCIT v. KSS Ltd. [2019] 101 taxmann.com 357 (Bom.).

Assessing Officer or TPO are not empowered to convert and re-characterize a transaction of share application into a loan transaction particularly when amounts paid by assessee-company were on account of investment in share capital of associates or subsidiaries—Strides Pharma Science Ltd. v. "One important aspect which has been ignored by NFRA reviewer due to lack of sector/industry experience and knowledge is that ITNL is not in lending/finance business, it is in infrastructure business where the projects are executed in SPVs where the entire equity/financing obligation is of the sponsor itself and hence the impact on the Company has to be assessed on a holistic basis and not in narrow sense."

7.6 NFRA's observations on each of the above contentions are as follows: 7.6-1 Contentions at (a) and (b) above are general understanding of the Audit Firm which NFRA has not disputed in the DAQRR. However, whether such matters are in fact factored into the terms of the loans, so that these are not prejudicial to the interest of the Company is a matter that requires documentation. There is no such documentation in the Audit File.

7.6-2 Regarding contention at (c) above, NFRA has not stated anywhere in the DAQRR that the terms of loans are prejudicial because of zero per cent interest. Paras 7.2-3 and 7.2-6 may be read in this regard.

7.6-3 The Audit Firm's contention in (d) above that the loans were expected to be fully recovered (based on cash flow projections) is without the support of adequate procedures. For e.g., in the case of TRDCL the projected shortterm loan from ITNL is Rs. 201.10 crore (it is noted against this line item in the WP, hardcopy file 13, that "ITNL has given a 0% loan to support the SPV to repay the external debt obligation") over a period of 14 years. However, the WP shows no evidence of how the Audit Firm has verified the projections and assumptions to verify the recoverability of the loan.

7.6-4 Contention in (e) above is a general understanding which was not disputed by NFRA. However, there is no evidence that this is in fact the view of the management.

7.6-5 Contention in (f) and (g) above is not acceptable due to the absence of clear evidence as explained above. More importantly, the Audit Firm itself admits that "the impact on the Company has to be assessed on a holistic basis and not in narrow sense" (contention at (h) above). It can be seen from the above explanations that the Audit Firm has not done any holistic assessment as it clearly failed to verify the factors such as negative indicators that will have an impact on the recoverability of the loans, the repayment capacity of the SPVs, the feasibility of the projects etc. as detailed in para 7.2-8 above. Depending on such factors, even a repayment schedule that does not factor in the ground realities could be prejudicial to the interest of the Company, since such conditions may cause unwarranted defaults and repayment pressures on the SPVs, which in turn would increase their market borrowing costs beyond affordable limits. If the term loans have certain conditions similar to that of a financing company, which the SPVs cannot meet because of specific circumstances applicable to each SPVs, even such conditions, which are normal in other cases, could be prejudicial to the interest of the company. The company has stated in its 'Chairman's Message' that "In the process, the Company's debt position worsened and, the Company also incurred additional interest cost. With the intent to overcome these hurdles, we plan to critically reassess our project portfolio and take appropriate actions, including stake sale, divestment and refinancing". Such plans may have a dependency on the terms and conditions of the existing financing arrangements.

Failure of such plans may not be in the interest of the Company in any case. Even providing a loan, with or without interest, when the situation demands equity, might itself prove prejudicial to the interest of the company depending on the ground realities.

7.7 Thus, it is clear from the replies that the Audit Firm has not done any holistic examination to ascertain whether the terms of the loans are prejudicial to the interest of the Company or not. The company's decision to provide interestfree loans indicates the distress situation of the SPVs. Any failure of the SPVs in honouring the conditions of the loans could prove prejudicial to the Company as a whole. The Audit Firm's examination was based on the general, historical, and theoretical understanding of the company and its business and also based on certain projections provided by the management. There is no examination of the ground realities, i.e., the factors other than the interest rate, to confirm the conclusions apparently reached based on such a highlevel understanding. In that context, the contention at 7.5(h) above is a welldrafted guidance for the Audit Firm itself.

Rathi Graphics Technologies Ltd. [2015] 64 taxmann.com 65 (Delhi)] .

Similarly, in cases of one-time settlement, depending on the facts, there is generally no conversion involved. The liability is settled for a lesser amount. That being the case, it is submitted that in the absence of conversion and in acceptance of discharge of liability, disallowance is not warranted.

Furthermore, if instead of conversion of existing interest into a loan, borrowing etc., a fresh loan is obtained and the interest obligation is paid, the same shall not be covered by the Explanation and accordingly disallowance under section 43B shall not be attracted. In ACIT v. Ashok Radhakishen Mehra [2021] 127 taxmann.com 468/188 ITD 663 (Mum.-Trib.), the Tribunal relying on the decision of Madras High Court in CIT v. Prakash Food & Feed Mills (P.) Ltd. [T.C. Appeal Nos. 775 & 808 of 2014, dated 26-11-2014] held where interest amount had actually been paid by the assessee through overdraft/cash credit account and same had not been converted into loan or borrowing (or) loan or advance, disallowance of interest under section 43B(d)/(e)read with Explanation 3C/3D could not have been made.

4.3-6 Instrument

The expression used in the Explanation is "any other instrument by which the liability to pay is deferred to a future date". The term instrument has not been defined under the Act or the General Clauses Act.

The Indian Stamp Act, 1899 under section 2(14) defines instrument as:

"(14) "Instrument" – "instrument" includes every document by which any right or liability is, or purports to be, created, transferred, limited, extended, extinguished or recorded:"

In general parlance, the instrument is understood as writing of a document which is formal in nature and executed between two parties.

4.3-7 Conversion of interest into equity shares

The Delhi High Court in the case of Rathi Graphics Technologies Ltd. (supra) held that when pursuant to a settlement, creditor agrees to convert a portion of interest into shares, it must be treated as an extinguishment of liability to pay interest to that extent and, thus, said conversion of interest into shares should be taken to be 'actual payment' within the meaning of Section 43B.

The Mumbai ITAT in the case of Garware Chemicals Ltd. v. Dy. CIT [2015] 54 taxmann.com 86/68 SOT 223 (Mum. - Trib.) held that there could be no disallowance under Section 43B(1)(d) by invoking Explanation 3C, where interest payable was converted into equity shares as interest liability stood ceased to exist and not deferred as in case of conversion of interest loan or borrowing. The Ahmedabad ITAT also held the same ratio in the case of Marwar Hotel Ltd. v. Asstt. CIT [2015] 62 taxmann.com 385/155 ITD 655 (Ahd. - Trib.).

Also from clauses (d), (da) and (e) of Section 43B(1) read with Explanation 3C/3CA/3D and Circular No. 7 of 2006, it is evident that the deduction is allowed when the liability is discharged and not merely on deferring the same by conversion. The transaction of conversion of interest payable into loan or borrowing is deferment of payment of the amount. But when the interest payable is converted into equity capital, the liability of interest payable ceases to exist and stands discharged.

Therefore, in case of discharge of liability by converting it into equity shares would not fall under the ambit of Explanations as the liability is no more in existence once it is discharged.

The above cases still hold good after the amendment by the Finance Act, 2022 as the conversion of interest into equity shares does not defer the liability to pay to a future date, and any conversion of interest into equity shares should be deemed as an actual payment for the purpose of Section 43B.

4.3-8 Conversion of interest into preference shares

The above cases still hold good after the amendment by the Finance Act, 2022 as the conversion of interest into equity shares does not defer the liability to pay to a future date, and any conversion of interest into equity shares should be deemed as an actual payment for the purpose of Section 43B.

4.3-8 Conversion of interest into preference shares Section 55(1) of the Companies Act, 2013 provides that no company limited by shares shall issue irredeemable preference shares. Further, Section 55(2) of the Companies Act, 2013 provides that a company limited by shares may, if so authorised by its articles, issue preference shares that are liable to be redeemed within a period not exceeding twenty years from the date of their issue subject to such conditions as may be prescribed. Redeemable preference shares can be convertible or non-convertible. Convertible preference shares are converted into equity shares, and non-convertible preference shares are redeemed by repaying the capital.

Should the conversion of interest into the preference shares be treated at par with the conversion into debentures or equity shares?

There are two schools of thought on the same. The first school of thought says conversion of interest into preference shares could not be brought within ambit of Explanation 3C to Section 43B as holder of such shares could not be treated as lender of the assessee, and in fact, lender became an owner with certain rights2. This is further supported by the fact that conversion of interest into equity shares is considered as a discharge of interest liability.

However, on the other hand, due to the redeemable character of preference shares, it should be prudent to treat them like debentures for Section 43B. A preference share is an instrument, and since, in India, irredeemable preference shares cannot be issued, the liability to pay against the preference shares continues to exist, although it may be deferred. Hence both the conditions in Explanation 3C are satisfied, and consequently, conversion of interest into preference shares should not be regarded as actual payment of interest under Section 43B, till the preference shares are redeemed.

The CBDT should clarify this issue to avoid any litigation on the same.

4.3-9 Whether IBC overrides Section 43B?

Section 43B contains a non-obstante clause that has overriding effect over any of the provisions contained in the Act. However, the overriding effect is not with respect to any other law. In this regard, it would be helpful to refer to the case of CIT v. Tube Investments of India Ltd. [2012] 18 taxmann.com 90/204 Taxman 686 (Mad.). The Madras High Court held that the provisions of section 32 of Sick Industrial Companies (Special Provisions) Act, 1985, have overriding effect over provisions of section 43B of the Act. Thus, where a scheme provided that the tax authorities shall provide a deduction for the interest, even though the same is not paid, the assessee was eligible to get the deduction, even if not permitted by Section 43B.

Further, section 238 of the IBC has an overriding effect over all statutes [Principal CIT v. Monnet Ispat & Energy Ltd. [2018] 18 SCC 786]. Thus, if in a scheme approved under IBC, it is provided that deduction is to be allowed for outstanding interest, the same shall be an allowable deduction, irrespective of the requirement of Section 43B.

5.6-3 Amendments in brief

5.6-3a Clause (da) is inserted in section 43B to include therein payment of interest on loan or borrowing from certain NBFCs. It means, any sum payable as interest on any loan or borrowings from certain NBFCs, shall be allowed as deduction only if it is actually paid, in the manner as discussed earlier.

As mentioned in Memorandum, amendment is made pursuant to amendment made in section 43D as per matching principle. Section 43D is amended to provide that interest income in relation to only certain categories of bad debts (commonly known as interest on non-performing assets) shall be chargeable to tax in the previous year in which it is credited to profit and loss account for that year or the previous year in which it is actually received, whichever is earlier. However, in terms of the amendment in section 43B, any interest payable to certain NBFCs would be allowed as deduction on actual payment basis, whether or not such loan or borrowing has become non-performing assets in hands of the certain NBFCs. In other words, even interest, on loans, not treated as bad debt/non-performing asset, would be allowed only on actual payment and not on accrual basis.

5.6-3b Explanation 3AA is inserted to provide that if deduction in respect of interest referred to in clause (da) is allowed in earlier assessment years i.e. prior to assessment year 2019-20, on accrual basis, no deduction under this section is allowed again on payment basis in respect of same amount of interest.

5.6-3c Explanation 3CA is inserted to provide that deduction of interest referred to in clause (da) shall be allowed, if interest is actually paid, and if it is converted into loan or borrowing, it will not be considered as interest actually paid for the purpose of its allowability.

The above Explanation 3CA is similar to the Explanation 3C which presently exists in section 43B and provides that if any sum payable by the assessee as interest on any loan or borrowing from public financial institution or a State financial corporation or a State Industrial Investment Corporation is converted into a loan or borrowing, the interest so converted and not 'actually paid', shall not be deemed as 'actual payment' and not allowed as deduction in the computation of income under section 43B. The said amendment was made effective from assessment year 1989-90.

It is so because, pursuant to a settlement, the creditor agrees to convert a portion of interest into shares, it must be treated as an extinguishment of liability to pay interest to that extent. In essence, there will be no further outstanding interest to that extent. It is different from the situation envisaged in Explanation 3C to section 43B of the Act viz., conversion of interest into 'a loan or borrowing' where liability continues, although in a different form.

1.6-29 Adjustment - Whether a deemed advance resulting in deemed dividend under section 2(22)(e)?

Section 2(22)(e) provides that any payment by a company of any sum by way of advance to a specified shareholder or to a concern in which he is interested shall be regarded as deemed dividend.

A question that arises is what happens if the associated enterprise is a shareholder covered by section 2(22)(e) or is an interested concern within the meaning of the said section? Will the deemed advance be treated as a deemed dividend under section 2(22)(e)? If yes, will it result in violation of TDS provision under section 195?

There could be two views regarding taxability of the deemed advance under section 2(22)(e).

According to one view a fiction has to be carried to its logical conclusion [CIT v. G. Narasimhan [1999] 102 Taxman 66 (SC)]. Hence once the adjustment is treated as advance for the purpose of section 92CE, it ought to be regarded as advance for the purpose of section 2(22)(e) and the adjustment should be regarded as liable to dividend under the said section.

According to the other view, section 2(22)(e) should not apply in such a situation for following reasons:

(a)

Section 2(22)(e) applies only if there is a payment by a company. It appears that a statutorily deemed advance cannot be regarded as a "payment" within the meaning of section 2(22)(e).

(b)

It is now well settled that legal fictions are created only for some definite purpose and these must be limited to that purpose and should not be extended beyond that legitimate field [CIT v. Mother India Refrigeration Industries (P.) Ltd. [1985] 23 Taxman 8 (SC); CIT v. Vadilal Lallubhai [1972] 86 ITR 2 (SC); ITO v. M. C. Ponnoose [1970] 75 ITR 174 (SC); CIT v. Amar Chand N. Shroff [1963] 48 ITR 59 (SC)]. It could be argued that the fiction of excess money be deemed as an advance should be restricted to section 92CE and not extended to other purposes of the Act.

(c)

A legal fiction cannot be expanded by giving purposive interpretation particularly if the result of such interpretation is to transform the concept of chargeability. [Vodafone International Holdings B. V. v. UOI [2012] 17 taxmann.com 202 (SC)]. Now, in section 92CE, the fiction does not result in any chargeable income: the secondary adjustment is not taxable; however, if section 2(22)(e) regarded as applicable, then a fiction which does not initially result in taxable income is transformed into a fiction resulting in taxable income under section 2(22)(e)! Obviously, such an interpretation cannot be attributed.

(d)

The word "deemed" refers to "what is supposed to be, not to "what actually is" [A.C. Goel v. First National Bank Ltd. (1960) 30 Comp. Cas. 317 (Punj)]. What is deemed as advance made by the assessee is not actually an advance made by him. The nomenclature "advance" is to facilitate recovery of excess money and charge of interest. However, it is not a loan or advance within the meaning of section 2(22)(e). Now, section 2(22)(e) would require an actual advance by the assessee and since there is no actual advance upon the adjustment being deemed as advance section 2(22)(e) should not apply.

(e)

It is clear that unless and until there is created in favour of an assessee a debt due by somebody, it cannot be said that he has acquired a right to receive the income or that income has accrued to him.

... Thus, a mere claim to income without an enforceable right thereto cannot be regarded as accrued income for the purposes of the Act. [CIT v. Govind Prasad Prabhu Nath [1987] 35 Taxman 513 (All.)2] It is a moot point as to whether a unilateral entry by the Indian entity is legally binding on the associated enterprise and whether there is a legal liability on its part to pay and if it does not accept the liability, can the Indian entity be really taxed on the ground that income has accrued to it.

Explanations 3C, 3CA and 3D of section 43B provide that if the outstanding interest (as referred to above) is converted into a loan or borrowing or advance, the same shall not be considered as actually paid for the purpose of Section 43B and accordingly, disallowance shall get attracted.

The term actually paid has been a bone of contention. Some of the rulings dealing with the expression 'actually paid' have been given below:

(a)

Furnishing of bank guarantee is not actual payment for the purpose of section 43B [CIT v. McDowell & Co. Ltd. [2009] 180 Taxman 514 (SC)];

(b)

Advance deposit of central excise duty in Personal Ledger Account [PLA] constitutes actual payment of duty within the meaning of section 43B [CIT v. Modipon Ltd. [2017] 87 taxmann.com 275 [2018] 252 Taxman 123 (SC)];

(c)

Mere postponement of the liability to pay interest does not amount to discharge, whether actual or constructive and, therefore, the conversion of the outstanding interest into a term loan liability, though with the consent of the lender, cannot be considered as a constructive discharge of the interest liability [Kalpana Lamps and Components Ltd. v. Dy. CIT [2002] 125 Taxman 1045 (Mad.)];

(d)

Transfer of statutory liability in a slump sale shall not be considered as actual payment for the purpose of section 43B [Pembril Engineering (P.) Ltd. v. DCIT [2015] 61 taxmann.com 222/155 ITD 72 (Mum.-Trib.)];

(e)

If instead of paying the outstanding interest liability, a further loan is obtained and the same is tendered for payment of outstanding interest liability, Explanation 3C to section 43B is attracted, and deduction of interest is not available [CIT v. Gujarat Cypromet Ltd. [2019] 103 taxmann.com 346/262 Taxman 93 (SC)];

(f)

Outstanding interest on loan, being converted into debentures would be hit by Explanation 3C to section 43B and accordingly, even if the issuance of debentures is with the consent of the lender, the same shall not be considered as actually paid and disallowance shall get attracted [CIT v. M.M. Aqua Technologies Ltd. [2015] 60 taxmann.com 237/233 Taxman 397 (Delhi)];

(g)

The Supreme Court in M.M. Aqua Technologies Ltd. v. CIT [2021] 129 taxmann.com 145/282 Taxman 281 (SC) overturned the Delhi High Court decision. It held that issuing debenture in lieu of outstanding interest would tantamount to actual payment of outstanding interest. The Apex Court distinguished the decision of Gujarat Cypromet (supra) on facts and, without affording much discussion, held the issuance of the debenture to be sufficient discharge of liability as the liability to pay interest was extinguished.

4.3-2 Amendment by the Finance Act, 2022

In order to overcome and nullify the decision of the Supreme Court in the case of M.M. Aqua Technologies (supra), the Finance Act, 2022 has inserted the words "debentures or any other instrument by which the liability to pay is deferred to future date" in Explanation 3C, 3CA and 3D to Section 43B. Thus, henceforth, conversion of the outstanding interest into debenture or deferring the interest payment through any instrument shall not be considered actual payment of interest liability. Consequently, no deduction shall be allowed for the interest which has been converted into:

(a)

Loan;

(b)

Advance;

(c)

Debenture; or

(d)

Any other instrument by which the liability to pay is deferred to a future date.

4.3-3 Purpose of Amendment

The relevant extract from the Explanatory Memorandum is as under:

"However, certain taxpayers are claiming deduction under section 43B on account of conversion of interest payable on an existing loan into a debenture on the ground that such conversion is a constructive discharge of interest liability and, therefore, amounted to actual payment which has been upheld by several Courts.

Such interpretation is against the intent of legislation. The section was introduced to curb the mischief of claiming deduction by the assessee, without paying interest to financial institutions/NBFC/scheduled bank or a co-operative bank. Section 43B makes a departure from other sections in the Act, as indicated by its non obstante clause. Under the provisions of this section conversion of the outstanding interest liability into debentures is not an actual payment and cannot be claimed as deduction.

Achenbach Buschhutten GmbH & Co. v. Arcotech Ltd. [2017] 84 taxmann.com 262 (NCL-AT)

The appellant, a foreign company, claimed to be operational creditor. It filed an application under section 9 to initiate corporate insolvency resolution process in respect of the respondent corporate debtor. The Adjudicating Authority, referring to clause of arbitration, did not entertain the application on the ground that there was an existence of a dispute.

Held that, it was found that the appellant had enclosed one letter relating to 'confirmation of receipt of payment' from foreign institution known as 'Sparkasse Siegen'.

The question as to whether filing of a copy of the certificate from the financial institution, 'maintaining accounts of the operational creditor confirming that there was no payment of unpaid operational debt by the corporate debtor' as prescribed under clause (c) of sub-section (3) of section 9 is mandatory or directory, was considered by the Appellate Tribunal in 'Smart Timing Steel Ltd. v. National Steel & Agro Industries Ltd. [2017] 82 taxmann.com 136 (NCL-AT)'. The Appellate Tribunal held that certificate from the 'financial institution' maintaining accounts of the operational creditor confirming that there is no payment of unpaid operational debt by the 'corporate debtor', as prescribed under clause (c) of sub-section (3) of section 9 mandatory.

Admittedly, the bank in question was not a scheduled bank, nor is a 'financial institution' as defined under section 45-I of Reserve Bank of India Act, 1934 (2 of 1934). The Bank aforesaid also did not come within the meaning of 'Public Financial Institution' as defined in clause (72) of section 2 of Companies Act, 2013. The Central Government has also not issued any Notification specifying the bank in question for the purpose of sub-section (14) of section 3 read with section 9.

In the circumstances, the application preferred by the appellant was not maintainable in the absence of record of financial institution as defined in sub-section (14) of section 3.

10.5-1 Amendment regarding computation of deduction - Section 36(1)(viii) has been amended still further. Under the second proviso to the said section as it stood prior to the amendment, the allowance in respect of special reserve was allowable only till such period upto which the aggregate of the amounts carried to such reserve from time to time did not exceed twice the amount of share capital. Further, in computing the share capital, the amounts capitalised from reserves were to be excluded.

The said second proviso is now amended with effect from assessment year 1997-98 so as to provide that:

◆ the allowance will be allowed till such period upto which the aggregate of special reserve does not exceed the aggregate of share capital and general reserves; and

◆ in computing the share capital, the amounts capitalised from reserves are no longer required to be excluded.

Thus, in case of corporations making profits consistently and ploughing back the profits regularly by increasing the general reserves, the deduction in respect of special reserve could be allowed year after year almost perpetually.

3.2-3 Meaning of 'debt', financial debt, claim, operational debt

The definitions of debt, claim, financial debt, operational debt are highly relevant under Insolvency Code.

Debt - "Debt" means a liability or obligation in respect of a claim which is due from any person and includes a financial debt and operational debt - section 3(11) of Insolvency Code, 2016.

Debt due means debt due and payable. If the debt is barred by law under Limitation Act, it is not 'debt due' - B K Educational Services v. Parag Gupta and Associates (2018) 150 SCL 293 = 98 taxmann.com 213 (SC) = (2019) 11 SCC 633 - followed in SK Systems v. Hamtek Infra Projects India (2020) 157 SCL 678 = 113 taxmann.com 201 (NCLT).

If recovery certificate was issued on 24-12-2001, petition for CIRP on 21-7-2017 is barred. Section 23 of Limitation Act applies to continuous wrong and not to continuous right - Vashdeo R Bhojwani v. Abhyudaya Cooperative Bank (2019) 9 SCC 158.

Compulsorily Convertible Debenture (CCD) is equity. It is not debenture simpliciter. It is not a 'debt' under section 3(11) of Insolvency Code - IFCI Ltd. v. Sutanu Sinha [2023] 156 taxmann.com 681 (SC 3 member bench).

Claim - "Claim" means— (a) a right to payment, whether or not such right is reduced to judgment, fixed, disputed, undisputed, legal, equitable, secured or unsecured (b) right to remedy for breach of contract under any law for the time being in force, if such breach gives rise to a right to payment, whether or not such right is reduced to judgment, fixed, matured, un-matured, disputed, undisputed, secured or unsecured - section 3(6) of Insolvency Code, 2016.

Financial Debt - "Financial debt" means a debt along with interest, if any, which is disbursed against the consideration for the time value of money and includes—

(a)

money borrowed against the payment of interest.

(b)

any amount raised by acceptance under any acceptance credit facility or its de-materialised equivalent.

(c)

any amount raised pursuant to any note purchase facility or the issue of bonds, notes, debentures, loan stock or any similar instrument.

(d)

the amount of any liability in respect of any lease or hire purchase contract which is deemed as a finance or capital lease under the Indian Accounting Standards or such other accounting standards as may be prescribed.

(e)

receivables sold or discounted other than any receivables sold on non-recourse basis.

The said sections read as follows:

“Section 59 : Application of payment where debt to be discharged is indicated - Where a debtor, owing several distinct debts to one person, makes a payment to him, either with express intimation, or under circumstances implying, that the payment is to be applied to the discharge of some particular debt, the payment, if accepted, must be applied accordingly.

Section 60 : Application of payment where debt to be discharged is not indicated - Where the debtor has omitted to intimate, and there are no other circumstances indicating to which debt the payment is to be applied, the creditor may apply it at his discretion to any lawful debt actually due and payable to him from the debtor, whether its recovery is or is not barred by the law in force for the time being as to the limitation of suits.

Section 61 : Application of payment where neither party appropriates - Where neither party makes any appropriation, the payment shall be applied in discharge of the debts in order of time, whether they are or are not barred by the law in force for the time being as to the limitation of suits. If the debts are of equal standing, the payment shall be applied in discharge of each proportionably.”

5.7 Mode of receipt of consideration for transfer of certain assets other than capital asset [Section 43CA]1

5.7-1 Background

Section 43CA provides that where the consideration for the transfer of an asset (other than capital asset), being land or building or both, is less than the stamp duty value, the stamp duty value so adopted or assessed or assessable shall be deemed to be the full value of the consideration for the purposes of computing income under the head 'Profits and gains of business of profession'.

Section 43CA(3) provides that where the date of agreement fixing the value of consideration for transfer of asset and the date of registration of such transfer of asset are not the same, the stamp duty value on the date of agreement shall be compared with the declared consideration in order to decide whether such stamp duty value is higher than the declared consideration or not.

Further, section 43CA(4) provides that the aforesaid provision is applied only in case where the amount of consideration or a part thereof was received only through specified modes on or before the date of agreement for transfer of the asset.

5.7-2 Amendment

Finance (No. 2) Act, 2019 has amended sub-section (4) to include therein 'such other electronic mode as may be prescribed' in addition to specified modes of receipt.

Thus, the receipt of consideration through prescribed electronic mode would be in compliance with the requirement.

The amendment will take effect from 1-4-2020 and will accordingly, apply to assessment year 2020-21 and subsequent assessment years.

The following points are noteworthy:

The Debt must be issued by a non-resident, which must be an associated enterprise of the borrower Indian company or Indian PE of a foreign company.

However, debt issued by a lender not associated with an associated enterprise either provides an implicit or explicit guarantee to such lender or deposits a corresponding and matching amount of funds with the lender; such debt shall be deemed to have been issued by an associated enterprise.

The word "implicit guarantee" recognises the possibility that whilst a guarantee may not be formally documented, the parties' behaviour indicates that a guarantee exists.

Implicit guarantees are difficult to evaluate since their terms are not explicitly stated, and motivation may be mixed and obscure.

A major multinational may wish to protect its own credit status and reputation by making good any debts that its subsidiaries are unable to meet, but is it difficult to discern whether that is primarily a service provided to the subsidiary, whether it arises from a policy aimed at protecting the MNE's credit rating, or a mixture of both.

An implicit guarantee is perhaps more likely to exist where the recipient has an important role within the group or shows a close identification with the name or brand of the group.

The proviso to section 94B(1) provides that where the borrowing is from a non-resident third party but the debt is implicitly or explicitly guaranteed by an associated enterprise or an associated enterprise has deposited a corresponding and matching amount of funds with the third party, then the non-resident third party shall be deemed to be associated enterprise. "Long-term finance" is defined in clause (h) of the Explanation to section 36(1)(viii) to mean "any loan or advance where the terms under which moneys are loaned or advanced provide for repayment along with interest thereof during a period of not less than five years". This takes us to the question whether a preference share can be held to be a loan or advance. The investment in redeemable preference shares cannot be considered as a loan or advance made by the assessee to the company for interest. The basic characteristic of a loan is that the person advancing the loan has the right to sue on the debt, whereas the preference shareholders cannot sue for the money due on the shares undertaken to be redeemed and as of right claim a return of the share money except in a winding up and that to after the redemption date. Similarly, a preference shareholder stands on a different footing from a person who has advanced monies to another. Thus an advance is also quite different from preference shares in nature and character. Thus there is no merit in the assessee's claim that the dividend received in interest of the redeemable preference shares amounts to profits derived from providing long term finance within the meaning of section 36(1)(viii) of the Act read with clause (h) of the Explanation to the section.

Union of India [1991] 70 Comp. Cas. 210 (Bom.). In the said case petitioners were directors of the company. The company purchased a flat for accommodating the seventh petitioner who was an employee of the company and its whole time director. It was agreed when the purchase was made that the seventh petitioner would have the option to purchase the flat during the course of his employment or within 12 months thereafter. An agreement was entered into between the company and the seventh petitioner giving him such option. On 29-11-1978, the seventh petitioner exercised the option. He then paid to the company half of the purchase price and requested that he be allowed to pay the balance in three equal instalments. The company's board of directors, thereupon, passed a resolution. It approved the transfer of the flat to the seventh petitioner on the basis that half of the purchase price should be paid immediately and the balance in three yearly instalments with interest accruing at the rate of 6 per cent per annum. The Registrar of Companies filed a prosecution against the petitioners and stated that the seventh petitioner had paid the sum of ` 92,000 on 29-11-1978, and the balance amount of ` 92,000 together with interest in the sum of ` 6,685 only on 20-2-1980. He alleged that the amount due from the seventh petitioner was not on account of any of the normal trading or business activities of the company as it was not the business of the company to deal in immovable property and, therefore, the amount of ` 92,000 due from him to the company and such financial assistance and deferred part payment amounted to, and should be treated as, a loan to a director without the previous approval of the Central Government and thereby the accused had contravened the provisions of section 295(1)(a) of the Companies Act, 1956 ('the 1956 Act') punishable under section 295(4) of the 1956 Act. The Court held that the essential requirement of a loan is the advance of money (or of some article) upon the understanding that it shall be returned, and it may or may not carry interest. The debt here arose not out of an advance but out of the sale of the flat by the company to the seventh petitioner. The company gave to the seventh petitioner time to pay a part of the purchase price. The seventh petitioner was, thus, given financial accommodation by the company in the matter of payment of the debt. Such financial accommodation was not and did not amount to a loan.

9.3-3 Indirect loan

When the section refers to an indirect loan to a director, what it means is that the company shall not give a loan to a director through the agency of one or more intermediaries.- Dr. Fredie Ardeshir Mehta v. Union of India [1991] 70 Comp. Cas. 210 (Bom.). The word 'indirectly' in the section cannot be read as converting what is not a loan into a loan.

22.4

Is interest-free loan received liable to be treated as sum of money received without consideration?

The consideration in an interest-free loan is to return the money. The detriment suffered by lender in parting with use of funds is valid consideration to support promise of repayment of the loan by the borrower. This view is supported by the following observations of the Hon'ble Delhi High Court in CIT v. Mridu Hari Dalmia [1982] 8 Taxman 138/133 ITR 550 :

'A transaction of a loan implies an agreement to repay the money that is borrowed. Shri Harihar Lal cited a definition of 'loan' from Corpus Juris Secundum (Vol. 54, p. 654). According to this passage a loan of money is defined as 'a contract by which one delivers a sum of money to another and the latter agrees to return at a future time a sum equivalent to that which he borrows'; and again as the delivery by one party and the receipt by the other party of a given sum of money on an agreement, express or implied, to repay the sum lent with or without interest. These definitions can be accepted, succinctly summarising or analysing the ingredients of a loan. They are in line with the definitions enunciated by our Supreme Court (vide K.M.S. Lakshmanier & Sons v. CIT [1953] 23 ITR 202, Badridas Daga v. CIT [1958] 34 ITR 10 and other cases). They make it clear that a loan, involves an enforceable agreement between two parties, one of whom is the lender and the other the borrower. The former lends monies to the latter. The latter receives the sum and promises to repay it by an equivalent amount at a future date with or without interest. . . .'

In Chandrakant H. Shah v. ITO [2009] 28 SOT 315 (Mum.), the Tribunal held that 'consideration for a promise may consist of either some benefit conferred on the promisor or detriment suffered by the promisee or both, hence, on this criteria the assessee has gained by way of interest-free loan and the lenders have suffered by or giving interest-free loans and such suffering has got some value and, therefore, the said transaction cannot be said to be without consideration'.

In view of the above, interest free loan cannot be said to be sum of money received without consideration and is not taxable u/s 56(2)(x)(a).

Amount claimed to be transferred to corporate debtor couldn’t be termed as ‘financial debt’ without any evidence

HEADNOTE: Section  5(8), read with section  3(12), of the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016 -  Corporate insolvency resolution process -  Financial debt - Applicant - financial creditor claimed that it had disbursed a loan to corporate debtor - On corporate debtor’s failure to pay, an application under section 7 was filed against corporate debtor - It was noted that there was no credible evidence to establish that alleged disbursal was made against time value of money (an essential element for qualifying a claim as a ‘financial debt’ under Section 5(8)) - Transaction in question neither involved any stipulated interest component nor any contractual arrangement indicating accrual of financial gain, return, or profit to alleged Financial Creditor - Furthermore, there were no agreed terms of repayment, nor was there any contemporaneous communication or correspondence evidencing a request for a loan or acknowledgment of such a financial arrangement - Whether in absence of foundational elements, disbursal lacked commercial character necessary to constitute a financial debt under IBC - Held, yes - Whether application under Section 7 was barred by limitation as purported recall of an alleged loan was made nearly 17 years after its initial disbursal - Held, yes - Whether in absence of a categorical admission, a time-barred claim could not be revived - Held, yes - Whether financial creditor had failed to demonstrate, with cogent evidence, existence of a legally enforceable financial debt as defined under Section 5(8) and correspondingly, had not substantiated occurrence of a default as per Section 3(12), and, therefore, instant application was to be dismissed - Held, yes [Paras 14, 16, 22 and 24]

FACT: ■

The applicant- financial creditor claimed that it had extended a loan to the Corporate Debtor during the period from 13.06.2007 to 27.03.2009. The said loan was extended in his personal capacity and was repayable on demand.

■

Corporate Debtor had consistently acknowledged the said loan in its Audited Financial Statements over the years, classifying it as an “Unsecured Loan”.

■

A loan recall notice was issued by the financial creditor on 04.07.2022 demanding immediate repayment of the full outstanding loan. A reminder for payment was further issued via email on 01.08.2022. In response to the aforementioned notice, the Corporate Debtor, through its Financial Controller acknowledged the communication and expressed an intention to amicably settle the matter. Since no steps were taken by the Corporate Debtor to repay the debt a legal notice was issued by the financial creditor.

■

Thus, financial creditor filed instant petition under section 7 to initiate CIRP against corporate debtor for the alleged default on the part of the corporate debtor in repayment of financial debt.

■

The Corporate Debtor raised a dispute that the application under Section 7 was barred by limitation, as the alleged financial debt was stated to have arisen in the year 2005-06, and the demand was purportedly made for the first time in July 2022- after a lapse of nearly 17 years. The corporate debtor argued that such a stale claim could not be revived by unilateral recall or reliance upon self-serving accounting entries. Further, it was contended that the application failed to satisfy the statutory preconditions of Section 7.

■

The corporate debtor also claimed that financial creditor had failed to produce any loan agreement, repayment schedule, or even a basic acknowledgment of terms such as interest, tenure, or security. No board resolution or authorization was passed by corporate debtor to borrow funds from the financial creditor. The absence of any documentation, along with the lack of demand for repayment for nearly two decades, was said to indicate that the financial creditor never extended any loan capable of forming a financial debt.

HELD: ■

The Financial Creditor has pleaded that the loan advanced by him was a loan recallable on demand and qualifies as a financial debt under Section 5 (8). He has further pleaded that even though the loan was interest-free but qualified as disbursal against time value of money. (Para 11)

■

In order for an interest-free debt to qualify as financial debt, an financial creditor must show that the funds were disbursed with ‘consideration for time value of money’. The question of what constitutes ‘time value of money’ varies depending on the facts and circumstances; nonetheless, the financial creditor must demonstrate that it had an interest in the subject matter for which the loan was disbursed and was profiting from it. The pre-requisite is disbursal of money to the borrower for utilization by the borrower and that the disbursal must be against consideration for time value of money even if it is not interest bearing. (Para 13)

■

HEADNOTE: Section 5(8), read with section 7, of the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016 - Corporate insolvency resolution process - Financial debt - Corporate debtor, being respondent company, was engaged in business of leather processing and finished leather products - Nephew of petitioner was majority shareholder and managing director of corporate debtor - Under an understanding between petitioner, corporate debtor and said nephew, petitioner advanced loan of Rs. 1.29 crore to corporate debtor to meet its funds requirements - Said loan was payable on demand but such an understanding did not include payment of any interest against loan - There was also no material to show that loan amount was disbursed against consideration for time value of money - Whether said loan would not be covered under any of sub-clauses of definition of financial debt - Held, yes [Para 12]  Section 238A, read with section 7, of the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016 - Corporate insolvency resolution process - Limitation period - Petitioner provided loan to respondent in 2007 and 2008 - Understanding between petitioner and respondent did not provide a time limit for repayment of debt - Whether in absence of any contract between parties, amount needed to be repaid within three years from date when loan was advanced; thus, loan amount advanced by cheque dated 15-12-2007, 11-2-2008 and 26-3-2008 would have become due and payable on or before 14-12-2010, 10-2-2011 and 25-3-2011, respectively - Held, yes - Whether since there was no material to show that respondent made any admission of debt within such period or even subsequent thereto, instant CIRP application for non-payment filed in 2018 was grossly time barred and, hence, not maintainable - Held, yes [Para 19]IBC : Where unsecured loan was advanced which did neither bear interest nor was same disbursed against consideration for time value of money, said loan would not be financial debt   IBC : In absence of any contract between parties, loan amount needed to be repaid within 3 year from date when loan was advanced; in absence of any admission of debt by debtor company within such period or subsequent thereto, CIRP petition filed beyond three years was grossly time barred

Section 238A, read with section 7, of the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016 - Corporate insolvency resolution process - Limitation period - Petitioner provided loan to respondent in 2007 and 2008 - Understanding between petitioner and respondent did not provide a time limit for repayment of debt - Whether in absence of any contract between parties, amount needed to be repaid within three years from date when loan was advanced; thus, loan amount advanced by cheque dated 15-12-2007, 11-2-2008 and 26-3-2008 would have become due and payable on or before 14-12-2010, 10-2-2011 and 25-3-2011, respectively - Held, yes - Whether since there was no material to show that respondent made any admission of debt within such period or even subsequent thereto, instant CIRP application for non-payment filed in 2018 was grossly time barred and, hence, not maintainable - Held, yes [Para 19]

FACT: The respondent-company was engaged in the business of leather processing and finished leather products. The nephew of the petitioner was the majority shareholder and managing director of the respondent-company at the relevant time. The petitioner advanced unsecured loan of Rs. 1.30 crore to the respondent-company between 2007 and 2008, which was payable on demand.

It was submitted that the petitioner demanded payment in 2016, but to no avail; that the respondent-company had made a payment of Rs. 5 lakh in 2016; however, it failed to make further payments despite several requests. A demand notice was issued to which the company issued a reply denying its liability.

On instant CIRP petitioner filed by the petitioner:

HELD: Issue of financial debt

The Respondent company has admitted that the petitioner being the maternal uncle of the Managing Director, had given Rs. 1.25 lakh. initially. In addition, he had also given Rs. 1.29 crore under cheques dated 15-12-2007, 11-2-2008, 26-3-2008. [Para 6]

From the materials, it is clear that the petitioner had paid Rs. 1.29 crore to the respondent-company to meet its fund requirements.

The definition of financial debt is inclusive one. It indicates that debt along with interest 'if any' is disbursed against the consideration for time value of money. [Para 11]

had filed an application under section 7 to initiate CIRP against the corporate debtor.

The respondent submitted that petitioner had advanced an unsecured loan to the respondent on 9-1-2007 however, petition filed by the appellant in 2020 i.e., after a lapse of 13 years further, petitioner through letter dated 14-9-2017 himself had claimed that the amount was paid for acquisition of 25 per cent equity interest in the development project of the corporate debtor. HELD: By way of instant petition under section 7, the petitioner claims himself to be a financial creditor having an advance unsecured loan equivalent to Rs. 1.11 crores as on 31-3-2007 and presently Rs. 1.85 crores considering the enhanced value of USD. However, the petitioner has not relied upon any loan document which might have been executed between the petitioner and the corporate debtor with regard to the terms and conditions of the said loan transaction along with any repayment schedule or the rate of interest. However, surprisingly, the petitioner has relied upon the notice dated 14-9-2017, which was served upon a Director of the corporate debtor wherein it was stated that the petitioner wired USD 2,50,000/- and further that the petitioner was entitled to obtain 25 per cent equity interest in the corporate debtor, i.e., U.S. Hospitality Private Limited in exchange for the said sum of money. In response to the notice dated 14-9-2017, reply dated 18-9-2017 was sent on behalf of corporate debtor stating that the payment of USD 2,50,000/- was not towards 25 per cent equity interest but was rather an investment in a specific project of U.S. Co., as the said Company was involved in the Project to lease Real Estate in India with a hope of building a hospital on the said property. The petitioner has further relied upon notice dated 24-7-2020 got served by the petitioner upon the corporate debtor and its directors and in of the notice, it has been reiterated by the petitioner that on 1-9-2007, he wired a sum of USD 2,50,000/- from his Bank Account to the corporate debtor.

If the notices dated 14-9-2017 and 24-7-2020 are taken into account, it emerges that it is the specific and definite case of the petitioner that he transferred the amount of USD 2,50,000/- with an intent to buy a 25 per cent stake in the assets of the corporate debtor. [Para 20]

It is well settled that an investment cannot be equated with a loan. In the commercial word, equity financing and debt financing are altogether different modes of finance which are distinct from each other. Equity financing carries no repayment obligation while debt financing involves borrowing of money which is often repayable along with interest or other charges as may be settled between the parties. Therefore, a sum of money invested with an intent of requiring equity stake in a company or some other interest in some of the properties of the company cannot be dubbed as a financial debt or for that matter a loan transaction. [Para 21]

Besides, one cannot be oblivious of the facts that in the notices dated 14-9-2017 and 24-7-2020, the petitioner himself has claimed that the payment in question was made with intent to buy 25 per cent equity stake in the respondent's Company, on the basis of which, it could be safely concluded that the money was given as a loan. In this regard, a reference can be made to the Remittance Certificate Exhibit whereby the money was wired by the petitioner from Spain to the account of the corporate debtor and in the Bank note, it is specifically mentioned that the purpose of remittance was an investment in purchasing, constructing and operating a hotel business in India. [Para 23]

Therefore, by looking at the instant case, it cannot be said to be a case of money having been borrowed by the corporate debtor from the petitioner nor the transaction can be dubbed as a loan transaction. The so-called admission made by the corporate debtor in the reply dated 18-9-2017 that the transaction was invested is of no consequence. In this context, it is further pertinent to mention that the respondent has claimed in the reply that an amount of Rs. 20 lacs were paid back to the petitioner as on 11-2-2008 as is evident from the statement of account (Exhibit G) attached with the reply. So far as the petitioner is concerned, in the rejoinder filed by him, the transfer of an amount of Rs. 20 lacs as on 11-2-2008 has not been specifically denied and it has only been stated that it was a personal transaction not relating to the transaction which took place in the year 2007. Even this plea raised on behalf of the petitioners seems to be a tentative one and does not really explains the exact position and circumstances under which a sum of Rs. 20 lacs were paid to the petitioner. [Para 24]

, the finding of the Adjudicating Authority that the amount of interest at the rate of 24 per cent claimed by the appellant being exorbitant, it was sufficient ground for rejection of the claim of the appellant could not be subscribed to. The Adjudicating Authority, at best, had a limited jurisdiction to examine the decision of the RP on the rejection on the claim and not on the reasonability of computation of the claim or quantum of the debt. [Para 21]

■ It is a well settled precept that in the judgment of the Supreme Court in Orator Marketing (P.) Ltd. v. Samtex Desinz (P.) Ltd. [2021] 128 taxmann.com 424, it has been clearly held that financial debt does not expressly exclude an interest free loan. Thus, financial debt also includes any sum raised under any other transaction having the commercial effect of borrowing even it does not carry an interest component. Be that as it may, the fact that the appellant in the present case has not demonstrated any efforts made by it to recover the loan amount since 2007 cannot be obliterated. There is no material on record to show that any notice or any demand was raised either for repayment of the purported loan or for payment of interest since 2007. If the loan agreement was a genuine one, then the expected course of action on the part of the appellant would have been to seek refund of the loan given by it when it exited the management of the corporate debtor if not earlier. The inordinate and unexplained delay in raising the demand until the corporate debtor was admitted into rigours of CIRP does cast doubts on the legitimacy and bona fide of the alleged transaction as a whole irrespective of the interest component. [Para 22]

■

The Adjudicating Authority has rightly taken note of the 13 years unusual and stony silence on the part of the appellant to recover their dues. This is clearly a case where the appellant seemed to have woken up from their slumber and suddenly remembered to have raised their claim in respect of loan-cum-interest coinciding with the corporate debtor getting admitted into CIRP. Given this fact situation, there is nothing arbitrary on the part of the Adjudicating Authority to find the conduct on the part of the management for maintaining uninterrupted silence for over 15 years on the recovery of their dues including unclaimed interest amount of Rs. 1.04 crores rather unusual lending credence to the fact that the loan agreement was prepared as an after-thought to tailor the filing of their claims. [Para 23]

■

In result, there is substance in the contention raised by the respondents that the claim filed by the appellant was not bona fide as it was not premised on a genuine loan transaction and was bereft of cogent supporting proof. There is no error on the part of the Adjudicating Authority in passing the impugned order rejecting the claims filed by the appellant. [Para 24]

■

The Notes forming part of the balance sheet of the Corporate Debtor as on 31.03.2017 provides separate categories for "Long Term Borrowings" under Note 3 and "Other Long Term Liabilities" under Note 4. The audited balance sheet of the Corporate Debtor also classifies the amount claimed by the Appellant to be a loan to figure under the head of 'Other Advances' which does not denote any financial liability or loan obligation. Moreover, there being no record of TDS deduction reflected in the financial records in respect of the Corporate Debtor, there is no provision of interest. It is also clear therefrom that Rs 30,95,000/-appearing against the name of the Appellant company appears in the head of 'Other Advances' rather than as an unsecured loan as claimed by the Appellant. However, the sum appears under the sub-category of "Other Advances" under the category of "Other Long Term Liabilities". It is clear from the above categorisation that the sum was provided as an advance and was treated as a liability and not a borrowing in the balance sheet and therefore does not partake the character of financial debt. Hence the transaction was not in the nature of a financial debt and could not have been claimed in Form-C. Thus, there is no infirmity in the finding recorded by the Adjudicating Authority that the claim filed by the Appellant does not find support in the books of the Corporate Debtor as a loan.[Para 34]

■

HEADNOTE: Section 5(8), read with sections 7 and 60, of the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016 - Corporate Insolvency Resolution Process - Financial debt - Petitioner-financial creditor issued a demand notice against respondent-corporate debtor alleging that he had provided an unsecured loan to respondent, which respondent failed to repay - In reply to said notice, respondent submitted that petitioner had transferred said amount with an intention to buy 25 per cent equity in corporate debtor's development project - On default in making re-payment, petitioner filed a petition under section 7 against respondent - Whether an investment could not be equated with a loan and a sum of money invested with an intention to acquire equity stake or some other interest in company could not be referred as a financial debt - Held, yes - Whether since petitioner had made payment with an intention to acquire 25 per cent equity in corporate debtor's project, said transaction could not be classified as financial debt and, therefore, petition filed under section 7 for initiation of CIRP against corporate debtor was to be dismissed - Held, yes [Paras 21, 28 and 29]IBC : Where petitioner-financial creditor had made payment with an intention to buy 25 per cent equity stake in corporate debtor's development project, money had been invested with an intention to acquire equity stake or some other interest and, therefore, same could not be classified as a financial debt under section 5(8)

Section 5(8), read with sections 7 and 60, of the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016 - Corporate Insolvency Resolution Process - Financial debt - Petitioner-financial creditor issued a demand notice against respondent-corporate debtor alleging that he had provided an unsecured loan to respondent, which respondent failed to repay - In reply to said notice, respondent submitted that petitioner had transferred said amount with an intention to buy 25 per cent equity in corporate debtor's development project - On default in making re-payment, petitioner filed a petition under section 7 against respondent - Whether an investment could not be equated with a loan and a sum of money invested with an intention to acquire equity stake or some other interest in company could not be referred as a financial debt - Held, yes - Whether since petitioner had made payment with an intention to acquire 25 per cent equity in corporate debtor's project, said transaction could not be classified as financial debt and, therefore, petition filed under section 7 for initiation of CIRP against corporate debtor was to be dismissed - Held, yes [Paras 21, 28 and 29]

FACT: The petitioner-financial creditor had provided an unsecured loan of Rs. 1.11 crores to the respondent-corporate debtor on 9-1-2007.

The petitioner had issued a demand notice dated 14-9-2017. In reply to said notice, the corporate debtor submitted that the payment of Rs. 1.11 crores was not towards 25 per cent equity interest but was rather an investment in a development project of a corporate debtor.

On default in making payment, the petitioner had filed an application under section 7 to initiate CIRP against the corporate debtor.

The respondent submitted that petitioner had advanced an unsecured loan to the respondent on 9-1-2007 however, petition filed by the appellant in 2020 i.e., after a lapse of 13 years further, petitioner through letter dated 14-9-2017 himself had claimed that the amount was paid for acquisition of 25 per cent equity interest in the development project of the corporate debtor.

HEADNOTE: Section 5(8), read with  section 7, of the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016 and regulation 8 of the IBBI (Insolvency Resolution Process for Corporate Persons) Regulations, 2016 - Corporate insolvency resolution process - Financial debt - Whether financial debt can be proved from other relevant documents and it is not mandatory as per regulation 8(2) that written financial contract can be only basis for proving financial debt - Held, yes - Appellant-financial creditor granted unsecured term loan to respondent-corporate debtor by way of RTGS and, it was agreed between parties that repayment of unsecured term loan would be made on demand - On default in making repayment, appellant filed an application under section 7 against corporate debtor - NCLT by impugned order held that financial creditor failed to show nature of transaction between parties and, therefore, application filed by financial creditor was dismissed - Whether since payment of interest had been shown from corporate debtor in Form 26AS and Form No. 26AS entries corroborated to claim of financial debt, said document was a piece of evidence to prove that it was a financial debt - Held, yes - Whether since NCLT itself had given finding that disbursement was with interest and repayment was on demand, two essential conditions of financial debt were present with regard to time value of money - Held, yes - Whether pre-condition for establishing financial debt was proved by appellant and, therefore, order passed by NCLT rejecting section 7 application holding that appellant failed to show nature of transaction was to be set aside - Held, yes [Paras 11, 21, 23, 26 and 29]IBC : Financial debt can be proved from other relevant documents and, it is not mandatory in terms of regulation 8(2) of IBBI (Insolvency Resolution Process for Corporate Persons) Regulations, 2016 that a written financial contract can be only basis for proving financial debt

FACT: The respondent-corporate debtor sought financial assistance from the appellant-corporate debtor.

The appellant granted an unsecured term loan of Rs. 75 lakhs to the corporate debtor and, by way of RTGS payment of Rs. 50 lakhs, Rs. 5 lakhs and Rs. 20 lakhs were disbursed and, it was agreed between the parties that the repayment of the unsecured term loan will be made on demand.

The corporate debtor deducted tax on the interest amount in the financial year 2017-18. A total amount of Rs. 52.250 thousand was incurred as interest on the principle amount and, the corporate debtor deducted the TDS of Rs. 5250 thousand on 31-3-2018 but, had not paid it to the financial creditor.

The appellant sent a letter to the corporate debtor for the repayment of unsecured loan along with interest within two months and, the board of directors of the appellant had passed resolution to file a case against the corporate debtor in the NCLT.

The application under section 7 was filed by the appellant before the NCLT.

The NCLT directed the appellant to demonstrate that Income Tax for the assessment year 2018-19 had been taken into account and, the TDS deducted was adjusted and credited.

HEADNOTE: Section 7 of the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016 - Corporate insolvency resolution process - Initiation by financial creditor - With a view to set up a plant, all shareholders of corporate debtor company including applicant had given interest free unsecured loan to be used as margin money to enabling company to get loan facility from bank - Applicant admitted that unsecured loan would be subordinate to claim made by bank and agreed not to seek recovery of his unsecured loan till liability of bank stood extinguished - Corporate debtor failed to repay - Thus, applicant initiated insolvency resolution process against company - However, corporate debtor submitted that amount being claimed was not a loan in terms of financial debt, nor was there any agreement to pay interest on such loan and that said loan amount was not repayable on demand as it was part of working capital for procuring financial assistance from bank - Further, principal money lender i.e. Bank had not made any claim - Whether, instant insolvency resolution process could not be admitted - Held, yes [Para 9]Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code: Where promoter of company had given interest free unsecured loan to company to be used as margin money enabling it to get loan facility from bank which became part of company's working capital and further promoter agreed not to seek recovery till liability of bank stood extinguished, on company's failure to repay, promoter could not initiated insolvency resolution process

FACT: The corporate debtor, with an intention of setting up a project for the manufacture of flexible packaging material under co-extension process at an estimated cost of Rs.30 crores, had approached Canara Bank for financial assistance. While the said bank sanctioned a term loan of Rs.14.2 crores for construction of the building and purchase of plant and machinery, the promoters of corporate debtor were required to meet the condition of investing the margin money. Accordingly, all six promoters, including the financial creditor, had given interest free unsecured loan to the corporate debtor.

The financial creditor alleged that the corporate debtor failed to take any steps to liquidate or reduce the liability qua him despite various reminders. Thus, he issued demand notice under section 8. In response to the said notice, corporate debtor submitted that the amount being claimed was not a loan in terms of financial debt, nor was there any agreement to pay interest thereon. It was not to be repaid on demand as it was the basis of procuring financial assistance from their bank for establishing the corporate debtor for its working capital. The financial creditor was an equity holder and with a view to set up a plant, all shareholders had paid various amounts as the margin money to enable them to get the loan facility from Canara bank.

HELD: All Promoters including the Financial Creditor herein, have confirmed the Subordination Agreement with their Bank, for and on behalf of the Corporate Debtor, and have undertaken that the unsecured creditors had extended or continued to extend interest free unsecured loan on the express understanding that all their claims against the respondent company would be subject to the claims of Canara Bank; that all the claims of the unsecured creditors against the respondent company would at all times be subordinate and be subject to any claims of Canara Bank; that unsecured creditors agree not to sue the respondent company for recovering any money tendered to the respondent company as unsecured loan until all the claims of Canara Bank get settled; that the unsecured creditors agree not to join in any bankruptcy or any assignment.

It is therefore submitted by the respondent that since the unsecured loans were interest-free, no interest was promised. Further, it is stated that the transaction inter se the parties does not fall within the definition of financial debt nor is the financial creditor a person to whom a financial debt is owed. [Para 8]

In view of the facts and circumstances of the case, the present claim does not fall within the definition of a financial debt nor is it an unsecured loan repayable on demand. There is not Demand Promissory Note executed, nor is there any agreement for payment of any interest. As submitted by the corporate debtor and not denied by the operational creditor, the amount given by him along with 6 others was for promoting and setting up a business. The terms for raising the bank loan necessitated investment of the margin money. This was done by all the promoters and is reflected as unsecured loans, subordinate to the claim of the bank. The bank agreement corroborating this is on record.
