Appellant submitted that funds given were for share allotment and unsecured loan, and due to non-allotment of shares, amount was repayable under section 42(6) with interest - It was noted that corporate debtor did not issue any private placement offer in pursuance of which appellant made any application of allotment of shares i.e., amount advanced by appellant could not be treated in response of private placement and, hence, said amount could not be related to section 42 - Whether advanced amount was not towards any private placement - Held, yes - Whether since. there was no consideration for time value of money - Held, yes - Whether since, said amount could not be treated as financial debt - Held, yes [Para 20]  Section 5(8), read with section 7, of the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016 - Corporate insolvency resolution process - Financial debt - Appellant transferred an amount of Rs. 2.60 crores to corporate debtor - Thereafter, appellant sent legal notices to corporate debtor asking for repayment including interest - Corporate debtor in a reply stated that appellant never gave any advance or loan to them - Thereafter, appellant filed a section 7 application claiming amount as financial debt but same was dismissed by NCLT - In view of an e-mail between parties, NCLT held that no amount was outstanding as said Rs. 2.60 crores was to be adjusted by sale of summit units - Appellant submitted that NCLT's findings that no debt was due was incorrect and without any basis - It was noted that corporate debtor did not support NCLT findings of amount being paid from sale of summit units and propounded a new theory about repayment - Whether since there was lack of record to indicate that Rs. 2.6 crores was paid to appellant, said findings of NCLT were to be removed - Held yes - Whether thus, said issue was to be dealt separately and decided in appropriate proceedings in accordance with law - Held, yes [Para 15]

FACT: The appellant transferred an amount of Rs. 2.6 crores to the corporate debtor. With regard to amount transferred by the appellant to the corporate debtor, different e-mails were exchanged between the parties for execution of Memorandum of Understanding, however, no concluded contract could be executed between the parties.

Exchange of e-mails took place between the parties from November, 2017 till 9-4-2018. Appellant sent a legal notice to the corporate debtor asking the corporate debtor to refund the amount of Rs. 2.6 crore with interest. After the aforesaid notice, reply was given to the noticee stating that the Appellant never gave any advance or loan to the company.

Thereafter, the appellant filed a petition under section 7. The appellant in section 7 Application claimed an amount of Rs. 2.6 crores as financial debt along with the interest of 24 per cent. The Adjudicating Authority by the impugned order dated 6-7-2022 dismissed section 7 application holding that the appellant failed to prove the financial debt. The Adjudicating Authority also observed that it cannot be said that a sum of Rs. 2.6 crores was still outstanding from the corporate debtor. Aggrieved by NCLT's order, appellant filed instant appeal.

Appellant submitted that an amount of Rs. 2.6 crores was given to the corporate debtor for allotment of share of Rs. 2 crore against the investment made by the appellant and rest Rs. 60 Lakhs was to be treated as unsecured loan. The corporate debtor failed to allot shares to the appellant and, thus, the amount was repayable as per section 42(6) of the Companies Act, 2013 along with the statutory interest at the rate of 12 per cent per annum. It was further submitted that the amount was not repaid till date. It was submitted that the Adjudicating Authority committed error in making observations in the judgment that no debt is due on the corporate debtor. The said observations were without any basis and incorrect.

HEADNOTE: Section 5(8), read with sections 5(7) and 7, of the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016 - Corporate insolvency resolution process - Financial debt - Appellant entered into Letter of Intent (LoI) for disbursing advance for marketing/financial requirements of development project to be undertaken by respondent corporate debtor - Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) was also enclosed containing terms and conditions and manner of advance to be made by appellant for development of property of corporate debtor - In pursuance of said letter, appellant had advanced different amounts to corporate debtor totalling Rs. 41.75 crores - Corporate debtor sent a letter denying signing and executing MoU - It was also alleged that appellant had failed to raise required funds as promised - Appellant filed a Commercial Suit for recovery wherein an interim injunction order was issued expressing opinion that there was a clear admission of liability - Thereafter, an application was filed under section 7 by appellant claiming as financial creditor for recovery of amount of Rs. 41.75 crores together with interest accrued thereon at rate of 18 per cent - Adjudicating Authority rejected application filed under section 7, holding that arrangement between parties was in nature of business sharing and there was no 'financial debt' - However, on consideration of documents and correspondences, including balance sheets, it was evident that amount paid to corporate debtor as advance for marketing/financial requirements of development project undertaken by corporate debtor was nothing but a financial debt within meaning of IBC - Whether therefore, Adjudicating Authority committed error in holding that appellant was not a financial creditor and rejecting application filed by appellant under section 7 - Held, yes [Paras 19, 21 and 25]IBC : Where on consideration of documents and correspondences, including balance sheets, it was evident that amount paid to corporate debtor as advance for marketing/financial requirements of development project undertaken by corporate debtor was nothing but a financial debt, Adjudicating Authority committed error in holding that appellant was not a 'financial creditor'  IBC : There being acknowledgement of debt in balance sheet, there shall be fresh period of limitation on each acknowledgement, thereby, attracting provisions of section 18 of limitation Act, 1963

Section 238A of the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016, read with section 18 of the Limitation Act, 1963 - Corporate insolvency resolution process - Limitation period - Whether where there was acknowledgement of debt in balance sheet, there shall be fresh period of limitation on each acknowledgement, thereby, attracting provisions of section 18 of limitation Act, 1963 - Held, yes - Whether however, balance sheet would have to be examined on a case-to-case basis to establish whether acknowledgement of liability in fact had been made - Held, yes [Paras 23 and 25]

FACT: The corporate debtor owned 8 acres of land situated at Mumbai. The appellant agreed to provide marketing and financial assistance for development of land of the corporate debtor. Accordingly, the corporate debtor issued a Letter of Intent for marketing/financial assistance and along with the letter, Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) was also enclosed containing the terms and conditions and the manner of advance to be made by the appellant for development of the property of the corporate debtor. In pursuance of the said letter, the appellant had advanced different amounts to the corporate debtor. In the balance sheet of the corporate debtor for the year 2014-15 as on 31-3-2015 for the years 2015-16, 2016-17, 2017-18 and 2018-19, the corporate debtor had acknowledged the receipt of financial assistance of Rs. 40.75 crores, which was duly reflected in the balance sheet. On 26-6-2015, the appellant addressed a letter to the corporate debtor stating that sum of Rs. 41.75 crores had been paid under the MoU.

The corporate debtor sent a letter dated 8-7-2015 denying signing and executing the MoU. It was also alleged that the appellant had failed to raise the required funds as promised. The appellant came to know that the respondent intended to sell the property in question for which offers were invited. The appellant filed a Commercial Suit for recovery of Rs. 41.75 crores wherein an injunction order was passed.

Thereafter, an application was filed under section 7 by the appellant claiming as financial creditor for recovery of amount of Rs. 41.75 crores together with interest accrued thereon at the rate of 18 per cent per annum. In the application the date of default was mentioned as 12-7-2017 which was date of filing of the suit for recovery in the High Court.

HEADNOTE: Section 5(8) of the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016 - Corporate insolvency resolution process - Financial debt - Corporate debtor had been incurring losses and defaulted in re-payment of loan - Financial creditor as a prospective investor came out to take charge and run corporate debtor company - As per terms of MoU, financial creditor brought in funds from time to time for corporate debtor's working capital, cleared its liabilities and paid other expenses - However, corporate debtor did not perform its obligation to proceed to negotiate terms of definitive agreement as envisaged for implementation of provisions of MoU - Therefore, money infused by financial creditor was demanded back which corporate debtor failed to pay - Whether since money brought by financial creditor into corporate debtor company was part of purchase agreement for purchase of corporate debtor in terms of MoU, which did not happen, amount raised fell within purview of financial debt - Held, yes [Para 19]IBC: Where money brought by financial creditor into corporate debtor company was part of Agreement for purchase of corporate debtor company, but said purchase did not happen, amount raised by financial creditor would fall within purview of financial debt  IBC: Where financial creditor made payment in 2014 and Whatsapp messages were exchanged till 2016, through which corporate debtor assured to make payment, CIRP application filed in 2018, being within limitation period of 3 years, was to be admitted

Section 238A, read with  section 7, of the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016 - Limitation period - Corporate debtor took plea that last payment was made by financial creditor in 2014 while instant CIRP application was filed in 2018 which was beyond three years period of limitation and, thus, same was time barred - However, Whatsapp massages were exchanged between parties till year 2016 by which corporate debtor assured to make payments - Whether Whatsapp messages were admissible under Evidence Act and, hence, instant CIRP application being within limitation period, was to be admitted - Held, yes [Paras 21 and 24]

FACT: The corporate debtor had been incurring losses and defaulted in payment of the loan to SBI bank and other creditors including vendors. At that juncture, the financial creditor as a prospective investor came out to take charge and run the company on behalf of the existing management. Accordingly, an MoU was entered into between the corporate debtor and the financial creditor.

The financial creditor submitted that the amounts were disbursed by the financial creditor on various dates. There were various e-mail requests by the corporate debtor to the financial creditor for transfer of funds towards salary of the employees and statutory expenses to be incurred.

The financial creditor further contended that in terms of the MoU, the corporate debtor did not proceed to negotiate the terms of definitive agreement, as was necessary to implement the provisions of the MoU. Therefore, the corporate debtor was liable to return the money provided by the financial creditor.

The corporate debtor, on the other hand, contended that there was no debt, and even assuming that there was debt, it was not financial debt as there was no time value for money, neither was there any default.

HELD: Whether unpaid amount claimed by financial creditor was financial debt

The corporate debtor has admitted that the amount paid by the applicant-financial creditor was towards an arrangement entered into between the parties as per the MoU. [Para 16]

On perusal of the pleadings and looking in to the terms and conditions contained in the MoU, it appears that the intentions of the parties were to give life to the corporate debtor which was facing a financial crisis. The financial creditor was under the obligation to arrange for working capital and took responsibilities of the day-to-day management of the corporate debtor. The applicant-financial creditor was also made responsible for payments of statutory dues and other administrative expenses including liabilities as on the 'effective date' given in the MoU. [Para 17]

In pursuant to the terms and conditions of the MoU, the applicant-financial creditor had started to make payments to the corporate debtor as reflects from the Certificate issued by the Bank of Maharahstra. The total amount now claimed is Rs. 2.14 crore along with further interest at the rate of 18 per cent per annum. [Para 18]

and filed an application under section 7 against the corporate debtor.

The NCLT, by an impugned order, admitted said application.

On appeal, the appellant suspended director of the corporate debtor submitted that there was no loan agreement entered into between the corporate debtor and there was no financial debt.

The appellant further submitted that the respondents were not registered under the Banking Regulation Act, 1949, and respondents had no license and, therefore, could not have extended any loan to the corporate debtor. HELD: For proving a debt to be financial debt, pre-condition which is required to be proved is that debt is disbursed against the consideration for the time value of money. The definition of financial debt is inclusive definition. [Para 8]

The word transaction has also been defined in section 3(33) which also contains an inclusive definition. [Para 9]

There is no loan agreement between the parties which fact is undisputed. Whether there are any other materials on record which may prove that there was any financial debt by the transaction between the parties is the question to be answered. [Para 10]

All the demand notices and the replies received from the corporate debtor are part of section 7 application. Demand notices were sent separately by all the respondents. The notice dated 11-2-2019 demanded principal amount as well as the amount of interest by the financial creditor. [Para 11]

A perusal of the demand notice indicates that in addition to repayment of principal debt and interest lacs has been claimed. The notices dated 11-2-2019 by all the respondents were replied by the corporate debtor in its reply dated 21-2-2019. [Para 12]

From the reply given by the corporate debtor, the conclusions are inescapable, firstly, the corporate debtor admitted grant of loan. The plea taken in the reply was that loan was granted for a tenure of 5 years. The second conclusion which may be drawn from the reply is that the claim of interest which was claimed by the demand notice was not refuted. The corporate debtor did not take any plea that no interest is payable. [Para 13]

In section 7 application, the financial creditors have also brought on record Form 16A for the financial year ending 31-3-2018 which Form 16A indicates that TDS was deducted by the corporate debtor and deposited under section 194A of Income-tax Act, 1961. [Para 14]

It is true that deduction of TDS and deposit by the corporate debtor does not itself prove that there is any financial debt but deduction of TDS and deposit in Form 16A under section 194A of Income-tax Act clearly proves that the deduction which was deposited was TDS relating to 'Interest other than interest on securities'. Form 16A which was filed by the financial creditor along with section 7 application at least support the case of the financial creditors that loan which was granted to the corporate debtor was with interest. [Para 15]

When demand notice was issued demanding both principal and interest, the corporate debtor never at the relevant time refuted that no interest is payable or there was no interest with the loan. [Para 16]

There can be no dispute to the proposition that on the basis of deduction of TDS it cannot be concluded that transaction in question is a financial debt. [Para 18]

Form 1 under Rule, 2016 contains the details which are required to be submitted in an application by the financial creditors. Part-V of the Form 1. [Para 19]

Part-V refers to list of other documents to prove the existence of financial debt. The Rules thus clearly contemplates that financial debt can be proved on 'Other Documents' also. [Para 20]

Instant Tribunal in Pawan Kumar v. Utsav Securities (P.) Ltd. [2021] 131 taxmann.com 211/168 SCL 692 has held in that financial creditor has not furnished any document to show that the transaction is a loan transaction. Instant is not a case where no documents have been submitted by the financial creditor to prove the transaction as a financial transaction. The documents which were filed, included the demand notice dated 11-2-2019. Reply notice dated 21-2-2019 (containing the admission of loan by the corporate debtor), Form 16A as well as balance sheets were filed. [Para 21]

Instant Tribunal in the case of Arrow Engineering Ltd. v. Golden Tobacco Ltd. [2022] 134 taxmann.com 272, referring to documents and correspondences between the parties concluded that financial debt was there despite there being no MoU formerly executed between the parties containing the terms and conditions of transaction. Further when one looks into the definition of transaction as contained in section 3(33), the definition is an inclusive definition and the provision does not lead to the conclusion that unless there is written transaction between the parties incorporating the terms and conditions of the loan, no transaction can come within the meaning of section 5(8). Financial debt can be proved from other documents as contemplated in Column 8 of Part-V of Form 1 of Insolvency and Bankruptcy (Application to Adjudicating Authority) Rules, 2016. [Para 23]

HEADNOTE: Section 5(8), read with section 7, of the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016 - Corporate insolvency resolution process - Financial debt - Applicant advanced Rs. 2.5 crores to respondent under a draft MoU for development of a project - An amount of Rs. 1.5 crore was admittedly returned - MoUs proposed between applicant and R1 were only draft documents and there was no document or agreement which showed terms on which money was given, nor did it specifically showed whether any interest or consideration against time value for money was payable - Further, there was no repayment schedule - Whether advance paid by applicant to R1 would have no commercial effect of borrowing and same was not financial debt - Held, yes - Whether, thus, CIRP petition was to be dismissed - Held, yes [Para 7]IBC: Where advance was paid and there was no document or agreement which showed terms of payment of any interest or consideration against time value for money, same was not a financial debt

FACT: The applicant stated that:—

-

Edge Dwarika JV (R4) was a joint venture formed by R1, R2 and R3. R1, on behalf of the joint venture consortium, potrayed to the applicant that they had exclusive rights of development and sale of approximately 39371.25 sq. mtr. of land.

-

The respondents approached the applicant to avail assistance in developing the project. Through a proposed MoU with DIPL, a group company of applicant, R1 proposed to give returns in form of 50 per cent of the share of 63 per cent of the total developed and constructed area on the land to the applicant and/or DIPL, including profit and benefits therein, in lieu of investment and assistance in development and construction of the said project.

-

Before MoU was finalized, R1 requested the applicant to pay a part of the requested amount towards the project as an urgent requirement with promise of substantial returns on the same. The applicant paid Rs. 2.5 crores into the project of the respondents.

-

Later on an amount of Rs. 1.5 crore was returned by R1 to the applicant. The respondents further informed the applicant that due to paucity of funds for initiation of construction and stamp duty for registration of the consortium MoU, the respondents had decided to discontinue with the original project and they would like to modify same to development of plots. The respondents went ahead with the revised plan. A legal notice was sent to the respondents calling upon them to repay the due amount of Rs. 1 crore along with interest.

-

A reply to the legal notice was sent by the respondents wherein they had categorically admitted the receipt of Rs. 1 crore from the applicant.

The R1 on the other hand contended that:—

-

As per the MoU, DIPL had to make payment of a sum of Rs. 9 crores which was to be upfront, non-refundable and non-adjustable amount. It was also agreed that in the event the applicant failed to make payment of the entire sum, then the applicant would not get participation in the project in any manner. DIPL made payment of only an amount of Rs. 5.5 crores, and complete payment was never made.

-

As far as balance sheet were concerned, the reflection as unsecured loan was only because of accounting practice, and the same did not mean that payment was actually a loan. The applicant itself had written to the tax authorities stating that the payment made to the R1 was not a loan. The loan taken were shown as Nil under Term Loans in the balance sheet filed by the applicant in its income tax return.

On the applicant's CIRP application under section 7:

HELD: The MoUs proposed between the applicant and R1, attached with the application, are only draft documents which cannot serve any purpose and cannot be pressed to support the contention of either side. It is also held that the explanation given by the R2 and R3 is persuasive because there is no privity between the applicant and R2, R3 and even R4. The money was paid to R1 only. R2, R3 and R4 cannot be pleaded as corporate debtors to the instant application. [Para 5]

HEADNOTE: Section 5(8), read with section 5(7), of the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016 - Corporate insolvency resolution process - Financial debt - Appellant filed its claim as a financial creditor to Resolution Professional (RP) for an amount advanced to corporate debtor as an earnest money for purpose of purchasing surplus land of corporate debtor - RP vide e-mail replied that funds remitted to corporate debtor were interest free advance and same was to be adjusted against sale consideration for proposed sale of land, which did not fall under category of 'financial debt' - Appellant filed application before NCLT seeking direction to RP to adjudicate its claim, revise list of CoC members, and admit him as CoC member - NCLT dismissed said application on ground that there was no contract between parties for sale of any land and, therefore, earnest money advanced by appellant could not be treated as a 'financial debt' - On appeal, appellant submitted that in annual reports of corporate debtor for financial years 2018-19 and 2019-20 earnest money had been classified as a 'financial debt' and, therefore, appellant's claim deserved to be admitted as a financial debt - It was noted that there was no agreement between parties and disbursement made by appellant to corporate debtor was only a payment, which was to be adjusted in sale of land - Whether since disbursement was not in consideration for time value of money, essential condition for accepting a debt to be financial debt was absent - Held, yes - Whether acknowledging liability of earnest money in annual return as financial debt was not akin to admitting same as a financial debt - Held, yes [Paras 18, 19 and 20]IBC : Where appellant had disbursed money to corporate debtor only as payment which was to be adjusted in sale of land and same was not in consideration for time value of money, sum disbursed was not financial debt under section 5(8)  IBC : Where CoC in its commercial decision decided not to allocate any amount to other creditors and appellant who was classified as other creditor was not be able to prove any violation of provisions of IBC, resolution plan approved by NCLT did not require any interference

FACT: An application under section 9 filed against the corporate debtor was admitted by the NCLT, initiated CIRP against the corporate debtor.

On 22-5-2019, the appellant filed its claim other than as a financial creditor and operational creditor, and thereafter filed its claim as a financial creditor.

The erstwhile RP sent an e-mail stating that the appellant had remitted funds to corporate debtor as an interest-free advance to be adjusted against sale consideration for the proposed sale of land, which shall not fall under 'financial debt'.

The appellant filed an application before NCLT seeking direction to RP to adjudicate the claim of the appellant and revise the list of the CoC to admit him as a member of the CoC.

The NCLT dismissed said application on ground that there was no contract between the parties for sale of any land, hence the earnest money advanced by appellant could not be treated as a financial debt.

Aggrieved by the NCLT order, the appellant filed instant appeal on ground that the NCLT committed error in passing an order rejecting the claim of the appellant as a financial creditor.

The appellant submitted that he paid sum of Rs. 7 crores as earnest money to the corporate debtor with regard to which receipt was issued by the corporate debtor and payment had not been disputed by the corporate debtor and the RP had also admitted the payment of earnest money by the appellant as another creditor but wrongly classified the appellant as other creditor.

The appellant also referred to the annual reports for the financial years 2018-19 and 2019-20, wherein earnest money had been classified as a 'financial debt' and therefore the appellant's claim deserve to be admitted as a financial debt.

HELD: The appellant has claimed the payment of amount to corporate debtor as an earnest money for purpose of purchase of surplus land belonging to the mills of the corporate debtor. The payment of earnest money began after letter dated 14-9-2018 was sent by the appellant to the corporate debtor. [Para 10]

The earnest money was paid by the appellant after submitting a proposal by the appellant himself without their being any acceptance. There is neither any agreement between the parties nor any agreement has been brought on record. It is true that contract between the parties can be oral as well as in writing however, there is no foundation in the application filed by the appellant or materials brought by him to indicate that there was even an oral agreement with the corporate debtor for sale of the land to the appellant. The Adjudicating Authority in the impugned order has discussed the entire sequence of the events and materials on record. The Adjudicating Authority considered the claim of the appellant based on clause (f) of section 5(8). [Para 11]

HEADNOTE: Section 5(8), read with sections 3(12) and 5(7), of the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016 - Corporate insolvency resolution process - Financial debt - Appellant had given unsecured loan facility to respondent-corporate debtor - Corporate debtor had been paying interest on unsecured loan and also had been deducting and depositing Tax Deducted at Source (TDS) on interest paid to appellant - Corporate debtor defaulted in payment of unsecured loan - Appellant issued demand notice to corporate debtor seeking repayment of unpaid financial debt - Appellant filed application under section 7 for initiation of CIRP against corporate debtor - NCLT by impugned order rejected said application holding that appellant had failed to establish that unsecured loan he had granted fell within scope of financial debt in absence of any loan agreement setting out terms and conditions of agreement - Whether there were no documents/records to prove that appellant was financial creditor - Held, yes - Whether audited balance sheet also did not prove existence of financial debt and default as defined under section 3(12) - Held, yes - Whether since there was no financial debt and default as proved by appellant, NCLT had rightly rejected application filed by appellant under section 7 - Held, yes [Paras 16 and 17]IBC : Where appellant - financial creditor had given unsecured loan to corporate debtor but failed to prove existence of financial debt and default, NCLT had rightly rejected application filed by appellant under section 7 for initiation of CIRP against corporate debtor

FACT: The appellant had given unsecured loan facility to the respondent-corporate debtor.

The corporate debtor had been paying interest on unsecured loan till 30-9-2018 and also had been deducting and depositing Tax Deducted on Source (TDS) on the interest paid to the appellant. Thereafter, 30-9-2018 neither principle amount nor any interest amount was paid by the corporate debtor to the appellant.

The appellant issued a demand notice to the corporate debtor seeking repayment of the unpaid financial debt by the corporate debtor.

Thereafter, the appellant had filed an application under section 7 for initiation of CIRP against corporate debtor.

NCLT by impugned order rejected said application holding that appellant had failed to establish that the unsecured loan he had granted fell within the scope of financial debt in absence of any loan agreement setting out terms and condition of agreement.

On appeal :

HELD: The appellant has given unsecured loan facility to the Respondent from time-to-time and the Respondent has been repaying part of the unsecured loan to the Appellant. On 31-3-2018, the amount of Rs. 1,95,00,000/- was outstanding as unsecured loan of the Appellant from the Respondent.

The respondent has been paying interest on the unsecured loan till 30-9-2018 and has also been deducting and depositing TDS on the interest paid to the Appellant and the same can be seen from the TDS certificate as well as the Ledger Accounts for the Financial Years 1-4-2014 to 31-3-2018 of the Respondent.

The appellant has concealed the facts namely (a) Civil Suit wherein the Appellant himself has inter alia claimed 40 per cent shares in the Respondent Company and IA interlocutory application filed by the Appellant before the NCLT. (b) Personal Identification. (c) Being Promoter, Director and Guarantor to the Credit Facilities. (d) Amount deposited towards promoter's contribution in terms of a stipulation of HDFC Bank. (e) Availing of Loan from the Respondent Company. (f) Ledger accounts from 1-4-2010 onwards. (g) Bank Account Statements proving the amount drawn by the Company. (h) Amount deposited from 10-1-2007 to 7-9-2016. (i) Working for computation of amount and days of default in tabular form. (j) Evidence of disbursement of loan. (k) Bank Statement of IDBI Bank Account of the Appellant. (l) Dates of disbursements. (m) Conversion of Unsecured loan into Equity as and when required to maintain a positive tangible net worth.

HEADNOTE: Section 5(8), read with section 238A, of the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016 - Corporate insolvency resolution process - Financial debt - Corporate debtor entered into a Development Agreement with financial creditor, in which financial creditor was required to provide a refundable Security Deposit of Rs. 12 crores, with an option to add Rs. 3 crores more - In said agreement, additional amount (up to Rs. 3.5 crores) would bear 18 percent interest, payable quarterly - However, due to non-development, financial creditor filed a section 7 application claiming financial debt and highlighted corporate debtor's default in paying interest on Rs. 3.5 crores - Corporate debtor stated that no financial debt existed and that financial creditor was a related party holding 40 per cent equity - However, NCLT admitted said application - Aggrieved by NCLT's order, appellant-suspended director of corporate debtor filed instant appeal - It was noted that letter issued by corporate debtor to financial creditor clearly indicated that advance made over and above security deposit carried interest at a rate of 18 per cent per annum, which was compoundable and payable quarterly - Whether since payment of 18 per cent interest compoundable and payable quarterly clearly indicated time value of money, said transaction would fall within ambit of financial debt under section 5(8) - Held, yes - Whether corporate debtor had acknowledged in its financial statements, amount of interest as a long-term borrowing and had referred to same as loan from financial creditor and, thus, financial creditor had been able to prove debt and default - Held, yes - Whether therefore, NCLT did not commit any error in admitting section 7 application - Held, yes [Paras 28, 29 and 30]IBC : Where letter issued by corporate debtor to a financial creditor clearly showed that an advance made beyond a security deposit by financial creditor carried interest, which was compoundable and payable quarterly and, corporate debtor had acknowledged this interest in its financial statements as a long-term borrowing, referring to it as a loan, financial creditor had proved debt and default and, therefore, NCLT did not commit any error in admitting section 7 application  IBC : Where corporate debtor had acknowledged interest in books of account on 1-4-2013 and thereafter acknowledged that interest was due in financial statements for financial years 2013 to 2018 application filed under section 7 against corporate debtor on 30-9-2019 was within limitation period

Section 238A of the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016 - Limitation period - Whether where corporate debtor had acknowledged, interest in books of account on 1-4-2013 and thereafter acknowledged that interest was due in financial statements for financial years 2013 to 2018, application filed on 30-9-2019 was within limitation period - Held, yes [Para 28]

HEADNOTE: Section 5(8), read with section 7, of the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016 - Corporate insolvency resolution process - Financial debt - Applicant-financial creditor was in management of corporate debtor which had taken a loan from SBI - Later, management of corporate debtor was transferred to 'B' - Applicant filed application under section 7 against corporate debtor alleging that corporate debtor defaulted in repaying unsecured loan taken from applicant - Whether since terms and conditions of loan agreement with SBI of which applicant was party provided that unsecured loan made available by applicant to corporate debtor did not become due for payment till bank loan was fully liquidated i.e., on 16-2-2018, application filed on 3-7-2015 claiming that corporate debtor owed an amount to applicant was pre-matured and not maintainable - Held, yes - Whether since applicant had failed to bring on record any evidence to suggest that he disbursed money against consideration for time value of money and there was no information about rate of interest on principal amount, loan did not satisfy requirement of financial debt as contemplated under section 5(8) - Held, yes - Whether thus, applicant failed to show that corporate debtor owed an amount and there was a default in payment of such debt and, therefore, application under section 7 was to be dismissed - Held, yes [Paras 39, 40, 43, 44, 57 and 58]IB Code: Where applicant had failed to bring on record any evidence to suggest that he disbursed money against consideration for time value of money and there was no information about rate of interest on principal amount, loan did not satisfy requirement of financial debt as contemplated under section 5(8)

FACT: The application under section 7 had been preferred by financial creditor (FC) seeking initiation of Corporate Insolvency Resolution Process ('CIRP') against corporate debtor (CD).

In the application, it had been alleged that the CD had obtained an unsecured loan during the period between 11-11-2011 and 18-10-2014. However, the CD did not refund the loan nor did it pay the interest thereon to the FC as agreed upon for which an amount as on 3-7-2015, became due to the FC from the side of the CD.

The CD, on being served with notice, filed affidavit-in-opposition opposing the prayer of the FC alleging that the CD was not liable to pay any debt to the FC. In that connection, it had been alleged that a project, under the name and style of CD was established with much fanfare in 2008. In course of time, in 2010, CD obtained a term loan from State Bank of India (SBI). But such a project soon ran into rough weather and it was basically for inept handling of the company by the persons who were then in the management of the company and they were none other than applicant 'R', his son 'K' and his daughter-in-law 'J' who together held more than 94 per cent shareholdings in and of the CD.

Unfortunately, despite the flow of such additional fund to the company, it could do no better than before for which the management in the company once again approached 'B' (who was presently holding the post of MD of the CD) and requested him to bailout the company from its doldrums. After due consideration of the proposal from the side of the then management of the company, 'B' agreed to accept such proposal on certain terms and conditions which were, however, accepted by the then management of the company, vide agreement dated 15-12-2014.

Mere grant of loan and admission of taking loan will ipso facto not treat the applicant as 'financial creditor' within the meaning of section 5(8). [Para 15]

Precisely 'financial debt' is a debt along with interest, if any, which is disbursed against consideration for time value of money. [Para 16] In the instant case at Part-IV of the application pertaining to 'particulars of financial debt', applicant has claimed that the total amount in default is Rs. 1,77,71,974/- as on 31-12-2017, which includes Rs.80,00,000 towards Principal Loan and Rs. 97,71,974/- as interest at the rate of 18 per cent up to 31-12-2017. There is, thus, no dispute that Rs. 97,71,974/-, in addition to principal amount, has been claimed as interest at the rate of 18 per cent per annum. In the instant case interest has been claimed as a component of the claimed 'financial debt'. [Para 17]

However admittedly applicant has not produced any loan agreement nor there are details and particulars of any applicable interest mutually agreed between the parties. Respondent has alleged that interest has been wrongly claimed being never agreed to. There is nothing on record to show that the respondent company ever agreed to pay any such interest at any point of time. [Para 18]

It has, thus, been made clear that in the absence of evidence that the amount was disbursed for time value of money, applicant does not come within the meaning of 'financial creditor'. [Para 20]

It is well settled that the onus lies on the applicant to establish that the loan was given against the consideration for time value of money. Onus to prove also lies on the applicant to establish that the debt claimed in the application comes within the purview of 'financial debt' and that the applicant is a 'financial creditor' in respect of the instant claim in question. When the respondent debtor disputes that there is no question of payment of interest at any point of time on the debt in question; it becomes more onerous on the part of the applicant to prove that the amount was disbursed against the consideration for time value of money. Admittedly, no document in respect of the loan and to support the pleading that interest is payable on the loan has been furnished by the applicant. Applicant has miserably failed to substantiate with supporting documentary evidence that interest, as claimed at Part-IV of the application, is payable as per the agreed loan covenants. [Para 21]

Applicant has also taken a stand that the admitted high salary and perks given to his son is the consideration of time value of money against his loan. In support of such contention neither the applicant has made his son a party nor has placed any document to show that the loan was disbursed only to get such benefit. Without affording a minimal opportunity of hearing and at the back of applicant's son, no adverse finding on such person's efficiency could be passed. The son of the petitioner may be competent enough to receive the remuneration in question. At his back and in the absence of relevant documents, it cannot be said with certainty that he got the benefits only because of the loan. Mere pleading of the applicants in the absence supporting documentary evidence will not suffice to prove that the disbursements were made for such benefit. Besides this appears to be an afterthought. Applicant has not taken such stand in the original application and on the contrary has claimed interest as a component of financial debt. [Para 22]

It is pertinent to note that the balance sheets of the respondent company reveal that as on 31-3-2014 loan taken from the applicant stood at Rs. 80,00,000/-. However, subsequent balance sheets of the respondent company ending on 31-3-2015, 31-3-2016 and 31-3-2017 respectively show that the said loan has reduced to an amount of Rs. 65,00,000/-. It has not been made clear as to how the loan was shown as reduced to Rs. 65,00,000/-. Respondent in its reply has contended that the business of the group companies has gone down on account of faults of the applicant and his son. Respondent has also contended that there has been adjustment of value of shares allotted and the benefits enjoyed by the applicant's family in the form of drawing high salary, perks etc. Be that as it may it is seen from the various balance sheets of the respondent company that with the passage of time there has been no accumulation of interest in the loan amount. Any loan having been taken without interest or time value of money, cannot be termed to be a 'financial debt'. [Para 23]

It is reiterated that in the instant case neither any loan agreement has been placed on record nor there is any supporting evidence/document to establish applicable rate of interest to be paid on the said loan. The applicant has failed to prove that the loan was disbursed against consideration for time value of money, particularly when respondent company has affirmed that no interest has been paid nor payable at any point of time. [Para 25]

[Para 18] The Adjudicating Authority is obliged to investigate the nature of the transaction and should be very cautious in admitting the Application in order to prevent taking undue benefit of provisions of IBC to detriment of the rights of legitimate creditors as well as to protect the corporate debtor from being dragged into CIRP with mala fide. Section 65 provides that if any person initiates the Insolvency Resolution Process or liquidation proceedings fraudulently or with malicious intent for any purpose other than for resolution of Insolvency or Liquidation, the Adjudicating Authority may impose upon such person a penalty. Section 65 provides that where any person furnishes any information under section 7, which is false in material particulars, knowing it to be false or omits any material facts, knowing it to be material such person shall be punished with fine. Whether the transaction in question is Financial Debt and the corporate debtor has committed default?

As per the definition given in section 5(8), 'financial debt' means a debt along with interest, if any, which is disbursed against the consideration for the time value of money. The essential requirement is of disbursement and consideration for time value of money. [Para 21]

The Financial Creditor is not doing financial business but is engaged in manufacture of rice. On the other hand, the corporate debtor Company incorporated on 11-9-2018 having authorized and paid share capital of Rs.7 crores 30 lakhs, as per the MCA data filed by the financial creditor showed that the Bank of Baroda has sanctioned cash credit limit to the tune of Rs. 24 crores in the year October, 2018. According to the financial creditor, they have granted a loan of Rs. 10 lacs on 20-4-2019. It cannot be said that the corporate debtor Company having paid up share capital of Rs.7 crores 30 lacs and cash credit limit to the tune of Rs. 24 crores has to take a loan for Rs. 10 lacs from the financial creditor and that the corporate debtor is not able to make repayment of Rs. 10 lacs and has no objection if the Application under section 7 is allowed and the CIRP initiated against the corporate debtor Company. [Para 24]

Apart from this significant feature of the transaction, the other circumstances considered are as under :

'(a)

The transaction in question has no backing of the board resolution of the corporate debtor company.

(b)

There is no record to show that on date of disbursement i.e., 20-4-2019 the corporate debtor was in need of Rs. 10 lacs (As Loan) particularly when corporate debtor was having cash credit limit of Rs. 24 crores by Bank of Baroda.

(c)

There is no agreement of loan and interest.

(d)

No document is to stipulate the period of repayment.

(e)

The essential ingredients for financial debt disbursement and consideration for the time value of money are missing. On the other hand, the entries of ledger for the financial years 2018-19, 2019-20 reflect the inflow and outflow of funds which are in the nature of running account, indicating that the debit and credit balances lack of any commercial effect of borrowing which is an essential element in terms of section 5(8)(f) of the IBC. Adjudicating Authority on the basis of Financial Statement of the impugned order observed that "First transaction has been squared up on the same date i.e., 16-4-2018. Next transaction is squared up in two days. 3rd transaction is squared up on the same date. Thereafter two transactions for Rs. 20 lakhs and 10 lakhs respectively on 26-7-2018 and 10-8-2018 against which Rs. 10 lakhs have been repaid on 17-10-2018 and 20-12-2018. After sanctioned and disbursement of cash credit limit by Bank of Baroda on 12-10-2018. Thereafter a sum of Rs. 25 lakhs was given on 5-2-2019 which has been repaid on 15-2-2019, 18-2-2019 and 27-2-2019. Thus, Rs. 10 lakhs have remained outstanding as on 31-3-2019 in Financial Year 2019-20. A sum of Rs. 25 lakhs has been given on 17-4-2019 which has been repaid in two instalments within three days". These facts are undisputed. [Para 25]

The agreement dated 21-10-2017 which was entered between the directors of the financial creditor and the directors of the corporate debtor noted that the appellant is committed to return the principal amount of USD 1.5 million and Rs. 3.5 crores. [Para 12]

The agreement also mentions giving an IDBI cheque of Rs. 3.5 crores to the financial creditor which raise clear presumption of owing debt by the corporate debtor to the financial creditor. The agreement between the parties makes it clear that the corporate debtor has acknowledged the liability to refund aforesaid amount of Rs. 3.5 crores. The acknowledgement to refund the amount of Rs. 3.5 crores also proves that amount of Rs. 3.5 crores was a financial debt. [Para 13]

It was further noted that the e-mail dated 12-3-2018 which has been issued by the appellant - director of the corporate debtor to director of the financial creditor acknowledge payment of USD 1.5 million as well as Rs. 3.5 crores (0.5 million USD). [Para 14]

Further an e-mail dated 28-5-2018 written by the director of the corporate debtor was also part of section 7 application and was also relied by the Adjudicating Authority. [Para 15]

The e-mail also mentions that amount of Rs. 3.5 crores was a 'short term loan' given to corporate debtor by the financial creditor. In the e-mail director also conceded that maximum interest which can be considered is only 12 per cent. [Para 16]

The NCLT rightly refused to admit the application under section 7 of the IBC, holding the same to be barred by limitation. The Appellate Tribunal has erred in law in reversing the judgment and order of the earlier Adjudicating Authority. The Adjudicating Authority rightly rejected the application as barred by limitation. The Appellate Authority patently erred in law in reversing the decision of the adjudicating authority and admitting the application. [Para 38] As recorded in the said order dated 19-12-2018 passed by the NCLT Chennai, the respondent Nos. 1 and 2 jointly addressed the letter dated 11-1-2011 to the Income-tax department confirming that the respondent No. 1 had requested the appellant-company to transfer a sum of Rs. 90 lakhs to his wife, the respondent No. 2 for allotment of shares in the appellant company and further acknowledged that the amount outstanding from the erstwhile firm 'R' to the respondent was Rs. 1.40 crore as on 31-3-2004. [Para 39]

There are, as observed above cogent records including letters signed by the respondent Nos. 1 and 2 which evince that on 6-10-2007, respondent No. 2 resigned from the Board of the appellant-company and at that time the respondent no. 2 requested the appellant-company to treat the share application money of Rs. 90 lakhs as share application money of a promoter MK and to issue shares for aforesaid value to said promoter MK. The amount was to be treated as a personal loan from the respondent No. 2 to said promoter and a personal loan to a promoter or a Director of a company cannot trigger the Corporate Resolution Process under the IBC. Disputes as to whether the signatures of the respondents are forged or whether records have been fabricated can be adjudicated upon evidence including forensic evidence in a regular suit and not in proceedings under section 7. [Para 40]

The definition of 'financial debt' in section 5(8) makes it clear that 'financial debt' means a debt along with interest, if any, disbursed against the consideration from time value of money and would include money raised or borrowed against the payment of interest; amount raised by acceptance under any acceptance credit facility or its de-materialised equivalent; amount raised pursuant to any note purchase facility or the issue of bonds, notes, debentures, loan stock or any similar instrument; the amount of any liability in respect of any lease or hire purchase contract which is deemed as a finance or capital lease under the Indian Accounting Standards or such other accounting standards as may be prescribed; receivables sold or discounted other than any receivables sold on non-recourse basis or any amount raised under any other transaction, including any forward sale or purchase agreement, having the commercial effect of a borrowing. Explanation to section 5(8) which relates to real estate projects is of no relevance in the facts and circumstances of this case. The payment received for shares, duly issued to a third party at the request of the payee, as evident from official records, cannot be a debt, not to speak of financial debt. Shares of a company are transferable subject to restrictions, if any, in its Articles of Association and attract dividend when the company makes profits. [Para 43]

The appeal is to be allowed. The impugned judgment and order of the Appellate Tribunal is to be set aside and the order of the Adjudicating Authority dismissing the application, is to be restored. [Para 44]

■ From the audited financial statement for financial year 2016-17 of the corporate debtor, it is found that the notes forming part of the balance sheet of the corporate debtor as on 31-3-2017 provides separate categories for ''long-term borrowings'' under note 3 and ''other long-term liabilities'' under note 4. It is also clear therefrom that Rs 5.10 lakhs appearing against the name of SM appears in the head of ''other advances'' rather than as an unsecured loan as claimed by the appellant. Had the amount of Rs 5.10 lakhs appeared under the heading of ''long-term borrowings'', there would have been no doubt that the same was a transaction in the nature of financial debt. However, it is found that the sum appears under the sub-category of ''other advances'' under the category of ''other long-term liabilities''. It is clear from the above categorisation that the sum was provided as an advance and was treated as a liability and not a borrowing in the balance sheet and therefore does not partake the character of financial debt. Even the subsequent financial records do not show otherwise. Therefore, the Adjudicating Authority has not committed any infirmity in noting that the documents relied upon by the appellant to support their claim is ''deficient''. [Para 18]

■

More significantly, it is the contention of the respondents that the terms of the loan agreement contained gaping holes. There was no in-built clause therein on how default was to be calculated. Apart from the loan agreement being bereft of a repayment schedule, the loan agreement did not define any event of default prior to the winding up of the corporate debtor or it's becoming bankrupt in terms of IBC. It was equally unusual that for a loan given way back in 2007, there was no demand of repayment made by the appellant for 15 long years until the corporate debtor got admitted into CIRP. There is no evidence either of any communication sent to the corporate debtor seeking payment of interest. The records of the corporate debtor also do not reflect any provision for interest on the said loan having been credited to the account of the corporate debtor. Nor is there any proof for accrual of interest in any financial year or any evidence of TDS deduction such as Form 26AS. [Para 19]

■

It would be pertinent to outline the rival contention of the appellant that they cannot be denied the right to file their legitimate claim merely because no interest amount was reflected in the balance sheet of the corporate debtor. It was argued that if the corporate debtor did not deduct interest or make provision for interest payments in the balance sheet, the appellant cannot be held responsible for this lapse and put to prejudice. Since the appellant had already resigned from the management of the corporate debtor in 2012 and was not in control of the corporate debtor, they were not responsible in any manner for the corporate debtor not having levied the interest on the outstanding principal amount. Simply because interest was not paid by the corporate debtor, the sum advanced by the appellant cannot be denied the treatment of a financial debt. [Para 20]

■

The appellant was admittedly a shareholder of the corporate debtor when the loan agreement was signed in 2007 and later became one of the directors of the corporate debtor from 2009 to 2012. Thus, it is undisputable that the appellant was very much in control of the management of the corporate debtor until 2012. It is also noticed that either the appellant or his brother who was a signatory of the loan agreement remained at the helm of affairs of the corporate debtor all along. That being the case, the appellant cannot absolve itself of the responsibility of explaining as to why the financial statement of the corporate debtor did not reflect levy of interest till financial year 2011-12 even when they were in control of the corporate debtor. Having said that, the finding of the Adjudicating Authority that the amount of interest at the rate of 24 per cent claimed by the appellant being exorbitant, it was sufficient ground for rejection of the claim of the appellant could not be subscribed to. The Adjudicating Authority, at best, had a limited jurisdiction to examine the decision of the RP on the rejection on the claim and not on the reasonability of computation of the claim or quantum of the debt. Meaning thereby, there was no Financial Debt defined under section 5(8). Further the audited Balance Sheets also do not prove the existence of financial debt and default defined under section 3(12). These Balance Sheets do not prove that the whole loan or its instalment when became due and payable and the same is/are not repaid.

The Supreme Court had held in the matter of Innoventive Industries Ltd. v. ICICI Bank Ltd. [2017] 84 taxmann.com 320/143 SCL 625 of the Judgment that a 'Debt may not be due if it is not payable in law or in fact' and also held that the speed within which the 'adjudicating authority is to ascertain the existence of a default from the records of the information utility or on the basis of evidence furnished by the financial creditor, is important'. [Para 16]

Taking all the facts and circumstances of the case, it is held that there is no 'debt' and 'default' proved by the Appellant in the instant Appeal. Thus, there is no illegality committed by the Adjudicating Authority while passing the impugned order, therefore, the impugned order need not be interferred. The impugned order dated 12-1-2021 passed by the Adjudicating Authority is affirmed. There is no merit in the Appeal. The Appeal is dismissed. [Para 17]

The NCLT directed the appellant to demonstrate that Income Tax for the assessment year 2018-19 had been taken into account and, the TDS deducted was adjusted and credited. The appellant filed various documents including the Auditor's Report as well as copy of section 194A of the Income-tax Act.

The appellant filed instant appeal on ground that the NCLT committed error in holding that the appellant had not been able to prove financial debt, however, the documents brought on the record by the appellant including the balance sheets and bank transactions clearly proved the financial debt and, thus, NCLT committed an error in rejecting the application.

HELD: Whether written financial contract be the only material to prove the financial debt

The submission of the respondent that the written financial contract is necessary for proving debt. A financial contract supported by financial statements as evidence of the debt is one of the documents contemplated in regulation 8(2) of the IBBI (Insolvency Resolution Process for Corporate Persons) Regulation, 2016 but that is not exclusive requirement for proving existence of debt. Financial contract, thus, can very well be furnished to prove the financial debt but a plain reading of regulation 8(2) indicate that it is not mandatory that existence of financial debt has to be proved by a financial contract. For example: records available with an information utility can very well be used as proof for existence of financial debt. Further, financial statements showing that the debt has not been paid is also one of the clauses in regulation 8(2) by which existence of debt can be proved. [Para 11]

The Financial Creditor has failed to establish that the transaction in question is a Financial Debt and due and payable and the Corporate Debtor has committed default. The judgment Pawan Kumar v. Utsav Securities (P.) Ltd. [2021] 131 taxmann.com 211/168 SCL 692 (NCLAT - New Delhi), cannot be relied as laying down any preposition that unless there is Financial Contract to establish financial debt, Financial Creditor cannot prove the financial debt by any other document. [Para 15]

When one looks into the statutory scheme as reflected in the application to Adjudicating Authority Rules, 2016 and CIRP Regulations, 2016, it is clear that financial debt can be proved from other relevant documents and it is not mandatory that written financial contract can be only basis for proving the financial debt. Thus, it is not necessary that written financial contract be the only material to prove the financial debt. [Para 21]

FACT: The appellant-retd. captain on the request made by 'D' provided a loan help to the respondent no. 1-corporate debtor for construction of their hospital. The appellant had transferred Rs. 7.5 lakh, Rs. 2.5 lakh and Rs. 10 lakh to the bank account of 'D' for advancing the sum as loan to the corporate debtor at an agreed interest of 18 per cent.

The appellant further transferred Rs. 40 lakhs as per the request of R2 and R3-director of the corporate debtor and in return they transferred it from their personal account to corporate debtor. Thereafter the respondents started expressing huge financial crunch and inability to pay the monthly interest but promised to pay interest along with principal by mid july, 2017.

Thereafter, the appellant requested the R2 and R3 for return of money however, after repeated request R2 paid part of interest i.e., 2.5 lacs in 2017, but second cheque for part interest got dishonoured.

Thereafter, joint criminal complaint was filed ,in which corporate debtor approached the High Court for quashing the FIR but, the High Court found merit and substance in the FIR and ordered for continuation of case at district Court.

Thereafter, Police filed charge sheet and warrant for appearance was issued but the corporate debtor did not appear.

The appellant filed an application under section 7 against the corporate debtor before the NCLT.

The NCLT by impugned order rejected said application on ground that the appellant failed to produce any document to show that the appellant had given the money to the corporate debtor and further held that the amount was transferred to the personal account of the intermediary as well as the personal account of the directors and, therefore, the appellant did not come under section 5(8) and could not be considered as financial debt and neither the applicant comes under the definition of the financial creditor of 5(7).

Aggrieved by the impugned order, the appellant filed instant appeal on ground that there was no legal requirement for proving existence of any written contract to establish that a financial debt was owned by the corporate debtor.

HELD: It is pertinent to note that section 7(1) clearly spells out that a section 7 application can only be initiated only by a financial creditor either by itself or jointly. A perusal of the definition of expression financial creditor would show that it refers to a person to whom a financial debt is owed and includes even a person to whom such debt has been legally assigned or transferred to. The trigger for initiation of the CIRP by such a financial creditor under section 7 is the occurrence of a default by the corporate debtor a prescribed threshold limit. Default in the IBC framework means the incidence of non-payment of debt in whole or in part when the debt has become due and payable, in law and in fact. Debt means a liability or obligation in respect of a claim which is due from any person and claim means a right to payment even if it is disputed. [Para 13]

The relevant excerpts of the impugned order as to why it has held that the application filed under section 7 is not in accordance with law and not liable to be admitted.[Para 14]

From a bare reading of section 7, it is amply clear that insolvency process under IBC can be triggered only by a financial creditor either singularly or jointly. The primary and fundamental basis for a creditor to be treated as a financial creditor for the purpose of section 7 in Part II requires that a financial debt is owed to that person in terms of section 5(7). Such a financial debt could cover any of the transactions outlined in section 5(8) (a) to (i) of the IBC. That being so, the basic requirement of existence of financial debt being owed by the corporate debtor to the financial creditor has to be first satisfied and cannot be overlooked. [Para 19]

FACT: ■

The respondent/corporate debtor had undertaken to construct a project and for this purpose had approached the appellant for advancing a sum of Rs. 1 crore. The corporate debtor had purportedly assured to repay the advance with interest at the rate of 18 per cent per annum besides offering 15 per cent share in the profit of the project. The amount of Rs. 1 crore was given by appellant to the corporate debtor.

■

Though the corporate debtor was to repay the outstanding loan on completion of the project, they did not release payments to appellant as per the terms even though the project was purportedly completed. Appellant issued a Demand Notice claiming repayment of the outstanding amount from the corporate debtor.

■

Since payments were still not forthcoming from the corporate debtor, the appellant filed a section 7 petition seeking the admission of the corporate debtor into corporate insolvency resolution proceedings which was rejected by the Adjudicating Authority as non-maintainable.

Held, yes - Whether since money was advanced towards working capital needs of corporate debtor and for boosting its economic prospects, it was a disbursal against consideration for time value of money and, therefore NCLT had rightly admitted section 7 application and initiating CIRP - Section 5(8) of the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016 - Corporate insolvency resolution process - Financial debt - Whether for any debt to be treated as a financial debt, pre requisite is disbursal of money to borrower for utilization by borrower and that disbursal must be against consideration for time value of money even if it is not interest bearing - Held, yes - Respondent no. 1-financial creditor had disbursed a loan amount of Rs. 5 crores to corporate debtor - Financial creditor repeatedly demanded repayment of loan amount but no payment was received - Accordingly, an application under section 7 was filed against corporate debtor and same was admitted by NCLT vide impugned order - Aggrieved by NCLT's order, appellant, ex-Director of corporate debtor, filed instant appeal on ground that disbursal of Rs. 5 crores was not in nature of a loan but a part payment deposit for purpose of developing a land project and, thus, R1 did not fall in category of financial creditor - It was noted that money was actually disbursed to corporate debtor through RTGS and a letter from Bank authorities testified that an amount of Rs. 5 crore was paid from account of R1 to corporate debtor - It was further noted that in balance sheet of corporate debtor said amount was showed under head of 'Long Term Borrowings from Related Parties, which clearly evidenced that disbursal was a loan - Whether once a debt became due or payable, in law and in fact, and if there was an incidence of non-payment of said debt in full or even part thereof, CIRP may be triggered by financial creditor as long as amount in default was above threshold limit - Held, yes - Whether since money was advanced towards working capital needs of corporate debtor and for boosting its economic prospects, it was a disbursal against consideration for time value of money and, therefore NCLT had rightly admitted section 7 application and initiating CIRP - Held, yes [Paras 17, 18, 24 and 27]

FACT: The respondent no. 1-financial creditor had disbursed loan amount of Rs. 5 crore to the corporate debtor towards its working capital during the financial year 2013-14, which was repayable on demand.

and the disbursal must be against consideration for time value of money. Undoubtedly, the most typical illustration of time value of money is in the form of interest on the principal amount that has been borrowed. The present is a case where the disbursal of monies was clearly accompanied by interest amount leviable thereon, the disbursal has all the trappings of a financial debt and squarely falls within the purview of section 5(8) of IBC. ■ At this stage, it will be useful to look at the impugned order to see how it has analysed the facts of the case before arriving at its findings. The aspect of debt and default has been dwelt at length by the Adjudicating Authority in the impugned order. It is found that the Adjudicating Authority after relying on the judgements of the Supreme Court in Innoventive Industries Ltd. v. ICICI Bank Ltd. [2017] 84 taxmann.com 320/143 SCL 625 (SC) and Swiss Ribbons (P.) Ltd v. Union of India [2019] 101 taxmann.com 389/152 SCL 3 came to the conclusion that this is a fit case for admission of section 7 application against the Corporate Debtor since the sums taken by the Corporate Debtor had become due and payable on demand and inability to pay by the Corporate Debtor was clear. [Para 19]

■

Thus, to answer the second issue raised by the appellant, there are no reasons to disagree with the findings of the Adjudicating Authority that it has concluded the existence of debt on the basis of documents/records like the balance confirmation statement in the balance sheet of the Corporate Debtor to establish existence of debt. It maybe pertinent to add here that it has been rightly contended by the Financial Creditor that the quantum of debt is not to be looked at during the stage of admission as held by this Tribunal in Rajesh Kedia v. Phoenix Arc [CA(AT)(Ins.) No. 996 of 2021]. It is not for the Adjudicating Authority to decide on the quantum of debt but the only requirement for admission of section 7 petition is to see that the minimum outstanding amount should be more than the threshold amount under the IBC which clearly stands fulfilled in this case. [Para 20]

■

This brings to the last argument canvassed by the appellant that in terms of the order of this Tribunal, the appellant had deposited Rs 34.99 lakh along with interest at the rate of 12 per cent per annum for two years. However, the Financial Creditor has refused to accept this amount which shows that this is not a bona fide action on the part of the Financial Creditor. Reliance has been placed on the judgement of this Tribunal in Jag Mohan Daga v. Bimal Kanti Chowdhary [ CA(AT)(Ins.) No. 848 of 2022], wherein it has been held that when an offer is made by the Corporate Debtor to pay the entire demanded amount with interest but is refused by the Financial Creditor, it clearly indicates that the Financial Creditor wants to drag the CIRP process and is not interested in the debt. It was also added that the said judgment of this Tribunal also relied on the judgment of Supreme Court in Vidarbha Industries Pvt. Ltd. v. Axis Bank [2019] 101 taxmann.com 389/152 SCL 365 wherein it has been held that it is not mandatory to admit a section 7 application merely on proof of debt and default. CIRP should not be allowed to continue when Financial Creditor pushes for CIRP not for purposes of insolvency resolution of the Corporate Debtor but for pursuing some agenda other than insolvency resolution. Hence, on this very ground, the appeal ought to be allowed and the present section 7 petition is liable to be set aside. [Para 23]

■

It is trite law that under the IBC once a debt which becomes due or payable, in law and in fact, and if there is incidence of non-payment of the said debt in full or even part thereof, CIRP may be triggered by the financial creditor as long as the amount in default is above the threshold limit. It is also well accepted that debt means a liability in respect of a claim and claim means a right to payment even if it is disputed. It is found that the Corporate Debtor has nowhere countered that Corporate Debtor is not liable to pay the outstanding amount to the Financial Creditor except for questioning the quantum of debt. However, as long as the financial debt is more than the threshold limit, quantum of debt cannot be used as a ground of defence to assail the admission of section 7 application. [Para 25]

FACT: 'S', i.e. 'original lender', advanced a term loan of Rs. 1.60 crores to the corporate debtor for a period of two years, to enable the corporate debtor to meet its working capital requirement. The original lender had assigned the outstanding loan to the appellant.

According to the appellant the loan was due to be repaid by the corporate debtor in full within 1-2-2020. The appellant claimed that the corporate debtor made some payments, but Rs. 1.56 crores still remained outstanding.

The appellant filed a petition under section 7 in the NCLT for initiation of the Corporate Resolution Process. The petition was, however, rejected by a judgment and order dated 23-10-2020 holding that neither the claim could be termed to be a 'financial debt' nor did the applicant came within the meaning of 'financial creditor' and once the applicant did not come within the meaning of 'financial creditor' he became ineligible to file the application under section 7.

The appellant filed an appeal under section 61. The appeal has been dismissed by the NCLAT, by the impugned order and the order dated 23-10-2020 of the NCLT dismissing the petition filed by the appellant under section 7 with the finding that the appellant was not a financial creditor of the respondent was confirmed.

On appeal to the Supreme Court:

HELD: The judgment and order of the NCLAT, affirming the judgment and order of the Adjudicating Authority (NCLT) and dismissing the appeal is patently flawed. Both the NCLAT and NCLT have misconstrued the definition of 'financial debt' in section 5(8), by reading the same in isolation and out of context. [Para 8]

In construing and/or interpreting any statutory provision, one must look into the legislative intent of the statute. The intention of the statute has to be found in the words used by the legislature itself. [Para 9]

When a question arises as to the meaning of a certain provision in a statute, the provision has to be read in its context. The statute has to be read as a whole. The previous state of law, the general scope and ambit of the statute and the mischief that it was intended to remedy are relevant factors. [Para 10]

Section 7 enables a financial creditor to file an application for initiating Corporate Insolvency Resolution Process against a corporate debtor either by itself, or jointly with other financial creditors or any other person on behalf of the financial creditor, as may be notified by the Central Government, when a default has occurred. [Para 17]

The eligibility of a person, to initiate the Corporate Insolvency Resolution Process, if questioned, has to be adjudicated upon consideration of the key words and expressions in the aforesaid section and other related provisions. [Para 18]

Corporate resolution process gets triggered when a corporate debtor commits a default. A financial creditor may file an application for initiating a Corporate Insolvency Resolution Process against the corporate debtor, when a default has occurred. [Para 19]

A 'corporate debtor' means a corporate person who owes a debt to any person, as per the definition of this expression in section 3(8). [Para 20]

the NCLT in its order dated 19-7-2019 are to be argued with. NCLAT has also made an observation that AN, AA had created a web of companies in which both along with near and dear ones including R (Wife of AA) and S (Brother-in-law of AA) acted in concert with each other. It is to be noted that Ernst & Young were appointed as forensic/transactional auditors by the RP. [Para 49] As noted by NCLT, the Memorandum of Understanding on the basis of which Spade had filed its claim before the IRP, was signed two years after the commencement of the purported transaction. The execution of the Memorandum of Understanding was sought to be explained on the basis that a formal document was created for specifying the rate of interest on the ICDs given by Spade to the corporate debtor. However, despite the creation of a formal document, the rate of interest being charged on the ICDs was 12 per cent as mentioned in the claim before the IRP, which is half of the interest rate of 24 per cent stipulated in the Memorandum of Understanding. During the arguments, it is also brought to the notice of the Court that the Memorandum of Understanding is unregistered and unstamped. The IRP in his letter has noted that as per the ledger provided by Spade, no interest was claimed on the alleged debt and no adjustment was made regarding the payment of principal or interest by the corporate debtor to Spade. It has been submitted in the written submissions filed on behalf of Spade and AAA that the auditors of the corporate debtor had been putting a note in its balance sheets stating that the interest of 12 per cent was not being paid to Spade due to a dispute. This submission in fact further fortifies the finding of the IRP that no interest has been paid on the alleged loan. The IRP has also noted in his letter that the Memorandum of Understanding does not stipulate the period of repayment. Hence, the consideration for time value of money is absent, which is an essential ingredient of a financial debt. The NCLT has also noted that a major portion of the ICDs was credited in the account of AA holding that the entire amount was not 'disbursed' to the corporate debtor. NCLAT has also made a similar finding in its judgment. This finding has been disputed by Spade and AAA who argued that no amount of the ICDs has been credited to the account of AA and such an allegation has not been made by any of the parties including the RP. However, it is to be noted under clause 2 of the Memorandum of Understanding, the amount of Rs. 26.55 crores has been disbursed not only to the corporate debtor but also to "other companies on behalf of AKME". In any event, the entirety of the ICDs were not disbursed to Spade. Additionally, no Board resolution was passed by Spade approving the grant of ICDs and the charge created on the loan was not registered with the Registrar of Companies. In view of the above, Phoenix is agreed with that the Memorandum of Understanding was an eye-wash and collusive. [Para 50]

NCLT in its order dated 19-7-2019 has noted that AAA and the corporate debtor had entered into multiple agreements regarding the same property without giving any explanation or rationale regarding variation in the consideration. This showed that the transactions were collusive in nature entered with the purpose of diverting properties of the corporate debtor to AAA. Spade and AAA sought to explain the multiple agreements, and argued that AAA entered into a Development Agreement with the corporate debtor to obtain 38.3 per cent of development rights. Since the Development Agreement could not be implemented because the license for the project could not be split into two parts, an Agreement to Sell and a Side Letter were executed on 25-10-2012. The Agreement to Sell was entered to purchase FSI/flats equivalent to 38.3 per cent of the total FSI in relation to specific units identified and allotted in the agreement. Apparently, the sale consideration was re-negotiated and enhanced from Rs. 32.80 crores under the Development Agreement to Rs. 86.01 crores under the Agreement to Sell. Spade and AAA has submitted that there was no partnership clause in the Agreement to Sell. However, clause 3 of the Side Letter dated 25-10-2012 shows that the intent of the parties was to continue to codevelop the land.

It appears that the parties converted the Development Agreement into an Agreement to Sell executed along with a Side Letter to circumvent the legal prohibition on splitting a development license in two parts. The transaction between AAA and the corporate debtor was collusive in nature. [Para 51]

Since the commercial arrangements between Spade and AAA, and the corporate debtor were collusive in nature, they would not constitute a 'financial debt' under section 5(8) and, hence, Spade and AAA were not financial creditors of the corporate debtor. [Para 52]
