Section 5(8) of the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016 - Corporate insolvency resolution process - Financial debt - Applicant company which was also under CIRP claimed to have advanced a sum of certain amount as loan to respondent/corporate debtor - It contended that since corporate debtor failed to repay loan amount, same was to be considered as financial debt and accordingly applicant was a financial creditor - It was noted that there was no documentary evidence on record to suggest that amount claimed to have transferred by applicant to corporate debtor were advanced as loan - Balance sheet of applicant had shown certain amount given as loan to others but there was no mention of name of corporate debtor - Besides this, it was an admitted fact that applicant company and corporate debtor were group companies and directors on boards and promoters were common -Thus, money claimed to be financial debt did not change hands as it remained in same hands of directors and promoters who were common in both companies which were undergoing CIR process - Thus, there appeared to be round tripping of money and matter was under investigation of police - Whether, on facts, application filed by financial creditor was to be dismissed - Held, yes [Paras 14 to 17]IBC : Where financial creditor claimed to have advanced loan to corporate debtor, since financial creditor could not place on record any documentary evidence to suggest that amount claimed to have transferred by it to corporate debtor were advanced as loan, alleged loan amount could not be termed as 'financial debt'

Section 5(8), read with section  7, of the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016 - Corporate insolvency resolution process - Financial debt - Applicant-financial creditor claimed that it had advanced loan to respondent-corporate debtor - As respondent failed to repay loan, application was filed under section 7 against corporate debtor - It was noted that there was no loan agreement on record and no Board Resolution was placed or produced by applicant company empowering it to grant loan to corporate debtor and only document on strength of which applicant was claiming that debt had arisen out of loan transactions was Form 26AS reflecting credit of interest amount and deduction of TDS - Whether in absence of any loan agreement and relevant Board Resolution, merely on basis of Form 26AS, it could not be presumed that any loan was disbursed by applicant to corporate debtor, which could be treated as the financial debt - Held, yes - Whether since applicant/financial creditor had failed to demonstrate that debt claimed in its application was arising out of any loan transactions and was a financial debt, application under section 7 was to be dismissed - Held, yes [Paras 28 and 33]

Section 5(8), read with section 7, of the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016 - Corporate Insolvency Resolution Process - Financial debt - Corporate debtor availed financial assistance from applicant but committed default in repayment - Thus, applicant filed instant application under section 7 - Corporate debtor raised objections that applicant was neither a financial creditor nor debts claimed by applicant came within purview of financial debt - It also raised a dispute that amount was due and payable at convenience of corporate debtor within a period of seven years and not on demand by applicant - As regard to first objection, it was noted that loan was disbursed against consideration for time value of money with a clear commercial effect of borrowing, thus, not only present claim came within purview of financial debt but also applicant was a financial creditor - As regard to second objection, it was noted that corporate debtor had sent an email to financial creditor in which it had not only accepted its liability but also sought time to repay debt at earliest, therefore, contention of corporate debtor that amount was payable after seven years was baseless and same could not be sustained - Whether since applicant had placed on record documents to prove default in repayment and, moreover, application of applicant was complete and there was no disciplinary proceeding pending against proposed RP, said application was to be admitted - Held, yes [Paras 14, 25, 39 and 40]

Section 5(8), read with section 7, of the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016 - Corporate insolvency resolution process - Financial debt - Appellant-financial creditor advanced loan of Rs. 1 crore to respondent, a real estate company for construction of a project 'Madina Heights' - Respondent assured to repay loan with interest @ 18 per cent per annum besides offering 15 per cent share in profit of project - However, respondent failed to repay loan - Appellant issued demand notice - Since payments were still not forthcoming from respondent, appellant filed a section 7 petition seeking admission of respondent into corporate insolvency resolution process which was rejected by Adjudicating Authority as non-maintainable - It was an admitted fact that there was no written contract or agreement between appellant and respondent governing terms and conditions by which sum was advanced by appellant and disbursed to account of respondent - Whether since appellant had failed to muster clinching proof and evidence in terms of financial records to show that sum advanced by them was indisputably interest-bearing and that interest had continued to accrue and was being realized as consideration for time value of money, sum advanced by appellant to respondent did not satisfy ingredients of financial debt of disbursal, time value of money and commercial effect of borrowing - Held, yes - Whether further said project was still in progress and compliances, both procedural and regulatory, were still pending and hence no occasion for default could be said to have occurred as debt was not due or payable - Held, yes - Whether thus, debt and default not having been clearly established, there was no infirmity in impugned order rejecting Section 7 application - Held, yes [Paras 21, 25, 26 and 27]

facts.text:
The corporate debtor, with an intention of setting up a project for the manufacture of flexible packaging material under co-extension process at an estimated cost of Rs.30 crores, had approached Canara Bank for financial assistance. While the said bank sanctioned a term loan of Rs.14.2 crores for construction of the building and purchase of plant and machinery, the promoters of corporate debtor were required to meet the condition of investing the margin money. Accordingly, all six promoters, including the financial creditor, had given interest free unsecured loan to the corporate debtor.

The financial creditor alleged that the corporate debtor failed to take any steps to liquidate or reduce the liability qua him despite various reminders. Thus, he issued demand notice under section 8. In response to the said notice, corporate debtor submitted that the amount being claimed was not a loan in terms of financial debt, nor was there any agreement to pay interest thereon. It was not to be repaid on demand as it was the basis of procuring financial assistance from their bank for establishing the corporate debtor for its working capital. The financial creditor was an equity holder and with a view to set up a plant, all shareholders had paid various amounts as the margin money to enable them to get the loan facility from Canara bank.

■

The appellant was a financial creditor of the corporate debtor(CD). The appellant had advanced an interest free loan to the corporate debtor to discharge the liabilities of the other secured financial creditors. The loan advanced by the appellant did not bear interest and was to be repaid after the settlement of the secured financial loans of the CD under the one time settlement scheme but when the CD failed to repay the loan after settlement of the secured loans, the appellant issued notice and recalled its loan to be repaid within 15 days. The appellant alleged that the amount of loan was reflected in the financial statement of the Respondent as unsecured loan. The corporate debtor failed to repay the loan after settlement of the secured loans.

■

The appellant filed an application under section 7 for the resolution of an interest free loan. The NCLT dismissed the application on ground that amount given by the appellant to the corporate debtor was not a financial debt and, hence, the corporate debtor was not owed to pay the appellant and that the loan was advanced in violation of section 186(2) of the Companies Act, 2013 and, therefore, was void and unforceable.

■

On appeal:

The respondent-corporate debtor sought financial assistance from the appellant-corporate debtor.

The appellant granted an unsecured term loan of Rs. 75 lakhs to the corporate debtor and, by way of RTGS payment of Rs. 50 lakhs, Rs. 5 lakhs and Rs. 20 lakhs were disbursed and, it was agreed between the parties that the repayment of the unsecured term loan will be made on demand.

The corporate debtor deducted tax on the interest amount in the financial year 2017-18. A total amount of Rs. 52.250 thousand was incurred as interest on the principle amount and, the corporate debtor deducted the TDS of Rs. 5250 thousand on 31-3-2018 but, had not paid it to the financial creditor.

The appellant sent a letter to the corporate debtor for the repayment of unsecured loan along with interest within two months and, the board of directors of the appellant had passed resolution to file a case against the corporate debtor in the NCLT.

The application under section 7 was filed by the appellant before the NCLT.

The NCLT directed the appellant to demonstrate that Income Tax for the assessment year 2018-19 had been taken into account and, the TDS deducted was adjusted and credited.

The appellant filed various documents including the Auditor's Report as well as copy of section 194A of the Income-tax Act.

The NCLT by impugned order held that the financial creditor failed to show the nature of the transaction between the parties and that the amount paid did not come under the definition of financial debt and, therefore, application filed by the financial creditor was dismissed.

The appellant filed instant appeal on ground that the NCLT committed error in holding that the appellant had not been able to prove financial debt, however, the documents brought on the record by the appellant including the balance sheets and bank transactions clearly proved the financial debt and, thus, NCLT committed an error in rejecting the application.

The financial creditor granted financial assistance of Rs. 6.10 crores to the corporate debtor.

The corporate debtor paid interest once after deduction of TDS, thereafter, corporate debtor failed to pay further interest. The financial creditor recalled the loan.

The corporate debtor had not liquidated the outstanding liabilities. Hence, the financial creditor filed the application under section 7.

The corporate debtor filed the reply and resisted the application on various grounds inter alia lack of any contractual agreement, an undefined period of loan, absence of any agreement for payment of interest at any specific rate and the said transaction did not fall within the definition of financial debt.

NCLT found no substance in the defence raised by the corporate debtor and held that the transaction does not get vitiated for want of agreement in terms of section 186(ii) of the Companies Act, 2013. NCLT by impugned order admitted the application and initiated CIRP against the corporate debtor.

The appellant, ex-director of corporate debtor, filed instant appeal against the impugned order of NCLT.

The appellant submitted that the Adjudicating Authority failed to appreciate that the financial creditor did not produce any loan agreement or instrument along with its application, and there were no pleadings regarding the basic terms of the alleged financial contract or financial debt including the date of repayment, applicable interest and date of default.

■

The applicant- financial creditor claimed that it had extended a loan to the Corporate Debtor during the period from 13.06.2007 to 27.03.2009. The said loan was extended in his personal capacity and was repayable on demand.

■

Corporate Debtor had consistently acknowledged the said loan in its Audited Financial Statements over the years, classifying it as an “Unsecured Loan”.

■

A loan recall notice was issued by the financial creditor on 04.07.2022 demanding immediate repayment of the full outstanding loan. A reminder for payment was further issued via email on 01.08.2022. In response to the aforementioned notice, the Corporate Debtor, through its Financial Controller acknowledged the communication and expressed an intention to amicably settle the matter. Since no steps were taken by the Corporate Debtor to repay the debt a legal notice was issued by the financial creditor.

■

Thus, financial creditor filed instant petition under section 7 to initiate CIRP against corporate debtor for the alleged default on the part of the corporate debtor in repayment of financial debt.

■

The Corporate Debtor raised a dispute that the application under Section 7 was barred by limitation, as the alleged financial debt was stated to have arisen in the year 2005-06, and the demand was purportedly made for the first time in July 2022- after a lapse of nearly 17 years. The corporate debtor argued that such a stale claim could not be revived by unilateral recall or reliance upon self-serving accounting entries. Further, it was contended that the application failed to satisfy the statutory preconditions of Section 7.

■

The corporate debtor also claimed that financial creditor had failed to produce any loan agreement, repayment schedule, or even a basic acknowledgment of terms such as interest, tenure, or security. No board resolution or authorization was passed by corporate debtor to borrow funds from the financial creditor. The absence of any documentation, along with the lack of demand for repayment for nearly two decades, was said to indicate that the financial creditor never extended any loan capable of forming a financial debt.

The petitioner-financial creditor had provided an unsecured loan of Rs. 1.11 crores to the respondent-corporate debtor on 9-1-2007.

The petitioner had issued a demand notice dated 14-9-2017. In reply to said notice, the corporate debtor submitted that the payment of Rs. 1.11 crores was not towards 25 per cent equity interest but was rather an investment in a development project of a corporate debtor.

On default in making payment, the petitioner had filed an application under section 7 to initiate CIRP against the corporate debtor.

The respondent submitted that petitioner had advanced an unsecured loan to the respondent on 9-1-2007 however, petition filed by the appellant in 2020 i.e., after a lapse of 13 years further, petitioner through letter dated 14-9-2017 himself had claimed that the amount was paid for acquisition of 25 per cent equity interest in the development project of the corporate debtor.

The appellant-retd. captain on the request made by 'D' provided a loan help to the respondent no. 1-corporate debtor for construction of their hospital.

The appellant had transferred Rs. 7.5 lakh, Rs. 2.5 lakh and Rs. 10 lakh to the bank account of 'D' for advancing the sum as loan to the corporate debtor at an agreed interest of 18 per cent.

The appellant further transferred Rs. 40 lakhs as per the request of R2 and R3-director of the corporate debtor and in return they transferred it from their personal account to corporate debtor. Thereafter the respondents started expressing huge financial crunch and inability to pay the monthly interest but promised to pay interest along with principal by mid july, 2017.

Thereafter, the appellant requested the R2 and R3 for return of money however, after repeated request R2 paid part of interest i.e., 2.5 lacs in 2017, but second cheque for part interest got dishonoured.

Thereafter, joint criminal complaint was filed ,in which corporate debtor approached the High Court for quashing the FIR but, the High Court found merit and substance in the FIR and ordered for continuation of case at district Court.

Thereafter, Police filed charge sheet and warrant for appearance was issued but the corporate debtor did not appear.

The appellant filed an application under section 7 against the corporate debtor before the NCLT.

The NCLT by impugned order rejected said application on ground that the appellant failed to produce any document to show that the appellant had given the money to the corporate debtor and further held that the amount was transferred to the personal account of the intermediary as well as the personal account of the directors and, therefore, the appellant did not come under section 5(8) and could not be considered as financial debt and neither the applicant comes under the definition of the financial creditor of 5(7).

Aggrieved by the impugned order, the appellant filed instant appeal on ground that there was no legal requirement for proving existence of any written contract to establish that a financial debt was owned by the corporate debtor.

The respondent no. 1-financial creditor had disbursed loan amount of Rs. 5 crore to the corporate debtor towards its working capital during the financial year 2013-14, which was repayable on demand.

The financial creditor repeatedly demanded the repayment of the loan amount but no payment was received by the financial creditor.

Accordingly, a demand notice was issued and application under section 7 was filed against the corporate debtor.

The NCLT vide impugned order admitted said application.

Aggrieved by the NCLT's, the appellant, ex-Director of the corporate debtor filed instant appeal on ground that the disbursal of Rs. 5 crores was not in the nature of a loan but a part payment deposit for the purpose of developing the land project hence, respondent No. 1 did not fall in the category of 'financial creditor' and the outstanding amount claimed by respondent No. 1 was not in the nature of 'financial debt' in terms of the statutory construct of IBC, basis which section 7 application could not have been admitted.

The respondent corporate debtor availed a loan/inter corporate deposit from the applicant/financial creditor vide loan agreement.

As per the loan agreement executed between the parties, the loan was to be repaid with interest. In terms of agreement the interest was to become payable from the beginning of financial year following the moratorium period or upon demand by financial creditor whichever was later, the determination of which was to be at the sole option of financial creditor.

Thereafter, the financial creditor vide various communications requested the corporate debtor to repay the loan amount but the corporate debtor failed to repay the same. Thus, the financial creditor was constrained to issue a demand notice but the corporate debtor maliciously denied such admitted amount as due and payable to the financial creditor.

The corporate debtor in its reply had raised objection that the debt claimed in the petition was not disbursed against interest or consideration for time value of money and therefore the claim of the applicant was not a financial debt. It was contended that no interest or time period for repayment was ever prescribed on the alleged transaction.

Corporate debtor had also alleged that the sole loan agreement relied upon by the financial creditor was false and fabricated for the purpose of filing of the present application. It was claimed that apart from the alleged forged loan document, there was nothing on record to show that the corporate debtor ever agreed to pay any such interest component.

Accordingly, it was argued that the applicant was not a 'financial creditor' and the debt claimed in the application did not come within the purview of 'financial debt' and therefore the present application was not maintainable.

■

The appellant claimed that she had advanced loan to the respondent-corporate debtor for the purpose of repaying interest/instalments on bank loans taken by the respondent so that loans were not defaulted upon or rendered NPA and, ensuring payment of salaries and money due to suppliers/ vendors, so that business continues unabated.

■

According to appellant, though the terms of the loan were not recorded in writing, it was agreed that money advanced would carry interest.

■

The appellant issued demand notice for repayment of the loans. The respondents, in its reply claimed that the money had been repaid.

■

The appellant initiated insolvency resolution process against the corporate debtor.

■

The NCLT vide order held that the appellant did not come within the meaning of ''''financial creditor'''' and failed to satisfy the NCLT about requisite ingredients of section 7 to claim any relief and thereby rejected the application.

■

Aggrieved by the NCLT’s order, the appellant filed appeal before the NCLAT.

■

The NCLAT vide impugned order upheld the NCLT’s order on ground that the appellant had failed to bring on record any evidence to suggest that she had disbursed money to corporate debtor against ''''consideration for time value of money and, in absence of any such evidence, the appellant could not claim that loan amount.

■

On appeal to Supreme Court;

■

The respondent, a money lender, advanced loans of about Rs. 2.50 crores (interest 12.75% p.a., payable half-yearly) and Rs. 2 crores (interest 3% per month, payable half-yearly) to the appellant in 2010. After cheque dishonour and a 2013 compromise, the appellant had paid about Rs. 3.53 crores by July 2014. The respondent filed a summary suit in 2016 for about Rs. 4.38 crores; a second compromise in 2016 recorded a full and final settlement figure of about Rs. 2.39 crores. On 11.01.2018, the Delhi High Court decreed about Rs. 4.38 crores with 24% p.a. interest from 01.02.2016, after deducting Rs. 25 lakhs and awarding costs of Rs. 5 lakhs. The appeal was dismissed in 2018 and the SLP was dismissed in 2021, rendering the decree final.

■

On 13.12.2021, instead of pursuing execution of the money decree, the respondent filed a Section 7 application under the IBC before the NCLT alleging default of the decretal amount as a financial debt. On 20.06.2022, the NCLT dismissed the petition, recording that a decree holder under Section 3(10) is a distinct class and does not automatically become a financial creditor, that the debt did not qualify as a financial debt under Section 5(8), that the appellant was a solvent, functioning company (revenue about Rs. 35 crores, profits about Rs. 8 crores, 95 employees), and that the IBC is not a recovery mechanism and was being misused as the claim rested on the civil decree rather than the underlying loans.

■

On 01.11.2022, the NCLAT set aside the NCLT’s order and directed admission of the Section 7 petition, holding that the loan agreements stipulated interest and repayment periods satisfying the time value of money under Section 5(8), and relying on the proposition that a money decree can furnish a fresh cause of action for a Section 7 filing; it rejected the appellant’s fraud plea against the decree. Meanwhile, the appellant moved the Delhi High Court by I.A. No. 17634 of 2022 under Section 151 CPC for redetermination of the decretal dues, asserting uncredited payments and inconsistent stands. The High Court directed the respondent to file a computation after crediting all payments and directed the appellant to deposit Rs. 3 crores plus costs; Rs. 3 crores was deposited on 02.11.2022. Separately, for AY 2012-13, the tax authorities raised a demand on interest income in the respondent’s hands premised on TDS of about Rs. 9.23 lakhs on interest of about Rs. 92.29 lakhs deposited by the appellant; the CIT(A) dismissed the respondent’s appeal in 2020. In ITAT proceedings decided on 01.09.2022, the respondent placed a computation showing only about Rs. 96.48 lakhs outstanding as on 31.03.2012 after accounting for disbursals, repayments and adjustments, which conflicted with higher claims; the I.A. remains pending.

■

On appeal to the Supreme Court, the appellant deposited about Rs. 60.99 lakhs pursuant to this Court’s order dated 18.10.2024 and filed a compliance affidavit referring to further payments.

The corporate debtor asked the financial creditor to extend 50 per cent of total purchase price for the purpose of acquisition of a US company 'Sona', and the financial creditor were assured a 50 per cent equity share in the US Co. for its financial assistance.

The corporate debtor informed the financial creditor that the total expenses would be USD 11 million and requested the financial creditor to immediately transfer INR 3.5 crores to its account in India for its 50 per cent share to meet the expenses of the amount of INR 7 crores to be deposited in the USA court as the auction was fixed on 12-12-2016.

On 4-12-2016, an agreement was entered between the financial creditor and the corporate debtor for equal equity participation to bid and acquisition of sona.

The total amount disbursed by the financial creditor to corporate debtor was Rs. 3.5 crores.

However, the company (SPT) was declared the highest bidder at the auction of 'Sona'.

After SPT was declared highest bidder, the corporate debtor approached the financial creditor to send a further amount of Rs. 1.5 million USD directly to the (SPT) account and assured that (SPT) would issue equity shares for investment by the financial creditor.

The financial creditor approached the RBI for granting permission to transfer funds to the SPT towards share application money, and permission having been granted, an amount of USD 1.5 million was transferred to SPT by the financial creditor, after transferring USD 1.5 million, the financial creditor asked the corporate debtor to return 3.5 crores, which was disbursed by the financial creditor to the corporate debtor.

However, SPT failed to issue securities within period of 60 days and also failed to refund the share application money amount of Rs. 1.5 million.

The financial creditor demanded entire money back, both Rs. 3.5, crores, which was earlier disbursed, and amount of USD. 1.5 million directly transferred to the SPT.

The financial creditor filed an application under section 7 and the director of corporate debtor, vide e-mail dated 28-5-2018, stated that the corporate debtor was unable to pay interest at 18 per cent per annum as demanded by the financial creditor on amount of Rs. 3.5 crores, however, agreed to pay interest at 12 per annum.

On 14-7-2018, an agreement was entered between the corporate debtor, director of the corporate debtor and an investor, where it was admitted that the corporate debtor owed INR 3.5 crores from the financial creditor.

In view of the agreement dated 14-7-2018, the financial creditor withdrew its section 7 application, which had not been admitted at that time.

The corporate debtor also acknowledged, vide e-mail dated 12-3-2018 the return of the amount of Rs. 3.5 crores to the financial creditor.

However, the corporate debtor did not pay the amount with interest and, inspite of its commitment to return the money, the money was never returned to the financial creditor.

The financial creditor filed section 7 application before NCLT claiming the amount of Rs. 3.5 crores with interest at 18 per cent and same was admitted by the NCLT.

On appeal, the appellant submitted that the amount of Rs. 3.5 crores paid by the financial creditor was not a financial debt, rather the amount was given by the financial creditor towards 50 per cent equity shares for the investment only.

The appellant further submitted that it was categorically mentioned in agreement dated 14-7-2018 that on receipt of USD 0.80 million from investor, amount of Rs. 3.5 crores be returned within three days since return was based on contingency of receipt of an amount of USD 0.80 million from the investor, and the investor never made payment of USD 0.80 million, hence no claim could be raised by the financial creditor for a refund of Rs. 3.5 crores.

The appellant further alleged that the amount of Rs. 3.5 crores was given by the financial creditor to the appellant was deal free and the same was clearly mentioned in the agreement dated 14-6-2016 and, therefore, the appellant had no responsibility to return the deal fee of Rs. 3.5 crores.

The agreement was entered into between the corporate debtor and the respondent-financial creditor, wherein financial creditor had advanced a loan facility of total sum of Rs. 5.35 crores to the corporate debtor by two cheques dated 28-10-2009 and 18-12-2010 and the same was repayable on demand with interest at 18 per cent on quarterly rests.

The corporate debtor defaulted in making payment and therefore the financial creditor filed an application under section 7 to initiate CIRP against the corporate debtor.

The corporate debtor alleged that Rs. 5.35 crores was not provided as a loan but as an advance for acquiring from the corporate debtor, floor space index of 15,500 square meter to be consumed on portion of the larger property.

The financial creditor thereafter addressed a letter dated 28-3-2019, reiterating that the amount of Rs. 5.35 crores was an advance by way of a loan and that the same was repayable on demand along with interest at the rate 18 per cent interest on quarterly interest.

The NCLT admitted section 7 application filed by the financial creditor and initiated CIRP against the corporate debtor.

The appellant-shareholder of the corporate debtor, aggrieved by the order passed by the NCLT, filed instant appeal on the ground that the debt was time barred as on 31-3-2014 and that the confirmation of accounts for the period 1-4-2016 to 1-4-2017 to 31-3-2018 were not 'acknowledgement of debt' within the meaning of section 18 of the limitation act.

The appellant had given unsecured loan facility to the respondent-corporate debtor.

The corporate debtor had been paying interest on unsecured loan till 30-9-2018 and also had been deducting and depositing Tax Deducted on Source (TDS) on the interest paid to the appellant. Thereafter, 30-9-2018 neither principle amount nor any interest amount was paid by the corporate debtor to the appellant.

The appellant issued a demand notice to the corporate debtor seeking repayment of the unpaid financial debt by the corporate debtor.

Thereafter, the appellant had filed an application under section 7 for initiation of CIRP against corporate debtor.

NCLT by impugned order rejected said application holding that appellant had failed to establish that the unsecured loan he had granted fell within the scope of financial debt in absence of any loan agreement setting out terms and condition of agreement.

On appeal :

The corporate debtor was a family company that struggled financially and was indebted to various banks/financial institutions and there was no access to funds.

On request of other directors and to bail out the corporate debtor, the respondent No.-1 financial creditor, had lent a sum of Rs. 9.15 crores from time to time as financial loans.

The financial creditor also issued a loan of Rs. 13.84 crores and was entitled to interest at 14 per cent per annum.

Thereafter, the corporate debtor, was requested by financial creditor, to return amount, without any success, a letter dated 17-11-2021 was issued to corporate debtor in which it was stated that he had infused funds, into the company, for the past few years, and those monies were brought in as unsecured loans, to save the company, from its repayment obligations.

However, no reply was received from the corporate debtor, on default in making payment, the petition under section 7 was filed by the financial creditor against the corporate debtor.

The corporate debtor alleged that the financial debt of Rs. 13.84 crores without any basis and, it was the duty of the financial creditor to annex all material documents along with the Form I in order to substantiate its debt.

The corporate debtor further alleged that section 7 casts an obligation on the financial creditor to furnish the record of default and, the corporate debtor had three shareholders, who were also directors of the corporate debtor and, thus it was not out of place to state that the said shareholder directors were own brothers.

The NCLT admitted said petition under section 7 and, declared moratorium under section 14.
