Thus, the applicants filled instant petition to initiate corporate insolvency resolution process against the corporate debtor.

In instant petition, the corporate debtor raised objection that there was neither any document in respect of loan, nor there were details of any applicable interest agreed between the parties. The corporate debtor further alleged that the applicants were neither financial creditors nor the debts claimed in application came within purview of financial debt.

The corporate debtor was developing an office complex by the name of 'Q-City' in Hyderabad. While it was in developing process, the 'Quinn Logistics' (financial creditor) acquired the entirety/majority of the shareholding of the corporate debtor.

During the period 2007- 2010, the financial creditor disbursed an interest free unsecured loan of Rs. 62.90 crores to the corporate debtor for development of Q-City.

However, bankruptcy proceedings in Sweden were initiated against parent company 'Quinn Investments Sweden AB', wherein order was reserved. Subsequent to reserving of such order the Board of Directors of the corporate debtor purported to show dilution of the respondent's shareholding in corporate debtor by allegedly issuing 376,301 fresh equity shares to one 'Me', a Dubai Company. Since then corporate debtor ceased to be a subsidiary of the 'Quinn Logistics' (financial creditor).

The financial creditor called upon the corporate debtor to repay the alleged outstanding loan amount of Rs. 62,90,45,905 on or before 30-6-2017. In response, the corporate debtor sought time to verify its records to clarify the position. According to the corporate debtor, there was no amount outstanding in the books of account of the corporate debtor payable to the financial creditor.

Having not received the amount, the financial creditor filed an application under section 7 for initiation of the corporate insolvency resolution process against the corporate debtor.

The Adjudicating Authority by impugned order dated 11-8-2017, admitted the application, order of Moratorium was passed and interim resolution professional had been appointed with certain directions.

On appeal:

The petitioner claimed to be a financial creditor had invested Rs.25 Lakh with the corporate debtor in relation to the development of project promoted by corporate debtor. As per mutual agreement between parties based on which investment was made, corporate debtor assured the repayment and as a collateral security one flat was also given. An unconditional guarantee was also given for the buy back of the said flat at a pre-settled and determined sum of Rs.31 lakh in relation to which post dated cheques were also given.

Said cheques were dishonoured for want of sufficient funds. Thus, a demand notice was sent to the corporate debtor. However, there had been no response to the said notice. Thus, petitioner initiated insolvency resolution proceeding under section 7 against the corporate debtor and submitted that as per agreement, the impugned amount was to be treated as amount made available for time value for money as given in the definition of financial debt in section 5(8).

Per contra, the corporate debtor submitted that the sum of Rs.25 lakh could not be treated as investment and for which assured returns were promised but on the other hand was only an advance received by the corporate debtor towards the purchase of immovable properties by the petitioner from the corporate debtor. It was further submitted that the subject matter of the agreement on which reliance had been placed by the petitioner discloses that relationship between the petitioner and the corporate debtor was that of only a purchaser and seller.

■

The appellant–NBFC/financial creditor had extended financial assistance to the corporate debtor on the basis of an oral understanding, disbursing loans aggregating about Rs. 22.75 crores in several tranches between 2011 and 2016, carrying interest. These transactions were reflected in the parties’ books and bank statements, including bank statements evidencing disbursals from FY 2013-14 till July 2016. The corporate debtor acknowledged liability through confirmation letters, loan-renewal acknowledgments for 2013–2017, demand promissory notes, and signed confirmations of account for FY 2013-14 to FY 2017-18; it issued post-dated cheques (some dishonoured) and deducted TDS on interest. After the last repayment made in 2021, the corporate debtor defaulted, leading to a recall notice in 2022.

■

The appellant filed a first Section 7 petition, which was withdrawn pursuant to a Settlement Agreement in 2022 wherein the corporate debtor acknowledged outstanding liability and agreed to a repayment schedule. On breach of the settlement, the appellant filed a fresh Section 7 petition (CP(IB) No. 146 of 2023). In the fresh proceedings, despite initial ex parte admission following non-filing of reply, the admission order was recalled on the debtor’s application and the debtor was allowed to reply. The Adjudicating Authority thereafter dismissed the Section 7 petition, holding that a fresh petition on the same subject matter was not maintainable after withdrawal of the earlier Section 7 petition without liberty, that withdrawal amounted to abandonment unless liberty to refile was granted, and that an explicit written loan agreement was necessary for an NBFC to determine the nature of transactions and debt.

■

On appeal to the NCLAT.

■

The appellant infused funds as share application money in the corporate debtor and in return, the corporate debtor allotted 3000 equity shares to the appellant. Subsequently, the appellant paid another sum as share application money for allotment of equity shares. However, no shares were allotted and only a part of the share application money was refunded.

■

The corporate debtor was not able to refund the balance amount of share application money purportedly on account of liquidity crunch, instead agreed to allot shares for the balance amount subject to the appellant providing additional funds to the corporate debtor. The appellant thereafter provided additional funds.

■

Since neither the shares were allotted nor the share application money was refunded, the appellant sent a demand notice to the corporate debtor for repayment of the share application money with statutory interest of 12 per cent in terms of section 42(6) of the Companies Act, 2013. Since the corporate debtor failed to repay the amount, the appellant filed a section 7 application before the Adjudicating Authority.

■

The Adjudicating Authority held that share application money in respect of the shares not allotted could not be deemed to be a financial debt. The impugned order further held that the requirements of section 7 application under the IBC were not fulfilled and therefore rejected the section 7 application.

■

On appeal:

■

The applicant, financial creditor (FC) had given an unsecured loan of Rs. 20 lakhs to the respondent-corporate debtor (CD) through RTGS with interest at the rate of 24 per cent per annum.

■

Since, the CD failed to pay the said loan, the FC filed a petition under section 7 seeking to initiate Corporate Insolvency Resolution Process (CIRP) against the CD.

■

The CD had filed a counter, questioning the maintainability of the petition, on the ground that there was no creditor and debtor relationship between the parties. It was further stated that the CD paid the amount to the FC through one ''A'' who was an elder known to both the parties and who was doing business in the State of Andhra Pradesh.

The assessee-firm showed certain borrowings on 2-1-1963 in its books. The loan was shown to have been taken from R against four pronotes. This loan was shown to have been returned on 19-7-1965. The assessee filed confirmation letter from the aforesaid creditor. In a statement and cross-examination, the creditor affirmed that the money transactions with the assessee were not of a genuine nature, that he had never advanced any money to the assessee nor received back any money from the assessee and that the transaction was a mere Havala or accommodation entry in which no money had passed whatsoever. As the assessment involved an addition of more than Rs. 1 lakh, the Assessing Officer referred the matter to the IAC. The IAC, on the basis of the aforesaid facts, held that there was no bona fide transaction between the assessee and the alleged lender. On the basis of the directions of the IAC under section 144B the ITO added back the aforesaid cash credit and also disallowed the interest claim on the aforesaid loan. On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) upheld the aforesaid addition.

On second appeal:

■

The corporate debtor, a power generation company, was admitted into CIRP on 2 January 2024 on a Section 7 application by a financial creditor. Following admission, the IRP/RP took over management and made a public announcement on 4 January 2024 inviting claims.

■

In June 2015, the corporate debtor had entered into a fully and compulsorily convertible debentures subscription agreement with an investor-company for issuance of 0% FCCDs up to Rs. 500 crores; the investor subscribed to about 49.04 crore FCCDs of face value Rs. 10 each. The agreement contemplated equity infusion, compulsory conversion of each FCCD into one equity share upon specified events, pari passu ranking with existing equity post-conversion, and no interest on FCCDs.

■

In March 2017, the investor agreed to sell these FCCDs to a promoter trust of the corporate debtor, and on 1 April 2017 the applicant entered into an advance agreement with the promoter trust for purchase of those FCCDs, paying about Rs. 306 crores. On 9 January 2024, the promoter trust informed the applicant that lender approvals for transfer of FCCDs were pending and asked the applicant to claim the advance directly from the corporate debtor. In the corporate debtor’s balance sheet as at 31 March 2023, the FCCDs were classified under equity.

■

Treating itself as a financial creditor on the basis of the FCCDs, the applicant filed Form-C claiming about Rs. 1,847.32 crores. By email dated 26 January 2024, the IRP informed the applicant that the claim towards FCCDs could not be verified with the corporate debtor’s records and therefore could not be admitted, noting that the FCCDs were not issued to the applicant and that no money was disbursed by the applicant to the corporate debtor. The applicant replied on 6 February 2024 asserting entitlement. By email dated 28 March 2024, the IRP/RP reiterated rejection, maintaining that the FCCDs were never issued to the applicant as per the corporate debtor’s records and that FCCDs were not treated as financial debt under Section 5(8) of the IBC.

■

Before the Adjudicating Authority (NCLT).

The applicant-financial creditor claimed to have disbursed a total amount of Rs. 70 lakhs in favour of the respondent-corporate debtor, out of which an amount of Rs. 40 lakhs was repaid by the corporate debtor. It was claimed that the remaining amount of Rs. 30 lakhs had not been paid till date.

The financial creditor filed relevant statement of bank accounts along with auditor's report. The financial creditor also filed the calculation sheet providing the calculation of the financial debt along with the ledger account of the corporate debtor maintained by the financial creditor. In addition, the copies of balance sheets of the corporate debtor had also been placed on record.

The financial creditor issued a demand notice to the corporate debtor for repayment of the remaining debt, but the respondent committed default in payment of the outstanding debt.

In the instant CIRP application, the respondent contended that amount that was given by the applicant was given under an oral agreement. It was due and payable at the convenience of the respondent within a period of seven years. The respondent thus contended that applicant was not a financial creditor, nor debt claimed came within purview of financial debt. The respondent further contended that there were pending disputes between the management of the applicant company before the NCLT and, thus, the instant CIRP application was not maintainable.

The corporate debtor was engaged in the construction business and, entered into an amended and restated share subscription and shareholders agreement (ARSSHA) with the respondent no. 1 financial creditors, in which the financial creditors gave a certain amount to the corporate debtor for implementation of an ongoing real estate project.

Thereafter, the parties to the 'ARSSHA' entered into a Supplementary Share Subscription and Shareholders Agreement (Supplementary SSHA) under which the financial creditors gave an additional amount to the corporate debtor.

However, the corporate debtor failed to comply with the terms of said agreements and hence, a binding term sheet was executed.

Thereafter, the corporate debtor once again failed to pay the amount under the binding term sheet.

Since, the corporate debtor failed to pay the exit consideration under the 'ARSSHA', 'supplementary SSHA' as well as failed to comply with the terms of the 'binding term sheet' consequently, the financial creditors invoked the Arbitration Clause under the 'ARSSHA'.

In the Arbitral proceedings, the parties arrived at a settlement, on basis of which consent term arbitration proceedings were disposed of by consent Award, in which a sum of Rs. 72.85 crores was agreed to be paid to respondent Nos. 1 and 2 on or before 25-8-2021 and a further sum of Rs. 47.14 crores was agreed to be paid to the respondent Nos. 1 and 2 on or before expiry of 15 months from 25-11-2020 and, in terms of the consent Terms, failure to pay one of the tranches, would render the amount of Rs. 120 crores along with interest at 15 per cent per annum.

Since, the amount as contemplated under the consent award were not paid, the respondent Nos. 1 and 2 issued legal notices to the corporate debtor as well as to the promoters, in which it was stated that corporate debtor and the promoters were jointly and severally liable to pay the amount as per the consent award.

Since, no payment had been made, the financial creditors filed an application under section 7 against against the corporate debtor claiming total default amount of Rs. 133,75 crores being amount payable under the Consent Award amounting to Rs. 120 crores and interest accrued thereupon till 31-5-2022. The date of default was 25-8-2021 as per the Part IV of the application, date when the corporate debtor failed to pay first tranche of award under the consent award.

The NCLT by impugned order admitted section 7 application and appointed Interim Resolution Professional (IRP).

Aggrieved by the NCLT's order, the appellant-suspended director of the corporate debtor filed instant appeal on ground that there was no commercial borrowing for time value of money involved in the transaction. The appellant further stated that the transaction was for consideration for exchange and sale/purchase of shares and, thus, transaction did not constitute a financial debt under the IBC nor did it have a commercial effect of a borrowing not was it disbursement for time value of money.

■

The Government of India launched the Scheme for Integrated Textile Parks in 2005, under which a special purpose vehicle (SPV), the financial creditor (a public company), was incorporated to implement a textile park at Kathua. J&K SIDCO leased 200 kanals to the SPV for 90 years; premium of about Rs. 3 crores and advance ground rent of about Rs. 12 lakhs were paid. The SPV executed a Memorandum of Agreement with the Ministry of Textiles, which sanctioned a project cost of about Rs. 39.70 crores. The SPV allotted plots to nine unit-holders (the corporate debtors) through tripartite agreements with J&K SIDCO, conferring leasehold rights of 20 kanals each.

■

A loan agreement dated 16.10.2018 between the SPV and each unit-holder, exemplified by Silklon Processors Pvt. Ltd., recorded (i) Rs. 3.20 crores as consideration towards land, and (ii) an unsecured loan of Rs. 3.55 crores for building/project with interest at 13% p.a., interest payable yearly from 01.01.2018, principal repayable over 36 monthly instalments starting 01.01.2020, and penal interest at 2% p.a. quarterly on defaults. The unit-holders also availed bank finance from Punjab National Bank. Upon defaults in lease rent, interest and principal on the unsecured loan, the SPV issued a recall notice on 22.04.2020 (e.g., demanding about Rs. 4.68 crores from Silklon). The corporate debtor replied enclosing post-dated cheques of about Rs. 4.70 crores, which were dishonoured, followed by notices for action under Section 138 of the NI Act. PNB initiated action under the SARFAESI Act, conducted auctions and issued sale certificates. The SPV filed nine Section 7 applications in December 2023 against the corporate debtors. In these petitions, PNB and a minority shareholder of the SPV (Sunder Lal Aggarwal) sought intervention and imposition of penalty under Section 65, and the shareholder additionally questioned the SPV’s authorisation to file under Section 7. The SPV objected to the maintainability of these Section 65 applications and produced the Board Resolution dated 21.11.2014; NeSL records were also filed to evidence debt and default.

■

The Adjudicating Authority framed issues on limitation, authorisation, existence of financial debt, related-party/collusion, and intervention. It held the petitions within limitation; found the Section 7 petitions unauthorised on the ground that the Board Resolution dated 21.11.2014 predated the IBC and was under challenge in pending proceedings under Sections 241–242 of the Companies Act; held that the amounts claimed did not constitute “financial debt”; and held the SPV and the corporate debtors to be related parties and the petitions to be collusive. It dismissed all nine Section 7 petitions and imposed costs of Rs. 25 lakhs each on the SPV and on each corporate debtor under Section 65, citing filing of false, frivolous, collusive and malicious petitions and alleged false affidavits regarding non-related-party status.

■

The SPV filed nine appeals challenging rejection of the Section 7 applications and the penalties, seeking admission of the petitions. The corporate debtors filed nine separate appeals challenging the penalties imposed on them.

■

On appeal to the NCLAT.

■

The applicant–NBFC (financial creditor) filed a Section 7 application to initiate CIRP against the corporate debtor. It stated that between May 2019 and August 2019 it disbursed five Inter-Corporate Deposits aggregating about Rs. 4.05 crores at 13% p.a., four tranches repayable in about 90 days and one in 18 days, supported by bank statements and contemporaneous emails/letters recording interest and due dates; it issued demands after default, received balance confirmations from the corporate debtor, and reflected TDS on interest and part-payments, claiming about Rs. 6.74 crores outstanding as on 30.04.2025, above the Section 4 threshold.

■

In reply, the corporate debtor contended the transfers were commercial advances for joint trades and not ICDs; that there was no loan agreement, stipulated interest or structured repayment; that RBI Fair Practices/Companies Act requirements were not complied with; and that Section 7 was being used as a recovery tool.

■

Before the National Company Law Tribunal.

The respondent no. 1-financial creditor had advanced various amounts to the corporate debtor from the year December, 2013 to December, 2017.

Thereafter, insolvency proceedings were initiated against the financial creditor and, RP of the financial creditor wrote to the corporate debtor seeking confirmation of the balance amount of Rs. 17.47 crores payable to the financial creditor, in a further letter, RP of the financial creditor wrote to the corporate debtor for making payment of Rs. 27.69 crores.

Meanwhile, liquidation proceedings were initiated against the financial creditor by the NCLT's order.

The Liquidator filed an application before the NCLT seeking approval for the initiation of proceedings under section 7 against the corporate debtor.

The NCLT allowed said application and granted permission to the Liquidator to file a section 7 application.

The financial creditor through liquidator filed a section 7 application against the corporate debtor for the initiation of CIRP.

The NCLT admitted said application on ground that the balance sheet of the corporate debtor showed that the corporate debtor had availed a loan facility from the financial creditor, thus, there was a financial debt and default.

The appellant, being shareholder and suspended director of the corporate debtor aggrieved by the NCLT's order had filed appeal before the NCLAT on ground that as per the MoU signed between parties, the amount advanced by the financial creditor was only an investment in the corporate debtor and hence it was not a financial debt.

The NCLAT, by the impugned order, held that the MoU brought on record by the appellant in appeal for the first time and balance sheet of the corporate debtor as on 31-3-2017 acknowledged a loan advanced from the corporate debtor.

The NCLAT further held that the financial statement of the financial creditor was also filed along with section 7 application, where under the heading short-term loan and advance against the name of corporate debtor was shown, thus, NCLT had rightly placed reliance on the financial statement of the corporate debtor as well as those of financial creditor, both reflecting the amount as a short-term loan thus, there was no error in the order passed by the NCLT admitting section 7 application.

The appellant filed instant appeal before the Supreme Court:

For taking over the controlling interest and management of a sick industry, the assessee-company, as per the order of the BIFR, had provided Rs. 1.08 crores to the said sick industry after taking loan` from a bank. The said loan of the bank was repaid along with interest by the assessee after taking an interest-free loan from ‘R Ltd.’ in the same accounting year itself and, thus, during the year itself the account of the bank was squared up by the assessee-company in its books of account. The assessee-company had claimed interest of Rs. 5,92,840 which was disallowed by the Assessing Officer on the ground that from the balance sheet and the copy of account, it transpired that the assessee-company never took loan from the aforesaid bank. On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) deleted the disallowance.

On the revenue’s appeal :

The corporate debtor was incorporated as a wholly owned subsidiary of IIL, wherein 'IIL' was holding more than 50 per cent of the shares.

The corporate debtor had approached IIL for financial assistance, which assistance was received.

The corporate debtor had sent an e-mail to IIL confirming an amount of Rs. 5.58 crores as due and payable by them to IIL.

Subsequently, the IIL was admitted into CIRP and Information Memorandum prepared by the Resolution Professional (RP) had shown Rs. 5.11 crores as receivable from the corporate debtor.

Later, Liquidation proceedings were admitted against IIL and, the liquidator had published the Process Memorandum, wherein the amount in default by the corporate debtor was recorded as Rs. 5.10 crores.

The appellant-financial creditor had bid for the assets/receivables of IIL and entered into a Deed of Assignment on 21-7-2021 with the Liquidator of IIL whereby the assets of IIL were transferred in favour of the financial creditor.

In terms of the Deed of Assignment, the debt of Rs. 5.10 crores of the corporate debtor was transferred in favour of the financial creditor.

The financial creditor issued legal notice calling upon the corporate debtor for repayment of the said debt.

The corporate debtor in reply to said legal notice on 30-9-2021 and 26-10-2021 denyied the claims of the financial creditor.

Since, the financial creditor had not received any amount from the corporate debtor filed a section 7 application before the NCLT.

However, said application was rejected by the NCLT on the ground that debt and default did not exist.

On appeal :

An operating agreement was executed between Marriott hotel and corporate debtor for construction of a hotel which started functioning in mid-2017.

The corporate debtor took a loan of Rs. 50 crore from ILFS and in 2018 the loan was assigned to TFCI.

On 28-3-2018, a loan agreement was executed between the corporate debtor and TFCI regarding repayment of loan till 15-1-2031 and shares of corporate debtor were pledged in favour of financial creditor to secure that loan.

The corporate debtor defaulted in payment of instalments. TFCI issued notice under section 13(2) of SARFAESI Act, 2002 to the corporate debtor for the payment of Rs. 50,78,74,188.00 and on 19-2-2020. But there was no response from corporate debtor.

TFCI as financial creditor filed an application under section 7 against corporate debtor for initiation of CIRP against corporate debtor.

The Adjudicating Authority by impugned order admitted said application.

On appeal; the appellant, suspended director of corporate debtor contended that TFCI was only interested in enforcing a security interest over the assets of corporate debtor and had no interest in the growth and survival of the corporate debtor and, thus, it did not satisfy the test of being a financial creditor under the IBC. The Appellant had also claimed that the Adjudicating Authority had failed to appreciate the meaning of debt and default and no default had occurred under the loan agreement as loan instalments were to be paid till 15-1-2031 and TFCI could not recall the loan at any earlier date. Further grounds raised by the Appellant were that the corporate debtor was not a failing business but it was a new and a profit making hotel and CIRP would put the entire business in jeopardy. The Appellant also claimed that 'N', who filed the section 7 application, did not have the necessary authorization to file the section 7 application and, hence, it was not maintainable.

held.text:
■

The Financial Creditor has pleaded that the loan advanced by him was a loan recallable on demand and qualifies as a financial debt under Section 5 (8). He has further pleaded that even though the loan was interest-free but qualified as disbursal against time value of money. (Para 11)

■

In order for an interest-free debt to qualify as financial debt, an financial creditor must show that the funds were disbursed with ‘consideration for time value of money’. The question of what constitutes ‘time value of money’ varies depending on the facts and circumstances; nonetheless, the financial creditor must demonstrate that it had an interest in the subject matter for which the loan was disbursed and was profiting from it. The pre-requisite is disbursal of money to the borrower for utilization by the borrower and that the disbursal must be against consideration for time value of money even if it is not interest bearing. (Para 13)

■

It is opined that there is no credible evidence to establish that the alleged disbursal was made against the time value of money- an essential element for qualifying a claim as a “financial debt” under Section 5(8). The transaction in question neither involved any stipulated interest component nor any contractual arrangement indicating the accrual of financial gain, return, or profit to the alleged Financial Creditor. Furthermore, there were no agreed terms of repayment, nor was there any contemporaneous communication or correspondence evidencing a request for a loan or acknowledgment of such a financial arrangement. In the absence of these foundational elements, the disbursal lacks the commercial character necessary to constitute a financial debt under the Code. (Para 14)

■

The purported recall of an alleged loan nearly 17 years after its initial disbursal- without any documented agreement, interest component, or discernible commercial consideration—raises serious doubts about the nature of the transaction and is inconsistent with the conduct ordinarily expected of a prudent financial creditor acting in the ordinary course of business. Furthermore, the email dated 05-08-2022, which the financial creditor has relied upon as an acknowledgment under Section 18 of the Limitation Act, falls short of constituting a clear or unequivocal admission of liability. Rather, it reads as a generalized and non-committal response, devoid of any express acknowledgment of debt or promise to repay. In the absence of a categorical admission, such communication cannot, by itself, revive a time-barred claim (Para 16)

■

The respondent- corporate debtor has further contended that the applicant- financial creditor exercised significant influence over the accounts and affairs of the Corporate Debtor by virtue of his position as a Key Managerial Personnel (KMP) and Director. It was asserted that the financial statements relied upon by the financial creditor were, in fact, authored and approved under his supervision, and that the relevant entries reflecting long-term borrowings were affected at his instance. (Para 17)

■

Moreover, the underlying transaction in question constitutes a Related Party Transaction. It is trite law that a company is governed by its Board of Directors, who bear primary responsibility for the management and conduct of its affairs. The record clearly establishes that the Applicant, was actively controlling and managing the operations of the Corporate Debtor during the relevant period in his capacity as Director. In view of the foregoing factual position, and considering that the Applicant had substantial control over the management and affairs of the Corporate Debtor, it is opined that the Applicant qualifies as a "related party" within the meaning of Section 5(24). Accordingly, his claim warrants close scrutiny under the heightened standards applicable to related party transactions under the Code. Hence the absence of a Board Resolution authorizing a borrowing from Related Party raises doubts with respect to legitimacy of the claim.(Para 18)

■

The Corporate Debtor has questioned the correctness of the record of Financial Information (Form-C) available with the Information Utility (NeSL) and submitted that no Record of Default with Information Utility in Form-D has been furnished in terms of Regulation 21(4) of IBBI (IU) Regulations 2017, which is a requirement as per Section 7(3)(a) of IBC. (Para 19)

■

On perusal of the Financial Information in Form-C of the Corporate Debtor maintained by the Information Utility namely National E-Governance Services Limited (NESL) dated, we find that the mere filing of record of Financial Information in Form-C with the Information Utility (NeSL) does not constitute the record of default. Therefore, there exists no debt and there is no default on the part of the Corporate Debtor. (Para 20)

■

■

For any debt to be treated as financial debt, the pre-requisite is disbursal of money to the borrower for utilization by the borrower and that the disbursal must be against consideration for time value of money even if it is not interest-bearing. As to when a Financial Creditor who has disbursed money to a Corporate Debtor against consideration for time value of money can trigger the insolvency resolution process against the Corporate Debtor, as per the scheme of IBC, that stage arises when a default arises in that a debt which has become due, in fact and in law, but has not been paid in whole or part thereof. [Para 12]

■

Submission has been made by the Appellant that an amount of Rs 1 crore had been disbursed to the Corporate Debtor which is validated by the certificate issued by ICICI Bank on 4-5-2021 which clearly states that Rs 1 crore had been credited to the account of the Corporate Debtor from the current account of the Appellant on 19-2-2010. It was also pressed that the disbursal of the above loan amount to the Corporate Debtor was substantiated by the fact that the Corporate Debtor had acknowledged the receipt of this amount in their balance sheets of 31-3-2010 and 31-3-2011 and is duly reflected as 'Loan from Directors and Shareholders'. It was further added that this sum had been disbursed with time value of money on the understanding with the Corporate Debtor that they would repay the amount with interest at the rate of 18 per cent per annum. That TDS was deducted by the Corporate Debtor on the interest amount payable to the Appellant as is evident from the TDS Certificate for the month of March 2010 shows that disbursal had been made against consideration for time value of money. [Para 13]

■

It was contended that there is no need of a written contract to prove the existence of a financial debt and in support of their contention reliance has been placed on the judgment of this Tribunal in Agarwal Polysacks Ltd. v. K.K. Agro Foods and Storage Ltd. in CA(AT)(Ins) No. 1126 of 2022 and Pradeep Tayal v. Essbert Fashion Pvt. Ltd. in CA(AT)(Ins) No. 950 of 2022 which have held that written contract is not mandatory nor a necessary pre-condition for the purpose of proving existence of financial debt. Submission was pressed that the terms and conditions of the loan including the period of loan and the purpose of the loan was not documented but rested on an oral understanding mutually arrived at between the two parties that the loan amount advanced would be returned by the Corporate Debtor on completion of the Madina Project. Since this project was already completed and yet no payment was forthcoming from the Appellant, a legal notice was served upon them claiming repayment of the amount financed by them. Thus, this was a case where a default had been committed by the Corporate Debtor which the Adjudicating Authority failed to appreciate. It was therefore contended that the Adjudicating Authority had committed a grave error by holding that the Appellant was not a financial creditor and that the amount advanced by the Appellant to the Corporate Debtor did not qualify as financial debt. [Para 14]

■

Per contra, it was contended by the Corporate Debtor that the Appellant has failed to show that any default had occurred on the part of the Corporate Debtor. Even if it is accepted that the right to payment arose on the completion of the Madina Project, the said project was not yet complete as procedural compliances were still in the pipeline. It was also submitted that since it is for the Appellant as Financial Creditor to substantiate that the project stood completed and until such substantiation is done, the claim made by the Appellant under Section 7 was pre-mature. Further as there was no tenure of the loan, it shows that the amount advanced was in the nature of an investment and not a loan. The Adjudicating Authority had therefore correctly held that the Appellant had invested money for speculative purposes and such a speculative investor cannot file a Section 7 petition. [Para 15]

■

-2018. The copy of the statement of account annexed with the Company Petition is signed by the same P. It is observed that this statement of account records free reserves of the Company as on 31-3-2015 to be Rs. 2,53,08,746/- which exceeds the 100 per cent benchmark set under section 186 of the Companies Act, 2013, as the loan amount is Rs. 12 crores. [Para 11] It is vehemently contended by the Respondent that an amount of Rs. 7 Crore was legally withdrawn by the Appellant and 'S' jointly from the account of the Respondent Company between January 2015 and April 2015 and an amount was paid to unknown parties 'J' and 'K'. The said transaction was written off in the books of account of the Respondent Company on 31-12-2017. A perusal of the Rejoinder filed by the appellant shows that there is no specific denial with respect to these amounts, though it was categorically pleaded by the Respondent. It is the case of the Respondent that the amount transferred to these parties is not recoverable as the same was executed in relation to satisfying some other transaction entered into with 'S' group. Garnishee Notices were issued by the Income Tax Department under section 226(3) of the Income-tax Act, 1961, against 'S' Realty, one of the entities of the 'S' group. It is strenuously contended that as no amount was payable to the Appellant Company, the 'Corporate Debtor Company' did not pay any amount to the Income Tax Department and have informed the same to the Appellant. [Para 12]

The Respondent relies on MOU dated 23-3-2018 filed before the Adjudicating Authority. It is the case of the Respondent that the MOU expressly mentions that the appellant shall not be entitled for interest at all. The said MOU also provides that if the advance amount of loan of Rs. 7 Crores given to two parties between January 2015 to April 2015 is not repaid, then the respondent is not liable to pay any amounts to the appellant. [Para 13]

The appellant contended that this MOU is forged and fabricated document and a Complaint has also been lodged with the Police and that the stamp and their signature is also fabricated. [Para 14]

Keeping in view the definition of 'Financial Debt' as defined under section 5(8); the nature of transactions entered into between both the parties; that there are several transactions some executed on the same day, between 'S' realty and 'S' properties together with the admitted fact that the Respondent Company was a part of the 'S' group; that the Directorship is common in all the 'S' Companies; it was only on 9-4-2018 that the name of the Respondent Company was changed to 'C' with the new management stepping in; that the statement of account appended to the petition is signed by 'P', the erstwhile Director of the Respondent Company; the entries of debit and credit dated 7-11-2015, 10-11-2015, 24-11-2015 establish several internal transactions between the 'S' group; the Auditor's Report detailing the Related Party transactions which figures the names of common Directors and the corresponding transactions; it is opined that the appellant has failed to satisfy that the transaction in question is a 'Financial Debt' as defined in the Code and a default has occurred. Therefore, the contention of the appellant that ratio of Innoventive Industries (supra) alone is to be applied, cannot be sustained. The scope and objective of the IBC is to be cautious in admitting an Application and not encourage recovery proceedings. For all these reasons, the ratio of 'Phoenix ARC (P.) Ltd. v. Spade Financial Services Ltd. [2021] 124 taxmann.com 24 (SC)' is squarely applicable to the facts of this case. Having held so, one does not wish to go into the technicalities of the authorization of the petition and also the issue of genuineness and veracity of the MOU. [Para 15]

The instant appeal is dismissed confirming the Impugned Order passed by the Adjudicating Authority. [Para 16]

■

The present Application has been filed by L H Sugar Factories Limited ("Applicant/Financial Creditor") under Section 7 of the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016 ("Code" or "IBC") seeking initiation of Corporate Insolvency Resolution Process against Oswal Overseas Limited ("Corporate Debtor") on the ground that the Corporate Debtor has committed default in repayment of financial debt. As per Part IV of Form 1, the amount claimed to be in default is Rs. 2,44,38,082.19/-, comprising principal amount of Rs. 2,25,00,000/- and interest, and the date of default is stated to be 10.02.2025. [Para 7]

■

The principal issue for consideration is whether the amount disbursed by the Financial Creditor constitutes financial debt within the meaning of Section 5(8) of the Code. The disbursal of Rs. 2,25,00,000/- by the Financial Creditor to the Corporate Debtor is not seriously disputed. The Corporate Debtor has, however, sought to contend that the amount was not a loan but was paid in connection with a proposed acquisition of the business of the Corporate Debtor. [Para 10]

■

Upon consideration of the material placed on record, it is noticed that the Corporate Debtor has relied upon a proposed Share Purchase Agreement to contend that the amount was paid towards a contemplated acquisition transaction. However, no executed Share Purchase Agreement or any concluded acquisition agreement has been placed on record. The proposed Share Purchase Agreement relied upon by the Corporate Debtor remained unexecuted and does not establish that the amount of Rs. 2,25,00,000/- stood finally adjusted or appropriated towards acquisition consideration. [Para 11]

■

It is further observed that the Financial Creditor's audited financial statements for the financial year ending 31.03.2025 record the amount of Rs. 225.00 lakhs under Note 10 as "Loan to Other Company" and specifically state that the same represents loan given to Oswal Overseas Limited. Correspondingly, the Corporate Debtor's audited financial statements record an amount of Rs. 2,25,00,000/- under Note 15 as "Intercorporate Advance" and further state that the Company has received an advance of Rs. 2,25,00,000/- from L.H. Sugar Factories Limited. Though the nomenclature employed by the parties is not identical, both sets of financial statements acknowledge the transaction and the subsisting outstanding amount between the parties. [Para 12]

■

The contention of the Corporate Debtor that the amount reflected as "Intercorporate Advance" cannot be treated as financial debt is not acceptable. Mere nomenclature employed in the books of accounts is not conclusive of the true nature of a transaction. The substance of the transaction and the attendant circumstances are required to be examined. In the present case, the receipt of Rs. 2,25,00,000/- from the Financial Creditor stands acknowledged in the audited financial statements of the Corporate Debtor. The said amount is reflected under the head "Intercorporate Advance" in Note 15 to the audited financial statements of the Corporate Debtor, wherein it is recorded that the Company has received an advance of Rs. 2,25,00,000/- from L.H. Sugar Factories Limited. Further, no material has been placed on record to demonstrate that the said amount stood finally adjusted or appropriated towards any concluded acquisition transaction. Therefore, the mere description of the amount as an "Intercorporate Advance" does not, by itself, alter the nature of the transaction. [Para 13]

■

It is also significant that the Corporate Debtor's Board Resolution dated 01.10.2024 refers to availing unsecured loan from the Financial Creditor. Though the Corporate Debtor disputes the effect of the said resolution, the same constitutes contemporaneous evidence emanating from the Corporate Debtor itself. Further, while acquisition discussions between the parties are borne out from the record, no executed Share Purchase Agreement or other concluded document has been produced to establish that the amount of Rs. 2,25,00,000/- stood finally adjusted towards acquisition consideration. The material on record, therefore, indicates that the amount continued to remain outstanding. [Para 14]

■

The Corporate Debtor has further contended that the transaction does not carry interest and therefore cannot be treated as financial debt. At this stage, it is relevant to refer to the judgment of the Hon'ble Supreme Court in Orator Marketing (P.) Ltd. v. Samtex Desinz (P.) Ltd. (2023) 3 SCC 753. [Para 15]

■

. Since this application has been filed on 21-6-2019, therefore, it is after the 3 years as provided under the law. So the instant application is also barred by law of limitation. [Para 17]

Apart from that, it is necessary to consider whether the applicant has succeeded to establish that the amount which it claimed to pay as debt to respondent, comes under the definition of 'Financial Debt' as referred in section 5 (8). [Para 18] Mere plain reading of provisions of section 5(8) shows that the financial debt means the debt along with interest, if any, which is disbursed against the consideration for time value of money and includes the debt which has been referred in clauses(a) to (i) and when one considers the amount which the applicant claim he has paid as per schedule shown in part IV of Form I, then one finds, nowhere in the application the applicant has mentioned that fact that it has deposited the amount against the consideration for time value of money, rather there are contradiction in the statements of the applicant regarding the payment of interest. [Para 19]

As the applicant failed to produce any document to show that what was the agreed interest in between the parties on the basis of which money was borrowed. Therefore, the case of the applicant did not comes under section 5(8)(a) and also does not come either under (b) or (c) or (d) or (e) or (f) or (g) or (h) or (i) of section 5(8) of the I&B Code. Therefore, the contention of the applicant that these payment shown in schedule Part IV of Form-1 comes under financial debt and the applicant comes under the definition of financial creditor in view of section 5(7) of the IB Code cannot be accepted. [Para 20]

In absence of any document, the contention of the applicant is not liable to accepted and the applicants fails to prove that payment shown in schedule Part IV of Form-1 comes under the definition of financial debt under section (8) of IBC and paid amount as claimed is not barred by law of limitation. [Para 21]

So for the reasons discussed above, the application filed under section 7 is not according to the provision of law and is not complete thus this application is not liable to be admitted. [Para 22]

by the appellant for 15 long years until the corporate debtor got admitted into CIRP. There is no evidence either of any communication sent to the corporate debtor seeking payment of interest. The records of the corporate debtor also do not reflect any provision for interest on the said loan having been credited to the account of the corporate debtor. Nor is there any proof for accrual of interest in any financial year or any evidence of TDS deduction such as Form 26AS. [Para 19]

■ It would be pertinent to outline the rival contention of the appellant that they cannot be denied the right to file their legitimate claim merely because no interest amount was reflected in the balance sheet of the corporate debtor. It was argued that if the corporate debtor did not deduct interest or make provision for interest payments in the balance sheet, the appellant cannot be held responsible for this lapse and put to prejudice. Since the appellant had already resigned from the management of the corporate debtor in 2012 and was not in control of the corporate debtor, they were not responsible in any manner for the corporate debtor not having levied the interest on the outstanding principal amount. Simply because interest was not paid by the corporate debtor, the sum advanced by the appellant cannot be denied the treatment of a financial debt. [Para 20]

■

The appellant was admittedly a shareholder of the corporate debtor when the loan agreement was signed in 2007 and later became one of the directors of the corporate debtor from 2009 to 2012. Thus, it is undisputable that the appellant was very much in control of the management of the corporate debtor until 2012. It is also noticed that either the appellant or his brother who was a signatory of the loan agreement remained at the helm of affairs of the corporate debtor all along. That being the case, the appellant cannot absolve itself of the responsibility of explaining as to why the financial statement of the corporate debtor did not reflect levy of interest till financial year 2011-12 even when they were in control of the corporate debtor. Having said that, the finding of the Adjudicating Authority that the amount of interest at the rate of 24 per cent claimed by the appellant being exorbitant, it was sufficient ground for rejection of the claim of the appellant could not be subscribed to. The Adjudicating Authority, at best, had a limited jurisdiction to examine the decision of the RP on the rejection on the claim and not on the reasonability of computation of the claim or quantum of the debt. [Para 21]

■

It is a well settled precept that in the judgment of the Supreme Court in Orator Marketing (P.) Ltd. v. Samtex Desinz (P.) Ltd. [2021] 128 taxmann.com 424, it has been clearly held that financial debt does not expressly exclude an interest free loan. Thus, financial debt also includes any sum raised under any other transaction having the commercial effect of borrowing even it does not carry an interest component. Be that as it may, the fact that the appellant in the present case has not demonstrated any efforts made by it to recover the loan amount since 2007 cannot be obliterated. There is no material on record to show that any notice or any demand was raised either for repayment of the purported loan or for payment of interest since 2007. If the loan agreement was a genuine one, then the expected course of action on the part of the appellant would have been to seek refund of the loan given by it when it exited the management of the corporate debtor if not earlier. The inordinate and unexplained delay in raising the demand until the corporate debtor was admitted into rigours of CIRP does cast doubts on the legitimacy and bona fide of the alleged transaction as a whole irrespective of the interest component. [Para 22]

■

The Adjudicating Authority has rightly taken note of the 13 years unusual and stony silence on the part of the appellant to recover their dues. This is clearly a case where the appellant seemed to have woken up from their slumber and suddenly remembered to have raised their claim in respect of loan-cum-interest coinciding with the corporate debtor getting admitted into CIRP. Given this fact situation, there is nothing arbitrary on the part of the Adjudicating Authority to find the conduct on the part of the management for maintaining uninterrupted silence for over 15 years on the recovery of their dues including unclaimed interest amount of Rs. 1.04 crores rather unusual lending credence to the fact that the loan agreement was prepared as an after-thought to tailor the filing of their claims. [Para 23]

■

In result, there is substance in the contention raised by the respondents that the claim filed by the appellant was not bona fide as it was not premised on a genuine loan transaction and was bereft of cogent supporting proof. There is no error on the part of the Adjudicating Authority in passing the impugned order rejecting the claims filed by the appellant. [Para 24]

■

By way of instant petition under section 7, the petitioner claims himself to be a financial creditor having an advance unsecured loan equivalent to Rs. 1.11 crores as on 31-3-2007 and presently Rs. 1.85 crores considering the enhanced value of USD. However, the petitioner has not relied upon any loan document which might have been executed between the petitioner and the corporate debtor with regard to the terms and conditions of the said loan transaction along with any repayment schedule or the rate of interest. However, surprisingly, the petitioner has relied upon the notice dated 14-9-2017, which was served upon a Director of the corporate debtor wherein it was stated that the petitioner wired USD 2,50,000/- and further that the petitioner was entitled to obtain 25 per cent equity interest in the corporate debtor, i.e., U.S. Hospitality Private Limited in exchange for the said sum of money. In response to the notice dated 14-9-2017, reply dated 18-9-2017 was sent on behalf of corporate debtor stating that the payment of USD 2,50,000/- was not towards 25 per cent equity interest but was rather an investment in a specific project of U.S. Co., as the said Company was involved in the Project to lease Real Estate in India with a hope of building a hospital on the said property. The petitioner has further relied upon notice dated 24-7-2020 got served by the petitioner upon the corporate debtor and its directors and in of the notice, it has been reiterated by the petitioner that on 1-9-2007, he wired a sum of USD 2,50,000/- from his Bank Account to the corporate debtor.

If the notices dated 14-9-2017 and 24-7-2020 are taken into account, it emerges that it is the specific and definite case of the petitioner that he transferred the amount of USD 2,50,000/- with an intent to buy a 25 per cent stake in the assets of the corporate debtor. [Para 20]

It is well settled that an investment cannot be equated with a loan. In the commercial word, equity financing and debt financing are altogether different modes of finance which are distinct from each other. Equity financing carries no repayment obligation while debt financing involves borrowing of money which is often repayable along with interest or other charges as may be settled between the parties. Therefore, a sum of money invested with an intent of requiring equity stake in a company or some other interest in some of the properties of the company cannot be dubbed as a financial debt or for that matter a loan transaction. [Para 21]

Besides, one cannot be oblivious of the facts that in the notices dated 14-9-2017 and 24-7-2020, the petitioner himself has claimed that the payment in question was made with intent to buy 25 per cent equity stake in the respondent's Company, on the basis of which, it could be safely concluded that the money was given as a loan. In this regard, a reference can be made to the Remittance Certificate Exhibit whereby the money was wired by the petitioner from Spain to the account of the corporate debtor and in the Bank note, it is specifically mentioned that the purpose of remittance was an investment in purchasing, constructing and operating a hotel business in India. [Para 23]

Therefore, by looking at the instant case, it cannot be said to be a case of money having been borrowed by the corporate debtor from the petitioner nor the transaction can be dubbed as a loan transaction. The so-called admission made by the corporate debtor in the reply dated 18-9-2017 that the transaction was invested is of no consequence. In this context, it is further pertinent to mention that the respondent has claimed in the reply that an amount of Rs. 20 lacs were paid back to the petitioner as on 11-2-2008 as is evident from the statement of account (Exhibit G) attached with the reply. So far as the petitioner is concerned, in the rejoinder filed by him, the transfer of an amount of Rs. 20 lacs as on 11-2-2008 has not been specifically denied and it has only been stated that it was a personal transaction not relating to the transaction which took place in the year 2007. Even this plea raised on behalf of the petitioners seems to be a tentative one and does not really explains the exact position and circumstances under which a sum of Rs. 20 lacs were paid to the petitioner. [Para 24]

receipts of Rs 1,01,07,836 from Meck Pharma and Chem. Pvt. Ltd. In view of the above, it is concluded that there exists sufficient proof that disbursal had taken place. Having satisfied that there was a disbursal of Rs. 1 crore to the Corporate Debtor by the Appellant sans any written contract or agreement between them, it is next seen whether there was a disbursal with the consideration of time value of money. [Para 20]

■ It is an admitted fact that there was no written contract or agreement between the Appellant and the Corporate Debtor governing the terms and conditions by which the sum was advanced by the Appellant and disbursed to the account of the Corporate Debtor. Be that as it may the decision of this Tribunal in Agarwal Polysacks (supra) is to be followed wherein it has been held that requirement of written financial contract between parties is not a pre-condition for determining whether any amount disbursed is financial debt or not. When there are no written agreements or financial contract between the parties as in the present case, the real nature of transaction becomes the key to decide as to whether the transaction is in nature of financial debt or not. Thus, even if there is no agreement/contract between the parties, nothing precludes the Adjudicating Authority or this Tribunal from looking into the real nature of transaction to determine whether the transaction in question is in the nature of financial debt in terms of the statutory construct of IBC. [Para 21]

■

Though the expression 'time value of money' finds mention in Section 5(8) of the IBC, the term has not been defined in the said enactment. It is well recognised that the most typical example of 'time value of money' is in the form of interest charged on the principal amount that has been borrowed. In the present case, the Appellant has claimed that there was an oral understanding between the two parties that the loan was interest-bearing at the rate of 18 per cent per annum, and that being so, the sum was disbursed with the intent of extending a financial debt to the Corporate Debtor. [Para 22]

■

To substantiate the fact that the loan was actually interest-bearing, the Appellant has contended that the TDS certificates placed on record corroborate that interest amount had been paid by the Corporate Debtor. Secondly, the Corporate Debtor had acknowledged the receipt of this amount in their balance sheets of 31-3-2010 and 31-3-2011 which is duly reflected as 'Loan from Directors and Shareholders'. [Para 23]

■

Even though it has been held by this Tribunal in Prayag Polytech Pvt. Ltd. v. Gem Batteries Pvt. Ltd. in CA(AT)(Ins) No. 713 of 2019 and in Pawan Kumar v. Utsav Securities Pvt. Ltd. in CA(AT)(Ins) No. 251 of 2020 that TDS deduction does not prove a debt, it does not restrain from noticing that TDS deductions were actually made which have corroborative value in substantiating the element of time value of money. When the material available on record is seen, it is noticed that the Appellant has been able to show TDS certificates on interest payment for only two financial years ending 2010 and 2011. For the subsequent years, the Appellant has not been able to submit any proof or evidence of TDS deductions to substantiate that interest liability was being enforced. There is no proof to show that any reminders were sent to the Corporate Debtor seeking interest payment. For the transaction to have been interest-bearing in the true sense, the interest payment should have been paid annually and by logical corollary corresponding TDS deductions ought to have been reflected. This does not seem to have happened. Thus, it is viewed that deduction of TDS for only two years is insufficient to determinatively conclude that interest liability was a quintessential adjunct of the sum disbursed by the Appellant. [Para 24]

■

Coming to the balance sheets of the Corporate Debtor, it is noticed that for financial years ending 2010 and 2011, the amount of loan of the Corporate Debtor qua the Appellant in both the years is shown as Rs. 1,01,07,836. However, no other balance sheets of subsequent years have been placed on record thereafter to show that the debt and interest amount continued to be reflected in their balance-sheets. Though the Appellant has claimed that the 2021 balance sheet of the Corporate Debtor also mentions unsecured loans from Director and other related parties, on a pointed query made by this Bench, it was admitted that the balance sheet ending 2021 had not been produced before the Adjudicating Authority. Hence, it is viewed that when this document was not placed before the Adjudicating Authority, this contention raised at the appellate stage cannot be relied on. Therefore, the Appellant has failed to muster clinching proof and evidence in terms of financial records to show that the sum advanced by them was indisputably interest-bearing and that interest had continued to accrue and was being realised as consideration for time value of money. [Para 25]

■

Under section 5(7), a person can be categorised as a financial creditor if a financial debt is owed to it. Section 5(8) stipulates that the essential ingredient of a financial debt is disbursal against consideration for the time value of money. [Para 43]

The money advanced as debt should be in the receipt of the borrower. The borrower is obligated to return the money or its equivalent along with the consideration for a time value of money, which is the compensation or price payable for the period of time for which the money is lent. A transaction which is sham or collusive would only create an illusion that money has been disbursed to a borrower with the object of receiving consideration in the form of time value of money, when in fact the parties have entered into the transaction with a different or an ulterior motive. In other words, the real agreement between the parties is something other than advancing a financial debt. [Para 46]

Phoenix argued that the transactions entered into between the corporate debtor and Spade and AAA are collusive in nature and do not constitute a financial debt. AAA & Spade have urged that the eligibility of Spade and AAA as financial creditors has conclusively been determined by the NCLT in its order dated 31-5-2018. It is already concluded that the above order would not operate as res judicata and it was within the jurisdiction of the NCLT to consider this issue afresh. NCLT in its order dated 19-7-2019 has undertaken a detailed analysis of the transactions to arrive at a finding that the transactions were collusive. The findings of the NCLT in its order dated 19-7-2019 are to be argued with. NCLAT has also made an observation that AN, AA had created a web of companies in which both along with near and dear ones including R (Wife of AA) and S (Brother-in-law of AA) acted in concert with each other. It is to be noted that Ernst & Young were appointed as forensic/transactional auditors by the RP. [Para 49]

As noted by NCLT, the Memorandum of Understanding on the basis of which Spade had filed its claim before the IRP, was signed two years after the commencement of the purported transaction. The execution of the Memorandum of Understanding was sought to be explained on the basis that a formal document was created for specifying the rate of interest on the ICDs given by Spade to the corporate debtor. However, despite the creation of a formal document, the rate of interest being charged on the ICDs was 12 per cent as mentioned in the claim before the IRP, which is half of the interest rate of 24 per cent stipulated in the Memorandum of Understanding. During the arguments, it is also brought to the notice of the Court that the Memorandum of Understanding is unregistered and unstamped. The IRP in his letter has noted that as per the ledger provided by Spade, no interest was claimed on the alleged debt and no adjustment was made regarding the payment of principal or interest by the corporate debtor to Spade. It has been submitted in the written submissions filed on behalf of Spade and AAA that the auditors of the corporate debtor had been putting a note in its balance sheets stating that the interest of 12 per cent was not being paid to Spade due to a dispute. This submission in fact further fortifies the finding of the IRP that no interest has been paid on the alleged loan. The IRP has also noted in his letter that the Memorandum of Understanding does not stipulate the period of repayment. Hence, the consideration for time value of money is absent, which is an essential ingredient of a financial debt. The NCLT has also noted that a major portion of the ICDs was credited in the account of AA holding that the entire amount was not 'disbursed' to the corporate debtor. NCLAT has also made a similar finding in its judgment. This finding has been disputed by Spade and AAA who argued that no amount of the ICDs has been credited to the account of AA and such an allegation has not been made by any of the parties including the RP. However, it is to be noted under clause 2 of the Memorandum of Understanding, the amount of Rs. 26.55 crores has been disbursed not only to the corporate debtor but also to "other companies on behalf of AKME". In any event, the entirety of the ICDs were not disbursed to Spade. Additionally, no Board resolution was passed by Spade approving the grant of ICDs and the charge created on the loan was not registered with the Registrar of Companies. In view of the above, Phoenix is agreed with that the Memorandum of Understanding was an eye-wash and collusive. [Para 50]

Issue of financial debt

The Respondent company has admitted that the petitioner being the maternal uncle of the Managing Director, had given Rs. 1.25 lakh. initially. In addition, he had also given Rs. 1.29 crore under cheques dated 15-12-2007, 11-2-2008, 26-3-2008. [Para 6]

From the materials, it is clear that the petitioner had paid Rs. 1.29 crore to the respondent-company to meet its fund requirements.

The definition of financial debt is inclusive one. It indicates that debt along with interest 'if any' is disbursed against the consideration for time value of money. [Para 11]

The petitioner in his petition pleaded that the loan was advanced as an understanding between him and the corporate debtor and its managing director, who happened to be his nephew and that the loan was payable on demand. It is nowhere pleaded that such understanding included the payment of interest against the loan and the rate thereof. There is also no pleading that the payment was made against the issue of shares at a future date. The advancement of the said loan accordingly is not covered under any of the clauses of the definition. There is also no material on record to show that the amount was disbursed against the consideration for the time value of the money. [Para 12]

The Respondent pleaded that it availed an unsecured loan of Rs. 5 lakh from the petitioner. The same is manifest from its annual report of 2013-14. Admittedly, the amount was repaid in 2016, which is apparent from the account statement filed along with the petition. According to the petitioner he did not make any payment during 2013-14, which the audited annual report of the respondent company shows as unsecured loan of Rs. 5 lakh. The report is not in dispute. Therefore, its repayment could not be taken as the payment towards interest of the loan amount of Rs. 1.29 crore. More so when the petitioner has credited this amount against the principal amount of Rs. 1.24 crore and showed a default of Rs. 1.24 crore. Besides the petition is completely silent as indicated before that the loan was advanced against an agreed interest. Taking all these aspects into consideration it is accordingly clear, for the purpose of instant case, that the amount would not come within the definition of a financial debt, though it is admitted that the petitioner had advanced said amount to meet the fund requirements of the company. [Para 13]

Issue of limitation

The first of the payments was made by cheque dated 15-12-2007 and was credited to the respondent's account on 18-12-2007. The last payment was made by cheque dated 26-3-2008, and was credited to the respondent's account on 27-3-2008. According to the petitioner, it was an understanding and was payable on demand. The understanding between the petitioner and the Respondent, which then was managed by the former's nephew, did not provide a time limit for repayment of the debt. [Para 15]

The Application under section 7 is not a suit. Suits relating to money needs to be filed within three years when the amount became due. In the instant case admittedly, there was no time limit agreed upon between the parties for repayment of the amount advanced. The amount payable on demand pleaded by the petitioner could not be extended for an uncertain period. In the absence of any contract between parties the amount needed to be repaid within three years from the date when they were respectively advanced. The amounts accordingly would have been due and payable on or before 14-12-2010, 10-2-2011 and 25-3-2011 respectively. There is no material on record to show that the respondent made any admission of debt respectively within these periods or subsequent thereso. [Para 17]

The Application having been filed only on 13-11-2018, was grossly time barred. The debt accordingly was not due and payable. In view of the discussions and the findings viewed from any perspective, the petition at the instance of the petitioner is not maintainable. The petitioner is not entitled to the relief sought. The petition thus cannot be admitted. [Para 19]

In the instant case, the corporate debtor in its reply to company petition No. 1347/2019 had admitted that the 'financial creditor' had paid a sum of Rs. 5.35 crores on 27-10-2009 to it but the 'corporate debtor' had taken a stand that no payment was ever made towards interest by it. Further, the claim of the financial creditor is repudiated by the 'corporate debtor' by stating that the total consideration agreed to be paid for by the financial creditor towards the purchase of FSI and its entitlement to consume the same on the said portion was Rs. 10 crores only of which only a sum of Rs. 5.35 crores was paid by the financial creditor to it. [Para 67]

The fact that a sum of Rs. 5.35 crores was paid by the financial creditor to the corporate debtor through two cheques (one cheque dated 28-10-2009 for Rs. 5.25 crores) and another cheque dated 18-12-2010 for Rs. 10 lacs is not disputed. Hence, a sum of Rs. 5.35 crores is a 'Financial Debt' coming under section 5(8)(f), in the considered opinion of this Tribunal. The 1st respondent/applicant is a 'financial creditor' as per section 5(7), even though the rate of interest at the rate of 18 per cent for Rs. 5.35 crores is disputed on the side of the 'corporate debtor' because of the fact that the sum paid was not provided as a 'loan' etc., the corporate debtor is clearly in 'Default' of the 'Debt' due and payable in law. [Para 68]

Before the Adjudicating Authority the financial creditor through the bank statement issued by the Bank of India and through its Bank certificate dated 30-3-2019 had shown that a sum of Rs. 5.35 crores was credited to the 'corporate debtor'. From the confirmation of accounts dated 1-4-2011, 1-4-2017 and 1-4-2018 the 'Debt' due of the corporate debtor is established. [Para 69]

Even though pleas are advanced on behalf of the appellant that for the alleged 'Default' which occurred from the time the interest was not paid viz 2010 or 2011 and from 2009 till date the interest accrued every quarter was not paid by the 'corporate debtor' and further that no action was taken, no claim was made from the company or no steps for recovery of interest was made by the financial creditor till 2018 when the 1st letter was issued to the 'corporate debtor' demanding the amount with interest. In the instant case, the 'Debt' of the corporate debtor is supported from the confirmation of accounts dated 1-4-2011, 1-4-2017 and 1-4-2018. Further, on 13-4-2018 the financial creditor had called upon the corporate debtor to repay the facility availed and that the corporate debtor had through a reply dated 7-6-2018 had mentioned that the sum of Rs. 5.35 crores was only provided as an 'advance' for acquiring from the corporate debtor floor space Index of 15,500 sq. mtrs. etc. and not as loan. The financial creditor through its letter dated 28-3-2019 had reiterated that the sum in question was an advance by way of loan and that the same was repayable on demand along with interest at the rate of 18 per cent on quarterly rests. As such, the section 7 application filed before the 'Adjudicating Authority' in CP No. 1347/MB/CII/2019 is well within the period of limitation. Moreover, the acknowledgements through confirmation letters on 1-4-2011, 1-4-2017, 1-4-2018 and balance sheets beginning from 31-3-2010 till 31-12-2019 will extend the period of limitation as per section 18. Viewed in that perspective, the contra pleas taken on behalf of the appellant on the aspect of limitation are unworthy of acceptance by this Tribunal. [Para 70]

It has also been clarified by the Liquidator that the receivables from the corporate debtor did not appear separately in the financials of IIL from 2017-18 onwards and that it was included under the overall trade receivables.
