For example:

(a)

a financial instrument may contain a non-financial obligation that must be settled if, and only if, the entity fails to make distributions or to redeem the instrument. If the entity can avoid a transfer of cash or another financial asset only by settling the non-financial obligation, the financial instrument is a financial liability.

(b)

a financial instrument is a financial liability if it provides that on settlement the entity will deliver either:

(i)

cash or another financial asset; or

(ii) its own shares whose value is determined to exceed substantially the value of the cash or other financial asset. Although the entity does not have an explicit contractual obligation to deliver cash or another financial asset, the value of the share settlement alternative is such that the entity will settle in cash. In any event, the holder has in substance been guaranteed receipt of an amount that is at least equal to the cash settlement option (see paragraph 21).

Settlement in the entity's own equity instruments [paragraph 16(b)]

21. A contract is not an equity instrument solely because it may result in the receipt or delivery of the entity's own equity instruments. An entity may have a contractual right or obligation to receive or deliver a number of its own shares or other equity instruments that varies so that the fair value of the entity's own equity instruments to be received or delivered equals the amount of the contractual right or obligation. Such a contractual right or obligation may be for a fixed amount or an amount that fluctuates in part or in full in response to changes in a variable other than the market price of the entity's own equity instruments (e.g. an interest rate, a commodity price or a financial instrument price). Two examples are (a) a contract to deliver as many of the entity's own equity instruments as are equal in value to Rs. 100, and (b) a contract to deliver as many of the entity's own equity instruments as are equal in value to the value of 100 ounces of gold. Such a contract is a financial liability of the entity even though the entity must or can settle it by delivering its own equity instruments. It is not an equity instrument because the entity uses a variable number of its own equity instruments as a means to settle the contract. Accordingly, the contract does not evidence a residual interest in the entity's assets after deducting all of its liabilities.

22. Except as stated in paragraph 22A, a contract that will be settled by the entity (receiving or) delivering a fixed number of its own equity instruments in exchange for a fixed amount of cash or another financial asset is an equity instrument. For example, an issued share option that gives the counterparty a right to buy a fixed number of the entity's shares for a fixed price or for a fixed stated principal amount of a bond is an equity instrument. Changes in the fair value of a contract arising from variations in market interest rates that do not affect the amount of cash or other financial assets to be paid or received, or the number of equity instruments to be received or delivered, on settlement of the contract do not preclude the contract from being an equity instrument. Any consideration received (such as the premium received for a written option or warrant on the entity's own shares) is added directly to equity. Any consideration paid (such as the premium paid for a purchased option) is deducted directly from equity. Changes in the fair value of an equity instrument are not recognised in the financial statements.

22A. If the entity's own equity instruments to be received, or delivered, by the entity upon settlement of a contract are puttable financial instruments with all the features and meeting the conditions described in paragraphs 16A and 16B, or instruments that impose on the entity an obligation to deliver to another party a pro rata share of the net assets of the entity only on liquidation with all the features and meeting the conditions described in paragraphs 16C and 16D, the contract is a financial asset or a financial liability. This includes a contract that will be settled by the entity receiving or delivering a fixed number of such instruments in exchange for a fixed amount of cash or another financial asset.

23. With the exception of the circumstances described in paragraphs 16A and 16B or paragraphs 16C and 16D, a contract that contains an obligation for an entity to purchase its own equity instruments for cash or another financial asset gives rise to a financial liability for the present value of the redemption amount (for example, for the present value of the forward repurchase price, option exercise price or other redemption amount). This is the case even if the contract itself is an equity instrument. One example is an entity's obligation under a forward contract to purchase its own equity instruments for cash. The financial liability is recognised initially at the present value of the redemption amount, and is reclassified from equity. Subsequently, the financial liability is measured in accordance with Ind AS 109. If the contract expires without delivery, the carrying amount of the financial liability is reclassified to equity. An entity's contractual obligation to purchase its own equity instruments gives rise to a financial liability for the present value of the redemption amount even if the obligation to purchase is conditional on the counterparty exercising a right to redeem (e.g. a written put option that gives the counterparty the right to sell an entity's own equity instruments to the entity for a fixed price).

In the recent judgment by the Hon'ble Supreme Court of India dated July 26, 2021, in the case of Orator Marketing (P.) Ltd. v. Samtex Desinz (P.) Ltd. [2021] 128 taxmann.com 424 (hereinafter referred to as "Orator's case"), it was held that the loans disbursed without interest shall be categorised as financial debt as under section 5(8) of the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code (IBC/Code). This has created a sensation in the market and a lot of uncertainty w.r.t. the definition of financial debt as to what exactly constitutes a financial debt. The authors through this article will analyse the above judgment in the light of various precedents given by the Supreme Court, NCLAT & NCLT and the Insolvency Committee Report and will analyse how the said judgment has created confusion on various aspects. But, before delving into the larger aspect let us look into the facts and the rationale behind the judgment of the NCLT, NCLAT and the Supreme Court.

NCLT's Decision

An application under section 7 of the IBC was filed by the Financial Creditor (FC)/Orator Marketing Pvt. Ltd. to initiate the Corporate Insolvency Resolution Process (CIRP) against the Corporate Debtor (CD)/M/s Samtex Desinz Private Limited for the default in making the payment of Rs. 1,56,89,740/-. The FC was assigned the debt via assignment agreement dated October 10, 2019, between the FC and M/s Sameer Sales Pvt. Ltd., who originally granted interest-free loans to the CD for the business operations of the CD. In the application, it was mentioned that the CD had acknowledged the debts in its books of accounts and had also pleaded regarding its inability to repay the debts.

The Adjudicating Authority (AA)/NCLT observed that there exist no dispute w.r.t. the fact that the CD was assigned a loan without any interest. The NCLT stated that in order to admit an application under section 7 of the Code an application has to be filed by the FC for the "financial debts" owned by it. It further referred to the definition of 'financial debt" under section 5(8) of the Code which runs as "financial debt means a debt alongwith interest, if any, which is disbursed against the consideration for the time value of money and includes money borrowed against the payment of interest etc." The AA also referred to various judgments of the NCLAT1 wherein it was held that to constitute a debt as financial debt, it has to have a component of interest and time value of money attached to it.

Thus, the AA held that the Appellant shall not be termed as FC as there was neither any component of interest attached with the loan amount nor it was disbursed against the consideration for the time value of money, both of which are quintessential for debt to qualify as financial debt. Lastly, it observed that it was merely a loan and not financial debt.

NCLAT's Decision

An appeal was filed by the Appellant/M/s Orator Marketing Pvt. Ltd. (who claims to be the FC) in the NCLAT against the impugned order passed by the NCLT. The Appellant stated that the loan was reflected in the balance sheet of the CD which was due. It argued that the money was given for the business operations of the CD and thus it categorises as having a component of the time value of money. Appellant further puts his reliance on the case of Pioneer Urban Land and Infrastructure Ltd. v. Union of India [2019] 108 taxmann.com 147/155 SCL 622 and argued that if the money is no longer with the person giving the money then it would qualify as financial debt.

The Appellate Tribunal rejected the arguments of the Appellant and concluded that for a loan to be a financial debt it should have consideration for the time value of money and the consideration should be for the FC and not the CD. It further rejected the Appellant's reliance on the Pioneer's case and stated that the Appellant is picking up the words in isolation which will not solve the purpose. The Appellate Tribunal then reiterated the position as held in Pioneer's case and concluded that the money given by the allottee even though was no longer with the allottee but was given with the objective of taking a flat (money's equivalent) from the developer which is the consideration for the allottee. Hence, the NCLAT rejected the appeal of the Appellant and upheld the decision of the AA by not categorising the Appellant as FC.

Supreme Court's Decision

The Appellate Tribunal then reiterated the position as held in Pioneer's case and concluded that the money given by the allottee even though was no longer with the allottee but was given with the objective of taking a flat (money's equivalent) from the developer which is the consideration for the allottee. Hence, the NCLAT rejected the appeal of the Appellant and upheld the decision of the AA by not categorising the Appellant as FC.

Supreme Court's Decision Aggrieved by the decision of the NCLAT, the Appellant/FC (who is claiming to be the FC) appealed before the Supreme Court under section 62 of the IBC (Orator Marketing (P.) Ltd. (supra). The question which was posed before the Supreme Court was "whether a person who has given interest free loan to a Corporate Person becomes incompetent to file a petition under section 7 of the Code?"

The Appellant challenged the impugned order of the NCLAT & NCLT and argued that while interpreting the provision of the legislation, the focus should be on the legislative intent, object & purpose of the statute. It was argued that both the Adjudicatory Tribunal have overlooked the words in section 5(8) of the Code, i.e., "if any". The interpretation of the words provides that the financial debt will not necessarily have the component of interest and if there is no interest still the principal debt will qualify to be as financial debt. He further argued that the NCLAT & NCLT have failed to take notice of Section 5(8) (f) of the IBC which provides that financial debt will include any amount which is raised under other transactions having the commercial effect of borrowing. The Appellant argued that the word "includes" as per the interpretation given in the case of Dilworth v. Commissioner of Stamps [1899] AC 99, will have connotation "means and includes" which will give an extensive explanation to the meaning attached to the words or expressions and thus lending of money for the financial requirements of the CD will in no way be discerned as it does not have the commercial effect of borrowing and thus, cannot be excluded from the definition of financial debt.

The Court further referred to the judgment of Anuj Jain, IRP for Anuj Jain v. Axis Bank Ltd. [2020] 114 taxmann.com 656, wherein the Supreme Court held that the basic element for the debt to be financial debt is that it should be disbursed against the consideration for the time value of money. Time value of money remains an essential part of the financial debt. The Court further stated that "the essential element of disbursal, and that too against the consideration for the time value of money, needs to be found in the genesis of any debt before it may be treated as financial debt within the meaning of Section 5(8) of the Code". The Apex Court, in the present matter, applied the ratio of the Jaypee Infratech case and held that the facts of the present matter are distinguishable from the above-mentioned case in a sense that the debt in the former case was in a form of a third-party guarantee which was given by the CD for securing the advances to the borrower, but, in the present case, the interest-free loan was given to meet out the working expenditures and financial requirements of the CD and thus, the ratio of the former case cannot be applied to the present case.

Further, the court relied on the case of Prabhudas Damodar Kotecha v. Manhabala Jeram Damodar [2013] 15 SCC 358, wherein the court applied the golden rule of interpretation while interpreting Section 41(1) of the Presidency Small Cause Courts Act, 1882 and observed that the words or phrase of the statute must be given ordinary meaning when the language used by the legislature is precise and plain and thus concluded that the gratuitous licensee will be considered as a general licensee unless specifically excluded. Thus, relying on the reasoning of the above case the Court in the present matter concluded that the loan given without interest will qualify to be treated as a financial debt unless specifically excluded. Hence, the Supreme Court set aside the judgment of the NCLAT & NCLT and ordered the NCLT to revive the petition under section 7 of the FC.

Divided Opinions of the Court/Tribunals on Interest as Prerequisite for Financial Debt

Section 5(8) of the Code defines financial debt which provides that it's a debt alongwith interest, if any, disbursed against the consideration for the time value of money and includes the debt and includes money borrowed against payment of interest. On the plain reading of the provision, it is evident that if there is any interest component in the debt then it will qualify as financial debt. However, if there is no interest component attached to the debt/loan amount then what treatment is to be provided to the loan is a question that seeks urgent attention. Although, the Supreme Court in the Orator's case has very clearly highlighted the fact that the debt having no interest constituent shall be termed as financial debt, but this judgment of the Hon'ble court cannot be read alone and should be read in the light of various judgments of various NCLTs and NCLAT wherein the position of law was divided.

Interest necessary part of Financial Debt

evidences the fact that there was the consideration of interest against time value of money.

Critical Analysis of the Supreme Court's Judgment in the Orator's case.

Considering the Orator's judgment by the Supreme Court in the light of various judgments and points discussed above, the authors vehemently states that the judgment has not removed the black cloud over the issue of interest not being an essential part of financial debt. Instead, it has brought forward various ambiguous points, upon which a necessary deliberation is required. Firstly , as observed from various judgments of the Supreme Court and the NCLAT, it can be concluded that the time value of money is the most important and quintessential part of the financial debt without which an application under section 7 will not get admitted. It is also evident from the various definitions as referred above that the time value of money includes the interest component, and is the difference between the present values of payment and the payment due and payable in future discounted by compound interest. Hence, for a debt to be disbursed against the consideration for the time value of money, it needs to have an interest component in it. Further, as can be seen from the Insolvency Committee Report, 2018, the time value of money has two components, i.e., interest or factoring in discount of payment. Though, the Supreme Court has clarified that the word "interest" before the phrase "if any" under the definition of financial debt is not required to file a case under section 7 if there is no interest attached to the loan, however, a lot of clarity is required upon the component of interest which also exist in the phrase "time value of money". Thus, it can be said that the consideration for the time value of money under section 5(8) also includes interest as a major component. Hence, in the humble submission of the authors, the interest constituent is necessary for a debt to qualify as financial debt and the ratio in the case of Narendra Kumar Agarwal v. Monotrone Leasing Private Limited should be taken into consideration which provides that the interest component in a transaction is the time value of money.

Secondly , seeing the factual matrix of the present case in hand, the Appellant/FC in its application has mentioned Rs. 1.56 cr as the total default by the CD. Here, it is important to bring to the notice that the total loan amount sanctioned was Rs. 1.60 cr out of which the CD had only paid Rs. 4 lakhs, thereby making default on Rs. 1.56 cr. Although the loan disbursed was interest-free, the Supreme Court didn't take notice of the same and allowed the application to be admitted in which only the principal amount was given, the principal amount was partly paid, and application was also filed for the principal amount without any interest, thereby implying that the amount disbursed was not in consideration against the time value of money.

Thirdly , the Supreme Court has failed to deliberate upon the point basing which the NCLAT had given its judgment, i.e., the consideration for the time value of money is for the benefits of the FC and not the CD. The Supreme Court has unforeseen this aspect of the judgment by the NCLAT. In the present case, there was no consideration for the time value of money for the FC as the loan agreement was interest-free and the CD was only liable to repay the principal amount even after maturity of the contract, i.e., only Rs. 1.56 cr. Also, the Supreme Court in the case of Pioneer's case has held that the definition of financial debt under section 5(8) should be read as "means and includes" thereby providing an extensive meaning to the definition. This means that clauses (a) to (i) under section 5(8) is an extension of the definition of financial debt and is not an exhaustive list and thus, the substantial part of the definition cannot be ignored. In the present case, the Supreme Court is only putting its reliance on the clause (f) of Section 5 which provides for commercial effect of borrowing but is completing ignoring the principal/substantial part of the definition which provides for the component of time value of money in the financial debt. Hence, the Appellant should not be termed as FC by the Supreme Court and his application should have been rejected.

Conclusion

From the point of view of the authors, it is evident that the Supreme Court's decision in Orator's case can have negative implications as the Court has predominantly based its reasoning taking into consideration Section 5(8)(f) of the IBC only and have ignored the principal aspect of the definition of financial debt, i.e., the consideration for the time value of money. This obstinate view of the Court has created ambiguity and vagueness in the understanding of the substantial part of the definition of financial debt and hence, a much-needed clarification is required on interest being an essential constituent of "time value of money".

Interest necessary part of Financial Debt Following are the judgments by the NCLAT highlighting the fact that the interest component is necessary to constitute a financial debt.

1.

Vishwa Nath Singh (supra), the NCLAT observed that the FC must prove that the loan amount given is a financial debt and was disbursed against the consideration for the time value of money and the payment of interest. The tribunal has used the term "and" in between the words "consideration of time value of money" and "payment of interest", thereby making it a mandatory condition for constituting a financial debt.

2.

Dr. B.V.S. Lakshmi (supra) wherein the Appellate Tribunal held that the for categorising a debt as financial debt it to be against payment of interest and consideration for the time value of money.

3.

Shreyans Realtors (P.) Ltd. (supra) wherein the NCLAT was of the view that if in the agreement the interest component was not accepted by the CD and the CD never paid or undertook to repay the loan with interest, the loan granted will not be termed as financial debt and the creditor will not be called as an FC.

Interest not necessary part of Financial Debt

Following are the judgments by the NCLAT highlighting the fact that the interest component is not necessary to constitute a financial debt.

1.

Shailesh Sangani v. Joel Cardoso [2019] 103 taxmann.com 181/152 SCL 657 : The NCLAT, in this case, had expressly observed that the suffix "if any" before the word "interest" in the definition of financial debt means that element of interest is not an essential requirement for claiming a debt to be a financial debt and further went on to say that the loan disbursed against the consideration for the time value of money "may or may not" have the component of interest attached to it. Lastly, it held that what prima facie is of importance is that the debt should be against the consideration for the time value of money.

2.

Sanjay Kewalramani v. Sunil Parmanand Kewalramani [Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 57 of 2018, dated 12-7-2018]: The Appellate Tribunal while dealing with the matter observed that the loan given by Respondent No. 2 & 3 in the present matter was not against consideration of time value of money and further held that mere granting of the loan will not make the Respondents as FC until they show that they have complied with the substantive definition or any clauses of Section 5(8) of the Code. Also, it held that mere payment of interest for a certain period will not make the debt to be a financial debt as under the IBC.

Hence, from the above-mentioned judgments, it is understood that the tribunals earlier had divided opinions w.r.t. interest being an essential part of the financial debt. However, the Supreme Court in the Orator's case has clarified the status. Now, the settled position of law is that the loans having no interest payable on them will be considered as a financial debt along with the interest payable loans.

CHAPTER 3

ESSENTIAL ELEMENTS OF FINANCIAL DEBT 3.1 Disbursement of Money

The first essential element of financial debt is disbursement. Disbursement refers to the transfer of money from the creditor to the debtor. Financial debt must involve the actual disbursal of funds, which creates a liability on the borrower. Without such disbursement, the transaction cannot ordinarily qualify as financial debt.

3.2Consideration for Time Value of Money

The time value of money is the most important characteristic of financial debt. It reflects the principle that money today is worth more than the same amount in the future. The elements generally are:

Interest payments

Financial returns

Compensation for delayed repayment

In the absence of such consideration, the transaction may not qualify as financial debt.

In the matter of Shivam Agrioils (P.) Ltd. v. Shree Krishna Vanaspati Industries (P.) Ltd. [Company Appeal (AT)(Insolvency) No. 982 of 2022] NCLAT observed that Interest on loan is not the only binding criterion for determining the time value of money for Financial Debt under IBC.

Whether disbursement for the time value of money is an essential ingredient to prove a Financial Debt? – Kesoram Industries Ltd. v. Pratim Bayal [2024] 159 taxmann.com 27 (NCLAT - New Delhi)

Hon'ble NCLAT held that: Disbursement against the consideration for the time value of money has to be proved for a financial debt. There is no disbursement by the Appellant to the Corporate Debtor. When there is no disbursement for the time value of money, essential ingredients to prove a financial debt are missing.

3.3 Commercial Effect of Borrowing

Section 5(8) also includes transactions that have the commercial effect of borrowing. This provision ensures that sophisticated financial arrangements designed to function like loans are also covered under the definition.

Examples include:

Structured finance transactions

Forward sale agreements

Certain investment arrangements

INTRODUCTION

Financial Debt has been clearly defined under the provisions of section 5(8) of the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016 (hereinafter referred to as 'IBC'). Also, in various judgements/orders by different NCLT/NCLAT benches, the definition has been well unleashed. Further, in the matter of Nikhil Mehta & Sons v. AMR Infrastructure (P.) Ltd. [2017] 84 taxmann.com 163/143 SCL 278, the Hon'ble NCLAT has very clearly explained the criteria to be checked for ascertaining if debt is a financial debt or not. Also, it is well settled that while dealing with the application under section 7 of the IBC the Hon'ble Adjudicating Authority(NCLT)has to only focus on the nature of debt i.e. if it is financial debt or not and whether it is due and defaulted and not having existence of any dispute.

In the recent matter of Drip Capital Inc. v. Concord Creations (India) P. Ltd. [Company Appeal (AT) (CH) (Ins.) No. 167 of 2021, dated 8-11-2021], the Hon'ble NCLT Bengaluru Bench in reference to and interpreting certain sayings of various courts in several judgements, considered the financial position of the corporate debtor even though the debt was duly acknowledged, and considering it as solvent granted 6 months' time to the Corporate Debtor to pay the sum and didn't admitted the application to initiate Corporate Insolvency Resolution Process (CIRP).

In this article, we will analyze the judgement(s) of NCLT and NCLAT in the matter of Drip Capital Inc. (supra)

PRE-REQUISITE FOR FINANCIAL DEBT UNDER SECTION 5(8) OF IBC-

The Hon'ble Appellate Tribunal in the matter of Nikhil Mehta & Sons (supra) has very precisely put forth the basic criteria for considering a debt as financial debt in the code which are mentioned as below-

1.

There must be disbursal of some money from the financial creditor to the corporate debtor,

2.

The same must has been disbursed keeping in consideration to time value of money, and

3.

It must fall in any of the transaction mentioned in sub-clauses of Section 5(8) of the Code.

CHECKPOINTS FOR ADMITTING APPLICATION UNDER SECTION 7 OF IBC-

In the matter of Innoventive Industries Ltd. v. ICICI Bank Ltd. [2017] 84 taxmann.com 320/143 SCL 625the Hon'ble Supreme Court in Para 30 of the judgement has very clearly worded that-

"In the case of a corporate debtor who commits a default of a financial debt, the adjudicating authority has merely to see the records of the information utility or other evidence produced by the financial creditor to satisfy itself that a default has occurred. It is of no matter that the debt is disputed so long as the debt is "due" i.e., payable unless interdicted by some law or has not yet become due in the sense that it is payable at some future date."

EMERGING ISSUES AND CONTROVERSIES

5.1 Whether Share Subscription Agreements Can Constitute Financial Debt under IBC?

Share Application Money in the event of non-allotment of shares can be treated as a loan/debt, and such an amount falls under the definition of Financial Debt as defined under Section 5(8) of the Code.

In the matter of Kushan Mitra v. Amit Goel [2022] 136 taxmann.com 313 (NCL-AT), NCLAT held that if the Shares are not allotted within 60 days of receiving the Share Application Money, and if the refund does not take place within 15 days form the expiry of 60 days' time limit, then this amount will be treated as a Deposit, advanced to the Company, which has to be returned by the Company at the rate of 12 percent per annum from the expiry of the 60th day. Thus, the concerned person would receive compensation for the time value of money given to the Company, which changes the nature and character of the money so given. Although the amount was initially paid towards Shares, the equity did not materialise because the allotment was revoked. Thereafter, by operation of law, Section 42(6) of the Companies Act, 2013, the amount has statutorily been given the character of a loan with interest. The same applies to amounts paid as optionally convertible debentures. It was held that share Application Money in the event of non-allotment of shares, attracts interest under Section 42(6) of the Companies Act, 2013 and therefore falls within the ambit of the definition of Financial Debt as defined under Section 5(8) of the Code.

However, after the same, on April 25, 2022, Hon'ble NCLAT in the matter of Pramod Sharma v. Karanaya Heart Care (P.) Ltd. [Comp. App. (AT) (Ins.) Blurring the Lines between Financial Creditor and Operational Creditor In order to qualify as a financial creditor under section 5(8) of the IBC, one should be owed a financial debt6 which includes two conditions, firstly, there should be a debt along with interest, if any, which is disbursed against the consideration for the time value of money,7 and secondly, it should be included in one of the specified categories.8 Moreover, a financial creditor must prove that a default has occurred, which takes place when a debt becomes due and payable as per the proof of claims submitted by the creditor.9 Since a claim/payment is flexible enough to include "recompense",10 an operational creditor who has suffered any harm or has to be compensated will become the stakeholder of the insolvencyprocess.11 With respect to the first requirement, any debt, with or without interest is covered under the scope of Section 5(7) of the code. The time value of money requirement, according to which any money we have right now is worth more than the identical sum in future, due to its potential earning capacity12 is present in any kind of transaction. The Court in the case of DF Deutsche Forfait AG v. Uttam Galva Steel Ltd.13 held that if a party fails to repay within the fixed time, then interest can be claimed over operational debt as well, and it is nowhere said that the operational creditor is barred from claiming interest. Therefore, since the premise of claim is based on whether the "X" has taken something from "Y' with an intention to pay back the value, then the law should be applied in a manner to ensure that it is repaid but not dismissed on the ground of procedural irregularities. We need not stick to the ground that procedural justice is always subservient to substantial justice.14

With respect to the second prong, the authors believe that such an operational creditor is at par with home buyers. It is submitted that since Section 5(8)(f) of the IBC uses the words 'any amount' and 'any other transaction', it means that the amounts that are "raised under transactions and not covered by any of the other clauses", would amount to a financial debt if they had the commercial effect of borrowing, making it a 'catch-all provision'.15 Section 3(33) of the IBC defines a 'transaction' as an agreement or arrangement in writing for the transfer of assets, or funds, goods or services, from or to the corporate debtor. Furthermore, the expression "borrow" means to obtain or receive something, on loan for temporary use, intending to give it, or something equivalent back to the lender.16 A perusal of these definitions shows that the expression borrow is wide enough to include an advance given by operational creditors in the form of their services, workmen/employees in the present case when the payment for the same was neglected by a company to keep its operations afloat. This implies that the same amount was borrowed for 'temporary use' i.e. for honouring their commitments and paying back other creditors as long as they intended to give 'something equivalent' back to the operational creditors. Additionally, the commercial aspect, which means transactions having profit as its main aim is present in such a situation of employees who have not been paid, since the company wants to keep its operations afloat by temporarily borrowing the requisite amount from operational creditors, and the operational creditors demanding interest due to delay in payments.17 Additionally, the proof of claim as per the IBBI (Insolvency Resolution Process for Corporate Persons) Regulations, 2016 can be proved by any contractual document indicating that the amount is due in case of employees or through muster rolls in case of workmen.18 It therefore follows that the employees/workmen in such a situation will be considered as a financial creditor at par with home buyers as per Pioneer since they qualify all the parameters based on which the home buyers have been considered as a financial creditor. Therefore, treating them differently will lead to gross violation of principles of natural justice.19

23. Collusive commercial arrangement between creditors and the corporate debtor wouldn't constitute a financial debt, rules SC

[Phoenix Arc (P.) Ltd. v. Spade Financial Services Ltd. [2021] 124 taxmann.com 24 (SC)]

The Supreme Court in an important ruling in the Phoenix Arc (P.) Ltd. v. Spade Financial Services Ltd. case held that entities having commercial arrangements of collusive nature with the corporate debtor could not be considered financial creditors under the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code (IBC) provisions.

Brief facts

In this case, the operational creditor initiated the corporate insolvency resolution process (CIRP) against AKME Projects Limited under section 9 of the IBC.

As part of the process, the Interim Resolution Professional invited claims. In response to the notice, Spade Financial Services Limited and its subsidiary AAA Landmark Private Limited filed claims as creditors.

Spade filed the claim based on an alleged Memorandum of Understanding executed with the Corporate Debtor, which stated that Inter Corporate Deposits (ICDs) of Rs. 26.55 crore have been granted to the Corporate Debtor by Spade, bearing interest of 24 per cent repayable in terms of the mutual agreement between the parties. AAA filed its claim before the IRP for a sum of Rs. 93.90 crore.

Later, the CoC was constituted on May 22, 2018. On May 25, 2018, the IRP rejected the claim of Spade, inter alia, on the ground that the claim was not in the nature of a financial debt in terms of Section 5(8) of IBC since consideration was absent for the time value of money, i.e., the period of repayment of the claimed ICDs was not stipulated.

The IRP also rejected the claim of AAA on the ground that its claim as a financial creditor in Form C was filed after the expiry of the period for filing such a claim.

Having gone through the National Company Law Tribunal (NCLT) and the National Company Law Appellate Tribunal (NCLAT), the dispute reached the Supreme Court.

Supreme Court

Based on the appeals, the Supreme Court framed three issues for consideration which are as follows:

(a)

Whether Spade and AAA are financial creditors of the Corporate Debtor;

(b)

Whether Spade and AAA are related parties of the Corporate Debtor; and

(c)

Whether Spade and AAA have to be excluded from the CoC.

In the present case, the Court said, there was a finding that AAA and Spade were related parties within the meaning of Section 5(24) at the time when the alleged financial debt based on which they assert a claim to be a part of the CoC was created.

"Further, we have also concluded that the transactions between Spade and AAA on the one hand, and the Corporate Debtor on the other hand, which gave rise to their alleged financial debts were deceitful in nature. Therefore, it is evident that there existed a deeply entangled relationship between Spade, AAA and Corporate Debtor, when the alleged financial debt arose," the Court said, adding, the pervasive influence of the promoter/director of the Corporate Debtor over the concerned entities was evident, and allowing them in the CoC would definitely affect the other independent financial creditors.

"Due to the collusive nature of their transactions alleged to be a financial debt under section 5(8), Spade and AAA cannot be labelled as financial creditors under section 5(7)," it added.

"Section 60 (5) Notwithstanding anything to the contrary contained in any other law for the time being in force, the National Company Law Tribunal shall have jurisdiction to entertain or dispose of

The Hon'ble SC held that a Court or Tribunal has the inherent power to recall an order to ensure justice is served and to prevent misuse of the legal process. Neither the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code (IBC) nor its related Regulations restrict the exercise of this inherent power.

Section 60(5)(c) of the IBC grants authority to the National Company Law Tribunal (NCLT) to address questions of priorities or legal and factual matters related to insolvency proceedings, regardless of any other provisions. Additionally, Rule 11 of the NCLT Rules, 2016 acknowledges the Tribunal's inherent power.

The Hon'ble Court has analysed various decisions on how the Tribunal, or a Court is invested with ancillary or incidental powers: -

In Manohar Lal Chopra v. Rai Bahadur Rao Raja Seth Hiralal3 while interpreting section 151 CPC it is observed that the inherent power has not been conferred upon the court; it is a power inherent in the Court by virtue of its duty to do justice between the parties before it.

In Grindlays Bank Ltd. v. Central Govt. Industrial Tribunal4 it is a well-known rule of statutory construction that a Tribunal or body should be considered to be endowed with such ancillary or incidental powers as are necessary to discharge its functions effectively for the purpose of doing justice between the parties. In a case of this nature, we are of the view that the Tribunal should be considered as invested with such incidental or ancillary powers unless there is any indication in the statute to the contrary.

In a recent decision (i.e., Union Bank of India v. Dinakar T. INTRODUCTION

The IBC was introduced to consolidate insolvency laws and provide a time-bound mechanism for the resolution of distressed companies. The Code seeks to maximise asset value, promote entrepreneurship, and balance stakeholders' interests.

A critical feature of the insolvency framework under the IBC is the classification of creditors, primarily into financial creditors and operational creditors. This classification determines the rights and powers of creditors in the Corporate Insolvency Resolution Process (CIRP).

Among these, financial creditors hold a dominant position, as they control the Committee of Creditors (CoC), which decides the corporate debtor's fate. Therefore, determining whether a claim qualifies as "financial debt" under Section 5(8) is central to insolvency jurisprudence.

CHAPTER 1

IMPORTANCE OF FINANCIAL CREDITORS IN THE INSOLVENCY PROCESS

Financial creditors occupy a significant role within the insolvency framework. They possess the right to initiate insolvency proceedings under Section 7 of the IBC and are the primary decision-makers during CIRP.

The Committee of Creditors, which comprises financial creditors, is responsible for evaluating and approving resolution plans. The CoC exercises its commercial wisdom in determining whether the corporate debtor should be revived or liquidated.

Section 5(7) of the IBC defines financial creditors- "means any person to whom a financial debt is owed and includes a person to whom such debt has been legally assigned or transferred to."

CHAPTER 2

MEANING AND SCOPE OF FINANCIAL DEBT

Section 5(8) of the IBC defines financial debt as: "A debt along with interest, if any, which is disbursed against the consideration for the time value of money."

The provision further provides an inclusive list of transactions that may constitute financial debt. These include:

Money borrowed against payment of interest

Amounts raised through credit facilities

Debentures, bonds, or other similar instruments

Finance or capital leases

Any transaction having the commercial effect of borrowing

In the matter of Agarwal Polysacks Ltd. v. K.K. Agro Foods and Storage Ltd. [2023] 155 taxmann.com 358 (NCLAT – New Delhi) A question which rose before NCLAT was – "Whether to prove a Financial Debt, a Financial Creditor has to enter into a 'written' Financial Contract?".

Hon'ble NCLAT held that - A bare perusal of Part V of Form-1 indicates that particulars of financial debt, several documents, records and evidence of default have been referred to, which documents are contemplated to be particulars of financial debt. Use of the word "or" in Regulation 8(2)(a) indicates that by any of the documents referred to in Sub-regulation (2), the existence of debt can be proved. A financial contract supported by financial statements as evidence of the debt is one of the documents contemplated in Regulation 8(2), but that is not an exclusive requirement for proving the existence of debt. When the statutory scheme as reflected in the Application to Adjudicating Authority Rules, 2016 and CIRP Regulations, 2016 is looked upon, it is clear that financial debt can be proved from other relevant documents, and it is not mandatory that a written financial contract can be the only basis for proving the financial debt."

The Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016 ("Code") was enacted for providing a comprehensive and uniform insolvency legislation by replacing the then prevailing ineffective and inadequate insolvency regime. Recently, the Economic Survey highlighted that, for the first time, India has leaped 30 spots to break into the top 100 in the World Bank's Ease of Doing Business Report, 20181. Also, India jumped 33 places in insolvency indices due to the legislative reforms in insolvency regime2.

For giving more teeth to the Code, certain amendments were made to Code by way of the Insolvency and Bankruptcy (Amendment) Act, 20183. Thereafter, for the purpose of evaluating the law and ascertain the key practical challenges in the implementation of the Code, the Government constituted a formal committee known as the Insolvency Law Committee ("Committee") on 16 November, 2017.

The 'Report of the Insolvency Law Committee'4 ("Report") prepared by the Committee has taken into account the market practices, legal principles, international jurisprudence and the views of various stakeholders to provide the following key recommendations to amend the Code:

I. Home-Buyers as Financial Creditors

While deliberating on this issue, the Committee placed reliance on Nikhil Mehta & Sons v. AMR Infrastructure Ltd.5 in which the home buyers were held to be financial creditors as the arrangement between the home buyers and the seller of the apartments was such that the latter had committed to pay assured returns to the former till the possession of the property was handed over. The Committee noted that significant amount of money is raised from the home buyers and is utilised for financing the construction of assets for a real estate project. On failure of completion of such project, the amount is repaid based on time value of money. Therefore, the amount so raised may be classified as 'financial debt' and the home buyers as 'financial creditors'. The Committee however cautioned that not all forward sale or purchase transactions can be classified as 'financial debt'.

II. Interim Finance

Interim finance is defined as a financial debt raised by Insolvency Resolution Professional ("IRP") for financing the cost of going through the Corporate Insolvency Resolution Process ("CIRP")6. Also, since 'financial debt' means 'debt along with interest'7 therefore interest will be charged on any amount raised as interim finance. As per R. 27 of Insolvency and Bankruptcy Board of India (Liquidation Process) Regulations, 2016, interest on interim finance is only calculated till the liquidation commencement date.

Since Interim finance is one of the most important aspects of CIRP therefore interest on interim finance must be calculated for one year after the liquidation commencement date or until repayment (whichever is earlier). This amount should be distributed in priority in order to encourage early repayment and preferential treatment of interim finance.

III. Regulatory dues vis-à-vis Operational Debts

The Committee noted that in case any claim arises due to non-payment by a corporate debtor in lieu any goods or services provided by a regulatory body then such debt may be categorised as 'operational debt' on case to case basis. Also, the regulators have wide ranging powers to recover their dues, therefore, regulatory dues are not required to be included within the purview of 'operational debt'8.

IV. "Payment" or "Repayment"

With respect to the term 'repayment' as provided in the definition of operational debt, the Committee recommended that such term should be substituted by the term 'payment' as the latter is of much wider import than the former. The term 'payment' means "performance of an obligation by the delivery of money or some other valuable thing accepted in partial or full discharge of the obligation". The term 'repay' means "to pay back" or "refund" and the term 'repayment' means "the act of repaying". Accordingly, appropriate amendments have been proposed in other provisions of the Code where words "repayment", "repaid" or "repay" have been used.

This period has witnessed the setting-up of the eco-system for the Code to function: the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Board of India (IBBI), National Company Law Tribunal (NCLT), development of the profession of insolvency professionals and establishment of information utilities (IU).

Being a new Act, some problems in its implementation were felt just after few months of its operation. Immediate amendments were made firstly by an ordinance, which was replaced by the Insolvency and Banking Code (Amendment) Act, 2018, which was made effective from 23.11.17. A new ordinance has since been promulgated, which is being considered in later discussion.

The Committee examined various provisions of the IBC and has given an exhaustive report on various provisions of IBC, which it felt, needed change. In India, inter-corporate loans are important sources of funds for many companies. Often inter-company loans have no written terms. Many loans to wholly owned subsidiaries often bear no (or a below market) interest rate; and/or do not have a fixed repayment date. Such features may pose real practical challenges when applying the classification and impairment provisions of Ind AS 109 Financial Instruments in separate financial statements.

Classification and measurement under Ind AS 109

Under Ind AS 109, a company is required to assess whether an inter-company loan receivable can be classified and subsequently measured at amortised cost. Ind AS 109 permits classification as amortised cost only if the instrument meets both the:

Business model test; and

'SPPI' contractual cash flow characteristics test.

It must be also noted that intercompany loan receivables don't qualify for the simplified approach to impairment available under Ind AS 109, and so the general approach (generally referred to as the three-bucket approach) must be applied when calculating the expected credit loss ('ECL'). These rules are complex enough to apply, but will prove particularly difficult in the absence of a contractual arrangement, as illustrated in the examples given below. A contractual arrangement may take different forms (written, oral, implied, explicit) but should have the following essential features: Offer and Acceptance; Consideration; Intention to create legal relations; Certainty of terms.

In India, typically, lending scenario considerations include:

-

Written agreement (fixed term or repayable on-demand): Consider whether a demand feature is genuine if the lender does not intend, and the circumstances do not indicate, calling repayment for many years.

-

Oral or implicit terms: Written confirmation of the terms

-

No agreed repayment terms: No documented formal terms

There are no specific issues that should arise when intercompany loans are given on normal commercial terms. There may not be any significant challenge with respect to meeting the first 'business model' test under Ind AS 109. However, issues may arise when considering the second 'SPPI' test when there are no formal terms, the terms are limited, or the terms are off-market.

'SPPI' test requires a loan to give rise to cash flows on 'specified dates' that are solely payments of principal and 'interest on the principal amount outstanding'. In practice, it's not always easy to determine the 'specified date' or what the return is as many group companies lend to other group companies without any written agreement, or if written, are not explicit with respect to a repayment date, or the repayment date is contingent on a future event. For example:

-

On-demand loans are repayable when demanded and so the 'specified date' is 'when demanded'. Where it is assumed, in the absence of this being formally stated, that the loan is repayable on demand, it is better to be documented between the parties.

-

Even when timing of repayment is contingent on a specified event occurring, the repayment date is nevertheless 'specified' as being the contingent event.

-

Where a contingent event only impacts the timing of repayment and not the contractual cash flows, then the SPPI test can still be met where the cash flows are solely principal and interest.

-

Interest-free terms do not fail the SPPI test even though the contractual cash flows are just repayment of the principal. Principal is defined in Ind AS 109 as the 'fair value of the financial asset at initial recognition' rather than the gross paramount. Interest will therefore be imputed for accounting purposes, so that interest-free loans have both a principal and interest for Ind AS 109 purposes

-

Some more unusual terms may not be consistent with a basic lending arrangement; eg interest calculated by reference to the borrower's profits will fail the SPPI test.

ECL provision is determined by taking into account the amount and the timing of payments and by considering both the possibility of a credit loss occurring and the possibility that no credit loss occurs, even if the most likely outcome is no credit loss. For these reasons, an impairment provision will always exist, even for intercompany loans receivables that are repayable on-demand, although it may not be material. However, there are generally some practical challenges arising from the need to consider the timing of payments and the probability of a credit loss occurring when repayment terms are fluid or not explicit. For example:

-

Determining when a default, such as becoming past due, occurs.

-

Lack of comparable default patterns from other intercompany loan receivables to consider, and so greater reliance on current and forecast information.

However, the impairment provisions of Ind AS 109 will be difficult to apply to those without formal repayment terms and so it is recommended that companies shall document their understanding of the lending arrangement to reflect its substance and so better enable the application of the standard. Tax implications and repercussions under Companies Act, 2013 also need consideration.

CIRP against Indus under section 7 of the IBC, was justified, the reasoning adopted by the NCLT in doing so was flawed. The NCLT dismissed the application on the grounds that since there is a dispute between the parties, it is not satisfied that a default has occurred. Had NCLT first inquired that whether there exists a financial debt; and whether Kotak is a financial creditor, there would not have been any need for determining the existence of default. As per section 7 of the IBC, an application for initiation of CIRP against a corporate debtor can be filed by a financial creditor. According to section 5(7) of the IBC, financial creditor is a person to whom financial debt is owed. According to section 5(8) of the IBC, there are two essential elements for any transaction to be termed as 'financial debt' i.e. 1) It should be a debt along with interest, which is disbursed against the consideration for the time value of money; and 2) It may include any of the events enumerated in sub clauses (a) to (i). On conjoint reading of section 5(7) and 5(8) of the IBC, it can be said that a person is not entitled to initiate CIRP under section 7 of the IBC unless financial debt is owed to him.

Whether failure to redeem OCRPS would fall within the ambit of financial debt?

According to section 5(8)(c) of the IBC, if the amount is raised by issuance of bonds, debentures, or any similar instrument, then such a transaction falls within the ambit of financial debt. There is a fundamental difference between the amount raised by issuing debentures and the amount raised by issuing OCRPS. The distinction was emphasized by the Calcutta High Court in Hindustan Gas and Industries Ltd. v. CIT, [1979] 1 Taxman 546/117 ITR 549 where it observed that in cases where money is raised by way of issuing redeemable convertible preference shares, such amount goes to the share capital of the company, and where money is raised by issuing debentures, such amount goes to loan capital of the company. Since the amount contributed by preference shareholders goes to the share capital, the company does not become debtor for such payment. In contrast, the amount raised by way of issuance of debentures goes to the loan capital of the company and consequently such debenture holders act as creditors of the company and are entitled to fixed rate of interest whether there are profits or not. In view of the above, it can be argued that there is no element of 'consideration for time value of money' when money is raised by issuing OCRPS as preference shareholders are not entitled to any fixed rate of interest but entitled to get dividends only out of profits. Therefore, it can be concluded that transaction of raising money by way of issuing OCRPS will not fall within the ambit of financial debt under section 5(8) of the IBC.

Whether Kotak can be termed as a financial creditor?

Moreover, the owner of a preference shareholder cannot be termed as a creditor of the company. The above view was fortified by Bombay High Court in Aditya Prakash Entertainment (P.) Ltd. v. Magikwand Media Pvt. Ltd.,[Co. Petition No. 404 of 2016, dated 15-3-2018] wherein the court observed that the shareholders of redeemable preference shares of a company do not become creditors of the company if their shares are not redeemed at appropriate time. Further, Gujarat High Court in Anarkali Sarabhai v. CIT, [1997] 90 Taxman 509/224 ITR 422 (SC) had observed that where the company defaults in redeeming the preference shares, holder of the redeemable preference shares cannot compel the company to redeem the shares by suing in debt for the return of its capital.

In the present case, Kotak has filed an application under section 7 of the IBC on the grounds that Indus has failed to redeem the OCRPS. From the foregoing, it is clear that neither Kotak can be classified as financial creditor of Indus nor failure of Indus to redeem OCRPS would fall within the ambit of financial debt. Therefore, had NCLT first determined whether there exists a financial debt or not, there would not have been any need to ascertain existence of default. Consequently, there would not have been any need to refer parties to arbitration in a petition filed under section 7 of the IBC.

IBC vis a vis Arbitration Act

In the present case, although, NCLT framed the question as to whether the provisions of Arbitration Act will prevail over the provisions of the IBC, it did not give a conclusive finding on the same, and kept the question open for debate in future cases. Despite, section 238 of the IBC provides for overriding effect of the IBC over any other law, the provisions of the IBC will not prevail over the provisions of the Arbitration Act in all the cases, and will vary from case to case.

NCLAT Distinguishes between Home-Buyer Simpliciter and Home-Buyers Under 'Committed Monthly Return Plan'

5. In a recent decision dated 21st July 2017, by the National Company Law Appellate Tribunal in Nikhil Mehta & Sons v. AMR Infrastructure Ltd. [2017] 84 taxmann.com 163 (NCLT - New Delhi), the Hon'ble Appellate Tribunal noted that pursuant to the Memorandum of Understanding dated 12th April 2008, reached between the appellant and the respondent-corporate debtor, in respect of booking and payment of Rs. 36,00,000/- for a commercial shop which was being developed by the respondent-corporate debtor, the debtor had treated the appellant as an investor and had agreed to a payment of a monthly 'Committed Interest/Return Plan'. The Hon'ble Appellate Tribunal also noted that from the annual return of the corporate-debtor and Form 16A with regard to tax deducted at source from the said returns under the "Committed Interest/Return Plan", the corporate-debtor had treated the appellant as an "investor" and borrowed the amount pursuant to sale/purchase agreement for their commercial purpose, treating it at par with "loan" in their return. Thereby, the amount invested by the appellant came within the meaning of "financial debt" as defined under section 5(8)(f) of the I&B Code 2016. It was further noted by the NCLAT that the amount disbursed by the appellant was "against the consideration of the time-value of the money" and that the respondent-corporate-debtor raised the amount by way of a sale/purchase agreement having a commercial effect of borrowing. Therefore, the NCLAT held that the respondent-corporate-debtor had treated the amount so raised/borrowed as commitment charges under the head "financial cost". Thus, the NCLAT held the appellant as a "financial creditor" within the meaning of section 5(7) of the I&B Code 2016, and remitted the case back to the adjudicating authority for further proceedings under section 7 of the I&B Code 2016, provided the appellant's application was otherwise complete in all respects.

Thus, the aforesaid NCLAT decision of Nikhil Mehta & Sons case (supra) makes a distinction between flat-buyers who had booked and paid money to the builder/corporate debtor for purchasing a flat on one hand and those flat-buyers who made payments for flats under a "Committed Monthly Return Plan" agreed to by the builder/corporate-debtor on the other hand, as such latter category of flat-buyers would be classified as "financial creditors" and would be entitled to maintain insolvency proceedings against the concerned builder/corporate-debtor under section 7 of the I&B Code 2016.

Following principles determines the validity of the acknowledgement of debt under IBC:

1.

Such acknowledgement must refer to a present subsisting liability.

2.

It was also asserted that the entries in balance sheet are made under the statutory force but there is no compulsion to make admission of debt in the balance sheet, therefore, such an admission would not constitute an acknowledgement for the purpose of section 18 of the Limitation Act.

However, the SCI upheld the Calcutta High Court Judgement of Padman Tea Co Ltd., that the balance sheet is prepared which ought to be signed and approved by the Board of Directors as per the section 134 of the Companies Act, 2013 further the copies of the balance sheet along with the Director's Report and Auditor's Report are to be sent to the Registrar of the Companies. The court considered the importance of the notes annexed or forming part of such financial statements as per section 134 of the Companies Act. In the case of Bhajan Singh Samra v. Wimpy International Ltd. [2011] 16 taxmann.com 329/[2012] 111 SCL 1 (Delhi),the court held that balance sheet would amount to an acknowledgement of debt if such entries made in the Balance Sheet.

However, in order to determine whether entries in the balance sheet are unqualified or unequivocal concerning the liability, the notes forming part of such financial statements can qualify an entry in the balance sheet as an acknowledgement of debt, also, attention is to be given to the observation made in the Auditor's Report for any specific comment made on the entry reflecting such debt. Therefore, whether an entry in a balance sheet amounts to acknowledgement of debt and such acknowledgement must be based on case-to-case basis.

Other documents that Constitute Acknowledgement

1.

Debentures are the instruments which acknowledges debts, as these are the documents carry indebtedness of a specific sum under the purview of section 18 of the Limitation Act.

2.

Cheque given to pay dues is an acknowledgement of debt.

3.

Written statement in an earlier suit is considered as an acknowledge of debt.

4.

E-mails acknowledging the debt creating a legal relationship is considered as acknowledge of debt.

Reasoning for upholding the decision of the Adjudicating Authority

The NCLAT further noted that in the present case of "Ferro Alloys", as per clause 1.2 of the 'Deed of Guarantee' dated 22nd January, 2015, there is a clear cut stipulation that "on the failure of principal borrower to pay and/or discharge the obligations, the guarantor shall, forthwith upon demand, pay to Rural Electrification Corporation Limited (Financial Creditor) without demur or protest", the amount stated in the demand made by Rural Electrification Corporation Limited to the guarantor thereby invoking the guarantee.

Admittedly, the guarantee was invoked by 'Rural Electrification Corporation Limited' against 'Ferro Alloys Corporation Ltd.' and demand was raised on 27th October, 2015 calling upon 'Ferro Alloys Corporation Ltd.' to pay the amount due within 21 days. Since then, Ferro Alloys Corporation Ltd. (Corporate Guarantor) became a 'corporate debtor' of 'Rural Electrification Corporation Limited' (Financial Creditor). In its Annual Report for the year ending 2016-17, 'Ferro Alloys Corporation Ltd.' has shown a sum of Rs. 517.90 crores payable to the 'financial creditor'. Therefore, it became clear that 'Ferro Alloys Corporation Ltd.' admitted the 'debt' and in absence of payment, there was no doubt to hold that there is a 'default'. The NCLAT also noted that the provision of the IBC do not bar a 'financial creditor' from initiating 'corporate insolvency resolution process' against the 'guarantor', who comes within the meaning of 'corporate debtor'. The aforesaid matter can be noticed from the statutory inter-se rights, obligations and liabilities of:

(i)

A surety qua the creditor (the relationship as defined under the Indian Contract Act); or

(ii)

Guarantor qua financial creditor.

It was argued before the NCLAT that the IBC does not exclusively delineate and/or prescribe any inter-se rights, obligation and liabilities of a guarantor qua 'financial creditor'. Thus, in absence of any express provision providing for inter-se rights, obligation and liabilities of guarantor qua 'financial creditor' under the IBC, the same will have to be noticed from the provisions of the Indian Contract Act, which exclusively and elaborately deals with the same.

4. CCD under the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016 ['IBC']

4.1 Debentures are prima facie considered to be financial debt as per the definition of financial debt given in the IBC. As per section 5(8), financial debt means a debt along with interest, if any, which is disbursed against the consideration for the time value of money and includes- (c) "any amount raised pursuant to any note purchase facility or the issue of bonds, notes, debentures, loan stock or any similar instrument";

Thus, it is interesting to know the classification of CCD under the IBC in a case where a Financial Creditor holding debentures of the Corporate Debtors.

4.2 The question was raised before the Hon'ble Supreme Court in IFCI Ltd. v. Sutanu Sinha [2023] 156 taxmann.com 681 (SC) whether CCDs can be treated in essence as a form of debt instead of an equity share. The court, having examined the definition of debt in the Code as a 'liability or obligation in respect of a claim,' concluded that the appellant can be deemed a part-owner (i.e. an equity participant) of the company. This is because (as per the subscription agreement), if the company fails to buy back the shares within a specific period, the debentures can automatically be converted into equity shares.

4.3 As a result, the company does not have the right to claim any dues or debt from the Corporate Debtor ("CD"). Therefore, in case such an instrument is treated as debt, it would go against the agreement terms. The court further went on to hold that the investment is essentially a form of debenture which must be compulsorily converted into equity shares, and thus, not specified to be considered as a financial debt under certain circumstances that means it will be part of equity.

4.4 Therefore, it has become a settled position of law that when an investment is made like debentures which are compulsory convertible into equity it will be treated as equity.

4.5 Whereas, the issue relating to Optionally Convertible Debentures [OCD] is still unclear wherein the judiciary has taken to different contradicting opinions. The Hon'ble NCLAT in MAIF Investments India PTE. Ltd. v. Bharath Energy (Utkal) Ltd. [2019] SCC Online NCLAT 825 held that OCDs are considered as financial debt in view of Section 5(8) of the code.

5. CCD under the Foreign Exchange Management Act [FEMA]

5.1 The investment by a non-resident in an Indian Company, in any form, is regulated by the Foreign Exchange Management Act, 1999 read with Foreign Exchange Management (Transfer or Issue of a Security by a Person Resident outside India) Regulations, 2017 as amended in 2019 ('FEMA Regulations').

5.2 Regulation 2(xviii) defines 'Foreign Investment' to mean any investment made by a person resident outside India on a repatriable basis in 'capital instruments' of an Indian company or to the capital of an LLP.

5.3 Regulation 2(v) 'defines Capital instruments' to mean equity shares, 'debentures', preference shares and share warrants issued by an Indian company. The Explanation further provides that the expression 'Debentures' means fully, compulsorily and mandatorily convertible debentures. Thus, the CCDs which are fully and mandatorily convertible into equity, are considered as 'capital instruments' being at par with equity shares.

5.4 As fully, compulsorily and mandatorily convertible debentures alone are regarded as capital instruments, optionally convertible or partially convertible debentures are treated as debt instruments under the FEMA Regulations. These debentures which do not fall within the ambit of 'capital instruments would have to conform to the guidelines on External Commercial Borrowings, i.e. Foreign Exchange Management (Borrowing and Lending in Foreign Exchange) Regulations, 2000.

6. CCD under Income Tax Law

CCDs are treated as equity rather than debt under FEMA regulations and IBC from the date on which the CCDs are issued. We can analyse from the viewpoint of income tax law whether till the time of conversion can the same be recharacterised as equity.

6.1 Allowability of interest deductions

The re-characterization of CCDs as equity and the disallowance of the interest expenditure claimed thereof, has been an issue for consideration under the IT Act.

Concluding Remarks

5. The reason given for the dismissal of the case raises debatable issue. To say that I&B Code is not an Act for recovery of claim may not be very correct. Explanation to s. 7 of the IBC clarifies that for the purpose of clause (i) of s.7, a default includes a default in respect of a financial debt owned not only to the applicant-financial creditor but to any other financial creditor of the corporate debtor. Hence, limitation period provided for the recovery of debts must apply to IBC also. Not to adhere to this proposition would lead to uncertainties, inter-alia, to a situation, where the swords of claims can continue to hang on the heads of corporate debtors indefinitely, which could not be said to be a very happy position. Hence, limitation periods need to apply to proceedings under the IBC also. There have to be limits for processes under the Code.

In a span of 2 years, the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016 ("Code") has witnessed two Ordinances viz. the IBC Ordinance 2018 and the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code (Amendment) Ordinance, 2017("IBC Ordinance 2017") which received President's assent on November 23, 20172 and became the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code (Amendment) Act, 2018 ("IBC Amendment Act") on January 18, 20183.

The IBC Ordinance 2018 has been formulated with the intent to balance the interest of stakeholders especially home buyers and micro, small and medium enterprises, promoting resolution over liquidation of the corporate debtor and streamlining provisions relating to eligibility of resolution applicant. The IBC Ordinance 2018 is a result of the Insolvency Law Committee ("ILC") report dated March 26, 20184. The ILC was set up on November 16, 2017 to make recommendations to the Government on issues arising from the implementation of the Code.

Home buyers to be treated as financial creditor:

The definition being an inclusive one, means a debt along with interest, if any, disbursed against the consideration for the time value of money. The Committee's mandate

3.1 The Committee was constituted with the mandate of making recommendations on (a) issues arising from the functioning and implementation of the Code; (b) issues that may impact the efficiency of the corporate insolvency and resolution and liquidation framework prescribed under the Code; and (c) any other relevant matters as it deems necessary.

Furthermore, on verification of the financial statements of the real estate developer, it was noticed that the real estate developer itself treated the amount paid to the home buyer as commitment charges under the head financial cost. Hon'ble NCLAT after considering all the facts of the case, held that the amount received by the real estate developer from the home buyer by way of sale and purchase agreement have a commercial effect of 'borrowing' and hence it is clear that the amount was paid by the home buyer against the consideration for time value of money. Hon'ble NCLAT held the home buyer to be the Financial Creditor eligible for instating insolvency resolution process against the real estate developer.

Albeit, pursuant to the introduction of Form F home buyers could file their claim before the interim resolution professional, however because the home buyers are not 'financial creditors' and not even 'operational creditors', the home buyers would be paid only after the secured and operational creditors are repaid.
