(c) Interest-free loans – This is undoubtedly one of the more debatable issues in the space of intragroup financial transactions. Often intra-group arrangements are designed so that interest on loan or guarantee fees is not charged due to various reasons like the poor credit position of the subsidiary, loan proceeds to be used for acquisition purposes furthering the interests of the lender (parent) etc. While there may be plausible reasons for not charging interest, defending the position before the Revenue can pose significant challenges in the absence of strong commercial reasons and robust documentation. The OECD Guidelines acknowledge that benefit accruing to a borrower on being part of a larger group ('implicit support') should not necessitate a charge and there can be situations where a debt provided by the parent can be construed as a 'shareholder service' or 'quasi-equity'4. Still, it would not be correct to conclude that the provision of loans or guarantees without charging interest or fees can always be defended by this argument. In fact, the Indian Transfer Pricing jurisprudence has more often than not quashed the argument of 'quasi-equity'5 and computed interest rates/guarantee fees based on the arm's length principle6. Hence unless several conditions like the use of funds, presence of relevant clauses in the loan agreement, regulatory restrictions on infusing equity etc. are met, an interest-free loan or zero guarantee fee situation would be considered as non-arm's length.

(d)

Internal guarantees: service provided or shareholder transaction?According to the OECD Guidelines: "the question whether an intra group service has been rendered…should depend on whether the [guarantee] provides a group [company] with economic or commercial value… This can be determined by considering whether an independent enterprise in comparable circumstances would have been willing to pay for the [guarantee]…"This basically means that for each intra-group guarantee (i) the underlying reason for the guarantee should be established and (ii) it should be determined whether the guarantee creates a benefit for which the guaranteed group company should pay a fee. As further explained in the OECD Guidelines, the guarantee fee should be established by taking into account the perspective of both the guaranteed group company and the guarantor (i.e. the group company issuing the guarantee). That is, the underlying reason for the guarantee should take both these perspectives into account. In the event that a third party (the creditor) would not under any circumstances have been willing to enter into the transaction with the guaranteed company (the debtor) had the guarantee not been issued, it could be concluded that the guaranteed company would not have been able to enter into the transaction on a standalone basis. In other words, the guaranteed group company is not considered by the third party to be financially strong enough to enter into this transaction on a standalone basis. In this case, the guarantee may have been provided by the guarantor in its capacity as a shareholder, as no third party would appear willing to accept the risk associated with the transaction. Hence, the intra-group guarantee may not qualify as a service being rendered and a guarantee fee would not be appropriate. As a further consequence, in many countries a loss resulting from such a guarantee being invoked may not be deductible. In India, however, the concept of 'shareholder services' has failed to cut ice with the Revenue authorities7, though the taxpayer at times, have obtained limited relief in the way of reversal of guarantee fee chargeable through external bank quotes by the Transfer Pricing Officer etc.

(e)

Hybrids: debt or equity? – Hybrid instruments are ones that encapsulate the characteristics of both debt and equity. A perfect example would be compulsorily convertible debentures ('CCDs'), which are generally structured in a way to provide interest repayments to the investor over a fixed period, and convert to equity shares on the expiry of the term. The conversion ratios are usually fixed during the issuance of the instrument itself. One of the preferred ways of financing debt for acquisition, CCDs have been frequently used. The advantage of the instrument lies in its characterization, as it is characterized as equity from a Foreign Direct Investment perspective8, yet from a tax perspective interest deductions are allowed on CCDs. However, while designing these instruments, adequate precautions must be taken so that the nature of the instrument is not construed as equity. The conversion ratio as well as the valuation might be scrutinized at the time of conversion, in case the market value of the equity shares at that point in time varies from the time of issuance.

C can never be treated as an exercise under its Commercial wisdom. It is a matter of applying the law of IBC, and if such factor is left to CoC, there would be a serious conflict of interest. Whether a person or entity is "Financial Creditor" as defined in Section 5(7) or "Operational Creditor" as defined in Section 5(20) is a matter of applying the law to facts. It cannot be a matter of voting. However, the Appellate Authority find that the Order of the NCLT that 'BVN Trader is a Financial Creditor' is not totally based on the decision of the 'CoC'. The NCLT has determined the status of 'BVN Traders' as a Financial Creditor "in view of provisions and the fact situation". It would have been ideal and rather expected that NCLT should have recorded reasons also, instead of taking a short cut by taking the support of Resolution of CoC.

Analyzing the Order passed by the NCLT relying upon the decision of CoC

In the instant Appeal, Rajnish Jain ('the Appellant') is seeking a declaration that 'BVN Traders' is not a 'Financial Creditors.' As per Section 5(7) of the Code, only such Creditor could be the 'Financial Creditor' of the 'Corporate Debtor' to whom a financial debt is owed by the 'Corporate Debtor,' and as per Section 5(8) of the Code, the critical requirement of the financial debt is disbursal against the 'Consideration for the time value of money'. The reliance was put on the judgments Pioneer Urban Land & Infrastructure Ltd. v. Union of India5, Swiss Ribbons Ltd.6 etc.

In the present case the record shows that the Appellant Company is a borrower, and the loan amount was directly disbursed to Appellant's Company for which the title deed was deposited with the BVN Traders. In the said transaction time value of money is unambiguously involved, and the Appellant Company's liability is regarding the debt owed by it. It is reiterated that the Appellant Company had raised the said amount from the BVN Traders to meet its working Capital Requirement. Hence the BVN Traders is a Financial Creditor within the meaning of Sections 5(7) and 5(8) of the Code. The transaction involved in the present case meets the root ingredients/basic element of 'financial debt' within the meaning of the Code.

Thus, the tribunal held that the Order of the NCLT dated 23rd Jan, 2020 is correct and needs no interference. However, it set aside the reasoning, relying on the decision of CoC for holding BVN Traders as Financial Creditor.

Conclusion

Many of the resolutions passed by the CoC at the 4th, 7th, and 8th meetings of the CoC, according to the NCLAT, were outside of their authority, rights, and duties. Furthermore, the CoC's action of sitting in appeal over the Impugned Order and passing resolutions to the contrary was ruled unconstitutional. It was also decided that the CoC's Second Resolution was illegal because it was based on the foul reconstitution of the CoC. The Impugned Order was upheld to the point that it made Respondent a financial creditor whereas on the other hand, it overturned the NCLT's logic. The NCLAT based its reasoning on the factors, conclusions, and instructions set forth in the Judgment.

Abstract

The Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code 2016 did away with the requirement of assessing the financial health of a company before initiating the Corporate Insolvency Resolution Process in order to further the aim of timely disposal of cases. The Hon'ble Supreme Court in Vidarbha Industries Power Ltd. v. Axis Bank Ltd [2022] 140 taxmann.com 252, however, has reinstated this requirement in case of admitting the applications filed by the financial creditors under section 7 of the Code.

This judgment may benefit certain sectors but is likely to defeat the very purpose for which the code was brought in. The Court through this judgment made it mandatory to admit the applications filed by the Operational Creditors whereas the applications filed by the Financial Creditors may or may not be admitted depending on the discretion of the Adjudicating Authority. Thus, the judgment is also likely to distort the settled order of preference of Financial Creditors over Operational Creditors under the code and is likely to result in unnecessary delays.

The Supreme Court went with the literal interpretation of the code without taking into context and purpose of the same. This judgment is likely to cause confusion due to lack of proper guidelines and may even turn the clock to pre-IBC period.

Introduction

The Financial Creditors ("FCs") and Operational Creditors ("OCs") of a corporate debtor ("CD") are empowered under S.7 and S. 9 of Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016 ("IBC"/ "Code") respectively to file an application for initiating a Corporate Insolvency Resolution Process ("CIRP") before National Company Law Tribunal ("NCLT"). The Hon'ble Supreme Court("SC") of India in its landmark ruling of Innoventive Industries Ltd. v. ICICI Bank Ltd. [2017] 84 taxmann.com 320/143 SCL 625 (SC) pronounced that according to S.7, if the Adjudicating Authority ("AA") is satisfied with the existence of a debt and a default, and no disciplinary proceedings lie against the proposed interim resolution professional, then the AA is bound to admit the application unless the application is incomplete.

However, the SC in its recent verdict of Vidarbha Industries Power Ltd. (supra) while dealing with the issue concerning the nature of S.7(5)(a) of the IBC, conferred a discretionary power on the NCLT not to admit a CIRP application filed by a FC even if it is satisfied that a debt exists and the CD is in default. The SC observed that the legislature deliberately used the expression "may admit" in S.7(5)(a), whereas the expression "shall admit" has been used in S.9(5) in order to convey a different meaning therefore intending section S.7(5)(a) to be discretionary while S.9(5) to be mandatory.

This post, therefore, seeks to examine the Vidarbha Industries judgment in the light of the objective behind the Code, which is speedy recovery and revival of financially distressed entities. Further, it tries to analyze its impact on the IBC regime and address the legal conundrum resulting therefrom.

Judgment & Analysis: A case of inconsistent precedents

Vidarbha Industries, the CD is a power generation company operating a coal-fired thermal power plant in Maharashtra. Aggrieved with the decision of the Maharashtra Electricity Regulatory Commission ("MERC") with regard to the determination of tariff, Vidarbha industries challenged the MERC's decision before the Appellate Tribunal for Electricity ("APTEL"). The APTEL allowed the appeal and consequently Vidarbha was to receive a sum of INR 1,730 crores in terms of APTEL's order.

Subsequently, Axis Bank Limited ("ABL"), the FC filed an application before the National Company Law Tribunal ("NCLT") u/s 7(2) of the Code to initiate CIRP against Vidarbha for non-payment of its debt amounting to INR 553 crore. Vidarbha challenged the admission of CIRP on the ground that its inability to repay the dues of ABL was directly attributable to the MERC's failure to pay INR 1,730 crore on account of litigation pending before the SC against the APTEL's order. Hence, Vidarbha sought a stay of the CIRP proceedings until the question in the appeal regarding the liability of MERC to pay the said amount is resolved by the SC.

The NCLT as well as the NCLAT citing previous SC judgements rejected Vidarbha's application and held that the only two things that the Adjudicating Authority is required to consider are the 'existence of debt' and 'default in servicing the debt', and the fulfillment of both these conditions will instantly trigger corporate insolvency. Further, it was emphatically held that the reason for non-payment of the debt is immaterial to the scheme of the code.

The recently enacted Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016 ('IBC' or 'Code'), was aimed at restructuring the insolvency laws and regulations pertaining to corporates, partnerships, individuals and other entities in India, and providing an effective and time bound resolution process to the creditors. Multiple laws and adjudicating forums governing the financial failures in India, prior to enactment of IBC, were not able to alleviate the distressed credit market and provide a time bound and effective mechanism to the stakeholders to resolve the issue.

The structure of the Code is laid down with an objective to maximize the value of the stakeholders; to restructure and consolidate the businesses; to balance the interest of all the stakeholders; to support the development of credit market; improving ease of doing business and facilitate more investment, leading to higher economic growth and development.

The objective of the new law is to generate a competitive revival or resolution plan, which benefits and maximizes the value of all the stakeholders. The aim was to restructure the businesses, if viable, rather than liquidation. However, the Code has been considered by the financial institutions and other creditors as a fast recovery channel rather than considering the option of restructuring and revival of the businesses. In last two years of enactment of IBC, over 800 companies1 have been going the liquidation process.

Amid financial institutions and other financial and operational creditors being successful in instituting insolvency resolution process against the corporate debtors, the plea of the home buyers for initiating the insolvency resolution process against the corporate debtors, being real estate developers was struck down by the Hon'ble National Company Law Tribunal ('NCLT'). In terms of the provisions of IBC, financial creditor, operation creditor and the corporate debtor itself can initiate the corporate insolvency resolution process. NCLT adjudicated that the home buyers who have invested their money in purchasing the real estate property are not operational creditors and not even financial creditors, hence their plea for initiation of insolvency resolution process cannot be accepted. One of the judgment of the NCLT in the catena of judgments with respect to claim of home buyers was of the Delhi Bench of NCLT in the case of Nikhil Mehta & Sons (HUF) v. AMR Infrastructure Ltd. [2017] 78 taxmann.com 302 (NCLT - New Delhi), wherein the Hon'ble Bench held that where the transaction was a pure and simple agreement of sale or purchase of piece of property, such a transaction would not acquire the status of a 'financial debt' as the transaction did not have consideration for time value of money, which is a substantive ingredient to be satisfied for fulfilling requirements of expression 'financial debt'. In other words, Hon'ble Bench held that, to qualify as a financial debt and thus as a financial creditor, in terms of the provisions of IBC, what is important that the money has been advanced for a consideration for time value of money. However, in the case of home buyers, the money was advanced for purchase of property and not with a consideration for return of any time value of money.

Tax implications and repercussions under Companies Act, 2013 also need consideration. Illustration 1: Inter company loan repayable on demand

Parent (P Ltd.) makes an interest free loan of Rs. 10 crores to its subsidiary (S Ltd). There is a written agreement in place which provides that the loan is repayable on-demand. Cash flow forecasts for the next 3 years indicate positive cash inflows in each year.

The loan is initially measured at its fair value. As the loan is repayable on-demand, it's fair value is the transaction price and the effective interest rate (EIR) is zero.

In determining a default event, P should consider a range of factors that would indicate that the loan is in default, and not only when the loan is 90 days past due. The factors considered relevant are the availability of liquid assets when the loan is called.

In assessing whether an increase in credit risk relative to the position at initial recognition is indicated, P decides that the availability of liquid assets at the reporting date together with forward looking information is most relevant. Therefore, P decides to rely on its review of S's management accounts and cash flow forecasts when assessing credit risk. Whether there has been a significant increase in credit risk (which determines whether 12-month or lifetime ECLs apply) is largely irrelevant because the maximum period over which ECLs can be measured is the maximum contractual period (including extension options) over which the lender has a contractual obligation to extend credit. This is the period over which the entity is exposed to credit risk, and not a longer period. Given the loan is repayable on-demand, the maximum contractual period, and hence period of exposure to credit risk, is 1 day. Credit losses arising from the risk of a default that may occur after 1 day are not included.

Whilst tracking credit risk for an on-demand loan may not be relevant when measuring ECLs, whether there has been a significant increase in credit risk will be relevant for disclosure purposes (Ind AS 107 requires qualitative and quantitative disclosures on the entity's credit risk exposure and significant credit risk concentrations)

In measuring the expected loss on default, P considers the expected manner of recovery. P judges that to maximise recovery of the loan it would allow S to continue trading for 2 years to fund repayment of the loan rather than arrange a fire sale of the less liquid assets.

Example 2 – impairment testing of an intercompany term loan with fluid terms

Parent (P Ltd) makes an interest free loan of Rs. 10 crores to its subsidiary (S Ltd). There is no written agreement, but the parties have documented in writing, their understanding of the terms and this is supported by cash flow forecasts. The understanding is that the loan could be repaid in around 3 years, as working capital permits, but may be extended to the end of year 6. S has no other debt obligations or credit facilities and is adequately capitalised. Repayments are forecast to begin slowly during year 2 and increase throughout year 3. The loan is initially measured at its fair value, which is determined to be Rs. 8.4 crores.

In determining a default event, P judges that 'days past due' will not be a relevant indicator due to the fluid terms of repayment. P therefore develops a policy on default that considers qualitative factors such as the expected life of the loan and the level of headroom in the cash flow forecasts of S. P judges based on the documented understanding and initial forecasts, that the period it expects to have credit risk exposure for is 3 years, and that if the loan is not fully repaid within 6 years it will consider the loan to be credit impaired. In assessing whether an increase in credit risk relative to the position at initial recognition is indicated, P decides that forward looking information is most relevant given the repayment terms. This is because the fluid terms and the expectation that repayments will most likely be back-ended make past behavioural patterns less relevant. Therefore, P decides to rely on its review of S's cash flow forecasts when assessing credit risk. P judges that an increase in credit risk is significant if the expected life of the loan is extended by more than 1 year, or that less than 1/3 of the loan can be recovered by the end of year 3. The maximum period to consider when measuring expected credit losses is the maximum contractual period (including extension options) over which the entity is exposed to credit risk and not a longer period. P judges that in substance the loan contains an option for S to extend the contractual period, but not beyond year 6, if working capital does not permit repayment as forecast, and that it would be contractually required to continue extending credit.

The advent of Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016 (Code) brought in new classification of Creditors like Financial and Operational and Financial Creditor has been given primacy among the Creditors.

As per Section 5(7) and 5(8) of the Code, a creditor under the Code can be a financial creditor mainly under two circumstances i.e., (i) when corporate debtor directly avails a debt from the creditor and (ii) if corporate debtor furnishes a guarantee to any person. It is undisputed that where a creditor lends money for time value is indeed a Financial Creditor. Further, in a claim based on Corporate Guarantee also, a Creditor would be a Financial Creditor. The moot question is whether a Creditor who has not advanced any money to the corporate debtor, but only a security interest is created by such Corporate Debtor in favour a Creditor to secure the payment of a third party can be termed as Financial Creditor under the Code? To simply put, whether a third party mortgagor, i.e., a Company which had created a security interest to secure the payment by a third party who had availed loan from a lender, is a Financial Creditor or Operational?.

This issue had arisen in the case of Anuj Jain v. Axis Bank Ltd. [2020] 114 taxmann.com 656 (SC). In this case, Jaypee Infratech Ltd. (JIL) had been referred to Corporate Insolvency Resolution Process (CIRP) by the NCLT, Allahabad. The said company had mortgaged its properties in favour of Axis Bank and ICICI Bank for a loan advanced to its holding Company Jaiprakash Associates Ltd. (JAL). Other than this, JIL did not directly avail any loan or Credit facilities from the said Banks. It was simply a case of third party mortgage created by JIL to secure the advances provided to JAL. Axis Bank and ICICI Bank had filed their claim with Interim Resolution Professional (IRP) claiming to be the Financial Creditors when the said IRP had rejected to treat them as Financial Creditors. The said Banks had moved an application before the NCLT against the order of the IRP when the NCLT rejected the same. However, the NCLAT had allowed their appeal when the said IRP had moved Supreme Court against the order of the NCLAT. After analyzing the nature of transaction involved, Supreme Court had held that the said the debts in question were in the form of a third party security which had been given by the corporate debtor JIL so as to secure the loans/advances/facilities obtained by JAL from the lenders. Such a 'debt' is not and cannot be a 'financial debt' within the meaning of the Code and hence, the said lenders, the mortgagees, are not the 'financial creditors' of the corporate debtor JIL.Supreme Court had further elaborated that for a person to be designated as a financial creditor of the corporate debtor, it has to be shown that the corporate debtor owes a financial debt to such person and it becomes clear that a third party to whom the corporate debtor does not owe a financial debt cannot become its financial creditor for the purpose of the Code.

Supreme Court further held as under:

"Keeping the objectives of the Code in view, the position and role of a person having only security interest over the assets of the corporate debtor could easily be contrasted with the role of a financial creditor because the former shall have only the interest of realising the value of its security while the latter would, apart from looking at safeguards of its own interests, would also and simultaneously be interested in rejuvenation, revival and growth of the corporate debtor. Thus understood, it is clear that if the former i.e., a person having only security interest over the assets of the corporate debtor is also included as a financial creditor and thereby allowed to have its say in the processes contemplated by Part II of the Code, the growth and revival of the corporate debtor may be the casualty. Such result would defeat the very objective and purpose of the Code, particularly of the provisions aimed at corporate insolvency resolution.

Saranga Anilkumar Aggarwal v. Bhavesh Dhirajlal Sheth [2025] 172 taxmann.com 145 (SC)/[2025] 188 SCL 286 (SC)/[2025] 255 COMP CASE 681 (SC) The Supreme Court held that penalties imposed by the National Consumer Disputes Redressal Commission are regulatory in nature and arise from non-compliance with consumer protection laws, and are therefore distinct from debt recovery proceedings under the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code. In the instant case, the appellant, claiming to be a financial creditor, had advanced funds to the respondent–corporate debtor as share application money for allotment of equity shares. No shares were allotted by the corporate debtor, and the amount was also not refunded. On account of such non-refund, the appellant filed an application under section 7 of the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code alleging default.

The Adjudicating Authority rejected the application holding that share application money, where shares were not allotted, could not be treated as a financial debt. On appeal, the NCLAT examined the applicability of the Companies (Acceptance of Deposits) Rules, 2014. It held that Rule 2 of the CADR Rules envisages that only where any amount is received pursuant to a private placement offer made in accordance with the provisions of the Companies Act, 2013 and no shares are allotted in respect thereof, the amount can be treated as a deposit.

The Tribunal noted that the appellant had failed to place on record any proof of a private placement offer made in accordance with the Companies Act, 2013. In the absence of any evidence of a valid and concluded agreement between the parties relating to allotment of shares, the amount advanced could not be treated as money received in response to a private placement offer. INTRODUCTION

The Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016 (hereinafter 'the Code') proved to be one of the most innovative and reformative legal amendments. It made a paradigm shift in the very approach to the notion of insolvency and bankruptcy by providing a great scope for reorganisation and insolvency resolution in addition to liquidation. The Code also promised to balance all stakeholders' interest and to ensure the availability of credit. The scheme of this Code came before the judicial lens on various occasions. In Innoventive Industries Ltd. v. ICICI Bank Ltd.1, the Hon'ble Supreme Court underscored the various changes in the policy outlook of the Code and highlighted its overriding effect on other pre-existing laws.

Another such interesting decision of the Hon'ble Supreme Court is Swiss Ribbons (P.) Ltd. v. Union of India2, (hereinafter 'the present case') where the Hon'ble Court upheld various provisions of the Code. In this paper, the author aims at examining the correctness of the decision regarding two specific parameters regarding the differential treatment given to the Operational Creditors and Financial Creditors, in view of changed circumstances and other pertinent factors.

FINANCIAL DEBT AND OPERATIONAL DEBT UNDER THE CODE

As the next move, it is relevant to look into the statutory description of Financial Creditor and Operational Creditor under the Code. Section 5(7)of the Code defines Financial Creditor as a person to whom a financial debt is owed and includes its assignees and transferees. Section 5(8) gives a substantive definition to Financial Debt and also provides for an inclusive list of debts falling within the category. As per the provision, Financial Debt is a debt including interest, if any, disbursed for the time value of money against consideration.

From the definition, it is clear that the phraseology is very broad so as to include all kinds of debts associating with the time value for money. Similarly, Section 5(20) defines Operational Creditor as a person to whom an operational debt is owed and includes its assignees and transferees. Operational Debt, as per Section 5(21), is a claim in respect of provision of goods or services including employment or repayment of dues payable to the Central or State Government under law. Here, the test is whether the debt has a bearing on provision of goods and services.

It is now relevant to look at what is 'Claim', since both the definitions employ the said word. Section 5(6) defines Claim as (i) A Right to Payment or (ii) A Right to Remedy for Breach of Contract under law, whether or not they are reduced to judgment, disputed, matured, secured or fixed. Hence, it is clear that the right must be one legally enforceable.

All these definitions appear to be clear and concrete yet there are several instances where the Courts have taken varying stands depending on the facts and circumstances of each case. Hence, what was Financial Debt in one case can easily become Operational Debt in another. For instance, according to Section 5(8)(e) of the Code, "Receivables sold or discounted other than any receivables sold on non-recourse basis" falls within the meaning of Financial Debt.

However, in the recent decision of the National Company Law Tribunal, Bengaluru in Invoice Discounters of BNH Infra Projects (India) (P.) Ltd. v. BNH Infra Projects (India) (P.) Ltd.3 the Hon'ble Tribunal came to the conclusion that Financiers discounting invoices of the corporate debtor become operational creditors by stepping into their shoes. The Tribunal referred to Supreme Court and NCLAT decisions to observe that since there is no disbursement of money to the corporate debtor by the financiers and it was only put in an escrow account maintained by KredX, the facilitator, the fundamental condition of Section 5(8) is not met.

While taking this decision, the Hon'ble Tribunal relied on the Supreme Court decision in Anuj Jain v. Axis Bank Ltd.4, and NCLAT decision in Minions Ventures (P.) Ltd. v. TDT Copper Ltd.5 where the Hon'ble Appellate Tribunal observed that since there is no disbursement of money happening in a discounting transaction and since the discounter steps into the shoes of the seller, he is an Operational Creditor and a Petition u/s. 7 of the Code.

Therefore, this explanation must be read in conjunction with section 92B of the Act. Accordingly, if guarantee has to be considered an international transaction, it should fall in the residuary clause of section 92B(1) which covers "any other transaction having a bearing on profits, income, losses, or assets of such enterprises." From the agreement/Memorandum of Understanding it was clear that appellants were 'investors' and had chosen 'committed return plan'. The respondent in their turn agreed upon to pay monthly committed return to investors. Thus, the amount due to the appellants came within the meaning of 'debt' as defined in section 3(11). Thereby, the amount invested by appellants came within the meaning of 'financial debt', as defined in section 5(8)(f) subject to satisfaction as to whether such disbursement against the consideration was for time value of money.

Thus, the Adjudicating Authority had rightly highlighted the opening word of the definition clause which indicate that a 'financial debt' is a debt along with interest which is disbursed against the consideration for the time value of money and may include any of the events enumerated in sub-clauses (a) to (i). Therefore, it was to be seen whether the amount paid by the appellants to the corporate debtor fulfilled the other condition of 'disbursement against consideration of time value and money' to come within the definition of 'financial creditor' having satisfied that the corporate debtor raised the amount through a transaction of sale and purchase of agreement having commercial effect of a borrowing [section 5(8)(f)].

The agreement showed that the respondent agreed to complete the construction of shopping mall on or before December, 2009, in all respects, and was required to complete and handover the shop in the shopping mall before the said date. It was not the case of the respondent that the construction was stopped or delayed on account of factors beyond the control of the respondent, as stipulated in the later part of the Memorandum of Understanding. It was agreed upon by the respondent that since the appellants had paid most of the amount the respondent was ready to pay 'monthly committed returns' to the appellants. However, as the appellants were not required the monthly return till December, 2008 i.e. for 9 months so the respondent-Corporate Debtor undertook to make a consolidated payment of Rs. 99,600 less TDS for every calendar month. The corporate debtor was liable to pay committed return with effect from January, 2009 till the date of handing over of the possession to the appellants. Therefore, it was clear that the amount disbursed by the appellants was 'against the consideration of time value of the money' and the respondent corporate debtor raised the amount by way of sale-purchase agreement, having a commercial effect or borrowing. This was also clear from annual returns filed by respondent and not disputed by the respondent-corporate debtor in their annual returns, wherein the amount so raised/borrowed had been shown as 'commitment charges' under the head 'financial cost'. The financial cost included 'Interest on loans' and other charges. 4.3-6 Instrument The expression used in the Explanation is "any other instru-ment by which the liability to pay is deferred to a future date". The term instrument has not been defined under the Act or the General Clauses Act.

The Indian Stamp Act, 1899 under section 2(14) defines instrument as:

"(14) "Instrument" - "instrument" includes every document by which any right or liability is, or purports to be, created, transferred, limited, extended, extinguished or recorded:"

In general parlance, the instrument is understood as writing of a document which is formal in nature and executed between two parties.

The Delhi High Court in the case of Rathi Graphics Technologies Ltd. (supra) held that when pursuant to a settlement, creditor agrees to convert a portion of interest into shares, it must be treated as an extinguishment of liability to pay interest to that extent and, thus, said conversion of interest into shares should be taken to be 'actual payment' within the meaning of Section 43B.

CIT [2015] 54 taxmann.com 86/68 SOT 223 (Mum. - Trib.) held that there could be no disallowance under Section 43B(1)(d) by invoking Explanation 3C, where interest payable was converted into equity shares as interest liability stood ceased to exist and not deferred as in case of conversion of interest loan or borrowing. The Ahmedabad ITAT also held the same ratio in the case of Marwar Hotel Ltd. v. Asstt. CIT [2015] 62 taxmann.com 385/155 ITD 655 (Ahd. - Trib.).

Also from clauses (d), (da) and (e) of Section 43B(1) read with Explanation 3C/3CA/3D and Circular No. 7 of 2006, it is evident that the deduction is allowed when the liability is discharged and not merely on deferring the same by conversion. The transaction of conversion of interest payable into loan or borrowing is deferment of payment of the amount. But when the interest payable is converted into equity capital, the liability of interest payable ceases to exist and stands discharged.

Therefore, in case of discharge of liability by converting it into equity shares would not fall under the ambit of Explanations as the liability is no more in existence once it is discharged.

The above cases still hold good after the amendment by the Finance Act, 2022 as the conversion of interest into equity shares does not defer the liability to pay to a future date, and any conversion of interest into equity shares should be deemed as an actual payment for the purpose of Section 43B.

4.3-8 Conversion of interest into preference shares

Section 55(1) of the Companies Act, 2013 provides that no company limited by shares shall issue irredeemable preference shares. Further, Section 55(2) of the Companies Act, 2013 provides that a company limited by shares may, if so authorised by its articles, issue preference shares that are liable to be redeemed within a period not exceeding twenty years from the date of their issue subject to such conditions as may be prescribed. Redeemable preference shares can be convertible or non-convertible. Convertible preference shares are converted into equity shares, and non-convertible preference shares are redeemed by repaying the capital.

Should the conversion of interest into the preference shares be treated at par with the conversion into debentures or equity shares?

There are two schools of thought on the same. The first school of thought says conversion of interest into preference shares could not be brought within ambit of Explanation 3C to Section 43B as holder of such shares could not be treated as lender of the assessee, and in fact, lender became an owner with certain rights2. This is further supported by the fact that conversion of interest into equity shares is considered as a discharge of interest liability.

However, on the other hand, due to the redeemable character of preference shares, it should be prudent to treat them like debentures for Section 43B. A preference share is an instrument, and since, in India, irredeemable preference shares cannot be issued, the liability to pay against the preference shares continues to exist, although it may be deferred. Hence both the conditions in Explanation 3C are satisfied, and consequently, conversion of interest into preference shares should not be regarded as actual payment of interest under Section 43B, till the preference shares are redeemed.

The CBDT should clarify this issue to avoid any litigation on the same.

5.11-2 Loan must be taken from another with an obligation to return Loan must be taken with an obligation to return. In a loan, the amount taken is returned or repaid to fulfil the contract. Return or repayment of the loan is the happy ending to the contract desired by both parties at the inception itself. Trade advances taken by the supplier of goods or services or advances taken by the vendor of property or share application money is not a loan. Return/repayment of such advances may happen when the original agreement or contract to supply goods/services/property/allot shares could not be fulfilled. In a loan, the original agreement is to return the money taken with or without interest. In trade advance, the original agreement is to supply goods/services in return. In share application money, the original contract is to allot shares. It is repaid/returned when the original contract cannot be fulfilled. 5.11-3 Unpaid/deferred purchase price is not a 'loan'

The following judicial decisions are noteworthy:

(a)

An agreement to pay the balance of consideration due by the purchaser does not give rise to a loan. A loan of money undoubtedly results in a debt, but every debt does not involve a loan. Liability to pay a debt may arise from diverse sources, and a loan is only one of such sources. Every creditor who is entitled to receive a debt cannot be regarded as a lender [Bombay Steam Navigation Co. (P.) Ltd. v. CIT [1965] 56 ITR 52 (SC)].

(b)

A loan is defined by the Oxford English Dictionary as 'a thing lent; something the use of which is allowed for a time, on the understanding that it shall be returned or an equivalent given; esp., a sum of money lent on these conditions and usually with interest'. The essential requirement of a loan is the advance of money (or of some article) upon the understanding that it shall be returned, and it may or may not carry interest. The debt here arose not out of an advance but out of the sale of the flat by the company to the seventh petitioner. The company gave to the seventh petitioner time to pay a part of the purchase price. The seventh petitioner was, thus, given financial accommodation by the company in the matter of payment of the debt. Such financial accommodation was not and did not amount to a loan [Dr. Fredie Ardeshir Mehta v. Union of India [1991] 70 Comp. Cas. 210 (Bom.)].

(c)

The legislative has, for reasons of policy, thought it fit not to define the term "loan" in an inelastic or rigid manner, and in every case, we have got to look to the substance or the essential nature of the transaction for the purpose of determining as to whether or not it is a "loan" within the meaning of the Act. If a vendor of property feeling unable to rely on the personal credit of the purchaser merely takes a bond or security from him in respect of unpaid purchase money the transaction by itself cannot rank as a loan because there is no element of advance involved in it [Kunja Behari Pal v. Satyendra Nath, AIR 1941 Cal. 689 cited in Radha Kisen Chamria v. Keshardeo Chamria, AIR 1954 Cal. 105].

(d)

The amount of the unpaid price (of plant & machinery supplied by a non-resident) cannot be said to be a loan advanced by the non-resident to the buyer, nor can be the non-resident be said to be a lender to the buyer so far as that amount was concerned [CIT v. Saurashtra Cement & Chemical Industries Ltd. [1975] 101 ITR 502 (Guj.)].

(e)

Amount payable to electricity company in respect of electricity charges is not a loan from the electricity company [Ashiana Paper Mills Pvt. Ltd. v. Punjab State Electricity Board, AIR 2008 P&H 119].

(f)

In PCIT v. Boeing India (P.) Ltd. Every creditor who is entitled to receive a debt cannot be regarded as a lender [Bombay Steam Navigation Co. (P.) Ltd. v. CIT [1965] 56 ITR 52 (SC)].

(b)

A loan is defined by the Oxford English Dictionary as 'a thing lent; something the use of which is allowed for a time, on the understanding that it shall be returned or an equivalent given; esp., a sum of money lent on these conditions and usually with interest'. The essential requirement of a loan is the advance of money (or of some article) upon the understanding that it shall be returned, and it may or may not carry interest. The debt here arose not out of an advance but out of the sale of the flat by the company to the seventh petitioner. The company gave to the seventh petitioner time to pay a part of the purchase price. The seventh petitioner was, thus, given financial accommodation by the company in the matter of payment of the debt. Such financial accommodation was not and did not amount to a loan [Dr. Fredie Ardeshir Mehta v. Union of India [1991] 70 Comp. Cas. 210 (Bom.)].

(c)

The legislative has, for reasons of policy, thought it fit not to define the term "loan" in an inelastic or rigid manner, and in every case, we have got to look to the substance or the essential nature of the transaction for the purpose of determining as to whether or not it is a "loan" within the meaning of the Act. If a vendor of property feeling unable to rely on the personal credit of the purchaser merely takes a bond or security from him in respect of unpaid purchase money the transaction by itself cannot rank as a loan because there is no element of advance involved in it [Kunja Behari Pal v. Satyendra Nath, AIR 1941 Cal 689 cited in Radha Kisen Chamria v. Keshardeo Chamria, AIR 1954 Cal 105].

(d)

The amount of the unpaid price (of plant & machinery supplied by a non-resident) cannot be said to be a loan advanced by the non-resident to the buyer, nor can be the non-resident be said to be a lender to the buyer so far as that amount was concerned [CIT v. Saurashtra Cement & Chemical Industries Ltd. [1975] 101 ITR 502 (Guj.)].

(e)

Amount payable to electricity company in respect of electricity charges is not a loan from the electricity company [Ashiana Paper Mills Pvt. Ltd. v. Punjab State Electricity Board, AIR 2008 P&H 119].

(f)

Provisions of section 68 are not attracted to amount representing purchases made on credits - Principal CIT v. Kulwinder Singh [2018] 99 taxmann.com 449 (Punj. & Har.). In CIT v. Pancham Dass Jain (2006) 156 Taxman 507 (All. HC) it was held that provisions of section 68 are not attracted to amounts representing purchases made on credit.

8.1-11d Whether renewal of loan is a loan? -Renewal of loan may be taken to be a payment by the debtor with one hand and a fresh borrowing with the other, and, in that view of the matter, a renewal amounted to a fresh loan [Pratap Singh v. Gulzari Lal, 1942 ALJ 3, AIR 1942 All 50 explained in Lachmi Lal v. Babu Narain Das, AIR 1950 All 152].

8.1-11e Whether overdraft facility is a loan? -In Bareilly Electricity Supply & Co. Ltd. v. State of U.P AIR 1977 Cal 426, it was held as under:

"In considering whether overdraft was loan it may be mentioned that in Halsbury Laws of England 4th Edn., Vol. 3 at paragraph 155 it has been stated that a customer might borrow from a banker by way of loan or by way of overdraft. A loan was a matter of special agreement. In the absence of agreement, express or implied from a course of business, a banker was not bound to allow his customer to overdraw.

(h)

"One important aspect which has been ignored by NFRA reviewer due to lack of sector/industry experience and knowledge is that ITNL is not in lending/finance business, it is in infrastructure business where the projects are executed in SPVs where the entire equity/financing obligation is of the sponsor itself and hence the impact on the Company has to be assessed on a holistic basis and not in narrow sense."

7.6 NFRA's observations on each of the above contentions are as follows: 7.6-1 Contentions at (a) and (b) above are general understanding of the Audit Firm which NFRA has not disputed in the DAQRR. However, whether such matters are in fact factored into the terms of the loans, so that these are not prejudicial to the interest of the Company is a matter that requires documentation. There is no such documentation in the Audit File.

7.6-2 Regarding contention at (c) above, NFRA has not stated anywhere in the DAQRR that the terms of loans are prejudicial because of zero per cent interest. Paras 7.2-3 and 7.2-6 may be read in this regard.

7.6-3 The Audit Firm's contention in (d) above that the loans were expected to be fully recovered (based on cash flow projections) is without the support of adequate procedures. For e.g., in the case of TRDCL the projected shortterm loan from ITNL is Rs. 201.10 crore (it is noted against this line item in the WP, hardcopy file 13, that "ITNL has given a 0% loan to support the SPV to repay the external debt obligation") over a period of 14 years. However, the WP shows no evidence of how the Audit Firm has verified the projections and assumptions to verify the recoverability of the loan.

7.6-4 Contention in (e) above is a general understanding which was not disputed by NFRA. However, there is no evidence that this is in fact the view of the management.

7.6-5 Contention in (f) and (g) above is not acceptable due to the absence of clear evidence as explained above. More importantly, the Audit Firm itself admits that "the impact on the Company has to be assessed on a holistic basis and not in narrow sense" (contention at (h) above). It can be seen from the above explanations that the Audit Firm has not done any holistic assessment as it clearly failed to verify the factors such as negative indicators that will have an impact on the recoverability of the loans, the repayment capacity of the SPVs, the feasibility of the projects etc. as detailed in para 7.2-8 above. Depending on such factors, even a repayment schedule that does not factor in the ground realities could be prejudicial to the interest of the Company, since such conditions may cause unwarranted defaults and repayment pressures on the SPVs, which in turn would increase their market borrowing costs beyond affordable limits. If the term loans have certain conditions similar to that of a financing company, which the SPVs cannot meet because of specific circumstances applicable to each SPVs, even such conditions, which are normal in other cases, could be prejudicial to the interest of the company. The company has stated in its 'Chairman's Message' that "In the process, the Company's debt position worsened and, the Company also incurred additional interest cost. With the intent to overcome these hurdles, we plan to critically reassess our project portfolio and take appropriate actions, including stake sale, divestment and refinancing". Such plans may have a dependency on the terms and conditions of the existing financing arrangements.

Failure of such plans may not be in the interest of the Company in any case. Even providing a loan, with or without interest, when the situation demands equity, might itself prove prejudicial to the interest of the company depending on the ground realities.

7.7 Thus, it is clear from the replies that the Audit Firm has not done any holistic examination to ascertain whether the terms of the loans are prejudicial to the interest of the Company or not. The company's decision to provide interestfree loans indicates the distress situation of the SPVs. Any failure of the SPVs in honouring the conditions of the loans could prove prejudicial to the Company as a whole. The Audit Firm's examination was based on the general, historical, and theoretical understanding of the company and its business and also based on certain projections provided by the management. There is no examination of the ground realities, i.e., the factors other than the interest rate, to confirm the conclusions apparently reached based on such a highlevel understanding. In that context, the contention at 7.5(h) above is a welldrafted guidance for the Audit Firm itself.

3.6-5 No admission of application if demand disputed

If demand is disputed, application will not be admitted - Philips India v. Goodwill Hospital (2017) 142 SCL 208 = 82 taxmann.com 366 (NCLAT).

If claim was disputed by debtor much prior to issue of demand notice, application to initiate insolvency resolution process cannot be filed -Uttam Galva Steels v. DF Deutsche Forfait AG (2017) 143 SCL 318 = 84 taxmann.com 183 (NCLAT).

Adjudicating Authority (NCLT) is not empowered to go into dispute i.e. whether dispute is genuine or bogus.

Thus, application will be admitted only if the demanded is undisputed or there is clear court order.

NCLT cannot decide question of legality of foreign decree - NCLT cannot decide on legality of foreign decree. Thus, it has to consider the decree as valid and proceed - Usha Holdings LLC v. Francorp Advisors (2019) 151 SCL 266 = 101 taxmann.com 73 (NCLAT).

The above circular can be applied mutatis mutandis in case of the repayment of debentures or any other debt instrument. However, it needs to be noted that the deduction, even after conversion, shall be allowable only on a payment basis.

4.3-5 Conversion The Explanations use the phrase 'converted', thereby signifying that conversion is a pre-requisite. Thus, in cases where there is no conversion but an altogether extinguishment, the Explanation shall not apply. Therefore, if the interest obligation is not deferred but is extinguished, the same shall amount to paid, and the disallowance as per the provisions of section 43B shall not be applicable [CIT v. Rathi Graphics Technologies Ltd. [2015] 64 taxmann.com 65 (Delhi)] .

Similarly, in cases of one-time settlement, depending on the facts, there is generally no conversion involved. The liability is settled for a lesser amount. That being the case, it is submitted that in the absence of conversion and in acceptance of discharge of liability, disallowance is not warranted.

Furthermore, if instead of conversion of existing interest into a loan, borrowing etc., a fresh loan is obtained and the interest obligation is paid, the same shall not be covered by the Explanation and accordingly disallowance under section 43B shall not be attracted. In ACIT v. Ashok Radhakishen Mehra [2021] 127 taxmann.com 468/188 ITD 663 (Mum.-Trib.), the Tribunal relying on the decision of Madras High Court in CIT v. Prakash Food & Feed Mills (P.) Ltd. [T.C. Appeal Nos. 775 & 808 of 2014, dated 26-11-2014] held where interest amount had actually been paid by the assessee through overdraft/cash credit account and same had not been converted into loan or borrowing (or) loan or advance, disallowance of interest under section 43B(d)/(e)read with Explanation 3C/3D could not have been made.

4.3-6 Instrument

The expression used in the Explanation is "any other instrument by which the liability to pay is deferred to a future date". The term instrument has not been defined under the Act or the General Clauses Act.

The Indian Stamp Act, 1899 under section 2(14) defines instrument as:

"(14) "Instrument" – "instrument" includes every document by which any right or liability is, or purports to be, created, transferred, limited, extended, extinguished or recorded:"

In general parlance, the instrument is understood as writing of a document which is formal in nature and executed between two parties.

4.3-7 Conversion of interest into equity shares

The Delhi High Court in the case of Rathi Graphics Technologies Ltd. (supra) held that when pursuant to a settlement, creditor agrees to convert a portion of interest into shares, it must be treated as an extinguishment of liability to pay interest to that extent and, thus, said conversion of interest into shares should be taken to be 'actual payment' within the meaning of Section 43B.

The Mumbai ITAT in the case of Garware Chemicals Ltd. v. Dy. CIT [2015] 54 taxmann.com 86/68 SOT 223 (Mum. - Trib.) held that there could be no disallowance under Section 43B(1)(d) by invoking Explanation 3C, where interest payable was converted into equity shares as interest liability stood ceased to exist and not deferred as in case of conversion of interest loan or borrowing. The Ahmedabad ITAT also held the same ratio in the case of Marwar Hotel Ltd. v. Asstt. CIT [2015] 62 taxmann.com 385/155 ITD 655 (Ahd. - Trib.).

Also from clauses (d), (da) and (e) of Section 43B(1) read with Explanation 3C/3CA/3D and Circular No. 7 of 2006, it is evident that the deduction is allowed when the liability is discharged and not merely on deferring the same by conversion. The transaction of conversion of interest payable into loan or borrowing is deferment of payment of the amount. But when the interest payable is converted into equity capital, the liability of interest payable ceases to exist and stands discharged.

Therefore, in case of discharge of liability by converting it into equity shares would not fall under the ambit of Explanations as the liability is no more in existence once it is discharged.

The above cases still hold good after the amendment by the Finance Act, 2022 as the conversion of interest into equity shares does not defer the liability to pay to a future date, and any conversion of interest into equity shares should be deemed as an actual payment for the purpose of Section 43B.

4.3-8 Conversion of interest into preference shares

converting it into equity shares would not fall under the ambit of Explanations as the liability is no more in existence once it is discharged.

The above cases still hold good after the amendment by the Finance Act, 2022 as the conversion of interest into equity shares does not defer the liability to pay to a future date, and any conversion of interest into equity shares should be deemed as an actual payment for the purpose of Section 43B.

4.3-8 Conversion of interest into preference shares Section 55(1) of the Companies Act, 2013 provides that no company limited by shares shall issue irredeemable preference shares. Further, Section 55(2) of the Companies Act, 2013 provides that a company limited by shares may, if so authorised by its articles, issue preference shares that are liable to be redeemed within a period not exceeding twenty years from the date of their issue subject to such conditions as may be prescribed. Redeemable preference shares can be convertible or non-convertible. Convertible preference shares are converted into equity shares, and non-convertible preference shares are redeemed by repaying the capital.

Should the conversion of interest into the preference shares be treated at par with the conversion into debentures or equity shares?

There are two schools of thought on the same. The first school of thought says conversion of interest into preference shares could not be brought within ambit of Explanation 3C to Section 43B as holder of such shares could not be treated as lender of the assessee, and in fact, lender became an owner with certain rights2. This is further supported by the fact that conversion of interest into equity shares is considered as a discharge of interest liability.

However, on the other hand, due to the redeemable character of preference shares, it should be prudent to treat them like debentures for Section 43B. A preference share is an instrument, and since, in India, irredeemable preference shares cannot be issued, the liability to pay against the preference shares continues to exist, although it may be deferred. Hence both the conditions in Explanation 3C are satisfied, and consequently, conversion of interest into preference shares should not be regarded as actual payment of interest under Section 43B, till the preference shares are redeemed.

The CBDT should clarify this issue to avoid any litigation on the same.

4.3-9 Whether IBC overrides Section 43B?

Section 43B contains a non-obstante clause that has overriding effect over any of the provisions contained in the Act. However, the overriding effect is not with respect to any other law. In this regard, it would be helpful to refer to the case of CIT v. Tube Investments of India Ltd. [2012] 18 taxmann.com 90/204 Taxman 686 (Mad.). The Madras High Court held that the provisions of section 32 of Sick Industrial Companies (Special Provisions) Act, 1985, have overriding effect over provisions of section 43B of the Act. Thus, where a scheme provided that the tax authorities shall provide a deduction for the interest, even though the same is not paid, the assessee was eligible to get the deduction, even if not permitted by Section 43B.

Further, section 238 of the IBC has an overriding effect over all statutes [Principal CIT v. Monnet Ispat & Energy Ltd. [2018] 18 SCC 786]. Thus, if in a scheme approved under IBC, it is provided that deduction is to be allowed for outstanding interest, the same shall be an allowable deduction, irrespective of the requirement of Section 43B.

The term "loan" generally refers to borrowing something, especially a sum of cash that is to be paid back along with interest decided mutually by the parties. In other terms, the debtor is under a liability to pay back the principal amount along with the agreed rate of interest within a stipulated time [CIT v. Mahindra and Mahindra Ltd. (b) The expression 'loan', though not defined under the Act, has a well-settled connotation, i.e., advancing of money by one person to another under an agreement by which the recipient of the money agrees to repay the amount on such agreed terms with regard to the time of repayment and the liability to pay interest. The person advancing the money is generally called a creditor, and the person receiving the money is generally called a borrower. The most simple form of a loan transaction is a contract by which the borrower agrees to repay the amount borrowed on demand by the creditor with such interest as stipulated under the agreement. Such a loan transaction may be attended by any security arrangement, a mortgage or pledge etc., depending upon the agreement of the parties [Keshavlal Khemchand And Sons (P.) Ltd. v. UOI [2015] 53 taxmann.com 470 (SC)/4 SCC 770];

(c)

If A pays money to B, who agrees to return not the identical currency in specie but an equivalent sum subsequently, no bailment arises but simply a loan owing by B to A. The fact that it is called a "deposit" can make no difference [K.M.S. Lakshmanier and Sons v. CIT and CEPT [1953] 23 ITR 202 (SC)];

(d)

A loan imports a positive act of lending coupled with an acceptance by the other side of the money as a loan. The relationship between borrower and lender cannot ordinarily come about by mere inaction. At the bottom, this is a question of fact. Of course, money so left could, by a proper agreement between the parties, be converted into a loan, but in the absence of an agreement, mere inaction on the part of the managing agents cannot convert the money due to them, and not withdrawn, into a loan [Shree Ram Mills Ltd. v. CEPT [1953] 23 ITR 120 (SC)];

(e)

A loan can be with interest or without interest because no condition exists in law of contract that a loan can be with interest only [Chandrakant H. Shah v. ITO [2009] 28 SOT 315/[2010] 3 ITR (Trib.) 398/124 ITD 177 (Mum. - Trib.)].

The following points flow as corollaries from the above judicial decisions:

(a)

Two parties: Loan involves two parties - the lender/creditor and borrower [seepara 8.1-11a];

(b)

Money is taken with Obligation to return: Loan involves taking money from another person lender under a contract whereby the person taking the loan (borrower/debtor/loanee) promises to repay the loan [seepara 8.1-11b];

(c)

Unpaid purchase price is not a loan: Where there has been no transaction of taking a loan but purchase of goods or property, the deferring or giving more time for payment by the vendor does not convert the unpaid purchase price into a loan [seepara 8.1-11c];

(d)

Loan may be interest-free: Loan may be interest-bearing or interest-free. If ingredients in (a) and (b) above are there, the loan does not cease to be so merely because it is to be repaid without any interest.

For a transaction to be considered as a loan, two different persons are required. A contract of loan requires two persons. Mridu Hari Dalmia [1982] 8 Taxman 138/133 ITR 550/27 CTR 20 (Delhi)].

The proprietorship concern could have borrowed any amount to be categorised as a 'loan', only if it was procured from some other source, then himself/the proprietor [CIT v. K. V. Mohammed Zakir [2017] 82 taxmann.com 96/396 ITR 180 (Ker.)].

5.6-3 Amendments in brief

5.6-3a Clause (da) is inserted in section 43B to include therein payment of interest on loan or borrowing from certain NBFCs. It means, any sum payable as interest on any loan or borrowings from certain NBFCs, shall be allowed as deduction only if it is actually paid, in the manner as discussed earlier.

As mentioned in Memorandum, amendment is made pursuant to amendment made in section 43D as per matching principle. Section 43D is amended to provide that interest income in relation to only certain categories of bad debts (commonly known as interest on non-performing assets) shall be chargeable to tax in the previous year in which it is credited to profit and loss account for that year or the previous year in which it is actually received, whichever is earlier. However, in terms of the amendment in section 43B, any interest payable to certain NBFCs would be allowed as deduction on actual payment basis, whether or not such loan or borrowing has become non-performing assets in hands of the certain NBFCs. In other words, even interest, on loans, not treated as bad debt/non-performing asset, would be allowed only on actual payment and not on accrual basis.

5.6-3b Explanation 3AA is inserted to provide that if deduction in respect of interest referred to in clause (da) is allowed in earlier assessment years i.e. prior to assessment year 2019-20, on accrual basis, no deduction under this section is allowed again on payment basis in respect of same amount of interest.

5.6-3c Explanation 3CA is inserted to provide that deduction of interest referred to in clause (da) shall be allowed, if interest is actually paid, and if it is converted into loan or borrowing, it will not be considered as interest actually paid for the purpose of its allowability.

The above Explanation 3CA is similar to the Explanation 3C which presently exists in section 43B and provides that if any sum payable by the assessee as interest on any loan or borrowing from public financial institution or a State financial corporation or a State Industrial Investment Corporation is converted into a loan or borrowing, the interest so converted and not 'actually paid', shall not be deemed as 'actual payment' and not allowed as deduction in the computation of income under section 43B. The said amendment was made effective from assessment year 1989-90.

5.6-3c1 WHETHER CONVERSION OF UNPAID INTEREST INTO SHARES WOULD BE TREATED AS ACTUAL PAYMENT? - Delhi High Court in case of CIT v. Rathi Graphics Technologies Ltd. [2015] 64 taxmann.com 65/[2016] 235 Taxman 550 (Delhi)] held that conversion of a portion of interest into shares should be considered as 'actual payment' within the meaning of section 43B. It is so because, pursuant to a settlement, the creditor agrees to convert a portion of interest into shares, it must be treated as an extinguishment of liability to pay interest to that extent. In essence, there will be no further outstanding interest to that extent. It is different from the situation envisaged in Explanation 3C to section 43B of the Act viz., conversion of interest into 'a loan or borrowing' where liability continues, although in a different form.

Similar view was taken by Tribunal in following cases:

JSW Steel Ltd. v. Asstt. CIT [2011] 9 taxmann.com 77 (Bang.-Trib.) [Explanation 3C being deeming provision strictly applies to conversion of outstanding interest amount into loans or borrowings and not to preference shares].

Garware Chemicals Ltd. v Dy. CIT [2015] 54 taxmann.com 86/68 SOT 223 (Mum.-Trib.) [Explanation 3C cannot be applied in case of interest payable, converted into share capital as the interest liability ceased to exist and not deferred as in case of conversion of interest loan or borrowing].

5.11

Definition of 'loan'

The term 'loan' is not defined in the Act. So, one would have to go by its ordinary meaning as explained in judicial decisions and law dictionaries.

The following judicial definitions of 'loan' are relevant:

(a)

The term "loan" generally refers to borrowing something, especially a sum of cash that is to be paid back along with interest decided mutually by the parties. In other terms, the debtor is under a liability to pay back the principal amount along with the agreed rate of interest within a stipulated time [CIT v. Mahindra and Mahindra Ltd. [2018] 93 taxmann.com 32/255 Taxman 305 (SC)];

(b)

The expression 'loan', though not defined under the Act, has a well-settled connotation, i.e., advancing of money by one person to another under an agreement by which the recipient of the money agrees to repay the amount on such agreed terms with regard to the time of repayment and the liability to pay interest. The person advancing the money is generally called a creditor, and the person receiving the money is generally called a borrower. The most simple form of a loan transaction is a contract by which the borrower agrees to repay the amount borrowed on demand by the creditor with such interest as stipulated under the agreement. Such a loan transaction may be attended by any security arrangement, a mortgage or pledge etc., depending upon the agreement of the parties[Keshavlal Khemchand and Sons (P.) Ltd. v. UOI [2015] 53 taxmann.com 470 (SC)/4 SCC 770];

(c)

If A pays money to B, who agrees to return not the identical currency in specie but an equivalent sum subsequently, no bailment arises but simply a loan owing by B to A. The fact that it is called a "deposit" can make no difference [K.M.S. Lakshmanier and Sons v. CIT and CEPT [1953] 23 ITR 202 (SC)];

(d)

A loan imports a positive act of lending coupled with an acceptance by the other side of the money as a loan. The relationship between borrower and lender cannot ordinarily come about by mere inaction. At the bottom, this is a question of fact. Of course, money so left could, by a proper agreement between the parties, be converted into a loan, but in the absence of an agreement, mere inaction on the part of the managing agents cannot convert the money due to them, and not withdrawn, into a loan[Shree Ram Mills Ltd. v. CEPT [1953] 23 ITR 120 (SC)];

(e)

A loan can be with interest or without interest because no condition exists in law of contract that a loan can be with interest only[Chandrakant H. Shah v. ITO [2009] 28 SOT 315/[2010] 3 ITR (Trib.) 398/124 ITD 177 (Mum. - Trib.)].

The following points flow as corollaries from the above judicial decisions:

(a)

Two parties: Loan involves two parties - the lender/creditor and borrower [see Para 5.11-1];

(b)

Money is taken with Obligation to return: Loan involves taking money from another person lender under a contract whereby the person taking the loan (borrower/debtor/loanee) promises to repay the loan [see Para 5.11-2];

(c)

Unpaid purchase price is not a loan: Where there has been no transaction of taking a loan but purchase of goods or property, the deferring or giving more time for payment by the vendor does not convert the unpaid purchase price into a loan [see Para 5.11-3];

(d)

Loan may be interest-free: Loan may be interest-bearing or interest-free. If ingredients in (a) and (b) above are there, the loan does not cease to be so merely because it is to be repaid without any interest.

1.6-29 Adjustment - Whether a deemed advance resulting in deemed dividend under section 2(22)(e)?

Section 2(22)(e) provides that any payment by a company of any sum by way of advance to a specified shareholder or to a concern in which he is interested shall be regarded as deemed dividend.

A question that arises is what happens if the associated enterprise is a shareholder covered by section 2(22)(e) or is an interested concern within the meaning of the said section? Will the deemed advance be treated as a deemed dividend under section 2(22)(e)? If yes, will it result in violation of TDS provision under section 195?

There could be two views regarding taxability of the deemed advance under section 2(22)(e).

According to one view a fiction has to be carried to its logical conclusion [CIT v. G. Narasimhan [1999] 102 Taxman 66 (SC)]. Hence once the adjustment is treated as advance for the purpose of section 92CE, it ought to be regarded as advance for the purpose of section 2(22)(e) and the adjustment should be regarded as liable to dividend under the said section.

According to the other view, section 2(22)(e) should not apply in such a situation for following reasons:

(a)

Section 2(22)(e) applies only if there is a payment by a company. It appears that a statutorily deemed advance cannot be regarded as a "payment" within the meaning of section 2(22)(e).

(b)

It is now well settled that legal fictions are created only for some definite purpose and these must be limited to that purpose and should not be extended beyond that legitimate field [CIT v. Mother India Refrigeration Industries (P.) Ltd. [1985] 23 Taxman 8 (SC); CIT v. Vadilal Lallubhai [1972] 86 ITR 2 (SC); ITO v. M. C. Ponnoose [1970] 75 ITR 174 (SC); CIT v. Amar Chand N. Shroff [1963] 48 ITR 59 (SC)]. It could be argued that the fiction of excess money be deemed as an advance should be restricted to section 92CE and not extended to other purposes of the Act.

(c)

A legal fiction cannot be expanded by giving purposive interpretation particularly if the result of such interpretation is to transform the concept of chargeability. [Vodafone International Holdings B. V. v. UOI [2012] 17 taxmann.com 202 (SC)]. Now, in section 92CE, the fiction does not result in any chargeable income: the secondary adjustment is not taxable; however, if section 2(22)(e) regarded as applicable, then a fiction which does not initially result in taxable income is transformed into a fiction resulting in taxable income under section 2(22)(e)! Obviously, such an interpretation cannot be attributed.

(d)

The word "deemed" refers to "what is supposed to be, not to "what actually is" [A.C. Goel v. First National Bank Ltd. (1960) 30 Comp. Cas. 317 (Punj)]. What is deemed as advance made by the assessee is not actually an advance made by him. The nomenclature "advance" is to facilitate recovery of excess money and charge of interest. However, it is not a loan or advance within the meaning of section 2(22)(e). Now, section 2(22)(e) would require an actual advance by the assessee and since there is no actual advance upon the adjustment being deemed as advance section 2(22)(e) should not apply.

(e)

It is clear that unless and until there is created in favour of an assessee a debt due by somebody, it cannot be said that he has acquired a right to receive the income or that income has accrued to him.

... Thus, a mere claim to income without an enforceable right thereto cannot be regarded as accrued income for the purposes of the Act. [CIT v. Govind Prasad Prabhu Nath [1987] 35 Taxman 513 (All.)2] It is a moot point as to whether a unilateral entry by the Indian entity is legally binding on the associated enterprise and whether there is a legal liability on its part to pay and if it does not accept the liability, can the Indian entity be really taxed on the ground that income has accrued to it.

1.6-29 Adjustment - Whether a deemed advance resulting in deemed dividend under section 2(22)(e)?

Section 2(22)(e) provides that any payment by a company of any sum by way of advance to a specified shareholder or to a concern in which he is interested shall be regarded as deemed dividend.

A question that arises is what happens if the associated enterprise is a shareholder covered by section 2(22)(e) or is an interested concern within the meaning of the said section? Will the deemed advance be treated as a deemed dividend under section 2(22)(e)? If yes, will it result in violation of TDS provision under section 195?

There could be two views regarding taxability of the deemed advance under section 2(22)(e).

According to one view a fiction has to be carried to its logical conclusion [CIT v. G. Narasimhan [1999] 102 Taxman 66 (SC)]. Hence once the adjustment is treated as advance for the purpose of section 92CE, it ought to be regarded as advance for the purpose of section 2(22)(e) and the adjustment should be regarded as liable to dividend under the said section.

According to the other view, section 2(22)(e) should not apply in such a situation for following reasons:

(a)

Section 2(22)(e) applies only if there is a payment by a company. It appears that a statutorily deemed advance cannot be regarded as a "payment" within the meaning of section 2(22)(e).

(b)

It is now well settled that legal fictions are created only for some definite purpose and these must be limited to that purpose and should not be extended beyond that legitimate field [CIT v. Mother India Refrigeration Industries (P.) Ltd. [1985] 23 Taxman 8 (SC); CIT v. Vadilal Lallubhai [1972] 86 ITR 2 (SC); ITO v. M. C. Ponnoose [1970] 75 ITR 174 (SC); CIT v. Amar Chand N. Shroff [1963] 48 ITR 59 (SC)]. It could be argued that the fiction of excess money be deemed as an advance should be restricted to section 92CE and not extended to other purposes of the Act.

(c)

A legal fiction cannot be expanded by giving purposive interpretation particularly if the result of such interpretation is to transform the concept of chargeability. [Vodafone International Holdings B. V. v. UOI [2012] 17 taxmann.com 202 (SC)]. Now, in section 92CE, the fiction does not result in any chargeable income: the secondary adjustment is not taxable; however, if section 2(22)(e) regarded as applicable, then a fiction which does not initially result in taxable income is transformed into a fiction resulting in taxable income under section 2(22)(e)! Obviously, such an interpretation cannot be attributed.

(d)

The word "deemed" refers to "what is supposed to be, not to "what actually is" [A.C. Goel v. First National Bank Ltd. (1960) 30 Comp. Cas. 317 (Punj)]. What is deemed as advance made by the assessee is not actually an advance made by him. The nomenclature "advance" is to facilitate recovery of excess money and charge of interest. However, it is not a loan or advance within the meaning of section 2(22)(e). Now, section 2(22)(e) would require an actual advance by the assessee and since there is no actual advance upon the adjustment being deemed as advance section 2(22)(e) should not apply.
