FACT: The corporate debtor had been incurring losses and defaulted in payment of the loan to SBI bank and other creditors including vendors. At that juncture, the financial creditor as a prospective investor came out to take charge and run the company on behalf of the existing management. Accordingly, an MoU was entered into between the corporate debtor and the financial creditor.

The financial creditor submitted that the amounts were disbursed by the financial creditor on various dates. There were various e-mail requests by the corporate debtor to the financial creditor for transfer of funds towards salary of the employees and statutory expenses to be incurred.

The financial creditor further contended that in terms of the MoU, the corporate debtor did not proceed to negotiate the terms of definitive agreement, as was necessary to implement the provisions of the MoU. Therefore, the corporate debtor was liable to return the money provided by the financial creditor.

The corporate debtor, on the other hand, contended that there was no debt, and even assuming that there was debt, it was not financial debt as there was no time value for money, neither was there any default.

HELD: Whether unpaid amount claimed by financial creditor was financial debt

The corporate debtor has admitted that the amount paid by the applicant-financial creditor was towards an arrangement entered into between the parties as per the MoU. [Para 16]

On perusal of the pleadings and looking in to the terms and conditions contained in the MoU, it appears that the intentions of the parties were to give life to the corporate debtor which was facing a financial crisis. The financial creditor was under the obligation to arrange for working capital and took responsibilities of the day-to-day management of the corporate debtor. The applicant-financial creditor was also made responsible for payments of statutory dues and other administrative expenses including liabilities as on the 'effective date' given in the MoU. [Para 17]

In pursuant to the terms and conditions of the MoU, the applicant-financial creditor had started to make payments to the corporate debtor as reflects from the Certificate issued by the Bank of Maharahstra. The total amount now claimed is Rs. 2.14 crore along with further interest at the rate of 18 per cent per annum. [Para 18]

IBC : Where financial creditor had failed to muster clinching proof and evidence in terms of financial records to show that sum advanced by them to corporate debtor was indisputably interest-bearing and that interest had continued to accrue and was being realized as consideration for time value of money, sum advanced by financial creditor to corporate debtor did not satisfy ingredients of financial debt of disbursal, time value of money and commercial effect of borrowing, and thus, instant

and filed an application under section 7 against the corporate debtor.

The NCLT, by an impugned order, admitted said application.

On appeal, the appellant suspended director of the corporate debtor submitted that there was no loan agreement entered into between the corporate debtor and there was no financial debt.

The appellant further submitted that the respondents were not registered under the Banking Regulation Act, 1949, and respondents had no license and, therefore, could not have extended any loan to the corporate debtor. HELD: For proving a debt to be financial debt, pre-condition which is required to be proved is that debt is disbursed against the consideration for the time value of money. The definition of financial debt is inclusive definition. [Para 8]

The word transaction has also been defined in section 3(33) which also contains an inclusive definition. [Para 9]

There is no loan agreement between the parties which fact is undisputed. Whether there are any other materials on record which may prove that there was any financial debt by the transaction between the parties is the question to be answered. [Para 10]

All the demand notices and the replies received from the corporate debtor are part of section 7 application. Demand notices were sent separately by all the respondents. The notice dated 11-2-2019 demanded principal amount as well as the amount of interest by the financial creditor. [Para 11]

A perusal of the demand notice indicates that in addition to repayment of principal debt and interest lacs has been claimed. The notices dated 11-2-2019 by all the respondents were replied by the corporate debtor in its reply dated 21-2-2019. [Para 12]

From the reply given by the corporate debtor, the conclusions are inescapable, firstly, the corporate debtor admitted grant of loan. The plea taken in the reply was that loan was granted for a tenure of 5 years. The second conclusion which may be drawn from the reply is that the claim of interest which was claimed by the demand notice was not refuted. The corporate debtor did not take any plea that no interest is payable. [Para 13]

In section 7 application, the financial creditors have also brought on record Form 16A for the financial year ending 31-3-2018 which Form 16A indicates that TDS was deducted by the corporate debtor and deposited under section 194A of Income-tax Act, 1961. [Para 14]

It is true that deduction of TDS and deposit by the corporate debtor does not itself prove that there is any financial debt but deduction of TDS and deposit in Form 16A under section 194A of Income-tax Act clearly proves that the deduction which was deposited was TDS relating to 'Interest other than interest on securities'. Form 16A which was filed by the financial creditor along with section 7 application at least support the case of the financial creditors that loan which was granted to the corporate debtor was with interest. [Para 15]

When demand notice was issued demanding both principal and interest, the corporate debtor never at the relevant time refuted that no interest is payable or there was no interest with the loan. [Para 16]

There can be no dispute to the proposition that on the basis of deduction of TDS it cannot be concluded that transaction in question is a financial debt. [Para 18]

Form 1 under Rule, 2016 contains the details which are required to be submitted in an application by the financial creditors. Part-V of the Form 1. [Para 19]

Part-V refers to list of other documents to prove the existence of financial debt. The Rules thus clearly contemplates that financial debt can be proved on 'Other Documents' also. [Para 20]

Instant Tribunal in Pawan Kumar v. Utsav Securities (P.) Ltd. [2021] 131 taxmann.com 211/168 SCL 692 has held in that financial creditor has not furnished any document to show that the transaction is a loan transaction. Instant is not a case where no documents have been submitted by the financial creditor to prove the transaction as a financial transaction. The documents which were filed, included the demand notice dated 11-2-2019. Reply notice dated 21-2-2019 (containing the admission of loan by the corporate debtor), Form 16A as well as balance sheets were filed. [Para 21]

Instant Tribunal in the case of Arrow Engineering Ltd. v. Golden Tobacco Ltd. [2022] 134 taxmann.com 272, referring to documents and correspondences between the parties concluded that financial debt was there despite there being no MoU formerly executed between the parties containing the terms and conditions of transaction. Further when one looks into the definition of transaction as contained in section 3(33), the definition is an inclusive definition and the provision does not lead to the conclusion that unless there is written transaction between the parties incorporating the terms and conditions of the loan, no transaction can come within the meaning of section 5(8). Financial debt can be proved from other documents as contemplated in Column 8 of Part-V of Form 1 of Insolvency and Bankruptcy (Application to Adjudicating Authority) Rules, 2016. [Para 23]

from the account of respondent No. 1 to corporate debtor on 1-1-2014 has been placed. That this money was received by the corporate debtor has also not been denied by the corporate debtor. Neither has any claim been made that any part of this sum was repaid by corporate debtor. Respondent No. 1 has thus produced incontrovertible and unimpeachable evidence to prove the existence of debt liability on the part of the corporate debtor. [Para 17] In the instant case, the respondent No. 1 has submitted a bank certificate to substantiate the disbursal of funds to the corporate debtor and validated the same with the Annual Reports and Balance Sheets of the corporate debtor to show that it was a loan. Respondent No. 1 has placed on record the Balance Sheet of the corporate debtor wherein this amount has been shown under the head of 'Long Term Borrowings - Unsecured loan from Related Parties'. This clearly evidences that the disbursal was a loan. Even the notice sent by the respondent No. 1 on 20-2-2018 as placed clearly stated that they had extended a loan to the corporate debtor to meet its working capital requirements repayable on demand at an interest rate of 15 per cent per annum. Keeping in mind that there was no document/agreement in respect of the loan amount, it is quite natural that there was no document/agreement which determined the payment of interest and the rate of interest but that cannot be a ground for assuming that the loan was not interest-bearing. It is an undisputed fact that the respondent No. 1 has not placed on record any document which shows that the disbursal made was in the nature of loan wherein interest was specifically payable. Be that as it may, it is opined that the IBC does not provide for any prescriptive requirement for the financial creditor to place on record formal written agreements/documents between the parties to establish that the disbursal made was in the form of loan with interest. Given this background therefore, the Adjudicating Authority committed no error in holding that there was a financial debt owed by the corporate debtor to Respondent No. 1. [Para 18]

As long as there are clear acknowledgements of such debts in the statements of accounts of the corporate debtor, the financial creditor is not impeded in filing a section 7 application and the Adjudicating Authority is required to look into the evidence of default as furnished in Part-V of Form-1 of the application filed by the financial creditor. Both these requirements have been met in the instant case. In terms of section 7, a financial creditor is entitled to file an application for initiation of CIRP of the corporate debtor when a default is committed by the corporate debtor. The financial creditor is required to file the section 7 application along with proof of default above the threshold limit. [Para 19]

The Adjudicating Authority in the instant matter gave a clear and specific opportunity to the corporate debtor to produce their books of account to defend their case as is recorded in the impugned order. The corporate debtor however did not avail of this opportunity to place on record the ledger copies of the Respondent No. 1 in the books of the corporate debtor or filed any documents of their own to controvert the alleged self-created books of their accounts by the corporate debtor. That being so it does not behove of the appellant to now cry hoarse that the Adjudicating Authority had wrongly shifted the onus on them to refute the claim of debt and default raised by the financial creditor. [Para 20]

This brings for consideration the tenability of the contention raised by the appellant that the transaction was not in the nature of a loan but a part payment deposit for developing a land project. To substantiate their contention, it has been stated that this amount was transferred by the corporate debtor, since in terms of an MOU, SKIL had to transfer Rs. 45 crore to the corporate debtor, which it was unable to do, on account of financial difficulties which made the corporate debtor step in to make part payment deposit of Rs. 5 crore. Hence it was contended that the disbursal was not made against the consideration of time value of money [Para 21]

Section 5(8) of the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016 - Corporate insolvency resolution process - Financial debt - Whether for any creditor to become financial creditor under section 5(7), there must be a financial debt which is owed to that person and such a person can either be principal creditor to whom financial debt is owed or may be a legal assignee to whom such debt has been transferred - Held, yes - Corporate debtor was a wholly owned subsidiary of IIL - Corporate debtor had approached IIL for financial assistance, which was provided - Meanwhile, liquidation proceedings commenced against IIL and liquidator published Process Memorandum, wherein amount defaulted by corporate debtor was recorded as Rs. 5.10 crores - Appellant-financial creditor had bid for assets/receivables of IIL and entered into a Deed of Assignment with Liquidator of IIL whereby assets of IIL were transferred in favour of financial creditor - Subsequently, financial creditor issued a legal notice and filed a section 7 application against corporate debtor before NCLT, which was rejected by NCLT on ground that debt and default did not exist - It was noted that Deed of Assignment showed that 'receivables' of IIL were assigned a sum of Rs. 25 lakh only on an 'as is where is', 'as is what is' and 'whatever there is' and 'no recourse' basis and Annual Report of IIL for financial year 2015-16 had shown sum given to corporate debtor under Head of 'Receivables' and not under Head of 'Intercorporate Loan', which should have been treatment, if amount was a loan - Whether since assigned amount had been clearly shown as trade receivable in Deed of Assignment, it could not be viewed as a loan particularly when there was no contract/agreement between corporate debtor and IIL recording advance of any loan - Held, yes - Whether there was nothing placed on record by appellant to substantiate that disbursement had been made for consideration for time value of money and, thus, NCLT did not commit any error in rejecting section 7 application filed by appellant - Held, yes [Paras 14, 25 and 26]IBC : Where appellant-financial creditor filed a section 7 application against corporate debtor on basis of a Deed of Assignment, where sum given to corporate debtor by IIL was transferred to appellant, however, said sum was clearly shown as a trade receivable rather than a loan and there was no contract or agreement between corporate debtor and IIL designating sum given as a loan, NCLT did not commit any error in rejecting section 7 application filed by appellant against corporate debtor
IBC : Where unsecured loan was advanced which did neither bear interest nor was same disbursed against consideration for time value of money, said loan would not be financial debt

HEADNOTE: Section 5(8), read with section 7, of the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016 - Corporate insolvency resolution process - Financial debt - Applicant advanced Rs. 2.5 crores to respondent under a draft MoU for development of a project - An amount of Rs. 1.5 crore was admittedly returned - MoUs proposed between applicant and R1 were only draft documents and there was no document or agreement which showed terms on which money was given, nor did it specifically showed whether any interest or consideration against time value for money was payable - Further, there was no repayment schedule - Whether advance paid by applicant to R1 would have no commercial effect of borrowing and same was not financial debt - Held, yes - Whether, thus, CIRP petition was to be dismissed - Held, yes [Para 7]IBC: Where advance was paid and there was no document or agreement which showed terms of payment of any interest or consideration against time value for money, same was not a financial debt

FACT: The applicant stated that:—

Before MoU was finalized, R1 requested the applicant to pay a part of the requested amount towards the project as an urgent requirement with promise of substantial returns on the same. The applicant paid Rs. 2.5 crores into the project of the respondents.

-

Later on an amount of Rs. 1.5 crore was returned by R1 to the applicant. The respondents further informed the applicant that due to paucity of funds for initiation of construction and stamp duty for registration of the consortium MoU, the respondents had decided to discontinue with the original project and they would like to modify same to development of plots. The respondents went ahead with the revised plan. A legal notice was sent to the respondents calling upon them to repay the due amount of Rs. 1 crore along with interest.

-

A reply to the legal notice was sent by the respondents wherein they had categorically admitted the receipt of Rs. 1 crore from the applicant.

The R1 on the other hand contended that:—

-

As per the MoU, DIPL had to make payment of a sum of Rs. 9 crores which was to be upfront, non-refundable and non-adjustable amount. It was also agreed that in the event the applicant failed to make payment of the entire sum, then the applicant would not get participation in the project in any manner. DIPL made payment of only an amount of Rs. 5.5 crores, and complete payment was never made.

-

As far as balance sheet were concerned, the reflection as unsecured loan was only because of accounting practice, and the same did not mean that payment was actually a loan. The applicant itself had written to the tax authorities stating that the payment made to the R1 was not a loan. The loan taken were shown as Nil under Term Loans in the balance sheet filed by the applicant in its income tax return.

On the applicant's CIRP application under section 7:

HELD: The MoUs proposed between the applicant and R1, attached with the application, are only draft documents which cannot serve any purpose and cannot be pressed to support the contention of either side. It is also held that the explanation given by the R2 and R3 is persuasive because there is no privity between the applicant and R2, R3 and even R4. The money was paid to R1 only. R2, R3 and R4 cannot be pleaded as corporate debtors to the instant application. [Para 5]

■

The applicant- financial creditor claimed that it had extended a loan to the Corporate Debtor during the period from 13.06.2007 to 27.03.2009. The said loan was extended in his personal capacity and was repayable on demand.

■

Corporate Debtor had consistently acknowledged the said loan in its Audited Financial Statements over the years, classifying it as an “Unsecured Loan”.

■

A loan recall notice was issued by the financial creditor on 04.07.2022 demanding immediate repayment of the full outstanding loan. A reminder for payment was further issued via email on 01.08.2022. In response to the aforementioned notice, the Corporate Debtor, through its Financial Controller acknowledged the communication and expressed an intention to amicably settle the matter. Since no steps were taken by the Corporate Debtor to repay the debt a legal notice was issued by the financial creditor.

■

Thus, financial creditor filed instant petition under section 7 to initiate CIRP against corporate debtor for the alleged default on the part of the corporate debtor in repayment of financial debt.

■

The Corporate Debtor raised a dispute that the application under Section 7 was barred by limitation, as the alleged financial debt was stated to have arisen in the year 2005-06, and the demand was purportedly made for the first time in July 2022- after a lapse of nearly 17 years. The corporate debtor argued that such a stale claim could not be revived by unilateral recall or reliance upon self-serving accounting entries. Further, it was contended that the application failed to satisfy the statutory preconditions of Section 7.

■

The corporate debtor also claimed that financial creditor had failed to produce any loan agreement, repayment schedule, or even a basic acknowledgment of terms such as interest, tenure, or security. No board resolution or authorization was passed by corporate debtor to borrow funds from the financial creditor. The absence of any documentation, along with the lack of demand for repayment for nearly two decades, was said to indicate that the financial creditor never extended any loan capable of forming a financial debt.

HEADNOTE: Section 5(8), read with section 5(7), of the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016 - Corporate insolvency resolution process - Financial debt - Appellant filed its claim as a financial creditor to Resolution Professional (RP) for an amount advanced to corporate debtor as an earnest money for purpose of purchasing surplus land of corporate debtor - RP vide e-mail replied that funds remitted to corporate debtor were interest free advance and same was to be adjusted against sale consideration for proposed sale of land, which did not fall under category of 'financial debt' - Appellant filed application before NCLT seeking direction to RP to adjudicate its claim, revise list of CoC members, and admit him as CoC member - NCLT dismissed said application on ground that there was no contract between parties for sale of any land and, therefore, earnest money advanced by appellant could not be treated as a 'financial debt' - On appeal, appellant submitted that in annual reports of corporate debtor for financial years 2018-19 and 2019-20 earnest money had been classified as a 'financial debt' and, therefore, appellant's claim deserved to be admitted as a financial debt - It was noted that there was no agreement between parties and disbursement made by appellant to corporate debtor was only a payment, which was to be adjusted in sale of land - Whether since disbursement was not in consideration for time value of money, essential condition for accepting a debt to be financial debt was absent - Held, yes - Whether acknowledging liability of earnest money in annual return as financial debt was not akin to admitting same as a financial debt - Held, yes [Paras 18, 19 and 20]IBC : Where appellant had disbursed money to corporate debtor only as payment which was to be adjusted in sale of land and same was not in consideration for time value of money, sum disbursed was not financial debt under section 5(8)  IBC : Where CoC in its commercial decision decided not to allocate any amount to other creditors and appellant who was classified as other creditor was not be able to prove any violation of provisions of IBC, resolution plan approved by NCLT did not require any interference

FACT: An application under section 9 filed against the corporate debtor was admitted by the NCLT, initiated CIRP against the corporate debtor.

On 22-5-2019, the appellant filed its claim other than as a financial creditor and operational creditor, and thereafter filed its claim as a financial creditor.

The erstwhile RP sent an e-mail stating that the appellant had remitted funds to corporate debtor as an interest-free advance to be adjusted against sale consideration for the proposed sale of land, which shall not fall under 'financial debt'.

The appellant filed an application before NCLT seeking direction to RP to adjudicate the claim of the appellant and revise the list of the CoC to admit him as a member of the CoC.

The NCLT dismissed said application on ground that there was no contract between the parties for sale of any land, hence the earnest money advanced by appellant could not be treated as a financial debt.

Aggrieved by the NCLT order, the appellant filed instant appeal on ground that the NCLT committed error in passing an order rejecting the claim of the appellant as a financial creditor.

The appellant submitted that he paid sum of Rs. 7 crores as earnest money to the corporate debtor with regard to which receipt was issued by the corporate debtor and payment had not been disputed by the corporate debtor and the RP had also admitted the payment of earnest money by the appellant as another creditor but wrongly classified the appellant as other creditor.

The appellant also referred to the annual reports for the financial years 2018-19 and 2019-20, wherein earnest money had been classified as a 'financial debt' and therefore the appellant's claim deserve to be admitted as a financial debt.

HELD: The appellant has claimed the payment of amount to corporate debtor as an earnest money for purpose of purchase of surplus land belonging to the mills of the corporate debtor. The payment of earnest money began after letter dated 14-9-2018 was sent by the appellant to the corporate debtor. [Para 10]

The earnest money was paid by the appellant after submitting a proposal by the appellant himself without their being any acceptance. There is neither any agreement between the parties nor any agreement has been brought on record. It is true that contract between the parties can be oral as well as in writing however, there is no foundation in the application filed by the appellant or materials brought by him to indicate that there was even an oral agreement with the corporate debtor for sale of the land to the appellant. The Adjudicating Authority in the impugned order has discussed the entire sequence of the events and materials on record. The Adjudicating Authority considered the claim of the appellant based on clause (f) of section 5(8). [Para 11]

Section 5(8), read with section 7, of the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016 - Corporate insolvency resolution process - Financial debt - Appellant-financial creditor advanced loan of Rs. 1 crore to respondent, a real estate company for construction of a project 'Madina Heights' - Respondent assured to repay loan with interest @ 18 per cent per annum besides offering 15 per cent share in profit of project - However, respondent failed to repay loan - Appellant issued demand notice - Since payments were still not forthcoming from respondent, appellant filed a section 7 petition seeking admission of respondent into corporate insolvency resolution process which was rejected by Adjudicating Authority as non-maintainable - It was an admitted fact that there was no written contract or agreement between appellant and respondent governing terms and conditions by which sum was advanced by appellant and disbursed to account of respondent - Whether since appellant had failed to muster clinching proof and evidence in terms of financial records to show that sum advanced by them was indisputably interest-bearing and that interest had continued to accrue and was being realized as consideration for time value of money, sum advanced by appellant to respondent did not satisfy ingredients of financial debt of disbursal, time value of money and commercial effect of borrowing - Held, yes - Whether further said project was still in progress and compliances, both procedural and regulatory, were still pending and hence no occasion for default could be said to have occurred as debt was not due or payable - Held, yes - Whether thus, debt and default not having been clearly established, there was no infirmity in impugned order rejecting Section 7 application - Held, yes [Paras 21, 25, 26 and 27]IBC : Where financial creditor had failed to muster clinching proof and evidence in terms of financial records to show that sum advanced by them to corporate debtor was indisputably interest-bearing and that interest had continued to accrue and was being realized as consideration for time value of money, sum advanced by financial creditor to corporate debtor did not satisfy ingredients of financial debt of disbursal, time value of money and commercial effect of borrowing, and thus, instant section 7 petition by financial creditor was to be dismissed

HEADNOTE: Section 5(8), read with sections 3(12) and 5(7), of the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016 - Corporate insolvency resolution process - Financial debt - Appellant had given unsecured loan facility to respondent-corporate debtor - Corporate debtor had been paying interest on unsecured loan and also had been deducting and depositing Tax Deducted at Source (TDS) on interest paid to appellant - Corporate debtor defaulted in payment of unsecured loan - Appellant issued demand notice to corporate debtor seeking repayment of unpaid financial debt - Appellant filed application under section 7 for initiation of CIRP against corporate debtor - NCLT by impugned order rejected said application holding that appellant had failed to establish that unsecured loan he had granted fell within scope of financial debt in absence of any loan agreement setting out terms and conditions of agreement - Whether there were no documents/records to prove that appellant was financial creditor - Held, yes - Whether audited balance sheet also did not prove existence of financial debt and default as defined under section 3(12) - Held, yes - Whether since there was no financial debt and default as proved by appellant, NCLT had rightly rejected application filed by appellant under section 7 - Held, yes [Paras 16 and 17]IBC : Where appellant - financial creditor had given unsecured loan to corporate debtor but failed to prove existence of financial debt and default, NCLT had rightly rejected application filed by appellant under section 7 for initiation of CIRP against corporate debtor

FACT: The appellant had given unsecured loan facility to the respondent-corporate debtor.

The corporate debtor had been paying interest on unsecured loan till 30-9-2018 and also had been deducting and depositing Tax Deducted on Source (TDS) on the interest paid to the appellant. Thereafter, 30-9-2018 neither principle amount nor any interest amount was paid by the corporate debtor to the appellant.

The appellant issued a demand notice to the corporate debtor seeking repayment of the unpaid financial debt by the corporate debtor.

Thereafter, the appellant had filed an application under section 7 for initiation of CIRP against corporate debtor.

NCLT by impugned order rejected said application holding that appellant had failed to establish that the unsecured loan he had granted fell within the scope of financial debt in absence of any loan agreement setting out terms and condition of agreement.

On appeal :

HELD: The appellant has given unsecured loan facility to the Respondent from time-to-time and the Respondent has been repaying part of the unsecured loan to the Appellant. On 31-3-2018, the amount of Rs. 1,95,00,000/- was outstanding as unsecured loan of the Appellant from the Respondent.

The respondent has been paying interest on the unsecured loan till 30-9-2018 and has also been deducting and depositing TDS on the interest paid to the Appellant and the same can be seen from the TDS certificate as well as the Ledger Accounts for the Financial Years 1-4-2014 to 31-3-2018 of the Respondent.

The appellant has concealed the facts namely (a) Civil Suit wherein the Appellant himself has inter alia claimed 40 per cent shares in the Respondent Company and IA interlocutory application filed by the Appellant before the NCLT. (b) Personal Identification. (c) Being Promoter, Director and Guarantor to the Credit Facilities. (d) Amount deposited towards promoter's contribution in terms of a stipulation of HDFC Bank. (e) Availing of Loan from the Respondent Company. (f) Ledger accounts from 1-4-2010 onwards. (g) Bank Account Statements proving the amount drawn by the Company. (h) Amount deposited from 10-1-2007 to 7-9-2016. (i) Working for computation of amount and days of default in tabular form. (j) Evidence of disbursement of loan. (k) Bank Statement of IDBI Bank Account of the Appellant. (l) Dates of disbursements. (m) Conversion of Unsecured loan into Equity as and when required to maintain a positive tangible net worth.

Section 5(8) of the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016 - Corporate insolvency resolution process - Financial debt - Whether for any creditor to become financial creditor under section 5(7), there must be a financial debt which is owed to that person and such a person can either be principal creditor to whom financial debt is owed or may be a legal assignee to whom such debt has been transferred - Held, yes - Corporate debtor was a wholly owned subsidiary of IIL - Corporate debtor had approached IIL for financial assistance, which was provided - Meanwhile, liquidation proceedings commenced against IIL and liquidator published Process Memorandum, wherein amount defaulted by corporate debtor was recorded as Rs. 5.10 crores - Appellant-financial creditor had bid for assets/receivables of IIL and entered into a Deed of Assignment with Liquidator of IIL whereby assets of IIL were transferred in favour of financial creditor - Subsequently, financial creditor issued a legal notice and filed a section 7 application against corporate debtor before NCLT, which was rejected by NCLT on ground that debt and default did not exist - It was noted that Deed of Assignment showed that 'receivables' of IIL were assigned a sum of Rs. 25 lakh only on an 'as is where is', 'as is what is' and 'whatever there is' and 'no recourse' basis and Annual Report of IIL for financial year 2015-16 had shown sum given to corporate debtor under Head of 'Receivables' and not under Head of 'Intercorporate Loan', which should have been treatment, if amount was a loan - Whether since assigned amount had been clearly shown as trade receivable in Deed of Assignment, it could not be viewed as a loan particularly when there was no contract/agreement between corporate debtor and IIL recording advance of any loan - Held, yes - Whether there was nothing placed on record by appellant to substantiate that disbursement had been made for consideration for time value of money and, thus, NCLT did not commit any error in rejecting section 7 application filed by appellant - Held, yes [Paras 14, 25 and 26]

HEADNOTE: Section 5(8), read with section 238A, of the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016 - Corporate insolvency resolution process - Financial debt - Corporate debtor entered into a Development Agreement with financial creditor, in which financial creditor was required to provide a refundable Security Deposit of Rs. 12 crores, with an option to add Rs. 3 crores more - In said agreement, additional amount (up to Rs. 3.5 crores) would bear 18 percent interest, payable quarterly - However, due to non-development, financial creditor filed a section 7 application claiming financial debt and highlighted corporate debtor's default in paying interest on Rs. 3.5 crores - Corporate debtor stated that no financial debt existed and that financial creditor was a related party holding 40 per cent equity - However, NCLT admitted said application - Aggrieved by NCLT's order, appellant-suspended director of corporate debtor filed instant appeal - It was noted that letter issued by corporate debtor to financial creditor clearly indicated that advance made over and above security deposit carried interest at a rate of 18 per cent per annum, which was compoundable and payable quarterly - Whether since payment of 18 per cent interest compoundable and payable quarterly clearly indicated time value of money, said transaction would fall within ambit of financial debt under section 5(8) - Held, yes - Whether corporate debtor had acknowledged in its financial statements, amount of interest as a long-term borrowing and had referred to same as loan from financial creditor and, thus, financial creditor had been able to prove debt and default - Held, yes - Whether therefore, NCLT did not commit any error in admitting section 7 application - Held, yes [Paras 28, 29 and 30]IBC : Where letter issued by corporate debtor to a financial creditor clearly showed that an advance made beyond a security deposit by financial creditor carried interest, which was compoundable and payable quarterly and, corporate debtor had acknowledged this interest in its financial statements as a long-term borrowing, referring to it as a loan, financial creditor had proved debt and default and, therefore, NCLT did not commit any error in admitting section 7 application  IBC : Where corporate debtor had acknowledged interest in books of account on 1-4-2013 and thereafter acknowledged that interest was due in financial statements for financial years 2013 to 2018 application filed under section 7 against corporate debtor on 30-9-2019 was within limitation period

Section 238A of the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016 - Limitation period - Whether where corporate debtor had acknowledged, interest in books of account on 1-4-2013 and thereafter acknowledged that interest was due in financial statements for financial years 2013 to 2018, application filed on 30-9-2019 was within limitation period - Held, yes [Para 28]

HEADNOTE: Section 5(8), read with section 7, of the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016 - Corporate insolvency resolution process - Financial debt - Applicant-financial creditor was in management of corporate debtor which had taken a loan from SBI - Later, management of corporate debtor was transferred to 'B' - Applicant filed application under section 7 against corporate debtor alleging that corporate debtor defaulted in repaying unsecured loan taken from applicant - Whether since terms and conditions of loan agreement with SBI of which applicant was party provided that unsecured loan made available by applicant to corporate debtor did not become due for payment till bank loan was fully liquidated i.e., on 16-2-2018, application filed on 3-7-2015 claiming that corporate debtor owed an amount to applicant was pre-matured and not maintainable - Held, yes - Whether since applicant had failed to bring on record any evidence to suggest that he disbursed money against consideration for time value of money and there was no information about rate of interest on principal amount, loan did not satisfy requirement of financial debt as contemplated under section 5(8) - Held, yes - Whether thus, applicant failed to show that corporate debtor owed an amount and there was a default in payment of such debt and, therefore, application under section 7 was to be dismissed - Held, yes [Paras 39, 40, 43, 44, 57 and 58]IB Code: Where applicant had failed to bring on record any evidence to suggest that he disbursed money against consideration for time value of money and there was no information about rate of interest on principal amount, loan did not satisfy requirement of financial debt as contemplated under section 5(8)

FACT: The application under section 7 had been preferred by financial creditor (FC) seeking initiation of Corporate Insolvency Resolution Process ('CIRP') against corporate debtor (CD).

In the application, it had been alleged that the CD had obtained an unsecured loan during the period between 11-11-2011 and 18-10-2014. However, the CD did not refund the loan nor did it pay the interest thereon to the FC as agreed upon for which an amount as on 3-7-2015, became due to the FC from the side of the CD.

The CD, on being served with notice, filed affidavit-in-opposition opposing the prayer of the FC alleging that the CD was not liable to pay any debt to the FC. In that connection, it had been alleged that a project, under the name and style of CD was established with much fanfare in 2008. In course of time, in 2010, CD obtained a term loan from State Bank of India (SBI). But such a project soon ran into rough weather and it was basically for inept handling of the company by the persons who were then in the management of the company and they were none other than applicant 'R', his son 'K' and his daughter-in-law 'J' who together held more than 94 per cent shareholdings in and of the CD.

Unfortunately, despite the flow of such additional fund to the company, it could do no better than before for which the management in the company once again approached 'B' (who was presently holding the post of MD of the CD) and requested him to bailout the company from its doldrums. After due consideration of the proposal from the side of the then management of the company, 'B' agreed to accept such proposal on certain terms and conditions which were, however, accepted by the then management of the company, vide agreement dated 15-12-2014.

The corporate debtor contended that the instant proceeding needs to be rejected.

HELD: There is no dispute that in 2013, the SBI on being approached by the then management of the CD, had restructured the term loan which it obtained from the bank in 2008, the said loan was restructured on some stringent terms & conditions which were duly accepted by the management of the CD at that point of time. [Para 36]

It is worth remembering that 'R', the applicant, had signed the loan agreement dated 30-07-2013 on behalf of the CD which was further approved by the other directors of the CD at that point, they being 'K' and 'N', who happened to be the son and daughter-in-law of 'R' respectively. [Para 37]

ursed against the time value of money which was borrowed against the payment of interest. Hence the transaction satisfies all the essential of it being a financial debt. [Para 7.18]

■

Another Contention of the Corporate Debtor is that the Applicant has failed to provide a loan agreement with respect to the Inter Corporate Deposits. The CD further contends that the applicant has failed to adhere to the guidelines of the RBI on fair Practices Code for Lenders. [Para 7.19]

■ In this regard, this Tribunal has relied on the Judgement of Hon'ble NCLAT in the matter of Sinki Commodities Pvt Ltd v. ABC Floors Pvt Ltd (2025 SCC Online 1657) wherein it was held that even if no financial contract exists between the parties, Court is not precluded from looking into the real nature of transaction, which can be proved by the Financial Creditor from the material bought on record. Further it was also held that when the amount is disbursed against time value of money the fact that there is a breach of some RBI guidelines, the CD cannot be permitted to contend that definition of financial debt under Section 5(8) need to be looked into with reference to the guidelines. [Para 7.20]

■

Considering the facts of this matter and applying the decision of the Hon'ble NCLAT in Sinki Commodities Pvt Ltd v. ABC Floors Pvt Ltd (supra) this Tribunal is of the view that the Applicant has placed enough documents including Statement of Account, which evidences disbursal and the letters dated 20.05.2019, 03.07.2019, 11.07.2019, 12.07.2019 and 14.08.2019 which states the terms and condition of the ICD including payment terms along with interest rates and due dates. Thus, even if there is some breach in adherence to the RBI guidelines, the contention of the CD is not sustained. [Para 7.21]

■

The contention of the Corporate Debtor that the Applicant has filed this Application for recovery rather than resolution is not maintainable as the applicant has established the existence of the Financial debt and default, which is way above the threshold limit of Rs. 1 Crore as stipulated under section 4 of the Code, which is beyond doubt. [Para 7.22]

■

The Corporate Debtor has relied upon the following judgments, which in our view do not help its case for the following reasons: - I. The Judgment of NCLT in the matter of Kalpesh Jaysukh Shah v. Arch Pharmalabs Limited [CP (IB) 3460/MB/2019] does not apply to the facts of this case as the Applicant has been able to demonstrate with the help of the documents placed on record that multiple acknowledgement vide various emails latest being 18.06.2022 have been made which extend the limitation period. II. The Judgments of Hon'ble Supreme Court in the matter of Innoventive Industries Ltd. v. ICICI Bank Ltd. [(2018) I SCC 407] and Phoenix ARC Pvt. Ltd. v. Spade Financial Services Ltd [2021] 124 taxmann.com 24 / 165 SCL 21 (SC) do not support the case of the Corporate Debtor rather the same support the case of the Applicant as the latter has been able to demonstrate that the transaction entered into by it are of the nature of financial debt. [Para 7.23]

■

Thus, this Tribunal is of the view that I. Applicant has proved the Disbursement. II. Applicant has proved interest @ 13% p.a. which was duly confirmed by letter dated 19.06.2020 III. Applicant has furnished form 26 AS Confirming deduction of TDS on interest IV. For limitation aspect there are repeated acknowledgement by the respondent more particularly letter dated 18.06.2022 where the CD committed itself for the repayment. V. Further no evidence is produced by the respondent that money was advanced for financing trades for commodity. [Para 7.26]

■

In view of the above discussion, the Applicant has successfully demonstrated the existence of a financial debt as the transaction involves amount raised under Section 5(8)(a) of the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016, the occurrence of default, and the continuing nature of such default and all supported by clear documentary evidence. [Para 7.27]

■

Financial Creditor has also proposed the name of an Insolvency Professional (IP) Mr. Navin Khandelwal as the proposed IRP, and as per the Form 2 attached along with the Application, no disciplinary proceedings are going on against the said IP. Further, this Application is complete as all the required documents have been attached along with the Application. Accordingly, the present Application is fit for admission under Section 7 of the IBC, 2016. [Para 7.28]

■

The primary issue before consideration is whether in the backdrop of the statutory provisions of IBC, the outstanding amount of Rs. 5 crore disbursed by respondent No. 1 to corporate debtor is in the nature of financial debt, and, whether in the facts of the instant case, there has been a default in the re-payment of the said loan by the corporate debtor which entitled the respondent No. 1 to file a section 7 application in the capacity of a financial creditor qua the corporate debtor. [Para 8]

Now, one have perused the definition clauses, it will be useful to take notice of the guiding principles laid down by the Apex Court as to when a debt is to be treated as a financial debt in the context of IBC. In Pioneer Urban Land and Infrastructure Ltd. v. Union of India [2019] 108 taxmann.com 147/155 SCL 622 (SC) it has been held that any debt to be treated as financial debt, there must happen disbursal of money and the disbursal must be against consideration for time value of money. The concept of time value of money has been further explained to also include a transaction which does not necessarily culminate into money being returned to the lender or interest being paid in respect of money that has been borrowed. Holding section 5(8) to be a residuary provision which has a catch-all nature, it held that it can include anything which is equivalent to the money that has been loaned as long as commercial effect of borrowing or profit as the aim is discernible. [Para 10]

It is settled law that for any debt to be treated as financial debt, the pre-requisite is disbursal of money to the borrower for utilization by the borrower and that the disbursal must be against consideration for time value of money even if it is not interest bearing. [Para 13]

This brings to the next logical corollary as to when a financial creditor who has disbursed money to a corporate debtor against consideration for time value of money can trigger the insolvency resolution process against the corporate debtor. As per the scheme of IBC, that stage arises when a default takes place, in the sense that a debt which has become due, in fact and in law, but has not been paid. 'Default' as defined in section 3(12) means non-payment of a debt once it becomes due and payable, and non-payment could be of the whole amount or even part thereof. This has been elaborately discussed by the Supreme Court in the case of Swiss Ribbons (P.) Ltd. v. Union of India [2019] 101 taxmann.com 389/152 SCL 365 (SC). [Para 14]

Given this backdrop, one may now analyse the rival submissions made by both parties to find out whether a case of financial debt and default thereof has been effectively made out in the facts of the present case. [Para 15]

While admitting that a sum of Rs. 5 crore was disbursed to the corporate debtor, it has been emphatically asserted by the appellant that a financial contract is a must between the corporate debtor and the financial creditor to establish that the disbursal made was in the form of a loan. The letter from the bank produced by Respondent No. 1 only shows that transfer of the sum of Rs. 5 crore took place but does not show it as a loan. It is contended that only a contract between the parties could have set out the terms of the financial debt including the tenure of the debt, the applicable rate of interest and date of repayment. In the absence of any document, mere assertion that it was a loan repayable on demand does not have any legs to stand on. [Para 16]

When one look at the facts of the instant case, instant Tribunal find that it is an undisputed fact that a sum of Rs. 5 crore was transferred to the account of corporate debtor and the disbursal of this amount took place on 1-1-2014. Sufficient material has been placed on record by the respondent No. 1 to prove that money was actually disbursed to the corporate debtor. The RTGS bank transfer details as well as a letter from the Bank authorities testifying that an amount of Rs. 5 crore was paid from the account of respondent No. 1 to corporate debtor on 1-1-2014 has been placed. That this money was received by the corporate debtor has also not been denied by the corporate debtor. Neither has any claim been made that any part of this sum was repaid by corporate debtor. Respondent No. 1 has thus produced incontrovertible and unimpeachable evidence to prove the existence of debt liability on the part of the corporate debtor. [Para 17]

The plea of the appellants, that no record of default, from information utility, was filed by the financial creditor, the instant Tribunal, poignantly points out that the ingredients of section 7(3)(a), latently and patently specify that the financial creditor, is required to furnish the record of default, recorded with an information utility or such other record or evidence of default. Viewed in that perspective, the contra plea taken on behalf of the appellants, is not acceded to, by the instant Tribunal. [Para 62]

In the instant case, it transpires that the financial creditor, had issued a letter dated 17-11-2021, to all the board of directors of the corporate debtor, stating that he had infused funds, into the company, for the past few years, and these monies were brought in as unsecured loans, to save the company, from its repayment obligations, and also meet the obligations, towards one-time settlement, entered into the SBI bank, and further he had infused funds, to meet the operational losses of the company, at various times. [Para 63]

Added further, the financial creditor, had averred in the said letter dated 17-11-2021 that the company, makes arrangement to compensate him for the monies brought in at various times and suggested that the company may allot equity shares, in the corporate debtor at valuation, as per I.T. Rules, in lieu of repayment of unsecured loans, brought in by him, and the same may be converted into equity shares, within 30 days of this notice serving date, by passing the necessary resolutions, in the board. [Para 64]

In the instant case, the sum of Rs. 13.84 crores infused by the financial creditor, is to be repaid to him, and section 5(8), defines financial debt, meaning a debt, along with Interest, if any, which is disbursed against the consideration for the time value of money, and by commercial practice, any loan, long-term or otherwise, in the absence of any agreement for repayment, falls due and payable on demand, made by the creditor, in the considered opinion of the instant Tribunal. [Para 65]

As regards to notice/letter, dated 17-11-2021, issued by the financial creditor, to all the directors of the corporate debtor, there was no reply, from the appellants, and there is non-payment of debt, by the appellants, and they have committed default, coming within the purview of section 3(12), as held by the instant Tribunal. [Para 66]

There is no embargo in law, for a director of a company, to infuse the funds, into the company, with a view to rescue a company from financial distress/crisis, and the monies advanced clearly come within the umbrage of section 5(8). [Para 67]

In the instant case on hand, the financial creditor, in its application, under section 7, is to prove the existence of debt, which is due from the corporate debtor. No doubt, the corporate debtor or its directors, can point out that the debt, is not payable, by the corporate debtor, in law, and also in fact. [Para 68]

In a section 7 application an Adjudicating Authority, is not required to go into the claim or counter claim, made by the parties, except to find out, whether or not, record is complete, and whether or not, there is debt and default, committed by the corporate debtor. [Para 69]

In law, an application, under section 7, deserves to be admitted, where the sum, is more than Rs. 1 lakh (now Rs. 1 crore) and default of the corporate debtor, was established. [Para 70]

It cannot be gainsaid that a financial debt, is to be understood to include interest free loans, given to a company/entity, for its business purpose/operations, as the case may be. [Para 71]

One cannot ignore a vital fact that the auditor of the corporate debtor, had issued a certificate, dated 8-5-2022, stating that an unsecured loan, was shown, in the balance sheet of the corporate debtor, as on 31-3-2021, which was advanced, by the financial creditor. [Para 72]

It is brought to the fore on behalf of the financial creditor, that a sum of Rs. 3.97 crores, was advanced to the corporate debtor, by the financial creditor, and the same was used by the corporate debtor, to repay the loans, taken by the corporate debtor, from the SBI bank, under the one-time settlement scheme, provided by the bank, to save the corporate debtor, from distress. [Para 73]

A plain reading of the definition clauses of 'financial debt' and 'financial creditor' shows that for any creditor to become financial creditor under section 5(7), there must be a financial debt and for any debt to qualify as a financial debt, that debt along with interest, if any, should have been disbursed against the consideration for the time value of money. Use of expression 'if any' as suffixed to the word 'interest' leaves no shadow of doubt that the component of interest is not a sine qua non for bringing the debt within the fold of financial debt. What is material however is that the disbursement of debt should be against consideration for the time value of money irrespective of whether the debt is interest bearing or not. [Para 11]

The clauses of 'financial debt' and 'financial creditor' and the guiding legal precepts of the Innoventive judgment, it can be safely concluded that for any creditor to become financial creditor under section 5(7), there must be a financial debt which is owed to that person and such a person can either be the principal creditor to whom the financial debt is owed or may be a legal assignee to whom such debt has been transferred. Furthermore, for a debt to become financial debt under the various transactions stated in sub-clauses (a) to (i) of section 5(8), the basic non-negotiable ingredients are that there has to be a disbursal against the consideration for time value of money as carved out in the principal clause which has already been noted above. Further, a financial creditor may file an application under section 7 for initiating CIRP against the corporate debtor when the default in respect of the financial debt owed to him has occurred. It is for the financial creditor to file an application along with the proof of default. If there is a financial debt, which is more than the prescribed threshold level and there is a default and if the application is complete, the application is required to be admitted by the Adjudicating Authority. It is for the Adjudicating Authority to look into the various documents, records and evidence of default as furnished in Part V of Form 1 of the application filed under section 7. [Para 13]

Coming to the instant case, it is the case of the appellant that IIL had provided financial assistance to the corporate debtor on their request and that these amounts were transferred in favour of the corporate debtor during November 2013 to March 2014. It is also contended that the corporate debtor had admitted the financial assistance provided by IIL by an e-mail dated 24-5-2014 sent by them to the IIL confirming Rs. 5.58 crores as due and payable to IIL. Moreover, the corporate debtor in its financial statements for financial years 2015-16 and 2016-17 had admitted that there were amounts due and payable to IIL. Subsequently, this financial debt of the corporate debtor qua IIL was assigned to the appellant by way of a Deed of Assignment which was executed on 21-7-2021. It is also their case that the debt was due and payable is recorded with the Information Utility. It is also an admitted fact that the appellant had served a legal notice on the corporate debtor on 16-9-2021 calling upon the corporate debtor for repayment of the said debt. [Para 14]

It is the rival submission of the corporate debtor that they did not owe any debt to the IIL and that in their replies to the legal notice of the appellant which was sent on 30-9-2021 and 26-10-2021 the claims of the appellant were categorically denied. It has also been contended that there is no documentary evidence on record to establish the alleged financial debt. Besides lack of material particulars produced by the appellant to establish the alleged financial debt there is lack of proof of disbursement of the alleged loan to the corporate debtor either by way of any financial contract or loan agreement; lack of bank account details from which the alleged loan was provided to the corporate debtor to establish disbursement/transfer of funds to the corporate debtor and there is nothing to show that the debt had become due and payable and that the corporate debtor had committed a default thereof. On the Deed of Assignment which has been relied upon by the appellant, it has been submitted that the alleged debt in the Deed of Assignment has been shown as 'trade-receivables' which cannot be held as a loan particularly so when there is no contract/agreement which was entered into between the corporate debtor and IIL recording advance of any loan. [Para 15]

The statutory construct of IBC enjoins upon the IRP/RP the duty to verify every claim which has been submitted by creditors while collating claims. Regulation 12 of IBBI (Insolvency Resolution Process for Corporate Persons) Regulations, 2016 provides that a creditor is required to submit his claim with proof. The RP is entitled under Regulation 10 to call for such other evidence or clarification for substantiation of claims and under Regulation 13 to verify the claims with supporting documents to determine their authenticity and accuracy. Given that the IBC enjoins upon the IRP/RP to verify claims submitted by creditors, there was nothing abnormal or unusual on the part of the Adjudicating Authority to have undertaken to satisfy itself on the genuineness of the loan agreement basis which the claims were filed by the appellant. [Para 13]

■

The Adjudicating Authority has held that the claim filed by the appellant was based on a loan agreement which was fundamentally flawed and that the absence of vendor stamps, serial numbers and date of purchase undermined its validity. It had also noticed that the alleged agreement was executed solely by two brothers, both of whom served as directors of the corporate debtor and that the loan agreement was devoid of any formal authorization by way of board resolution thus undermining its enforceability. [Para 14]

■

The stamp paper on which the loan agreement was executed does not carry the stamp of the licensed vendor, serial number and date of purchase. Clearly, therefore, the stamp paper was not obtained from regular, identifiable, authorised or verifiable sources. Further, no material has been placed on record to show that there was any formal authorisation from the corporate debtor by way of board resolution for execution of the loan agreement for any signatory to execute the loan agreement on their behalf. The corporate debtor had also allegedly not submitted the original loan agreement with the RP. All these factors, seen cumulatively, casts a shadow of doubt on the authenticity and bona fide of the loan agreement. Hence, there existed substantial and compelling grounds for the Adjudicating Authority to have exercised its inherent powers bestowed under rule 11 of the NCLT Rules to look into the authenticity of the loan agreement. [Para 15]

■

From the audited financial statement for financial year 2016-17 of the corporate debtor, it is found that the notes forming part of the balance sheet of the corporate debtor as on 31-3-2017 provides separate categories for ''long-term borrowings'' under note 3 and ''other long-term liabilities'' under note 4. It is also clear therefrom that Rs 5.10 lakhs appearing against the name of SM appears in the head of ''other advances'' rather than as an unsecured loan as claimed by the appellant. Had the amount of Rs 5.10 lakhs appeared under the heading of ''long-term borrowings'', there would have been no doubt that the same was a transaction in the nature of financial debt. However, it is found that the sum appears under the sub-category of ''other advances'' under the category of ''other long-term liabilities''. It is clear from the above categorisation that the sum was provided as an advance and was treated as a liability and not a borrowing in the balance sheet and therefore does not partake the character of financial debt. Even the subsequent financial records do not show otherwise. Therefore, the Adjudicating Authority has not committed any infirmity in noting that the documents relied upon by the appellant to support their claim is ''deficient''. [Para 18]

■

More significantly, it is the contention of the respondents that the terms of the loan agreement contained gaping holes. There was no in-built clause therein on how default was to be calculated. Apart from the loan agreement being bereft of a repayment schedule, the loan agreement did not define any event of default prior to the winding up of the corporate debtor or it's becoming bankrupt in terms of IBC. It was equally unusual that for a loan given way back in 2007, there was no demand of repayment made by the appellant for 15 long years until the corporate debtor got admitted into CIRP. There is no evidence either of any communication sent to the corporate debtor seeking payment of interest. The records of the corporate debtor also do not reflect any provision for interest on the said loan having been credited to the account of the corporate debtor. Nor is there any proof for accrual of interest in any financial year or any evidence of TDS deduction such as Form 26AS. [Para 19]

Section 5(8), read with sections 7 and 60, of the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016 - Corporate Insolvency Resolution Process - Financial debt - Petitioner-financial creditor issued a demand notice against respondent-corporate debtor alleging that he had provided an unsecured loan to respondent, which respondent failed to repay - In reply to said notice, respondent submitted that petitioner had transferred said amount with an intention to buy 25 per cent equity in corporate debtor's development project - On default in making re-payment, petitioner filed a petition under section 7 against respondent - Whether an investment could not be equated with a loan and a sum of money invested with an intention to acquire equity stake or some other interest in company could not be referred as a financial debt - Held, yes - Whether since petitioner had made payment with an intention to acquire 25 per cent equity in corporate debtor's project, said transaction could not be classified as financial debt and, therefore, petition filed under section 7 for initiation of CIRP against corporate debtor was to be dismissed - Held, yes [Paras 21, 28 and 29]

The Supreme Court in case of Swiss Ribbons (P.) Ltd. v. Union of India [2019] 101 taxmann.com 389/152 SCL 365 held that even if the application filed under section 7 meets all the requirements, then also the Adjudicating Authority has to exercise discretion carefully to prevent and protect the corporate debtor from being dragged into the Corporate Insolvency Resolution Process mala fide. [Para 18] The Adjudicating Authority is obliged to investigate the nature of the transaction and should be very cautious in admitting the Application in order to prevent taking undue benefit of provisions of IBC to detriment of the rights of legitimate creditors as well as to protect the corporate debtor from being dragged into CIRP with mala fide. Section 65 provides that if any person initiates the Insolvency Resolution Process or liquidation proceedings fraudulently or with malicious intent for any purpose other than for resolution of Insolvency or Liquidation, the Adjudicating Authority may impose upon such person a penalty. Section 65 provides that where any person furnishes any information under section 7, which is false in material particulars, knowing it to be false or omits any material facts, knowing it to be material such person shall be punished with fine. Whether the transaction in question is Financial Debt and the corporate debtor has committed default?

As per the definition given in section 5(8), 'financial debt' means a debt along with interest, if any, which is disbursed against the consideration for the time value of money. The essential requirement is of disbursement and consideration for time value of money. [Para 21]

The Financial Creditor is not doing financial business but is engaged in manufacture of rice. On the other hand, the corporate debtor Company incorporated on 11-9-2018 having authorized and paid share capital of Rs.7 crores 30 lakhs, as per the MCA data filed by the financial creditor showed that the Bank of Baroda has sanctioned cash credit limit to the tune of Rs. 24 crores in the year October, 2018. According to the financial creditor, they have granted a loan of Rs. 10 lacs on 20-4-2019. It cannot be said that the corporate debtor Company having paid up share capital of Rs.7 crores 30 lacs and cash credit limit to the tune of Rs. 24 crores has to take a loan for Rs. 10 lacs from the financial creditor and that the corporate debtor is not able to make repayment of Rs. 10 lacs and has no objection if the Application under section 7 is allowed and the CIRP initiated against the corporate debtor Company. [Para 24]

Apart from this significant feature of the transaction, the other circumstances considered are as under :

'(a)

The transaction in question has no backing of the board resolution of the corporate debtor company.

(b)

There is no record to show that on date of disbursement i.e., 20-4-2019 the corporate debtor was in need of Rs. 10 lacs (As Loan) particularly when corporate debtor was having cash credit limit of Rs. 24 crores by Bank of Baroda.

(c)

There is no agreement of loan and interest.

(d)

No document is to stipulate the period of repayment.

(e)

The essential ingredients for financial debt disbursement and consideration for the time value of money are missing. On the other hand, the entries of ledger for the financial years 2018-19, 2019-20 reflect the inflow and outflow of funds which are in the nature of running account, indicating that the debit and credit balances lack of any commercial effect of borrowing which is an essential element in terms of section 5(8)(f) of the IBC. Adjudicating Authority on the basis of Financial Statement of the impugned order observed that "First transaction has been squared up on the same date i.e., 16-4-2018. Next transaction is squared up in two days. 3rd transaction is squared up on the same date. Thereafter two transactions for Rs. 20 lakhs and 10 lakhs respectively on 26-7-2018 and 10-8-2018 against which Rs. 10 lakhs have been repaid on 17-10-2018 and 20-12-2018. ■ From the audited financial statement for financial year 2016-17 of the corporate debtor, it is found that the notes forming part of the balance sheet of the corporate debtor as on 31-3-2017 provides separate categories for ''long-term borrowings'' under note 3 and ''other long-term liabilities'' under note 4. It is also clear therefrom that Rs 5.10 lakhs appearing against the name of SM appears in the head of ''other advances'' rather than as an unsecured loan as claimed by the appellant. Had the amount of Rs 5.10 lakhs appeared under the heading of ''long-term borrowings'', there would have been no doubt that the same was a transaction in the nature of financial debt. However, it is found that the sum appears under the sub-category of ''other advances'' under the category of ''other long-term liabilities''. It is clear from the above categorisation that the sum was provided as an advance and was treated as a liability and not a borrowing in the balance sheet and therefore does not partake the character of financial debt. Even the subsequent financial records do not show otherwise. Therefore, the Adjudicating Authority has not committed any infirmity in noting that the documents relied upon by the appellant to support their claim is ''deficient''. [Para 18]

■

More significantly, it is the contention of the respondents that the terms of the loan agreement contained gaping holes. There was no in-built clause therein on how default was to be calculated. Apart from the loan agreement being bereft of a repayment schedule, the loan agreement did not define any event of default prior to the winding up of the corporate debtor or it's becoming bankrupt in terms of IBC. It was equally unusual that for a loan given way back in 2007, there was no demand of repayment made by the appellant for 15 long years until the corporate debtor got admitted into CIRP. There is no evidence either of any communication sent to the corporate debtor seeking payment of interest. The records of the corporate debtor also do not reflect any provision for interest on the said loan having been credited to the account of the corporate debtor. Nor is there any proof for accrual of interest in any financial year or any evidence of TDS deduction such as Form 26AS. [Para 19]

It would be pertinent to outline the rival contention of the appellant that they cannot be denied the right to file their legitimate claim merely because no interest amount was reflected in the balance sheet of the corporate debtor. It was argued that if the corporate debtor did not deduct interest or make provision for interest payments in the balance sheet, the appellant cannot be held responsible for this lapse and put to prejudice. Since the appellant had already resigned from the management of the corporate debtor in 2012 and was not in control of the corporate debtor, they were not responsible in any manner for the corporate debtor not having levied the interest on the outstanding principal amount. Simply because interest was not paid by the corporate debtor, the sum advanced by the appellant cannot be denied the treatment of a financial debt. [Para 20]

■

The appellant was admittedly a shareholder of the corporate debtor when the loan agreement was signed in 2007 and later became one of the directors of the corporate debtor from 2009 to 2012. Thus, it is undisputable that the appellant was very much in control of the management of the corporate debtor until 2012. It is also noticed that either the appellant or his brother who was a signatory of the loan agreement remained at the helm of affairs of the corporate debtor all along. That being the case, the appellant cannot absolve itself of the responsibility of explaining as to why the financial statement of the corporate debtor did not reflect levy of interest till financial year 2011-12 even when they were in control of the corporate debtor. Critical Analysis of the Supreme Court's Judgment in the Orator's case.

Considering the Orator's judgment by the Supreme Court in the light of various judgments and points discussed above, the authors vehemently states that the judgment has not removed the black cloud over the issue of interest not being an essential part of financial debt. Instead, it has brought forward various ambiguous points, upon which a necessary deliberation is required. Firstly , as observed from various judgments of the Supreme Court and the NCLAT, it can be concluded that the time value of money is the most important and quintessential part of the financial debt without which an application under section 7 will not get admitted. It is also evident from the various definitions as referred above that the time value of money includes the interest component, and is the difference between the present values of payment and the payment due and payable in future discounted by compound interest. Hence, for a debt to be disbursed against the consideration for the time value of money, it needs to have an interest component in it. Further, as can be seen from the Insolvency Committee Report, 2018, the time value of money has two components, i.e., interest or factoring in discount of payment. Though, the Supreme Court has clarified that the word "interest" before the phrase "if any" under the definition of financial debt is not required to file a case under section 7 if there is no interest attached to the loan, however, a lot of clarity is required upon the component of interest which also exist in the phrase "time value of money". Thus, it can be said that the consideration for the time value of money under section 5(8) also includes interest as a major component. Hence, in the humble submission of the authors, the interest constituent is necessary for a debt to qualify as financial debt and the ratio in the case of Narendra Kumar Agarwal v. Monotrone Leasing Private Limited should be taken into consideration which provides that the interest component in a transaction is the time value of money.

Secondly , seeing the factual matrix of the present case in hand, the Appellant/FC in its application has mentioned Rs. 1.56 cr as the total default by the CD. Here, it is important to bring to the notice that the total loan amount sanctioned was Rs. 1.60 cr out of which the CD had only paid Rs. 4 lakhs, thereby making default on Rs. 1.56 cr. Although the loan disbursed was interest-free, the Supreme Court didn't take notice of the same and allowed the application to be admitted in which only the principal amount was given, the principal amount was partly paid, and application was also filed for the principal amount without any interest, thereby implying that the amount disbursed was not in consideration against the time value of money.

Thirdly , the Supreme Court has failed to deliberate upon the point basing which the NCLAT had given its judgment, i.e., the consideration for the time value of money is for the benefits of the FC and not the CD. The Supreme Court has unforeseen this aspect of the judgment by the NCLAT. In the present case, there was no consideration for the time value of money for the FC as the loan agreement was interest-free and the CD was only liable to repay the principal amount even after maturity of the contract, i.e., only Rs. 1.56 cr. Also, the Supreme Court in the case of Pioneer's case has held that the definition of financial debt under section 5(8) should be read as "means and includes" thereby providing an extensive meaning to the definition. This means that clauses (a) to (i) under section 5(8) is an extension of the definition of financial debt and is not an exhaustive list and thus, the substantial part of the definition cannot be ignored. In the present case, the Supreme Court is only putting its reliance on the clause (f) of Section 5 which provides for commercial effect of borrowing but is completing ignoring the principal/substantial part of the definition which provides for the component of time value of money in the financial debt. Hence, the Appellant should not be termed as FC by the Supreme Court and his application should have been rejected.

Conclusion

From the point of view of the authors, it is evident that the Supreme Court's decision in Orator's case can have negative implications as the Court has predominantly based its reasoning taking into consideration Section 5(8)(f) of the IBC only and have ignored the principal aspect of the definition of financial debt, i.e., the consideration for the time value of money. This obstinate view of the Court has created ambiguity and vagueness in the understanding of the substantial part of the definition of financial debt and hence, a much-needed clarification is required on interest being an essential constituent of "time value of money".

HELD: Whether written financial contract be the only material to prove the financial debt

The submission of the respondent that the written financial contract is necessary for proving debt. A financial contract supported by financial statements as evidence of the debt is one of the documents contemplated in regulation 8(2) of the IBBI (Insolvency Resolution Process for Corporate Persons) Regulation, 2016 but that is not exclusive requirement for proving existence of debt. Financial contract, thus, can very well be furnished to prove the financial debt but a plain reading of regulation 8(2) indicate that it is not mandatory that existence of financial debt has to be proved by a financial contract. For example: records available with an information utility can very well be used as proof for existence of financial debt. Further, financial statements showing that the debt has not been paid is also one of the clauses in regulation 8(2) by which existence of debt can be proved. [Para 11]

The Financial Creditor has failed to establish that the transaction in question is a Financial Debt and due and payable and the Corporate Debtor has committed default. The judgment Pawan Kumar v. [Para 15]

When one looks into the statutory scheme as reflected in the application to Adjudicating Authority Rules, 2016 and CIRP Regulations, 2016, it is clear that financial debt can be proved from other relevant documents and it is not mandatory that written financial contract can be only basis for proving the financial debt.
