HELD: It is pertinent to note that section 7(1) clearly spells out that a section 7 application can only be initiated only by a financial creditor either by itself or jointly. A perusal of the definition of expression financial creditor would show that it refers to a person to whom a financial debt is owed and includes even a person to whom such debt has been legally assigned or transferred to. The trigger for initiation of the CIRP by such a financial creditor under section 7 is the occurrence of a default by the corporate debtor a prescribed threshold limit. Default in the IBC framework means the incidence of non-payment of debt in whole or in part when the debt has become due and payable, in law and in fact. Debt means a liability or obligation in respect of a claim which is due from any person and claim means a right to payment even if it is disputed. [Para 13]

The relevant excerpts of the impugned order as to why it has held that the application filed under section 7 is not in accordance with law and not liable to be admitted.[Para 14]

From a bare reading of section 7, it is amply clear that insolvency process under IBC can be triggered only by a financial creditor either singularly or jointly. The primary and fundamental basis for a creditor to be treated as a financial creditor for the purpose of section 7 in Part II requires that a financial debt is owed to that person in terms of section 5(7). Such a financial debt could cover any of the transactions outlined in section 5(8) (a) to (i) of the IBC. That being so, the basic requirement of existence of financial debt being owed by the corporate debtor to the financial creditor has to be first satisfied and cannot be overlooked. [Para 19]

In construing and/or interpreting any statutory provision, one must look into the legislative intent of the statute. The intention of the statute has to be found in the words used by the legislature itself. [Para 9]

Section 7 enables a financial creditor to file an application for initiating Corporate Insolvency Resolution Process against a corporate debtor either by itself, or jointly with other financial creditors or any other person on behalf of the financial creditor, as may be notified by the Central Government, when a default has occurred. Although, the Supreme Court in the Orator's case has very clearly highlighted the fact that the debt having no interest constituent shall be termed as financial debt, but this judgment of the Hon'ble court cannot be read alone and should be read in the light of various judgments of various NCLTs and NCLAT wherein the position of law was divided.

Interest necessary part of Financial Debt Following are the judgments by the NCLAT highlighting the fact that the interest component is necessary to constitute a financial debt.

1.

Vishwa Nath Singh (supra), the NCLAT observed that the FC must prove that the loan amount given is a financial debt and was disbursed against the consideration for the time value of money and the payment of interest. The tribunal has used the term "and" in between the words "consideration of time value of money" and "payment of interest", thereby making it a mandatory condition for constituting a financial debt.

2.

Dr. B.V.S. Lakshmi (supra) wherein the Appellate Tribunal held that the for categorising a debt as financial debt it to be against payment of interest and consideration for the time value of money.

3.

Shreyans Realtors (P.) Ltd. (supra) wherein the NCLAT was of the view that if in the agreement the interest component was not accepted by the CD and the CD never paid or undertook to repay the loan with interest, the loan granted will not be termed as financial debt and the creditor will not be called as an FC.

Interest not necessary part of Financial Debt

Following are the judgments by the NCLAT highlighting the fact that the interest component is not necessary to constitute a financial debt.

1.

Shailesh Sangani v. Joel Cardoso [2019] 103 taxmann.com 181/152 SCL 657 : The NCLAT, in this case, had expressly observed that the suffix "if any" before the word "interest" in the definition of financial debt means that element of interest is not an essential requirement for claiming a debt to be a financial debt and further went on to say that the loan disbursed against the consideration for the time value of money "may or may not" have the component of interest attached to it. Lastly, it held that what prima facie is of importance is that the debt should be against the consideration for the time value of money.

2.

Sanjay Kewalramani v. Sunil Parmanand Kewalramani [Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 57 of 2018, dated 12-7-2018]: The Appellate Tribunal while dealing with the matter observed that the loan given by Respondent No. 2 & 3 in the present matter was not against consideration of time value of money and further held that mere granting of the loan will not make the Respondents as FC until they show that they have complied with the substantive definition or any clauses of Section 5(8) of the Code. Also, it held that mere payment of interest for a certain period will not make the debt to be a financial debt as under the IBC.

Hence, from the above-mentioned judgments, it is understood that the tribunals earlier had divided opinions w.r.t. interest being an essential part of the financial debt. However, the Supreme Court in the Orator's case has clarified the status. Now, the settled position of law is that the loans having no interest payable on them will be considered as a financial debt along with the interest payable loans.

Meaning of Disbursement and Time Value of Money

The Supreme Court in the case of Pioneer Urban Land & Infrastructure Ltd. (supra) while interpreting the word "disbursed" under section 5(8) of the Code referred to the Black's Law Dictionary 10th Edition which provides that "disbursement means money paid for the settlement of a debt or for a particular purpose". The Court had applied the same interpretation while dealing with the above-said case and concluded that the "disbursement against consideration for the time value of money" means that the money has been disbursed from the creditor, i.e., it is no longer with the loan giver, and is with the debtor.

CHAPTER 3

ESSENTIAL ELEMENTS OF FINANCIAL DEBT 3.1 Disbursement of Money

The first essential element of financial debt is disbursement. Disbursement refers to the transfer of money from the creditor to the debtor. Financial debt must involve the actual disbursal of funds, which creates a liability on the borrower. Without such disbursement, the transaction cannot ordinarily qualify as financial debt.

3.2Consideration for Time Value of Money

The time value of money is the most important characteristic of financial debt. It reflects the principle that money today is worth more than the same amount in the future. The elements generally are:

Interest payments

Financial returns

Compensation for delayed repayment

In the absence of such consideration, the transaction may not qualify as financial debt.

In the matter of Shivam Agrioils (P.) Ltd. v. Shree Krishna Vanaspati Industries (P.) Ltd. [Company Appeal (AT)(Insolvency) No. 982 of 2022] NCLAT observed that Interest on loan is not the only binding criterion for determining the time value of money for Financial Debt under IBC.

Whether disbursement for the time value of money is an essential ingredient to prove a Financial Debt? – Kesoram Industries Ltd. v. Pratim Bayal [2024] 159 taxmann.com 27 (NCLAT - New Delhi)

Hon'ble NCLAT held that: Disbursement against the consideration for the time value of money has to be proved for a financial debt. There is no disbursement by the Appellant to the Corporate Debtor. When there is no disbursement for the time value of money, essential ingredients to prove a financial debt are missing.

3.3 Commercial Effect of Borrowing

Section 5(8) also includes transactions that have the commercial effect of borrowing. This provision ensures that sophisticated financial arrangements designed to function like loans are also covered under the definition.

Examples include:

Structured finance transactions

Forward sale agreements

Certain investment arrangements

A liability in respect of a claim arising out of a Recovery Certificate would be a Financial Debt within Section 5(8) of IBC. A limitation period of three years starts from the date of issuance of the Recovery Certificate – Kotak Mahindra Bank Ltd. v. A. Balakrishnan and Anr, Civil Appeal No. 689 of 2021 – Supreme Court.

Hon'ble Supreme Court concluded that a liability in respect of a claim arising out of a Recovery Certificate would be a "financial debt" within the meaning of clause (8) of Section 5 of the IBC. Consequently, the holder of the Recovery Certificate would be a financial creditor within the meaning of clause (7) of Section 5 of the IBC. As such, the holder of such a certificate would be entitled to initiate CIRP if initiated within a period of three years from the date of issuance of the Recovery Certificate.

Consequently, the situation where an interest payable on a loan is converted into shares in the name of the lender/creditor is different from the situation envisaged in Explanation 3C to section 43B of the Act, viz., conversion of interest into 'a loan or borrowing'. In the latter instance, the liability continues, although in a different form. However, where the interest or a part thereof is converted into equity shares, the said Interest amount for which the conversion is taking place is no longer a liability." [Para 40]

'Financial debt' and 'financial creditor'

The expressions 'financial creditor' and 'financial debt' have been defined in section 5(7) and 5(8) and precisely 'financial debt' is a debt along with interest, if any, which is disbursed against the consideration for time value of money. [Para 14]

In the instant case, the applicant disbursed the loan and the respondent in their reply has admitted that the amount of Rs. 30 lakhs was received from the applicant but as a long-term borrowing. The respondent, therefore, has accepted that the debt amount of Rs. 30 lakhs given by the applicant was in the nature of a loan. Once it is accepted that the amount of Rs. 30 lakhs was received as a long-term borrowing, it is evident that the said loan amount was clearly disbursed against the consideration for time value of money with a clear commercial effect of borrowing. Besides the amount of financial debt has been recorded in the balance sheets of the corporate debtor and Form 26AS of the financial creditor, which reveals that the debt was advanced against consideration for time value of money. Moreover, the debt claimed in the instant application includes both the component of outstanding principal and interest. [Para 15]

In that view of the matter not only the instant claim comes within the purview of 'Financial Debt' in terms of section 5(8) but also the applicant can clearly be termed as 'financial creditor' of the respondent-corporate debtor so as to prefer the instant application under section 7. [Para 16]

Conditions for Admission of CIRP application

The application filed by the applicant financial creditor has to be admitted under sub-section 5(a) of section 7 of the code, on satisfaction that (i) Default has occurred, (ii) Application is complete, and (iii) No disciplinary proceeding against the proposed IRP is pending. [Para 17]

An application under section 7 is acceptable so long as the financial debt is proved to be due and there has been occurrence of existence of default. What is material is that the default is at least 1 lakh. In view of section 4, the moment default is of Rs. 1 lakh or more, the application to trigger corporate insolvency resolution process under the code is maintainable. In the instant case the claimed financial debt exceeds Rupees 44 lakhs and the respondent has defaulted in making the payment of the debt. [Para 18]

In connection with the 2nd requirement of sub-section (5)(a) of section 7, it is seen that the instant application is complete and has been filed by the petitioner financial creditor in Form-1 in terms of rule 4 of the Insolvency and Bankruptcy (Application to Adjudicating Authority) Rules, 2016 accompanied with the required information, documents and records as prescribed under the Rules. [Para 19]

The applicant inter alia has annexed to the application detail particulars of 'financial debt' including documents and records as evidence of default as required under sub-section (3)(a) of section 7. It is reiterated that the Form-1 filed in the instant case under section 7 read with rule 4 of the Rules, shows that the Form is complete in all respect and there is no infirmity in the same. [Para 20]

It is, thus, seen that the requirement of sub-section (5)(a) of section 7 stands satisfied as default has occurred; the instant application filed under section 7 is complete. [Para 22]

Whether written financial contract be the only material to prove the financial debt

The submission of the respondent that the written financial contract is necessary for proving debt. A financial contract supported by financial statements as evidence of the debt is one of the documents contemplated in regulation 8(2) of the IBBI (Insolvency Resolution Process for Corporate Persons) Regulation, 2016 but that is not exclusive requirement for proving existence of debt. Financial contract, thus, can very well be furnished to prove the financial debt but a plain reading of regulation 8(2) indicate that it is not mandatory that existence of financial debt has to be proved by a financial contract. For example: records available with an information utility can very well be used as proof for existence of financial debt. Further, financial statements showing that the debt has not been paid is also one of the clauses in regulation 8(2) by which existence of debt can be proved. [Para 11]

The Financial Creditor has failed to establish that the transaction in question is a Financial Debt and due and payable and the Corporate Debtor has committed default. The judgment Pawan Kumar v. Utsav Securities (P.) Ltd. [2021] 131 taxmann.com 211/168 SCL 692 (NCLAT - New Delhi), cannot be relied as laying down any preposition that unless there is Financial Contract to establish financial debt, Financial Creditor cannot prove the financial debt by any other document. [Para 15]

When one looks into the statutory scheme as reflected in the application to Adjudicating Authority Rules, 2016 and CIRP Regulations, 2016, it is clear that financial debt can be proved from other relevant documents and it is not mandatory that written financial contract can be only basis for proving the financial debt. Thus, it is not necessary that written financial contract be the only material to prove the financial debt. [Para 21]

Nikhil Mehta & Sons (HUF) (supra): The NCLAT in the present case elaborately dealt with the question as to who is an FC and consequently upheld the decision of the AA on the said point which provides that the FC is a person to whom a financial debt is owed. The tribunal while understanding financial debt stated that as per the definition given under section 5(8), the financial debt has to have a disbursement which was against the consideration for the time value of money. It further went on to elaborate the phrase "time value of money" and referred to the Black's Law Dictionary which provides that it is the "price which is associated with the length of time that an investor has to wait until an investment matures or related income is earned". Hence, the investment and outcome are separated by time and the compensation for such time is the time value of money.

Time Value of Money Includes Interest

The NCLAT admits the contention of the FC who stated that even if an inter-corporate deposit was to be repaid within a certain period with interest then such transaction will fall within the definition of financial debt. The Appellate Tribunal further went on to say that the interest component in the present transaction is the time value of money. Hence, the decision was given in favour of the FC.

The Tribunal further held that at the most, the default will create a debt that can be recovered but not the financial debt and thus, the petition was dismissed.

Critical Analysis of the Supreme Court's Judgment in the Orator's case.

Considering the Orator's judgment by the Supreme Court in the light of various judgments and points discussed above, the authors vehemently states that the judgment has not removed the black cloud over the issue of interest not being an essential part of financial debt. Instead, it has brought forward various ambiguous points, upon which a necessary deliberation is required.

All Promoters including the Financial Creditor herein, have confirmed the Subordination Agreement with their Bank, for and on behalf of the Corporate Debtor, and have undertaken that the unsecured creditors had extended or continued to extend interest free unsecured loan on the express understanding that all their claims against the respondent company would be subject to the claims of Canara Bank; that all the claims of the unsecured creditors against the respondent company would at all times be subordinate and be subject to any claims of Canara Bank; that unsecured creditors agree not to sue the respondent company for recovering any money tendered to the respondent company as unsecured loan until all the claims of Canara Bank get settled; that the unsecured creditors agree not to join in any bankruptcy or any assignment.

It is therefore submitted by the respondent that since the unsecured loans were interest-free, no interest was promised. In view of the facts and circumstances of the case, the present claim does not fall within the definition of a financial debt nor is it an unsecured loan repayable on demand. There is not Demand Promissory Note executed, nor is there any agreement for payment of any interest. As submitted by the corporate debtor and not denied by the operational creditor, the amount given by him along with 6 others was for promoting and setting up a business. The terms for raising the bank loan necessitated investment of the margin money. This was done by all the promoters and is reflected as unsecured loans, subordinate to the claim of the bank. The bank agreement corroborating this is on record.

Though it is admitted by the financial creditor that this unsecured loan would be subordinate to the claim made by the Canara Bank, it appears that notwithstanding his agreement not to seek recovery of his unsecured loan till the liability of Canara Bank stands extinguished or his undertaking not to participate in Insolvency proceedings, it is his wish and desire that the resolution process be initiated and the entire project be dumped before it comes into operation, irrespective of whether he can realise any proceeds or not in the watershed for repayment should the assets of the corporate debtor be liquidated. It is being noted that Canara Bank is not an aggrieved party. [Para 9]

The said attitude of the financial creditor is irreprehensible as the principal money lender i.e., Canara Bank has not made any claim. Insolvency Resolution Process of a corporate entity cannot be initiated on such grounds which reek of personal vendetta. The financial creditor seeks to scuttle the project even before it get into operation. Such arm twisting tactics cannot be the basis for initiation of Insolvency Process. [Para 10]

The petition is, therefore, rejected. [Para 11]

5.2 Inter-Corporate Deposits

Inter-corporate deposits are commonly used as financing mechanisms between companies. Inter-Corporate Deposits (ICDs) are a common financing mechanism in which one company lends money to another, usually for a fixed period and often with interest.

NCLT Principal Bench, New Delhi in the matter of Proplarity Infratech (P.) Ltd. v. Sky High Technobuild (P.) Ltd. [CP (IB) No.607/(PB)/2023] rules that Inter Corporate deposits in balance sheet not sufficient to establish financial debt without documentation.

The CD contended that there was no formal loan agreement, and the amount was recorded as an "Inter-Corporate Deposit" rather than a financial debt. The CD argued that the FC did not meet the requirements of Sections 5(7) and 5(8) of the IBC, and that no default occurred under Section 3(12) of the Code.

The NCLT noted that the mere listing of the amount as an "Inter-Corporate Deposit" without detailed documentation or a formal loan agreement was insufficient to establish financial debt. The absence of a loan agreement and supporting documentation weakened the FC's claim.

FC submits it that alleged transaction of Rs. 2,00,00,000 was given as a loan @18%interest p.a. It is observed from the balance sheet of CD that the amount of Rs. 2,00,00,000 has been shown as Inter Corporate Deposit under the heading "Long Term Borrowing" from the period 2013- 2017 and from the period 2018-2021, the said amount has been shown as "Unsecured Loans" under the heading "Long Term Borrowing."

Mere recording of a transaction in the balance sheet of the CD as "Inter-Corporate Deposit" would not constitute it as Financial Debt unless proved by a supporting document.

Additionally, in the matter ofSeaview Merchants (P.) Ltd. v. Ashish Vincom (P.) Ltd. [C.P (IB) 2011/KB/2019], SRF Ltd. v. Birla Tyres Ltd. [2024] 159 taxmann.com 27 (NCLAT - New Delhi), stated that Inter- Corporate Deposit are not Financial Debt unless the loan advanced is proved by way of documentary evidence.

5.3 Convertible Debentures and Hybrid Financial Instruments as Financial Debt.

In terms of Section 5(8)(c), any amount raised pursuant to Optionally Convertible Debentures (OCDs) comes within the meaning of Financial Debt.MAIF Investments India Pte. Ltd. v. Ind-Barath Energy (Utkal) Ltd. [Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 597 of 2018].

In terms of Section 5(8)(c), any amount raised pursuant to any note purchase facility or the issue of bonds, notes, debentures, loan stock or any similar instrument comes within the meaning of 'financial debt'. Therefore, from the aforesaid fact. There is a disbursal of Rs. 102 Crores in favour of the 'Corporate Debtor' and the 'OCDs' originally met is against the time value of money and per se, constitutes 'financial debt' in the light of Section 5(8)(c) of the 'I&B Code'.

Whether unpaid amount claimed by financial creditor was financial debt

The corporate debtor has admitted that the amount paid by the applicant-financial creditor was towards an arrangement entered into between the parties as per the MoU. [Para 16]

On perusal of the pleadings and looking in to the terms and conditions contained in the MoU, it appears that the intentions of the parties were to give life to the corporate debtor which was facing a financial crisis. The financial creditor was under the obligation to arrange for working capital and took responsibilities of the day-to-day management of the corporate debtor. The applicant-financial creditor was also made responsible for payments of statutory dues and other administrative expenses including liabilities as on the 'effective date' given in the MoU. [Para 17]

In pursuant to the terms and conditions of the MoU, the applicant-financial creditor had started to make payments to the corporate debtor as reflects from the Certificate issued by the Bank of Maharahstra. The total amount now claimed is Rs. 2.14 crore along with further interest at the rate of 18 per cent per annum. [Para 18]

As per the terms and conditions of the MoU the financial creditor brought funds from time to time for corporate debtor's working capital, cleared its liabilities and paid other expenses. However, the corporate debtor did not perform its obligation, i.e., to proceed to negotiate the terms of definitive agreement, as was envisaged for implementation of provisions of the MoU. Therefore, money infused by the applicant-financial creditor into the corporate debtor is being demanded back by the applicant, which the corporate debtor failed to pay. The money brought by the financial creditor into the corporate debtor was part of a purchase agreement i.e., for the purchase of the corporate debtor company, including its subsidiary in terms of the MoU, which did not happen. Thus, the amount raised falls within the purview of 'any other transaction/purchase agreement, having the commercial effect of borrowing' which certainly carried the element of time value for money. Therefore, the debt claimed by the financial creditor falls within the purview of the provisions of section 5(8)(f).

The view is based on the well-established maxim of interpretation which says 'ut res magis valeat quam pereat'. This Latin maxim of interpretation when translated into English means that 'it is better for a thing to have effect than to be void'. In other words, where the provisions of a statute are plain, precise and unambiguous; it must be given the same meaning which it receives in ordinary parlance so as to give effect to same. Accordingly, the issue stands decided in favour of the financial creditor and against the corporate debtor. [Para 19]

Whether the amount claimed by the Financial Creditor is a Financial Debt under the IBC ?

(i) From a conjoint reading of the provisions of the Act and the documents executed between the parties, it can be safely concluded that JKSIDCO leased out 200 kanals of land to JKITPL for a period of 90 years, where JKITPL paid a premium of Rs.3 crore to JKSIDCO and further paid Rs.12 lakhs as an advance ground rent for two years. The ownership of the land vests with the JKSIDCO and the ownership of the building constructed upon that land vests with JKITPL. The industrial units were to pay annual lease rent to JKITPL for the use of the leased premises. Further, as mentioned in the Agreement dated 6-10-2015 between the Corporate Debtor and JKITPL, it is mentioned that the net cost of the project/building is Rs.3.04 crores for the construction of building and in the same project, the cost incurred by the party of the second part is Rs.3.04 crores for the component of building constructed.

(ii)

The amount of Rs.1.24 crores mentioned as cost of land to be paid by the Corporate Debtor to JKITPL is not a financial debt advanced by JKITPL to the Corporate Debtor. The annual lease rent, which the industrial units, including the Corporate Debtor were to pay to JKITPL, is not in nature financial debt, as it intends towards availing services from JKITPL by the Corporate Debtor, i.e., use of the leased premises and buildings.

(iii)

While determining, whether a debt falls within the definition of financial debt as defined under section 5(8), mere existence of the debt is not to be ascertained. In addition to the existence of the debt, the intended use of such debt is also to be seen in order to categorise it as a financial debt.

(iv)

Further, in the Petition filed under section 7, the Financial Creditor has not appended any cogent evidence of disbursal of the debt amount to the Corporate Debtor. On 4-12-2016, an agreement was entered between the financial creditor and the corporate debtor for equal equity participation to bid and acquisition of sona.

However, the company (SPT) was declared the highest bidder at the auction of 'Sona'.

After SPT was declared highest bidder, the corporate debtor approached the financial creditor to send a further amount of Rs. 1.5 million USD directly to the (SPT) account and assured that (SPT) would issue equity shares for investment by the financial creditor.

The financial creditor approached the RBI for granting permission to transfer funds to the SPT towards share application money, and permission having been granted, an amount of USD 1.5 million was transferred to SPT by the financial creditor, after transferring USD 1.5 million, the financial creditor asked the corporate debtor to return 3.5 crores, which was disbursed by the financial creditor to the corporate debtor.

However, SPT failed to issue securities within period of 60 days and also failed to refund the share application money amount of Rs. 1.5 million.

The financial creditor demanded entire money back, both Rs. 3.5, crores, which was earlier disbursed, and amount of USD. 1.5 million directly transferred to the SPT.

The financial creditor filed an application under section 7 and the director of corporate debtor, vide e-mail dated 28-5-2018, stated that the corporate debtor was unable to pay interest at 18 per cent per annum as demanded by the financial creditor on amount of Rs. 3.5 crores, however, agreed to pay interest at 12 per annum.

On 14-7-2018, an agreement was entered between the corporate debtor, director of the corporate debtor and an investor, where it was admitted that the corporate debtor owed INR 3.5 crores from the financial creditor.

The corporate debtor also acknowledged, vide e-mail dated 12-3-2018 the return of the amount of Rs. 3.5 crores to the financial creditor.

On appeal, the appellant submitted that the amount of Rs. 3.5 crores paid by the financial creditor was not a financial debt, rather the amount was given by the financial creditor towards 50 per cent equity shares for the investment only.

The appellant further submitted that it was categorically mentioned in agreement dated 14-7-2018 that on receipt of USD 0.80 million from investor, amount of Rs. 3.5 crores be returned within three days since return was based on contingency of receipt of an amount of USD 0.80 million from the investor, and the investor never made payment of USD 0.80 million, hence no claim could be raised by the financial creditor for a refund of Rs. 3.5 crores.

The appellant further alleged that the amount of Rs. 3.5 crores was given by the financial creditor to the appellant was deal free and the same was clearly mentioned in the agreement dated 14-6-2016 and, therefore, the appellant had no responsibility to return the deal fee of Rs. 3.5 crores.

The first issue for consideration is ‘Whether there is financial debt under section 5(8) of IBC?’

A perusal of the records reveals that the Corporate Debtor had availed credit facilities for a sum of Rs.295 crore. The next issue for consideration is ‘Whether there is a ‘default’ as defined under Section 3(12) of the IBC, 2016?’

As per the Rupee Loan Agreement, which is entered into between the Parties herein, the repayment of the loan starts from 09.08.2025. The Financial Creditor argued that the Corporate Debtor has deviated from Clause 2.1.8 of the Loan Agreement, which provides that the loan facility shall be utilized towards advance for development of the Project and general corporate purpose including refinance, and once the Corporate Debtor deviated the Clause 2.1.8 of Loan Agreement, the Financial Creditor is always having a right under Clause 8.1.22(g) of the Agreement, and they can recall the debt any time before the scheduled date of repayment in the given Agreement. Clause 2.1.8 of the Agreement provides that the “The Loan facility shall be utilized towards advance for development of the project and general corporate purpose including refinance”.

Further, Clause 8.1 of Article VIII of the Agreement defines an ‘Events of Default’ which provides the events and occurrences that shall constitute an Event of Default for the purposes of this Agreement.

At this juncture, it is pertinent to examine the meaning of the term ‘refinancing’ as referred to in the Clause 2.1.8 of the Rupee Loan Agreement. Since the term is not expressly defined in the Loan Agreement, reference may be made to the Cambridge Dictionary, which defines Refinance as “to replace a loan with a new one.” As per Webster Law Dictionary, “Refinancing means paying off one loan with another loan, often in order to get better terms”. In other words, it is replacing an existing loan with a new loan in order to change the repayment terms, such as the interest rate or the term of the loan.

■

It is also pertinent to examine the meaning of the term ‘general corporate purposes, as referred to in the Clause 2.1.8 of the Rupee Loan Agreement. Since the term is not expressly defined in the Loan Agreement, the Cambridge and Webster Law Dictionary is referred, but there not find the definition of the above term there also. Therefore, the definition given in Regulation 2(1)(r) of the Securities and Exchange Board of India (Issue of Capital and Disclosure Requirements) Regulations, 2018 is used. According to which, the term “general corporate purposes” encompasses identified objectives for which no specific amount is allocated, or any amount designated towards general corporate purposes or similar objectives by any name, as stated in the draft offer document, draft letter of offer, or offer document. However, it is explicitly provided that issue-related expenses shall not be considered part of general corporate purposes merely because no specific amount has been allocated for such expenses in the aforementioned documents.

Whether the Adjudicating Authority has exceeded in its jurisdiction while examining the nature of transaction in question?

IBC recognizes that for the success of Insolvency regime the real nature of transaction has to be unearthed in order to prevent any person from taking undue benefit of its provisions to the detriment of the rights of legitimate creditors. It means, while admitting the Application under section 7 of the IBC, it is the duty of the Adjudicating Authority to investigate the real nature of the transaction in order to prevent any person from taking undue benefit of its provisions to the detriment of the rights of legitimate creditors. [Para 16]

The Supreme Court in case of Swiss Ribbons (P.) Ltd. v. Union of India [2019] 101 taxmann.com 389/152 SCL 365 held that even if the application filed under section 7 meets all the requirements, then also the Adjudicating Authority has to exercise discretion carefully to prevent and protect the corporate debtor from being dragged into the Corporate Insolvency Resolution Process mala fide. [Para 18]

The Adjudicating Authority is obliged to investigate the nature of the transaction and should be very cautious in admitting the Application in order to prevent taking undue benefit of provisions of IBC to detriment of the rights of legitimate creditors as well as to protect the corporate debtor from being dragged into CIRP with mala fide. Section 65 provides that if any person initiates the Insolvency Resolution Process or liquidation proceedings fraudulently or with malicious intent for any purpose other than for resolution of Insolvency or Liquidation, the Adjudicating Authority may impose upon such person a penalty. Section 65 provides that where any person furnishes any information under section 7, which is false in material particulars, knowing it to be false or omits any material facts, knowing it to be material such person shall be punished with fine. [Para 19]

The argument of the appellant that Adjudicating Authority when entered into investigating the nature of the transaction then exceeded in its jurisdiction under section 7(5), is not convincing. [Para 20]

Point No.(i)

The financial creditor, in order to prove its claim as financial debt, has relied upon Loan Agreement dated 07.05.2015. The said loan agreement is executed between the Financial Creditor and Corporate Debtor. The Corporate Debtor has requested to provide a short-term loan of Rs. 2.50 Crores against security of first mortgage on property and the Financial Creditor has agreed to lend. (Para 29)

■

Section 3 (11) of the IBC defines ‘debt’ to mean a liability or obligation in respect of a claim which is due from any person and includes a financial debt and operational debt. Section 3(12) of IBC defines default to mean non-payment of debt when whole or any part or instalment of the amount has become due and payable and is not paid by the debtor or the corporate debtor, as the case may. (Para 30)

■

A perusal of the aforesaid provision reveals that for a transaction to be considered as a financial debt under the IBC, there should be disbursal against consideration for the time value of money. Similarly, for an applicant to be considered as a ‘Financial Creditor’ under the IBC, it is to be proved that such applicant had assessed the financial viability of the corporate debtor and would engage in restructuring of the loan or reorganization of the corporate debtor''s business if the latter would fall in a financial stress. (Para 31)

■

In the facts and circumstances of this case, a perusal of account statement of the financial creditor reveals that an amount of Rs. 2.50 Crores was disbursed in the account of the Corporate Debtor on 07.05.2015 and the same is not disputed by the Corporate Debtor. Said loan amount has been acknowledged by the Corporate Debtor in its audited Balance Sheet dated 31.3.2018, 31.3.2019, 31.3.2021, 31.3.2022 and 31.3.2023. Therefore, existence of financial debt has been proved on file. (Para 32)

The only issue arises in the instant appeal is whether the transaction in question is a financial debt. [Para 12]

Certain essential conditions are required to be satisfied by a financial creditor seeking to invoke the provisions of CIRP as against the corporate debtor. Following essential conditions are required to be satisfied by a financial creditor.

(i)

There must be disbursal of loan amount,

(ii)

Such disbursal should be made for a consideration for time value of money, and

(iii)

When the debt (Whole or any part of instalment) become due and payable and is not paid by the corporate debtor means committed default. [Para 13]

The above all conditions are to be satisfied by the financial creditor then the Adjudicating Authority may admit the application under section 7 and initiate the CIRP against the corporate debtor. In the instant case, it is an admitted fact that financial creditor transferred Rs. 6.10 crores to the corporate debtor's bank account. This fact is corroborated by the bank entries filed by the financial creditor and the corporate debtor has not denied that the corporate debtor has not received such amount. Thus, aforesaid amount has been disbursed by the financial creditor to the corporate debtor. However, there is no written agreement between the parties to show that the disbursement of such amount is a loan transaction. [Para 14]

Now, it is to be considered whether such amount is disbursed for a consideration for time value of money. [Para 15]

According to the financial creditor, the corporate debtor has paid interest of Rs. 6.05 lakhs after deduction of TDS and this fact is undisputed. Therefore, it is proved that such disbursal has been made for a consideration for time value of money. However, as per the corporate debtor, on the basis of deduction of TDS such inference cannot be drawn. [Para 16]

Thus, aforesaid amount after deduction of TDS has been paid to the financial creditor on this basis it cannot be concluded that the transaction in question is a financial debt. [Para 18]

According to the financial creditor an oral loan agreement can be enforceable in law in view of section 10 of the Indian Contract Act and section 186(11) of the Act. [Para 19]

On the other hand, as per the corporate debtor in absence of a financial contract defined in rule 3(1)(d) of the Insolvency and Bankruptcy (Application to Adjudicating Authority) Rules, 2016 between the corporate debtor and financial creditor, the transaction cannot be termed as financial debt. RBI on issued guidelines to Non-Banking Finance Companies for fair practices which states that the Non-Banking Finance Company should convey in writing to the borrower in vernacular language as understood by the borrower by means sanctioned letter or otherwise, the amount of loan sanctioned along with the terms and conditions including annualised rate of interest. Thus, it is obligatory on the part of the financial creditor that there should be a loan agreement in writing only. [Para 20]

The financial creditor has not furnished any document to show that the transaction in question is a loan transaction. [Para 21]

The financial contract as per the rule 3(1)(d) of the Insolvency and Bankruptcy (Application to Adjudicating Authority) Rules, 2016 is a must between the corporate debtor and the financial creditor for setting out the terms of a financial debt including the tenure of the debt, interest payable and the date of repayment. In the absence of such financial contract, the financial creditor has failed to satisfy that when the debt and interest became due and payable. [Para 22]

The financial creditor has not filed any writing to show that when the debt become due and payable. As per the financial creditor the debt in question is payable on demand. From the notice and the application, it is not clear that on which date the demand was made and the loan and interest became due and payable. [Para 24]

Section 7(3)(a) provides that the financial creditor shall along with the application is required to furnish, a record of default recorded with the information utility or such other record or evidence of default as may be specified. The financial creditor has not filed any evidence of default along with the application under section 7. [Para 25]

Thus, the financial creditor failed to establish when the debt became due and payable and the corporate debtor has committed default. [Para 26]

The Adjudicating Authority took a view that there is no written agreement to establish the nature of transaction between the parties, hence, appellant failed to prove the debt. It is already held that requirement of written financial contract is not a pre-condition for proving debt. When Adjudicating Authority itself given finding that the disbursement was with interest and repayment was on demand, two essential conditions of financial debt were present with regard to time value of money. When the financial statement indicate amount with interest since the loan of Rs. 75 lacs increased in the financial year 2017-18 and amount due was shown as Rs. 79.70 Lacs,which clearly was after adding the interest, disbursement has to be held for time value of money. Thus, are satisfied that all pre-conditions for establishing financial debt are proved by the financial creditor and the order of the Adjudicating Authority rejecting section 7 application is not sustainable. IBC : Definition of 'Financial Debt' in section 5(8) does not expressly exclude an interest free loan; a person who gives a term loan to a corporate person free of interest on account of its working capital requirements is a financial creditor, and, therefore, is competent to initiate Corporate Insolvency resolution process under section 7

A plain look at the definition of 'financial debt' brings it to notice that the debt along with interest, if any, should have been disbursed against the consideration for the time value of money. Use of expression 'if any' as suffix to 'interest' leaves no room for doubt that the component of interest is not a sine qua non for bringing the debt within the fold of 'financial debt'. The amount disbursed as debt against the consideration for time value of money may or may not be interest bearing. What is material is that the disbursement of debt should be against consideration for the time value of money. Clauses (a) to (i) of section 5(8) embody the nature of transactions which are included in the definition of 'financial debt'. It includes money borrowed against the payment of interest. Clause (f) of section 5(8) specifically deals with amount raised under any other transaction having the commercial effect of a borrowing which also includes a forward sale or purchase agreement. It is manifestly clear that money advanced by a promoter, director or a shareholder of the corporate debtor as a stakeholder to improve financial health of the company and boost its economic prospects, would have the commercial effect of borrowing on the part of corporate debtor notwithstanding the fact that no provision is made for interest thereon. Due to fluctuations in market and the risks to which it is exposed, a company may at times feel the heat of resource crunch and the stakeholders like promoter, director or a shareholder may, in order to protect their legitimate interests be called upon to respond to the crisis and in order to save the company they may infuse funds without claiming interest. In such situation such funds may be treated as long term borrowings. Once it is so, it cannot be said that the debt has not been disbursed against the consideration for the time value of the money. The interests of such stakeholders cannot be said to be in conflict with the interests of the company. Enhancement of assets, increase in production and the growth in profits, share value or equity ensures to the benefit of such stakeholders and that is the time value of the money constituting the consideration for disbursement of such amount raised as debt with obligation on the part of company to discharge the same. Viewed thus, it can be said without any amount of contradiction that in such cases the amount taken by the company is in the nature of a 'financial debt'. [Para 6]

The balance sheet as on 31-3-2017 filed by the R1, inter alia, reflects a non-current liability of Rs. 4.72 crores treated as 'long term borrowings' and not treated as shareholder's funds and the breakup showing the loan amount of Rs. 1.45 crores in the name of R1.

In the face of this documentary evidence it is abundantly clear that the amount disbursed by the R1 to the corporate debtor was in the nature of debt treated as long term loan and not as an investment in the nature of share capital or equity. Such disbursement cannot either be treated as largesse. We are convinced that the aforesaid amount outstanding as against corporate debtor, default whereof is not in issue, has all the trappings of a 'financial debt' and falls within the purview of section 5(8)(f) and the R1 is covered by the definition of 'financial creditor'. [Para 9]

For the foregoing reasons there is no merit in this appeal. There being no infirmity in the impugned order, this appeal is dismissed. [Para 11]

The Court had applied the same interpretation while dealing with the above-said case and concluded that the "disbursement against consideration for the time value of money" means that the money has been disbursed from the creditor, i.e., it is no longer with the loan giver, and is with the debtor. At the same time, the Court in the same case interpreted "Time Value of Money" and reference was made to Dictionary of Banking (2nd Edition) by Thomas P. It also provides that the time value of money is the difference in the value to be received today as compared to a greater value to be received in future. Also, the Insolvency Law Committee Report2 has the time value of money which means the compensation for the duration for which the money has been disbursed by the creditor to the debtor which can be in form of either interest or factoring of discount in payment. Further, in the case of Nikhil Mehta & Sons (HUF) v. AMR Infrastructure Ltd. [2017] 78 taxmann.com 302/140 SCL 135 (NCLT - New Delhi), the Appellate Tribunal referred to the Black's Law Dictionary, 9th Edition to construe the meaning of time value of money and concluded that it is the compensation or the price paid for the time during which the money was disbursed, i.e., the time between lending and repayment.

Time Value of Money a Prerequisite of Financial Debt

Below-mentioned is the judgments of the Supreme Court, NCLAT and the NCLT highlighting the "consideration for the time value of money" as an essential part of the financial debt.

1.

Pioneer Urban Land & Infrastructure Ltd. (supra) (Pioneer's case): The Supreme Court stated that the disbursal and consideration for the time value of money are the essential constituents of financial debt without which the application under section 7 of the IBC remains incomplete.

2.

State Bank of India v. Rajendra Bhuta, IRP of Prabhat Technologies (India) Limited (IA No. 440 of 2020, dated 6-1-2021] in C.P. No. 1874/MB/2019): The NCLT Mumbai Bench while dealing with the question of terming a Forward Purchase Agreement (FPA) under the category of financial debt or not and observed that in order to categorise a debt as financial debt, it necessarily has to be disbursed against the consideration for the time value of money. Further, if an FPA is to be termed as financial debt it has to have two attributes, i.e., a) should be against consideration for the time value of money and, b) should have the commercial effect of borrowing. The AA held that the transaction entered into by the parties was a mere sale and purchase agreement and should not come within the definition of financial debt.

3.

K. N. Mahesh Prasad v. Medinnbelle Herbalcare (P.) Ltd. [Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 512 of 2019, dated 22-1-2020]: The NCLAT upheld the decision of the AA which dismissed the application of the creditor stating that the transaction in the case in hand was a simple loan agreement which is denuded of any element of the time value of money and won't constitute a financial debt.

4.

Indiabulls Housing Finance Ltd. v. Rudra Buildwell Projects (P.) Ltd . [2019] 108 taxmann.com 57/155 SCL 32 (NCL-AT): An appeal was filed by the Appellant stating that it had given loans to the borrower vide loan agreement dated 6-4-2015. A subsequent agreement was entered into by the Respondent and the borrower wherein it was agreed that the interest for the former agreement shall be paid by the Respondent on behalf of the borrower. On default on repayment of the same, the FC filed an application under section 7 against the Respondent. The NCLAT dismissed the application highlighting the fact that though the disbursement of the loan was made against the consideration for the time value of money and the creditor was the FC still the application won't be accepted as the disbursement was made in favour of the borrower and not the Respondent.

5.

IBC : Where loan agreements between parties clearly showed that loans were interest bearing and were in nature of financial debts, which carried time value of money, NCLT erred in dismissing application filed by appellant-operational creditor under section 7 against respondent-corporate debtor on ground that amounts advanced were not financial debts

IBC : Where appellant filed an application under section 7 against corporate debtor but had failed to establish that he had given any loan to corporate debtor directly and no material was placed on record by appellant, in which corporate debtor had unambiguously admitted debt, in absence of financial debt qua corporate debtor,

IBC : Where appellant/financial creditor advanced interest free loan to corporate debtor to discharge its liabilities towards secured financial creditors and said loan was acknowledged by corporate debtor as it was reflected in its balance sheet as unsecured loan, said amount fell within definition of default on part of corporate debtor and, therefore, NCLT had committed a patent error in dismissing application filed under section 7.

I&B Code: Where applicant had failed to bring on record any evidence to suggest that he disbursed money against consideration for time value of money and there was no information about rate of interest on principal amount, loan did not satisfy requirement of financial debt as contemplated under section 5(8)

INTRODUCTION

Financial Debt has been clearly defined under the provisions of section 5(8) of the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016 (hereinafter referred to as 'IBC'). Also, in various judgements/orders by different NCLT/NCLAT benches, the definition has been well unleashed. Further, in the matter of Nikhil Mehta & Sons v. AMR Infrastructure (P.) Ltd. [2017] 84 taxmann.com 163/143 SCL 278, the Hon'ble NCLAT has very clearly explained the criteria to be checked for ascertaining if debt is a financial debt or not. Also, it is well settled that while dealing with the application under section 7 of the IBC the Hon'ble Adjudicating Authority(NCLT)has to only focus on the nature of debt i.e. if it is financial debt or not and whether it is due and defaulted and not having existence of any dispute.

In the recent matter of Drip Capital Inc. v. Concord Creations (India) P. Ltd. [Company Appeal (AT) (CH) (Ins.) No. 167 of 2021, dated 8-11-2021], the Hon'ble NCLT Bengaluru Bench in reference to and interpreting certain sayings of various courts in several judgements, considered the financial position of the corporate debtor even though the debt was duly acknowledged, and considering it as solvent granted 6 months' time to the Corporate Debtor to pay the sum and didn't admitted the application to initiate Corporate Insolvency Resolution Process (CIRP).

In this article, we will analyze the judgement(s) of NCLT and NCLAT in the matter of Drip Capital Inc. (supra)

PRE-REQUISITE FOR FINANCIAL DEBT UNDER SECTION 5(8) OF IBC-

The Hon'ble Appellate Tribunal in the matter of Nikhil Mehta & Sons (supra) has very precisely put forth the basic criteria for considering a debt as financial debt in the code which are mentioned as below-

1.

There must be disbursal of some money from the financial creditor to the corporate debtor,

2.

The same must has been disbursed keeping in consideration to time value of money, and

3.

It must fall in any of the transaction mentioned in sub-clauses of Section 5(8) of the Code.

CHECKPOINTS FOR ADMITTING APPLICATION UNDER SECTION 7 OF IBC-

In the matter of Innoventive Industries Ltd. v. ICICI Bank Ltd. [2017] 84 taxmann.com 320/143 SCL 625the Hon'ble Supreme Court in Para 30 of the judgement has very clearly worded that-

"In the case of a corporate debtor who commits a default of a financial debt, the adjudicating authority has merely to see the records of the information utility or other evidence produced by the financial creditor to satisfy itself that a default has occurred. It is of no matter that the debt is disputed so long as the debt is "due" i.e., payable unless interdicted by some law or has not yet become due in the sense that it is payable at some future date."

EMERGING ISSUES AND CONTROVERSIES

5.1 Whether Share Subscription Agreements Can Constitute Financial Debt under IBC?

Share Application Money in the event of non-allotment of shares can be treated as a loan/debt, and such an amount falls under the definition of Financial Debt as defined under Section 5(8) of the Code.

In the matter of Kushan Mitra v. Amit Goel [2022] 136 taxmann.com 313 (NCL-AT), NCLAT held that if the Shares are not allotted within 60 days of receiving the Share Application Money, and if the refund does not take place within 15 days form the expiry of 60 days' time limit, then this amount will be treated as a Deposit, advanced to the Company, which has to be returned by the Company at the rate of 12 percent per annum from the expiry of the 60th day. Thus, the concerned person would receive compensation for the time value of money given to the Company, which changes the nature and character of the money so given. Although the amount was initially paid towards Shares, the equity did not materialise because the allotment was revoked. Thereafter, by operation of law, Section 42(6) of the Companies Act, 2013, the amount has statutorily been given the character of a loan with interest. The same applies to amounts paid as optionally convertible debentures. It was held that share Application Money in the event of non-allotment of shares, attracts interest under Section 42(6) of the Companies Act, 2013 and therefore falls within the ambit of the definition of Financial Debt as defined under Section 5(8) of the Code.

However, after the same, on April 25, 2022, Hon'ble NCLAT in the matter of Pramod Sharma v. Karanaya Heart Care (P.) Ltd. [Comp. App. (AT) (Ins.) No. 426 of 2022] held that, as per the Appellant's case, the amount was given as Share Application Money on which no share was allotted. Under the settlement, the principal amount was refunded, and thereafter, the Application under Section 7 was filed by the Appellant. NCLAT was of the view that the Adjudicating Authority rightly took the view that the amount which the Appellant gave as Share Application Money cannot be treated as a financial debt to enable the Appellant to trigger the Insolvency Process under Section 7 of the Code.

The case of the appellant was that she had advanced loan to the respondent for the purpose of (a) repaying interest/instalments on bank loans taken by the respondent so that loans were not defaulted upon or rendered NPA; and (b) ensuring payment of salaries and money due to suppliers/ vendors, so that business continues unabated. According to appellant, though the terms of the loan were not recorded in writing, it was agreed that money advanced would carry interest.

The appellant issued demand notice for repayment of the loans. The respondents, in its reply claimed that the money had been repaid.

Appellant initiated insolvency resolution process against corporate debtor.

The Adjudicating Authority by impugned order held that the appellant did not come within the meaning of 'financial creditor' and failed to satisfy the Adjudicating authority about requisite ingredients of section 7 to claim any relief and thereby rejected the application.

From the agreement/Memorandum of Understanding it was clear that appellants were 'investors' and had chosen 'committed return plan'. The respondent in their turn agreed upon to pay monthly committed return to investors. Thus, the amount due to the appellants came within the meaning of 'debt' as defined in section 3(11). Thereby, the amount invested by appellants came within the meaning of 'financial debt', as defined in section 5(8)(f) subject to satisfaction as to whether such disbursement against the consideration was for time value of money.

Thus, the Adjudicating Authority had rightly highlighted the opening word of the definition clause which indicate that a 'financial debt' is a debt along with interest which is disbursed against the consideration for the time value of money and may include any of the events enumerated in sub-clauses (a) to (i). Therefore, it was to be seen whether the amount paid by the appellants to the corporate debtor fulfilled the other condition of 'disbursement against consideration of time value and money' to come within the definition of 'financial creditor' having satisfied that the corporate debtor raised the amount through a transaction of sale and purchase of agreement having commercial effect of a borrowing [section 5(8)(f)].

The agreement showed that the respondent agreed to complete the construction of shopping mall on or before December, 2009, in all respects, and was required to complete and handover the shop in the shopping mall before the said date. It was not the case of the respondent that the construction was stopped or delayed on account of factors beyond the control of the respondent, as stipulated in the later part of the Memorandum of Understanding. It was agreed upon by the respondent that since the appellants had paid most of the amount the respondent was ready to pay 'monthly committed returns' to the appellants. However, as the appellants were not required the monthly return till December, 2008 i.e. for 9 months so the respondent-Corporate Debtor undertook to make a consolidated payment of Rs. 99,600 less TDS for every calendar month. The corporate debtor was liable to pay committed return with effect from January, 2009 till the date of handing over of the possession to the appellants. Therefore, it was clear that the amount disbursed by the appellants was 'against the consideration of time value of the money' and the respondent corporate debtor raised the amount by way of sale-purchase agreement, having a commercial effect or borrowing. The financial cost included 'Interest on loans' and other charges. Blurring the Lines between Financial Creditor and Operational Creditor In order to qualify as a financial creditor under section 5(8) of the IBC, one should be owed a financial debt6 which includes two conditions, firstly, there should be a debt along with interest, if any, which is disbursed against the consideration for the time value of money,7 and secondly, it should be included in one of the specified categories.8 Moreover, a financial creditor must prove that a default has occurred, which takes place when a debt becomes due and payable as per the proof of claims submitted by the creditor.9 Since a claim/payment is flexible enough to include "recompense",10 an operational creditor who has suffered any harm or has to be compensated will become the stakeholder of the insolvencyprocess.11 With respect to the first requirement, any debt, with or without interest is covered under the scope of Section 5(7) of the code. The time value of money requirement, according to which any money we have right now is worth more than the identical sum in future, due to its potential earning capacity12 is present in any kind of transaction. The Court in the case of DF Deutsche Forfait AG v. Uttam Galva Steel Ltd.13 held that if a party fails to repay within the fixed time, then interest can be claimed over operational debt as well, and it is nowhere said that the operational creditor is barred from claiming interest. Therefore, since the premise of claim is based on whether the "X" has taken something from "Y' with an intention to pay back the value, then the law should be applied in a manner to ensure that it is repaid but not dismissed on the ground of procedural irregularities. We need not stick to the ground that procedural justice is always subservient to substantial justice.14

With respect to the second prong, the authors believe that such an operational creditor is at par with home buyers. It is submitted that since Section 5(8)(f) of the IBC uses the words 'any amount' and 'any other transaction', it means that the amounts that are "raised under transactions and not covered by any of the other clauses", would amount to a financial debt if they had the commercial effect of borrowing, making it a 'catch-all provision'.15 Section 3(33) of the IBC defines a 'transaction' as an agreement or arrangement in writing for the transfer of assets, or funds, goods or services, from or to the corporate debtor. Furthermore, the expression "borrow" means to obtain or receive something, on loan for temporary use, intending to give it, or something equivalent back to the lender.16 A perusal of these definitions shows that the expression borrow is wide enough to include an advance given by operational creditors in the form of their services, workmen/employees in the present case when the payment for the same was neglected by a company to keep its operations afloat. This implies that the same amount was borrowed for 'temporary use' i.e. for honouring their commitments and paying back other creditors as long as they intended to give 'something equivalent' back to the operational creditors. Additionally, the commercial aspect, which means transactions having profit as its main aim is present in such a situation of employees who have not been paid, since the company wants to keep its operations afloat by temporarily borrowing the requisite amount from operational creditors, and the operational creditors demanding interest due to delay in payments.17 Additionally, the proof of claim as per the IBBI (Insolvency Resolution Process for Corporate Persons) Regulations, 2016 can be proved by any contractual document indicating that the amount is due in case of employees or through muster rolls in case of workmen.18 It therefore follows that the employees/workmen in such a situation will be considered as a financial creditor at par with home buyers as per Pioneer since they qualify all the parameters based on which the home buyers have been considered as a financial creditor. Therefore, treating them differently will lead to gross violation of principles of natural justice.19

In the receipt-cum-acceptance letter, it was stated on face of it, that these were for acquisitions and registrations of plots booked and maturity date of agreement was given as one year after date of registration and projected value was more than consideration value.

On these facts, the issue for the consideration of the NCLT was whether the buyers advancing the money came within the category of financial creditors entitled to invoke IBC for the recovery of the sums advanced. The Petitioner's case before the NCLT was that it was clear that under the garb of allotting land to the public, the respondent had been borrowing/accepting deposits/loans from the public by showing it as investment against property, i.e., by showing the depositors to register for plots of specific measurements and also showing the projected value of the said investment/deposit/borrowing on the maturity date. S.5(7) defines 'financial creditor' to mean a person to whom a financial debt is owed. Financial debt is defined in s.5(8) to mean a debt along with interest, if any, which is disbursed against the consideration for the time value of money and includes, inter alia, any amount raised under any other transaction, including any forward sale or purchase agreement, having the commercial effect of a borrowing [clause (f) of s.5(8).

According to the NCLT, receipt-cum-acceptance letters, even though stated to be for registration of plot were for/time value of money and have the commercial effect of borrowing and, hence, sub-sections (7) & (8) of s.5 apply and, hence, the petitioner is to be taken as financial creditor. In coming to this view, the NCLT relied on the decision of the National Company Law Appellate Tribunal (NCLTA) in the case of Nikhil Mehta & Sons v. AMR Infrastructure Ltd. [2017] 84 taxmann.com 163/143 SCL 278 (NCL - AT) where the following decision was taken by the NCLTA:-

"….From the provisions of law and discussion as made and quoted above, we find following essential criterias, to be fulfilled for a creditor to come within the meaning of financial creditor:-

(i)

A person to whom a financial debt is owned and includes a person, whom such debt has been legally assigned transferred to;

(ii)

The debt along with interest, if any, is disbursed against the consideration for time value of money and include any one or more mode of disbursement as mentioned in clauses (a) to (i) of sub-section (8) of s.5".

The NCLT thus, pronounced its decision as under:-

"In the present case, the receipt-cum-acceptance letters (Annexure-A-1 to A-4 of the application) on the face of it state that they are for acquisition of plot and registration for plot booked. However, the maturity date of agreement is given as one year after the date of registration and the projected value is given, which is more than the consideration value given. Therefore, the time value of money has been built in and it has to be presumed that the receipt-cum-acceptance letters, even though stated to be for registration of plot, have the commercial effect of borrowing. In view of sub-ss.(7) & (8) of s.5 of the Code (supra), the petitioners are to be treated as financial creditors".

It may be stated in the context of this decision that in reply, the respondent did not raise any objection that the petitioners before NCLT are not financial creditors. Rather it specifically stated saying that "there is some delay on the corporate debtor's part in returning the amount of the financial creditor [emphasis is provided].

Hence, this decision may not be a binding authority to claim that a homebuyer comes in the category of 'financial creditor'.

23. Collusive commercial arrangement between creditors and the corporate debtor wouldn't constitute a financial debt, rules SC

[Phoenix Arc (P.) Ltd. v. Spade Financial Services Ltd. [2021] 124 taxmann.com 24 (SC)]

The Supreme Court in an important ruling in the Phoenix Arc (P.) Ltd. v. Spade Financial Services Ltd. case held that entities having commercial arrangements of collusive nature with the corporate debtor could not be considered financial creditors under the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code (IBC) provisions.

Brief facts

In this case, the operational creditor initiated the corporate insolvency resolution process (CIRP) against AKME Projects Limited under section 9 of the IBC.

As part of the process, the Interim Resolution Professional invited claims. In response to the notice, Spade Financial Services Limited and its subsidiary AAA Landmark Private Limited filed claims as creditors.

Spade filed the claim based on an alleged Memorandum of Understanding executed with the Corporate Debtor, which stated that Inter Corporate Deposits (ICDs) of Rs. 26.55 crore have been granted to the Corporate Debtor by Spade, bearing interest of 24 per cent repayable in terms of the mutual agreement between the parties. AAA filed its claim before the IRP for a sum of Rs. 93.90 crore.

Later, the CoC was constituted on May 22, 2018. On May 25, 2018, the IRP rejected the claim of Spade, inter alia, on the ground that the claim was not in the nature of a financial debt in terms of Section 5(8) of IBC since consideration was absent for the time value of money, i.e., the period of repayment of the claimed ICDs was not stipulated.

The IRP also rejected the claim of AAA on the ground that its claim as a financial creditor in Form C was filed after the expiry of the period for filing such a claim.

Having gone through the National Company Law Tribunal (NCLT) and the National Company Law Appellate Tribunal (NCLAT), the dispute reached the Supreme Court.

Supreme Court

Based on the appeals, the Supreme Court framed three issues for consideration which are as follows:

(a)

Whether Spade and AAA are financial creditors of the Corporate Debtor;

(b)

Whether Spade and AAA are related parties of the Corporate Debtor; and

(c)

Whether Spade and AAA have to be excluded from the CoC.

In the present case, the Court said, there was a finding that AAA and Spade were related parties within the meaning of Section 5(24) at the time when the alleged financial debt based on which they assert a claim to be a part of the CoC was created.

"Further, we have also concluded that the transactions between Spade and AAA on the one hand, and the Corporate Debtor on the other hand, which gave rise to their alleged financial debts were deceitful in nature. Therefore, it is evident that there existed a deeply entangled relationship between Spade, AAA and Corporate Debtor, when the alleged financial debt arose," the Court said, adding, the pervasive influence of the promoter/director of the Corporate Debtor over the concerned entities was evident, and allowing them in the CoC would definitely affect the other independent financial creditors.

"Due to the collusive nature of their transactions alleged to be a financial debt under section 5(8), Spade and AAA cannot be labelled as financial creditors under section 5(7)," it added.

[Phoenix ARC (P.) Ltd. v. Ketulbhai Ramubhai Patel [2021] 124 taxmann.com 90 (SC)]

In a critical judgment, the Supreme Court held that pledge of shares would not make an entity financial creditor of the corporate debtor for the purpose of the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code (IBC). The Supreme Court gave this ruling in the Phoenix Arc Private Limited v. Ketulbhai Ramubhai Patel case.

Brief facts

(PB)/2019, admitted on May 30, 2019. The Claims were invited through a public announcement.

The Greater Noida Industrial Development Authority ('appellant'), considering itself a financial creditor, submitted a claim of Rs. 43,40,31,951 in January 2020, representing unpaid instalments for the lease premium. However, the Resolution Professional (RP) treated the appellant as an operational creditor and requested it to submit the claim in Form B as such. The NCLAT dismissed the appeal, noting that the appellant had been informed of its status as an operational creditor and to resubmit its claim, which it failed to do so. It was held that disbursement is an indispensable requirement to constitute a financial debt within the meaning of Section 5(8) of the IBC and, that too, the disbursement must be from a creditor to a debtor, and as the lease executed by the appellant was not a financial lease or capital lease, the appellant does not qualify as a financial creditor2.

UNDERSTANDING THE COURT'S DECISION AND BACKGROUND

After reviewing the arguments, the following two moot questions have surfaced for deliberation in this appeal which both the NCLT and NCLAT failed to address them:

A. Whether in the exercise of powers under sub-section (5) of Section 60, the Adjudicating Authority (i.e., NCLT) can recall an order of approval passed under sub-section (1) of Section 31 of the IBC?

"Section 60 (5) Notwithstanding anything to the contrary contained in any other law for the time being in force, the National Company Law Tribunal shall have jurisdiction to entertain or dispose of

(a)

any application or proceeding by or against the corporate debtor or corporate person;

(b)

any claim made by or against the corporate debtor or corporate person, including claims by or against any of its subsidiaries situated in India; and

(c)

any question of priorities or any question of law or facts, arising out of or in relation to the insolvency resolution or liquidation proceedings of the corporate debtor or corporate person under this Code."

The Hon'ble SC held that a Court or Tribunal has the inherent power to recall an order to ensure justice is served and to prevent misuse of the legal process. Neither the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code (IBC) nor its related Regulations restrict the exercise of this inherent power.

Section 60(5)(c) of the IBC grants authority to the National Company Law Tribunal (NCLT) to address questions of priorities or legal and factual matters related to insolvency proceedings, regardless of any other provisions. Additionally, Rule 11 of the NCLT Rules, 2016 acknowledges the Tribunal's inherent power.

The Hon'ble Court has analysed various decisions on how the Tribunal, or a Court is invested with ancillary or incidental powers: -

In Manohar Lal Chopra v. Rai Bahadur Rao Raja Seth Hiralal3 while interpreting section 151 CPC it is observed that the inherent power has not been conferred upon the court; it is a power inherent in the Court by virtue of its duty to do justice between the parties before it.

In Grindlays Bank Ltd. v. Central Govt. Industrial Tribunal4 it is a well-known rule of statutory construction that a Tribunal or body should be considered to be endowed with such ancillary or incidental powers as are necessary to discharge its functions effectively for the purpose of doing justice between the parties. In a case of this nature, we are of the view that the Tribunal should be considered as invested with such incidental or ancillary powers unless there is any indication in the statute to the contrary.

In a recent decision (i.e., Union Bank of India v. Dinakar T. Vekatasubramanian & Ors.5), a five-member Full Bench of NCLAT held that though the power to review is not conferred upon the Tribunal but the power to recall its judgment is inherent in the Tribunal and is preserved by Rule 11 of the NCLT Rules, 2016. This decision of NCLAT was upheld by a two-judge Bench of this Court vide order dated 31.07.2023 in Civil Appeal No.4620 of 2023 (Union Bank of India v. Financial Creditors [2023] 154 taxmann.com 203/180 SCL 64 (SC)).

Therefore, even when there's no specific provision allowing the Tribunal to recall its order, it still holds the power to do so. However, this power must be used sparingly and not as a means to re-examine the entire case.

B. Whether the resolution plan put forth by the resolution applicant did not meet the requirements of sub-section (2) of Section 30 of the IBC read with Regulations 37 and 38 of the CIRP Regulations, 2016?

It was held by Hon'ble Apex Court that the resolution plan did not meet the requirements of Section 30(2) of the IBC read with Regulations 37 and 38 of the CIRP Regulations, 2016 for the following reasons:-

However, the NCLT vide impugned order admitted said application.

Aggrieved by the NCLT’s order, the appellant-ex-director of the corporate debtor filed instant appeal on ground that the financial creditor had failed to prove the existence of any financial contract between them and the corporate debtor and in the absence of any agreement or financial contract, the financial creditor had clearly failed to establish the existence of any debt or default.
