Bansi Lal Bhat, Judicial Member. - Appellant is Promoter/Shareholder/Director of Respondent No.2 Company 'Priority Marketing Private Limited' (Corporate Debtor). Being aggrieved of the impugned order dated 31st August, 2018 passed by the Adjudicating Authority (National Company Law Tribunal) Mumbai Bench in Company Petition No. 1732/I&BP/2018 by virtue whereof petition filed by Respondent No. 1 - 'Mr. Joel Cardoso' as a 'Financial Creditor' under Section 7 of the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016 (hereinafter referred to as 'I&B Code') has been admitted, moratorium slapped and Interim Resolution Professional appointed with certain directions, has assailed the impugned order primarily on the ground that the amount claimed by Respondent No. 1 is not a 'Financial Debt' within the meaning of Section 5(8) and Respondent No. 1 cannot be treated as a 'Financial Creditor' for the purposes of I&B Code.

2. For better understanding of the controversy involved in this appeal it would be apposite to refer to the factual matrix of the case. Respondent No.1, claiming to be a Shareholder of Respondent No. 2 (hereinafter referred to as Corporate Debtor), filed an application under Section 7 of I&B Code before the Adjudicating Authority (National Company Law Tribunal) Mumbai Bench, seeking initiation of Corporate Insolvency Resolution Process against the Corporate Debtor on the ground that the Respondent No. 1 had granted unsecured loan repayable on demand from time to time to the Corporate Debtor which stood at Rs.3,23,46,475/- as on 31st March, 2008, major portion whereof was repaid by the Corporate Debtor from years 2008 to 2010 leaving an amount of Rs.1,45,36,475/- as outstanding which was duly reflected in the financial statements of Corporate Debtor and in respect whereof the Corporate Debtor issued balance confirmation as on 1st April, 2016 which was confirmed by the statutory auditor in terms of email dated 5th October, 2017 and since the Corporate Debtor did not repay the aforesaid loan amount, Respondent No. 1 served a notice of demand upon the Corporate Debtor, which was not complied. Corporate Debtor raised the plea before the learned Adjudicating Authority that there were cross holdings inter se the respondents in various companies and the amounts so arrived at was a settlement amount which had not ended in compliance of mutual obligations between the parties. The Corporate Debtor further stated that the unsecured loan of Rs.1,45,36,475/- was a part of overall settlement and it was ready to settle the cross holding of shares and loans inter se the Respondents. Respondent further contended that none of the loans under the quasi partnership arrangement inter se the Respondents had any term for repayment or interest. The learned Adjudicating Authority found that the contention raised on behalf of Corporate Debtor was not plausible as the factum of amount advanced as loan by Respondent No.1 to Corporate Debtor was admitted and reflected in the accounts and confirmed by the Corporate Debtor. Learned Adjudicating Authority was of the view that the said amount was arrived at after the parties mutually agreed and the same was reflected in the books of the Corporate Debtor under the head 'long term borrowings', the amount of debt fell within the purview of 'financial debt' notwithstanding the fact that no interest was payable. The contention raised by the Corporate Debtor was accordingly repelled.

3. Learned counsel for the Appellant submits that the learned Adjudicating Authority landed in error in holding that the amount claimed by Respondent No.1 for triggering Corporate Insolvency Resolution Process, in respect whereof default on the part of Corporate Debtor was alleged, was not a 'Financial Debt' as defined under Section 5(8) of the I&B Code despite the admitted position that there was no consideration for the time value of money in the transaction. It is further submitted that learned Adjudicating Authority failed to notice that no interest was ever claimed by the Respondent No.1 or paid by the Corporate Debtor to Respondent No.1, that no TDS amount was ever deducted in respect of the part payments made, that there was no tenure for the repayment of amounts granted by Respondent No.1 to Corporate Debtor and that there was no time value of money in the transaction and no consideration for the time value of the money was agreed between the parties at the time of disbursement of moneys by Respondent No.1.

Issue of financial debt

The Respondent company has admitted that the petitioner being the maternal uncle of the Managing Director, had given Rs. 1.25 lakh. initially. In addition, he had also given Rs. 1.29 crore under cheques dated 15-12-2007, 11-2-2008, 26-3-2008. [Para 6]

From the materials, it is clear that the petitioner had paid Rs. 1.29 crore to the respondent-company to meet its fund requirements.

The definition of financial debt is inclusive one. It indicates that debt along with interest 'if any' is disbursed against the consideration for time value of money. [Para 11]

The petitioner in his petition pleaded that the loan was advanced as an understanding between him and the corporate debtor and its managing director, who happened to be his nephew and that the loan was payable on demand. It is nowhere pleaded that such understanding included the payment of interest against the loan and the rate thereof. There is also no pleading that the payment was made against the issue of shares at a future date. The advancement of the said loan accordingly is not covered under any of the clauses of the definition. There is also no material on record to show that the amount was disbursed against the consideration for the time value of the money. [Para 12]

The Respondent pleaded that it availed an unsecured loan of Rs. 5 lakh from the petitioner. The same is manifest from its annual report of 2013-14. Admittedly, the amount was repaid in 2016, which is apparent from the account statement filed along with the petition. According to the petitioner he did not make any payment during 2013-14, which the audited annual report of the respondent company shows as unsecured loan of Rs. 5 lakh. The report is not in dispute. Therefore, its repayment could not be taken as the payment towards interest of the loan amount of Rs. 1.29 crore. More so when the petitioner has credited this amount against the principal amount of Rs. 1.24 crore and showed a default of Rs. 1.24 crore. Besides the petition is completely silent as indicated before that the loan was advanced against an agreed interest. Taking all these aspects into consideration it is accordingly clear, for the purpose of instant case, that the amount would not come within the definition of a financial debt, though it is admitted that the petitioner had advanced said amount to meet the fund requirements of the company. [Para 13]

Issue of limitation

The first of the payments was made by cheque dated 15-12-2007 and was credited to the respondent's account on 18-12-2007. The last payment was made by cheque dated 26-3-2008, and was credited to the respondent's account on 27-3-2008. According to the petitioner, it was an understanding and was payable on demand. The understanding between the petitioner and the Respondent, which then was managed by the former's nephew, did not provide a time limit for repayment of the debt. [Para 15]

The Application under section 7 is not a suit. Suits relating to money needs to be filed within three years when the amount became due. In the instant case admittedly, there was no time limit agreed upon between the parties for repayment of the amount advanced. The amount payable on demand pleaded by the petitioner could not be extended for an uncertain period. In the absence of any contract between parties the amount needed to be repaid within three years from the date when they were respectively advanced. The amounts accordingly would have been due and payable on or before 14-12-2010, 10-2-2011 and 25-3-2011 respectively. There is no material on record to show that the respondent made any admission of debt respectively within these periods or subsequent thereso. [Para 17]

The Application having been filed only on 13-11-2018, was grossly time barred. The debt accordingly was not due and payable. In view of the discussions and the findings viewed from any perspective, the petition at the instance of the petitioner is not maintainable. The petitioner is not entitled to the relief sought. FACT: During years 2004 to 2013, applicant No. 1 and applicant No. 2 advanced loans to the respondent company amounting to an aggregate sum of Rs. 28.05 lakh and Rs. 27.68 lakh, respectively.

During the year 2012-13 the respondent company deposited TDS for the interest due to the applicants but failed to remit the interest amounts after deduction of TDS to the applicants' accounts.

During the financial years 2013-14 to 2016-17 the respondent company neither paid the interest not deposited the TDS, however, the original loan amounts were reflected in the balance sheets of the respondent company.

The applicants sent two separate notices calling upon the respondent company to repay outstanding debts. However, the acceptance of these notices was refused by the respondent company.

The applicants filed the present application to initiate insolvency resolution process in which the total amount due from the respondent company had been shown to be Rs. 1.20 crore including interest.

The applicants had placed on record Customer Account Ledger Report of applicant maintained by the Bank. The applicants had also placed on record the audited balance sheets of the respondent company for the years ended 31-3-2015 and 31-3-2016. The balance sheets reflect the amounts of Rs. 27.66 lakh and Rs. 28.05 lakh under the heading 'Unsecured Loan' as loan owed to applicants. Further, the applicants had also filed there income tax returns for the assessment year 2013-2014 wherein the payment of TDS by the respondent company on behalf of the applicants was reflected.

The respondent company on the other hand had made a submission that the funds were advanced as a contribution to the capital and was thus, not a financial debt and the categorization of the amount under the head of 'Unsecured Loan' in the balance sheet would not change the nature of the amount advanced.

The respondent had also submitted that debt extended by the applicants were set off with the loan given by Pawan Kumar Aneja's owned respondent company under the settlement agreement.

Further, it was the respondent's contention that since there was no written agreement for the extension of the amount from the applicants to the respondent company and there were no terms regarding repayment of the amount to the applicants the amount had not become due and payable and thus, there was no default.

FACT: The respondent no. 1-financial creditor had disbursed loan amount of Rs. 5 crore to the corporate debtor towards its working capital during the financial year 2013-14, which was repayable on demand.

The financial creditor repeatedly demanded the repayment of the loan amount but no payment was received by the financial creditor. Accordingly, a demand notice was issued and application under section 7 was filed against the corporate debtor.

The NCLT vide impugned order admitted said application.

Aggrieved by the NCLT's, the appellant, ex-Director of the corporate debtor filed instant appeal on ground that the disbursal of Rs. 5 crores was not in the nature of a loan but a part payment deposit for the purpose of developing the land project hence, respondent No. 1 did not fall in the category of 'financial creditor' and the outstanding amount claimed by respondent No. 1 was not in the nature of 'financial debt' in terms of the statutory construct of IBC, basis which section 7 application could not have been admitted.

HELD: The primary issue before consideration is whether in the backdrop of the statutory provisions of IBC, the outstanding amount of Rs. 5 crore disbursed by respondent No. 1 to corporate debtor is in the nature of financial debt, and, whether in the facts of the instant case, there has been a default in the re-payment of the said loan by the corporate debtor which entitled the respondent No. 1 to file a section 7 application in the capacity of a financial creditor qua the corporate debtor. [Para 8]

Now, one have perused the definition clauses, it will be useful to take notice of the guiding principles laid down by the Apex Court as to when a debt is to be treated as a financial debt in the context of IBC. In Pioneer Urban Land and Infrastructure Ltd. v. Union of India [2019] 108 taxmann.com 147/155 SCL 622 (SC) it has been held that any debt to be treated as financial debt, there must happen disbursal of money and the disbursal must be against consideration for time value of money. The concept of time value of money has been further explained to also include a transaction which does not necessarily culminate into money being returned to the lender or interest being paid in respect of money that has been borrowed. Holding section 5(8) to be a residuary provision which has a catch-all nature, it held that it can include anything which is equivalent to the money that has been loaned as long as commercial effect of borrowing or profit as the aim is discernible. [Para 10]

It is settled law that for any debt to be treated as financial debt, the pre-requisite is disbursal of money to the borrower for utilization by the borrower and that the disbursal must be against consideration for time value of money even if it is not interest bearing. [Para 13]

This brings to the next logical corollary as to when a financial creditor who has disbursed money to a corporate debtor against consideration for time value of money can trigger the insolvency resolution process against the corporate debtor. As per the scheme of IBC, that stage arises when a default takes place, in the sense that a debt which has become due, in fact and in law, but has not been paid. 'Default' as defined in section 3(12) means non-payment of a debt once it becomes due and payable, and non-payment could be of the whole amount or even part thereof. This has been elaborately discussed by the Supreme Court in the case of Swiss Ribbons (P.) Ltd. v. Union of India [2019] 101 taxmann.com 389/152 SCL 365 (SC). [Para 14]

Given this backdrop, one may now analyse the rival submissions made by both parties to find out whether a case of financial debt and default thereof has been effectively made out in the facts of the present case. [Para 15]

While admitting that a sum of Rs. 5 crore was disbursed to the corporate debtor, it has been emphatically asserted by the appellant that a financial contract is a must between the corporate debtor and the financial creditor to establish that the disbursal made was in the form of a loan. The letter from the bank produced by Respondent No. 1 only shows that transfer of the sum of Rs. 5 crore took place but does not show it as a loan. It is contended that only a contract between the parties could have set out the terms of the financial debt including the tenure of the debt, the applicable rate of interest and date of repayment. In the absence of any document, mere assertion that it was a loan repayable on demand does not have any legs to stand on. [Para 16]

On June 6, 2018, the President approved promulgation of the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code (Amendment) Ordinance, 20181 ("IBC Ordinance 2018"). In a span of 2 years, the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016 ("Code") has witnessed two Ordinances viz. the IBC Ordinance 2018 and the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code (Amendment) Ordinance, 2017("IBC Ordinance 2017") which received President's assent on November 23, 20172 and became the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code (Amendment) Act, 2018 ("IBC Amendment Act") on January 18, 20183.

The IBC Ordinance 2018 has been formulated with the intent to balance the interest of stakeholders especially home buyers and micro, small and medium enterprises, promoting resolution over liquidation of the corporate debtor and streamlining provisions relating to eligibility of resolution applicant. The IBC Ordinance 2018 is a result of the Insolvency Law Committee ("ILC") report dated March 26, 20184. The ILC was set up on November 16, 2017 to make recommendations to the Government on issues arising from the implementation of the Code.

The author had analysed the IBC Ordinance 2017 in write-up titled 5"IBC Ordinance: either run or lose your company". This write-up analyses the impact of IBC Ordinance 2018.

Definition of "financial debt"

Home buyers to be treated as financial creditor:

Section 5 (8) of the Code defines the term "financial debt". The definition being an inclusive one, means a debt along with interest, if any, disbursed against the consideration for the time value of money. While the Code categorised the creditors into two viz., 'financial' and 'operational' creditors; home buyers witnessed various judgements categorising them as neither fitting within the definition of 'financial' nor 'operational' creditors. The only exception being, Nikhil Mehta & Sons v. AMR Infrastructure Ltd.6 (Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 07 of 2017, dated 21-7-2017) and Anil Mahindroo v. Earth Iconic (P.) Infrastructure Ltd.7 (Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 74 of 2017, dated 2-8-2017).

In Nikhil Mehta (supra), the NCLAT categorised the home buyer Mr. Nikhil Mehta as financial creditor due to the assured return scheme in the contract, in which there was an arrangement wherein it was agreed that the seller of the apartments would pay 'assured returns' to the home buyers till the date of handing over of the possession. Consequently, the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Board of India ("IBBI") amended the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Board of India (Insolvency Resolution Process for Corporate Persons) Regulations, 2016 ("CIRP Regulations")and introduced a separate claim form for "creditors other than financial or operational creditors".

The ILC after drawing an analogy, in the case of home buyers, concluded that the amounts raised under the contracts of home buyers are in effect for the purposes of raising finance, and are a means of raising finance. And, recommended inclusion of home buyers within the definition of "financial debt".

Accordingly, the IBC Ordinance 2018provides for inclusion of home buyers within the definition of the 'financial debt' by inclusion of an explanation to section 5 (8) (f) of the Code as follows:

"Explanation: For the purposes of this sub-clause, -

(i)

any amount raised from an allottee under a real estate project shall be deemed to be an amount having the commercial effect of a borrowing; and

(ii)

the expressions, "allottee" and "real estate project" shall have the meanings respectively assigned to them in clauses (d) and (zn) of section 2 of Real Estate (Regulation and Development) Act, 2016;"

From the materials, it is clear that the petitioner had paid Rs. 1.29 crore to the respondent-company to meet its fund requirements.

The definition of financial debt is inclusive one. It indicates that debt along with interest 'if any' is disbursed against the consideration for time value of money. [Para 11] The petitioner in his petition pleaded that the loan was advanced as an understanding between him and the corporate debtor and its managing director, who happened to be his nephew and that the loan was payable on demand. It is nowhere pleaded that such understanding included the payment of interest against the loan and the rate thereof. There is also no pleading that the payment was made against the issue of shares at a future date. The advancement of the said loan accordingly is not covered under any of the clauses of the definition. There is also no material on record to show that the amount was disbursed against the consideration for the time value of the money. [Para 12]

The Respondent pleaded that it availed an unsecured loan of Rs. 5 lakh from the petitioner. The same is manifest from its annual report of 2013-14. Admittedly, the amount was repaid in 2016, which is apparent from the account statement filed along with the petition. According to the petitioner he did not make any payment during 2013-14, which the audited annual report of the respondent company shows as unsecured loan of Rs. 5 lakh. The report is not in dispute. Therefore, its repayment could not be taken as the payment towards interest of the loan amount of Rs. 1.29 crore. More so when the petitioner has credited this amount against the principal amount of Rs. 1.24 crore and showed a default of Rs. 1.24 crore. Besides the petition is completely silent as indicated before that the loan was advanced against an agreed interest. Taking all these aspects into consideration it is accordingly clear, for the purpose of instant case, that the amount would not come within the definition of a financial debt, though it is admitted that the petitioner had advanced said amount to meet the fund requirements of the company. [Para 13]

Issue of limitation

The first of the payments was made by cheque dated 15-12-2007 and was credited to the respondent's account on 18-12-2007. The last payment was made by cheque dated 26-3-2008, and was credited to the respondent's account on 27-3-2008. According to the petitioner, it was an understanding and was payable on demand. The understanding between the petitioner and the Respondent, which then was managed by the former's nephew, did not provide a time limit for repayment of the debt. [Para 15]

The Application under section 7 is not a suit. Suits relating to money needs to be filed within three years when the amount became due. In the instant case admittedly, there was no time limit agreed upon between the parties for repayment of the amount advanced. The amount payable on demand pleaded by the petitioner could not be extended for an uncertain period. In the absence of any contract between parties the amount needed to be repaid within three years from the date when they were respectively advanced. The amounts accordingly would have been due and payable on or before 14-12-2010, 10-2-2011 and 25-3-2011 respectively. There is no material on record to show that the respondent made any admission of debt respectively within these periods or subsequent thereso. [Para 17]

The Application having been filed only on 13-11-2018, was grossly time barred. The debt accordingly was not due and payable. In view of the discussions and the findings viewed from any perspective, the petition at the instance of the petitioner is not maintainable. The petitioner is not entitled to the relief sought. The petition thus cannot be admitted. [Para 19]

Under section 5(7), a person can be categorised as a financial creditor if a financial debt is owed to it. Section 5(8) stipulates that the essential ingredient of a financial debt is disbursal against consideration for the time value of money. [Para 43]

The money advanced as debt should be in the receipt of the borrower. The borrower is obligated to return the money or its equivalent along with the consideration for a time value of money, which is the compensation or price payable for the period of time for which the money is lent. A transaction which is sham or collusive would only create an illusion that money has been disbursed to a borrower with the object of receiving consideration in the form of time value of money, when in fact the parties have entered into the transaction with a different or an ulterior motive. In other words, the real agreement between the parties is something other than advancing a financial debt. [Para 46]

Phoenix argued that the transactions entered into between the corporate debtor and Spade and AAA are collusive in nature and do not constitute a financial debt. AAA & Spade have urged that the eligibility of Spade and AAA as financial creditors has conclusively been determined by the NCLT in its order dated 31-5-2018. It is already concluded that the above order would not operate as res judicata and it was within the jurisdiction of the NCLT to consider this issue afresh. NCLT in its order dated 19-7-2019 has undertaken a detailed analysis of the transactions to arrive at a finding that the transactions were collusive. The findings of the NCLT in its order dated 19-7-2019 are to be argued with. NCLAT has also made an observation that AN, AA had created a web of companies in which both along with near and dear ones including R (Wife of AA) and S (Brother-in-law of AA) acted in concert with each other. It is to be noted that Ernst & Young were appointed as forensic/transactional auditors by the RP. [Para 49]

As noted by NCLT, the Memorandum of Understanding on the basis of which Spade had filed its claim before the IRP, was signed two years after the commencement of the purported transaction. The execution of the Memorandum of Understanding was sought to be explained on the basis that a formal document was created for specifying the rate of interest on the ICDs given by Spade to the corporate debtor. However, despite the creation of a formal document, the rate of interest being charged on the ICDs was 12 per cent as mentioned in the claim before the IRP, which is half of the interest rate of 24 per cent stipulated in the Memorandum of Understanding. During the arguments, it is also brought to the notice of the Court that the Memorandum of Understanding is unregistered and unstamped. It has been submitted in the written submissions filed on behalf of Spade and AAA that the auditors of the corporate debtor had been putting a note in its balance sheets stating that the interest of 12 per cent was not being paid to Spade due to a dispute. This submission in fact further fortifies the finding of the IRP that no interest has been paid on the alleged loan. The IRP has also noted in his letter that the Memorandum of Understanding does not stipulate the period of repayment. Hence, the consideration for time value of money is absent, which is an essential ingredient of a financial debt. The NCLT has also noted that a major portion of the ICDs was credited in the account of AA holding that the entire amount was not 'disbursed' to the corporate debtor. NCLAT has also made a similar finding in its judgment. This finding has been disputed by Spade and AAA who argued that no amount of the ICDs has been credited to the account of AA and such an allegation has not been made by any of the parties including the RP. However, it is to be noted under clause 2 of the Memorandum of Understanding, the amount of Rs. 26.55 crores has been disbursed not only to the corporate debtor but also to "other companies on behalf of AKME". In any event, the entirety of the ICDs were not disbursed to Spade. Additionally, no Board resolution was passed by Spade approving the grant of ICDs and the charge created on the loan was not registered with the Registrar of Companies. In view of the above, Phoenix is agreed with that the Memorandum of Understanding was an eye-wash and collusive. [Para 50]

The NCLT rightly refused to admit the application under section 7 of the IBC, holding the same to be barred by limitation. The Appellate Tribunal has erred in law in reversing the judgment and order of the earlier Adjudicating Authority. The Adjudicating Authority rightly rejected the application as barred by limitation. The Appellate Authority patently erred in law in reversing the decision of the adjudicating authority and admitting the application. [Para 38] As recorded in the said order dated 19-12-2018 passed by the NCLT Chennai, the respondent Nos. 1 and 2 jointly addressed the letter dated 11-1-2011 to the Income-tax department confirming that the respondent No. 1 had requested the appellant-company to transfer a sum of Rs. 90 lakhs to his wife, the respondent No. 2 for allotment of shares in the appellant company and further acknowledged that the amount outstanding from the erstwhile firm 'R' to the respondent was Rs. 1.40 crore as on 31-3-2004. [Para 39]

There are, as observed above cogent records including letters signed by the respondent Nos. 1 and 2 which evince that on 6-10-2007, respondent No. 2 resigned from the Board of the appellant-company and at that time the respondent no. 2 requested the appellant-company to treat the share application money of Rs. 90 lakhs as share application money of a promoter MK and to issue shares for aforesaid value to said promoter MK. The amount was to be treated as a personal loan from the respondent No. 2 to said promoter and a personal loan to a promoter or a Director of a company cannot trigger the Corporate Resolution Process under the IBC. Disputes as to whether the signatures of the respondents are forged or whether records have been fabricated can be adjudicated upon evidence including forensic evidence in a regular suit and not in proceedings under section 7. [Para 40]

The definition of 'financial debt' in section 5(8) makes it clear that 'financial debt' means a debt along with interest, if any, disbursed against the consideration from time value of money and would include money raised or borrowed against the payment of interest; amount raised by acceptance under any acceptance credit facility or its de-materialised equivalent; amount raised pursuant to any note purchase facility or the issue of bonds, notes, debentures, loan stock or any similar instrument; the amount of any liability in respect of any lease or hire purchase contract which is deemed as a finance or capital lease under the Indian Accounting Standards or such other accounting standards as may be prescribed; receivables sold or discounted other than any receivables sold on non-recourse basis or any amount raised under any other transaction, including any forward sale or purchase agreement, having the commercial effect of a borrowing. Explanation to section 5(8) which relates to real estate projects is of no relevance in the facts and circumstances of this case. The payment received for shares, duly issued to a third party at the request of the payee, as evident from official records, cannot be a debt, not to speak of financial debt. Shares of a company are transferable subject to restrictions, if any, in its Articles of Association and attract dividend when the company makes profits. [Para 43]

The appeal is to be allowed. The impugned judgment and order of the Appellate Tribunal is to be set aside and the order of the Adjudicating Authority dismissing the application, is to be restored. [Para 44]

In the instant case admittedly, applicants issued notices both in Form 3 as well as in Form 4 under rule 5 of the Rules on 3-1-2018 claiming themselves as financial creditors. Secondly, neither any document has been placed on record pertaining to the loan nor there is any supporting evidence to establish applicable rate of interest to be paid on the said loan. Thirdly, the applicants have failed to prove that the loan was disbursed against consideration for time value of money, particularly when respondent company has affirmed that no interest has been paid nor payable at any point of time. [Para 22]

It is pertinent to refer here that the balance sheets of the respondent company reveal that as on 31-3-2015 loans taken from both the applicants stands at Rs. 13 lakhs and Rs. 12 lakhs respectively. Similarly the balance sheet of the respondent company as on 31-3-2016 reflects the same amount of Rs. 13 lakhs and Rs. 12 lakhs as due to both the applicants. The position as on 31-3-2017 also remains the same as per the balance sheet of the respondent company. The position of the loans for the aforesaid three consecutive year endings shows that the amount of loan remains the same all through and with passage of time there has been no accumulation of interest or any other consideration therein. [Para 23]

It is reiterated that in the instant case, neither any loan agreement has been placed on record nor there is any supporting evidence/document to establish applicable rate of interest to be paid on the said loan. The applicant has failed to prove that the loan was disbursed against consideration for time value of money, particularly, when respondent company has affirmed that no interest has been paid nor payable at any point of time. [Para 27]

In the instant case also, there is no document to show that the respondent company either accepted or undertook to repay the loan with interest. The applicant has failed to justify, how without any provision of interest the debt can be termed as a financial debt. Once the claim made in the application does not pertain to 'disbursement against consideration for time value of money', the present claim will not come within the purview of 'Financial Debt' and consequently the applicants cannot be termed as 'Financial Creditor' in respect of the present claim in question. [Para 29]

Needless to say, that the onus to prove lies on the applicants to establish that 'interest' is payable on the loan amount as claimed in the instant application. The burden of proof becomes more onerous particularly when the claim is disputed. It is reiterated that neither any document has been placed on record pertaining to the loan nor there is any supporting evidence to establish applicable rate of interest to be paid on the said loan. Therefore, the applicants miserably failed to substantiate that the amount was disbursed against the consideration for time value of money with supporting documentary evidence nor could satisfactorily repudiate the contention of the respondent. Mere pleading of the applicants, in the absence supporting documentary evidence, will not suffice to prove that the disbursements were made for time value of money. [Para 30]

Therefore, neither the instant claim can be termed to be a 'financial debt' nor does the applicants come within the meaning of 'financial creditors'. Once the applicants do not come within the meaning of 'financial creditors', they become ineligible to file the application under section 7 [Para 31]

For the reasons stated above this petition fails and the same stands dismissed as not maintainable. [Para 32]

INTRODUCTION

The Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016 (hereinafter 'the Code') proved to be one of the most innovative and reformative legal amendments. It made a paradigm shift in the very approach to the notion of insolvency and bankruptcy by providing a great scope for reorganisation and insolvency resolution in addition to liquidation. The Code also promised to balance all stakeholders' interest and to ensure the availability of credit. The scheme of this Code came before the judicial lens on various occasions. In Innoventive Industries Ltd. v. ICICI Bank Ltd.1, the Hon'ble Supreme Court underscored the various changes in the policy outlook of the Code and highlighted its overriding effect on other pre-existing laws.

Another such interesting decision of the Hon'ble Supreme Court is Swiss Ribbons (P.) Ltd. v. Union of India2, (hereinafter 'the present case') where the Hon'ble Court upheld various provisions of the Code. In this paper, the author aims at examining the correctness of the decision regarding two specific parameters regarding the differential treatment given to the Operational Creditors and Financial Creditors, in view of changed circumstances and other pertinent factors.

FINANCIAL DEBT AND OPERATIONAL DEBT UNDER THE CODE

As the next move, it is relevant to look into the statutory description of Financial Creditor and Operational Creditor under the Code. Section 5(7)of the Code defines Financial Creditor as a person to whom a financial debt is owed and includes its assignees and transferees. Section 5(8) gives a substantive definition to Financial Debt and also provides for an inclusive list of debts falling within the category. As per the provision, Financial Debt is a debt including interest, if any, disbursed for the time value of money against consideration.

From the definition, it is clear that the phraseology is very broad so as to include all kinds of debts associating with the time value for money. Similarly, Section 5(20) defines Operational Creditor as a person to whom an operational debt is owed and includes its assignees and transferees. Operational Debt, as per Section 5(21), is a claim in respect of provision of goods or services including employment or repayment of dues payable to the Central or State Government under law. Here, the test is whether the debt has a bearing on provision of goods and services.

It is now relevant to look at what is 'Claim', since both the definitions employ the said word. Section 5(6) defines Claim as (i) A Right to Payment or (ii) A Right to Remedy for Breach of Contract under law, whether or not they are reduced to judgment, disputed, matured, secured or fixed. Hence, it is clear that the right must be one legally enforceable.

All these definitions appear to be clear and concrete yet there are several instances where the Courts have taken varying stands depending on the facts and circumstances of each case. Hence, what was Financial Debt in one case can easily become Operational Debt in another. For instance, according to Section 5(8)(e) of the Code, "Receivables sold or discounted other than any receivables sold on non-recourse basis" falls within the meaning of Financial Debt.

However, in the recent decision of the National Company Law Tribunal, Bengaluru in Invoice Discounters of BNH Infra Projects (India) (P.) Ltd. v. BNH Infra Projects (India) (P.) Ltd.3 the Hon'ble Tribunal came to the conclusion that Financiers discounting invoices of the corporate debtor become operational creditors by stepping into their shoes. Interest necessary part of Financial Debt Following are the judgments by the NCLAT highlighting the fact that the interest component is necessary to constitute a financial debt.

1.

Vishwa Nath Singh (supra), the NCLAT observed that the FC must prove that the loan amount given is a financial debt and was disbursed against the consideration for the time value of money and the payment of interest. The tribunal has used the term "and" in between the words "consideration of time value of money" and "payment of interest", thereby making it a mandatory condition for constituting a financial debt.

2.

Dr. B.V.S. Lakshmi (supra) wherein the Appellate Tribunal held that the for categorising a debt as financial debt it to be against payment of interest and consideration for the time value of money.

3.

Shreyans Realtors (P.) Ltd. (supra) wherein the NCLAT was of the view that if in the agreement the interest component was not accepted by the CD and the CD never paid or undertook to repay the loan with interest, the loan granted will not be termed as financial debt and the creditor will not be called as an FC.

Interest not necessary part of Financial Debt

Following are the judgments by the NCLAT highlighting the fact that the interest component is not necessary to constitute a financial debt.

1.

Shailesh Sangani v. Joel Cardoso [2019] 103 taxmann.com 181/152 SCL 657 : The NCLAT, in this case, had expressly observed that the suffix "if any" before the word "interest" in the definition of financial debt means that element of interest is not an essential requirement for claiming a debt to be a financial debt and further went on to say that the loan disbursed against the consideration for the time value of money "may or may not" have the component of interest attached to it. Lastly, it held that what prima facie is of importance is that the debt should be against the consideration for the time value of money.

2.

Sanjay Kewalramani v. Sunil Parmanand Kewalramani [Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 57 of 2018, dated 12-7-2018]: The Appellate Tribunal while dealing with the matter observed that the loan given by Respondent No. 2 & 3 in the present matter was not against consideration of time value of money and further held that mere granting of the loan will not make the Respondents as FC until they show that they have complied with the substantive definition or any clauses of Section 5(8) of the Code. Also, it held that mere payment of interest for a certain period will not make the debt to be a financial debt as under the IBC.

Hence, from the above-mentioned judgments, it is understood that the tribunals earlier had divided opinions w.r.t. interest being an essential part of the financial debt. However, the Supreme Court in the Orator's case has clarified the status. Now, the settled position of law is that the loans having no interest payable on them will be considered as a financial debt along with the interest payable loans.

The recently enacted Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016 ('IBC' or 'Code'), was aimed at restructuring the insolvency laws and regulations pertaining to corporates, partnerships, individuals and other entities in India, and providing an effective and time bound resolution process to the creditors. Multiple laws and adjudicating forums governing the financial failures in India, prior to enactment of IBC, were not able to alleviate the distressed credit market and provide a time bound and effective mechanism to the stakeholders to resolve the issue.

The structure of the Code is laid down with an objective to maximize the value of the stakeholders; to restructure and consolidate the businesses; to balance the interest of all the stakeholders; to support the development of credit market; improving ease of doing business and facilitate more investment, leading to higher economic growth and development.

The objective of the new law is to generate a competitive revival or resolution plan, which benefits and maximizes the value of all the stakeholders. The aim was to restructure the businesses, if viable, rather than liquidation. However, the Code has been considered by the financial institutions and other creditors as a fast recovery channel rather than considering the option of restructuring and revival of the businesses. In last two years of enactment of IBC, over 800 companies1 have been going the liquidation process.

Amid financial institutions and other financial and operational creditors being successful in instituting insolvency resolution process against the corporate debtors, the plea of the home buyers for initiating the insolvency resolution process against the corporate debtors, being real estate developers was struck down by the Hon'ble National Company Law Tribunal ('NCLT'). In terms of the provisions of IBC, financial creditor, operation creditor and the corporate debtor itself can initiate the corporate insolvency resolution process. NCLT adjudicated that the home buyers who have invested their money in purchasing the real estate property are not operational creditors and not even financial creditors, hence their plea for initiation of insolvency resolution process cannot be accepted. One of the judgment of the NCLT in the catena of judgments with respect to claim of home buyers was of the Delhi Bench of NCLT in the case of Nikhil Mehta & Sons (HUF) v. AMR Infrastructure Ltd. [2017] 78 taxmann.com 302 (NCLT - New Delhi), wherein the Hon'ble Bench held that where the transaction was a pure and simple agreement of sale or purchase of piece of property, such a transaction would not acquire the status of a 'financial debt' as the transaction did not have consideration for time value of money, which is a substantive ingredient to be satisfied for fulfilling requirements of expression 'financial debt'. In other words, Hon'ble Bench held that, to qualify as a financial debt and thus as a financial creditor, in terms of the provisions of IBC, what is important that the money has been advanced for a consideration for time value of money. However, in the case of home buyers, the money was advanced for purchase of property and not with a consideration for return of any time value of money.

If the notices dated 14-9-2017 and 24-7-2020 are taken into account, it emerges that it is the specific and definite case of the petitioner that he transferred the amount of USD 2,50,000/- with an intent to buy a 25 per cent stake in the assets of the corporate debtor. [Para 20]

It is well settled that an investment cannot be equated with a loan. In the commercial word, equity financing and debt financing are altogether different modes of finance which are distinct from each other. Equity financing carries no repayment obligation while debt financing involves borrowing of money which is often repayable along with interest or other charges as may be settled between the parties. Therefore, a sum of money invested with an intent of requiring equity stake in a company or some other interest in some of the properties of the company cannot be dubbed as a financial debt or for that matter a loan transaction. [Para 21]

Besides, one cannot be oblivious of the facts that in the notices dated 14-9-2017 and 24-7-2020, the petitioner himself has claimed that the payment in question was made with intent to buy 25 per cent equity stake in the respondent's Company, on the basis of which, it could be safely concluded that the money was given as a loan. In this regard, a reference can be made to the Remittance Certificate Exhibit whereby the money was wired by the petitioner from Spain to the account of the corporate debtor and in the Bank note, it is specifically mentioned that the purpose of remittance was an investment in purchasing, constructing and operating a hotel business in India. [Para 23]

Therefore, by looking at the instant case, it cannot be said to be a case of money having been borrowed by the corporate debtor from the petitioner nor the transaction can be dubbed as a loan transaction. The so-called admission made by the corporate debtor in the reply dated 18-9-2017 that the transaction was invested is of no consequence. In this context, it is further pertinent to mention that the respondent has claimed in the reply that an amount of Rs. 20 lacs were paid back to the petitioner as on 11-2-2008 as is evident from the statement of account (Exhibit G) attached with the reply. So far as the petitioner is concerned, in the rejoinder filed by him, the transfer of an amount of Rs. 20 lacs as on 11-2-2008 has not been specifically denied and it has only been stated that it was a personal transaction not relating to the transaction which took place in the year 2007. Even this plea raised on behalf of the petitioners seems to be a tentative one and does not really explains the exact position and circumstances under which a sum of Rs. 20 lacs were paid to the petitioner. Supreme Court's Decision Aggrieved by the decision of the NCLAT, the Appellant/FC (who is claiming to be the FC) appealed before the Supreme Court under section 62 of the IBC (Orator Marketing (P.) Ltd. (supra). The question which was posed before the Supreme Court was "whether a person who has given interest free loan to a Corporate Person becomes incompetent to file a petition under section 7 of the Code?"

The Appellant challenged the impugned order of the NCLAT & NCLT and argued that while interpreting the provision of the legislation, the focus should be on the legislative intent, object & purpose of the statute. It was argued that both the Adjudicatory Tribunal have overlooked the words in section 5(8) of the Code, i.e., "if any". The interpretation of the words provides that the financial debt will not necessarily have the component of interest and if there is no interest still the principal debt will qualify to be as financial debt. He further argued that the NCLAT & NCLT have failed to take notice of Section 5(8) (f) of the IBC which provides that financial debt will include any amount which is raised under other transactions having the commercial effect of borrowing. The Appellant argued that the word "includes" as per the interpretation given in the case of Dilworth v. Commissioner of Stamps [1899] AC 99, will have connotation "means and includes" which will give an extensive explanation to the meaning attached to the words or expressions and thus lending of money for the financial requirements of the CD will in no way be discerned as it does not have the commercial effect of borrowing and thus, cannot be excluded from the definition of financial debt.

The Court further referred to the judgment of Anuj Jain, IRP for Anuj Jain v. Axis Bank Ltd. [2020] 114 taxmann.com 656, wherein the Supreme Court held that the basic element for the debt to be financial debt is that it should be disbursed against the consideration for the time value of money. Time value of money remains an essential part of the financial debt. The Court further stated that "the essential element of disbursal, and that too against the consideration for the time value of money, needs to be found in the genesis of any debt before it may be treated as financial debt within the meaning of Section 5(8) of the Code". The Apex Court, in the present matter, applied the ratio of the Jaypee Infratech case and held that the facts of the present matter are distinguishable from the above-mentioned case in a sense that the debt in the former case was in a form of a third-party guarantee which was given by the CD for securing the advances to the borrower, but, in the present case, the interest-free loan was given to meet out the working expenditures and financial requirements of the CD and thus, the ratio of the former case cannot be applied to the present case.

Further, the court relied on the case of Prabhudas Damodar Kotecha v. Manhabala Jeram Damodar [2013] 15 SCC 358, wherein the court applied the golden rule of interpretation while interpreting Section 41(1) of the Presidency Small Cause Courts Act, 1882 and observed that the words or phrase of the statute must be given ordinary meaning when the language used by the legislature is precise and plain and thus concluded that the gratuitous licensee will be considered as a general licensee unless specifically excluded. Thus, relying on the reasoning of the above case the Court in the present matter concluded that the loan given without interest will qualify to be treated as a financial debt unless specifically excluded. Hence, the Supreme Court set aside the judgment of the NCLAT & NCLT and ordered the NCLT to revive the petition under section 7 of the FC.

Divided Opinions of the Court/Tribunals on Interest as Prerequisite for Financial Debt

Section 5(8) of the Code defines financial debt which provides that it's a debt alongwith interest, if any, disbursed against the consideration for the time value of money and includes the debt and includes money borrowed against payment of interest. On the plain reading of the provision, it is evident that if there is any interest component in the debt then it will qualify as financial debt. However, if there is no interest component attached to the debt/loan amount then what treatment is to be provided to the loan is a question that seeks urgent attention. Although, the Supreme Court in the Orator's case has very clearly highlighted the fact that the debt having no interest constituent shall be termed as financial debt, but this judgment of the Hon'ble court cannot be read alone and should be read in the light of various judgments of various NCLTs and NCLAT wherein the position of law was divided.

3.2-3 Meaning of 'debt', financial debt, claim, operational debt

The definitions of debt, claim, financial debt, operational debt are highly relevant under Insolvency Code.

Debt - "Debt" means a liability or obligation in respect of a claim which is due from any person and includes a financial debt and operational debt - section 3(11) of Insolvency Code, 2016.

Debt due means debt due and payable. If the debt is barred by law under Limitation Act, it is not 'debt due' - B K Educational Services v. Parag Gupta and Associates (2018) 150 SCL 293 = 98 taxmann.com 213 (SC) = (2019) 11 SCC 633 - followed in SK Systems v. Hamtek Infra Projects India (2020) 157 SCL 678 = 113 taxmann.com 201 (NCLT).

If recovery certificate was issued on 24-12-2001, petition for CIRP on 21-7-2017 is barred. Section 23 of Limitation Act applies to continuous wrong and not to continuous right - Vashdeo R Bhojwani v. Abhyudaya Cooperative Bank (2019) 9 SCC 158.

Compulsorily Convertible Debenture (CCD) is equity. It is not debenture simpliciter. It is not a 'debt' under section 3(11) of Insolvency Code - IFCI Ltd. v. Sutanu Sinha [2023] 156 taxmann.com 681 (SC 3 member bench).

Claim - "Claim" means— (a) a right to payment, whether or not such right is reduced to judgment, fixed, disputed, undisputed, legal, equitable, secured or unsecured (b) right to remedy for breach of contract under any law for the time being in force, if such breach gives rise to a right to payment, whether or not such right is reduced to judgment, fixed, matured, un-matured, disputed, undisputed, secured or unsecured - section 3(6) of Insolvency Code, 2016.

Financial Debt - "Financial debt" means a debt along with interest, if any, which is disbursed against the consideration for the time value of money and includes—

It noted that it was an admitted fact that the loan was interest free. It also found that there was no evidence that the amount was disbursed for time value of money. The Adjudicating Authority thus concluded that the Appellant could not be treated as a Financial Creditor. The Application thus came to be dismissed.

'Financial debt' and 'financial creditor'

The expressions 'financial creditor' and 'financial debt' have been defined in section 5(7) and 5(8) and precisely 'financial debt' is a debt along with interest, if any, which is disbursed against the consideration for time value of money. [Para 14]

In the instant case, the applicant disbursed the loan and the respondent in their reply has admitted that the amount of Rs. 30 lakhs was received from the applicant but as a long-term borrowing. The respondent, therefore, has accepted that the debt amount of Rs. 30 lakhs given by the applicant was in the nature of a loan. Once it is accepted that the amount of Rs. 30 lakhs was received as a long-term borrowing, it is evident that the said loan amount was clearly disbursed against the consideration for time value of money with a clear commercial effect of borrowing. Besides the amount of financial debt has been recorded in the balance sheets of the corporate debtor and Form 26AS of the financial creditor, which reveals that the debt was advanced against consideration for time value of money. Moreover, the debt claimed in the instant application includes both the component of outstanding principal and interest. [Para 15]

In that view of the matter not only the instant claim comes within the purview of 'Financial Debt' in terms of section 5(8) but also the applicant can clearly be termed as 'financial creditor' of the respondent-corporate debtor so as to prefer the instant application under section 7. [Para 16]

Conditions for Admission of CIRP application

The application filed by the applicant financial creditor has to be admitted under sub-section 5(a) of section 7 of the code, on satisfaction that (i) Default has occurred, (ii) Application is complete, and (iii) No disciplinary proceeding against the proposed IRP is pending. [Para 17]

An application under section 7 is acceptable so long as the financial debt is proved to be due and there has been occurrence of existence of default. What is material is that the default is at least 1 lakh. In view of section 4, the moment default is of Rs. 1 lakh or more, the application to trigger corporate insolvency resolution process under the code is maintainable. In the instant case the claimed financial debt exceeds Rupees 44 lakhs and the respondent has defaulted in making the payment of the debt. [Para 18]

In connection with the 2nd requirement of sub-section (5)(a) of section 7, it is seen that the instant application is complete and has been filed by the petitioner financial creditor in Form-1 in terms of rule 4 of the Insolvency and Bankruptcy (Application to Adjudicating Authority) Rules, 2016 accompanied with the required information, documents and records as prescribed under the Rules. [Para 19]

The applicant inter alia has annexed to the application detail particulars of 'financial debt' including documents and records as evidence of default as required under sub-section (3)(a) of section 7. It is reiterated that the Form-1 filed in the instant case under section 7 read with rule 4 of the Rules, shows that the Form is complete in all respect and there is no infirmity in the same. [Para 20]

It is, thus, seen that the requirement of sub-section (5)(a) of section 7 stands satisfied as default has occurred; the instant application filed under section 7 is complete. [Para 22]

Whether amount was payable after 7 years:

In this regard it is seen that even if there is no written loan agreement, the disbursal of loan amount of Rs. 30 lakhs has not been disputed. It is clearly accepted in the reply of respondent that the amount of Rs. 30 lakhs was received as a long-term borrowing. An agreement can either be oral or written and, therefore, an admitted loan given on oral request can be enforceable in law. [Para 24]

As regards the objection that the loan is recoverable only after 7 years, it is seen from the email letter written by corporate debtor that the corporate debtor has accepted its liability to pay the debt amount and its willingness to pay the debt to the applicant financial creditor. In the aforesaid email the respondent not only has accepted its liability but also has sought time to repay the amount of debt at the earliest. It is further stated in the email that the amount of debt could not be paid by the respondent due to its financial crisis. The email states that the debt shall be paid in the next month. The contention of the corporate debtor, therefore, that the amount was payable after seven years is baseless and without any proof and as such cannot sustain. [Para 26]

6. As stated earlier, IBC was enacted for the first time in 2016. All sections of the IBC were not made applicable from a single date. The provisions relating to corporate insolvency in the Code came into effect on 1 December, 2016 and have completed approx. more than one and a half years on its operation. This period has witnessed the setting-up of the eco-system for the Code to function: the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Board of India (IBBI), National Company Law Tribunal (NCLT), development of the profession of insolvency professionals and establishment of information utilities (IU).

Being a new Act, some problems in its implementation were felt just after few months of its operation. Immediate amendments were made firstly by an ordinance, which was replaced by the Insolvency and Banking Code (Amendment) Act, 2018, which was made effective from 23.11.17. A new ordinance has since been promulgated, which is being considered in later discussion.

6.1 Appointment of committee: While the 1st ordinance was yet to be replaced by an amendment Act (supra), the MCA constituted the Insolvency Law Committee (the Committee) under the Chairmanship of Injeti Srinivas, Secretary, MCA, vide an office order dt. 16.11.2017. The Committee, besides the Chairman, comprised of 13 members – 14 in all. The Committee submitted its report on 26.3.2018.

The Committee examined various provisions of the IBC and has given an exhaustive report on various provisions of IBC, which it felt, needed change. The report deals with the recommendations of the Committee and the rationale for such recommendations in relation to the Code and the relevant subordinate legislation, viz., Insolvency and Bankruptcy (Application to Adjudicating Authority) Rules, 2016 [CIRP Rules], Insolvency and Bankruptcy Board of India (Insolvency Resolution Process for Corporate Persons) Regulations, 2016 [CIRP Regulations], Insolvency and Bankruptcy Board of India (Liquidation Process) Regulations, 2016 (Liquidation Regulations].

The only change suggested by the Committee in the definition of 'financial debt' relevant for homebuyers is being considered in the present article.

6.2 S.5(8) of the Code defines 'financial debt': to mean a debt along with interest, if any, which is disbursed against the consideration for the time value of money and, inter alia, includes money borrowed against payment of interest, etc. The Committee's attention was drawn to the significant confusion regarding the status of buyers of under-construction apartments (homebuyers) as creditors under the Code. Multiple judgments were found to have categorized them as neither fitting within the definition of the 'financial nor operational creditors. In one particular case they have been classified as financial creditors due to the assured returns scheme in the contract, in which there was an arrangement wherein it was agreed that the seller of the apartments would pay assured returns to the homebuyers till possession of property was given. It was held that such a transaction was in the nature of a loan and constituted a financial debt within the Code. A similar judgment was given in Anil Mahindroo v. Earth Organics Infrastructure [2018] 91 taxmann.com 143 (NCL - AT). These judgments were given considering the terms of contracts between the homebuyers and the seller and are fact specific. Further, the IBBI issued a claim form for creditors, other than financial or operational creditors, which gave an indication that homebuyers are neither financial nor operational creditors.

The contention of the Corporate Debtor that the amount reflected as "Intercorporate Advance" cannot be treated as financial debt is not acceptable. Mere nomenclature employed in the books of accounts is not conclusive of the true nature of a transaction. The substance of the transaction and the attendant circumstances are required to be examined. In the present case, the receipt of Rs. 2,25,00,000/- from the Financial Creditor stands acknowledged in the audited financial statements of the Corporate Debtor. The said amount is reflected under the head "Intercorporate Advance" in Note 15 to the audited financial statements of the Corporate Debtor, wherein it is recorded that the Company has received an advance of Rs. 2,25,00,000/- from L.H. 14. It is also significant that the Corporate Debtor's Board Resolution dated 01.10.2024 refers to availing unsecured loan from the Financial Creditor. Though the Corporate Debtor disputes the effect of the said resolution, the same constitutes contemporaneous evidence emanating from the Corporate Debtor itself. Further, while acquisition discussions between the parties are borne out from the record, no executed Share Purchase Agreement or other concluded document has been produced to establish that the amount of Rs. 2,25,00,000/- stood finally adjusted towards acquisition consideration. The material on record, therefore, indicates that the amount continued to remain outstanding.

15. The Corporate Debtor has further contended that the transaction does not carry interest and therefore cannot be treated as financial debt. At this stage, it is relevant to refer to the judgment of the Hon'ble Supreme Court in Orator Marketing Pvt. Ltd. (supra), wherein the Hon'ble Supreme Court has observed as under:

"22. The NCLT and NCLAT have overlooked the words "if any" which could not have been intended to be otiose. 'Financial debt' means outstanding principal due in respect of a loan and would also include interest thereon, if any interest were payable thereon. If there is no interest payable on the loan, only the outstanding principal would qualify as a financial debt. Both NCLAT and NCLT have failed to notice clause(f) of Section 5(8), in terms whereof 'financial debt' includes any amount raised under any other transaction, having the commercial effect of borrowing."

"29....Having regard to the Aims, Objects and Scheme of the IBC, there is no discernible reason, why a term loan to meet the financial requirements of a Corporate Debtor for its operation, which obviously has the commercial effect of borrowing, should be excluded from the purview of a financial debt."

"31....The definition of 'Financial Debt' in Section 5(8) of IBC does not expressly exclude an interest free loan. 'Financial Debt' would have to be construed to include interest free loans advanced to finance the business operations of a corporate body."

16. In view of the aforesaid law laid down by the Hon'ble Supreme Court, the contention of the Corporate Debtor that the transaction cannot constitute financial debt merely because it was interest-free cannot be accepted. Section 5(8) itself employs the expression "interest, if any". The material placed on record demonstrates disbursal of funds by the Financial Creditor, acknowledgment of the transaction in the audited financial statements of both parties, reflection of the amount as an outstanding liability in the books of the Corporate Debtor and absence of any concluded document evidencing final adjustment of the amount towards acquisition consideration. In the facts of the present case, the transaction has not been shown to have culminated into a completed acquisition arrangement and, therefore, is liable to be treated as a transaction having the commercial effect of borrowing within the meaning of Section 5(8)(f) of the Code. Consequently, the same falls within the ambit of financial debt under Section 5(8) of the Code.

A plain reading of the definition clauses of 'financial debt' and 'financial creditor' shows that for any creditor to become financial creditor under section 5(7), there must be a financial debt and for any debt to qualify as a financial debt, that debt along with interest, if any, should have been disbursed against the consideration for the time value of money. Use of expression 'if any' as suffixed to the word 'interest' leaves no shadow of doubt that the component of interest is not a sine qua non for bringing the debt within the fold of financial debt. What is material however is that the disbursement of debt should be against consideration for the time value of money irrespective of whether the debt is interest bearing or not. [Para 11]

The clauses of 'financial debt' and 'financial creditor' and the guiding legal precepts of the Innoventive judgment, it can be safely concluded that for any creditor to become financial creditor under section 5(7), there must be a financial debt which is owed to that person and such a person can either be the principal creditor to whom the financial debt is owed or may be a legal assignee to whom such debt has been transferred. Furthermore, for a debt to become financial debt under the various transactions stated in sub-clauses (a) to (i) of section 5(8), the basic non-negotiable ingredients are that there has to be a disbursal against the consideration for time value of money as carved out in the principal clause which has already been noted above. Further, a financial creditor may file an application under section 7 for initiating CIRP against the corporate debtor when the default in respect of the financial debt owed to him has occurred. It is for the financial creditor to file an application along with the proof of default. If there is a financial debt, which is more than the prescribed threshold level and there is a default and if the application is complete, the application is required to be admitted by the Adjudicating Authority. It is for the Adjudicating Authority to look into the various documents, records and evidence of default as furnished in Part V of Form 1 of the application filed under section 7. [Para 13]

HELD: The judgment and order of the NCLAT, affirming the judgment and order of the Adjudicating Authority (NCLT) and dismissing the appeal is patently flawed. In construing and/or interpreting any statutory provision, one must look into the legislative intent of the statute. The intention of the statute has to be found in the words used by the legislature itself. [Para 9]

When a question arises as to the meaning of a certain provision in a statute, the provision has to be read in its context. The statute has to be read as a whole. The previous state of law, the general scope and ambit of the statute and the mischief that it was intended to remedy are relevant factors. [Para 10]

Section 7 enables a financial creditor to file an application for initiating Corporate Insolvency Resolution Process against a corporate debtor either by itself, or jointly with other financial creditors or any other person on behalf of the financial creditor, as may be notified by the Central Government, when a default has occurred. The eligibility of a person, to initiate the Corporate Insolvency Resolution Process, if questioned, has to be adjudicated upon consideration of the key words and expressions in the aforesaid section and other related provisions. [Para 18]

Corporate resolution process gets triggered when a corporate debtor commits a default. A financial creditor may file an application for initiating a Corporate Insolvency Resolution Process against the corporate debtor, when a default has occurred. [Para 19]

The loan advanced by the appellant did not bear interest and was to be repaid after the settlement of the secured financial loans of the CD under the one time settlement scheme but when the CD failed to repay the loan after settlement of the secured loans, the appellant issued notice and recalled its loan to be repaid within 15 days. The appellant alleged that the amount of loan was reflected in the financial statement of the Respondent as unsecured loan. The corporate debtor failed to repay the loan after settlement of the secured loans.

■

The appellant filed an application under section 7 for the resolution of an interest free loan. The NCLT dismissed the application on ground that amount given by the appellant to the corporate debtor was not a financial debt and, hence, the corporate debtor was not owed to pay the appellant and that the loan was advanced in violation of section 186(2) of the Companies Act, 2013 and, therefore, was void and unforceable.

■

On appeal:

HELD: ■

There is no dispute to the fact that the amount in question is continuously reflected in the balance sheet of the respondent from 2016-17 to 2020-21 in schedule 3A as unsecured loan without any caveat, therefore, such entry without any qualification/caveat is acknowledgment of debt by the CD as unsecured loan is having commercial effect of borrowing. [Para 20]

■

Much emphasis has been laid by the respondent as well as the Tribunal about non-adherence to the provision of section 186 of the Companies Act. Section 186(2)(a) of the Companies Act says that 'no company can directly or indirectly give any loan exceeding 60 per cent of its paid up share capital free reserves and securities premium account of its free reserves and securities premium account whichever is more'. However, section 186(13) provides for punishment for violation of the provisions of the section. It provides that 'the Company shall be punishable with fine which shall not be less than Rs. 25000 but which may extend to Rs. 5 lakh and officer of the company who is in default shall be punishable with imprisonment for a term which may extend to two years and with fine which shall not be less than Rs. 25000 but which may extend to Rs. 1 lakh.' [Para 21]

■

But in no case the debt advanced by the company to a corporate body can be held to be unrecoverable only because of the reason that there was a irregularity in advancement of the loan which became a debt to a third party or in other words the CD cannot take the shelter of section 186 of the Act to deny its liability to return the amount taken by it being a corporate body which is due and payable. [Para 22]

FACT: The corporate debtor, with an intention of setting up a project for the manufacture of flexible packaging material under co-extension process at an estimated cost of Rs.30 crores, had approached Canara Bank for financial assistance. While the said bank sanctioned a term loan of Rs.14.2 crores for construction of the building and purchase of plant and machinery, the promoters of corporate debtor were required to meet the condition of investing the margin money. Accordingly, all six promoters, including the financial creditor, had given interest free unsecured loan to the corporate debtor.

The financial creditor alleged that the corporate debtor failed to take any steps to liquidate or reduce the liability qua him despite various reminders. Thus, he issued demand notice under section 8. In response to the said notice, corporate debtor submitted that the amount being claimed was not a loan in terms of financial debt, nor was there any agreement to pay interest thereon. It was not to be repaid on demand as it was the basis of procuring financial assistance from their bank for establishing the corporate debtor for its working capital. The financial creditor was an equity holder and with a view to set up a plant, all shareholders had paid various amounts as the margin money to enable them to get the loan facility from Canara bank.

HELD: All Promoters including the Financial Creditor herein, have confirmed the Subordination Agreement with their Bank, for and on behalf of the Corporate Debtor, and have undertaken that the unsecured creditors had extended or continued to extend interest free unsecured loan on the express understanding that all their claims against the respondent company would be subject to the claims of Canara Bank; that all the claims of the unsecured creditors against the respondent company would at all times be subordinate and be subject to any claims of Canara Bank; that unsecured creditors agree not to sue the respondent company for recovering any money tendered to the respondent company as unsecured loan until all the claims of Canara Bank get settled; that the unsecured creditors agree not to join in any bankruptcy or any assignment.

It is therefore submitted by the respondent that since the unsecured loans were interest-free, no interest was promised. Further, it is stated that the transaction inter se the parties does not fall within the definition of financial debt nor is the financial creditor a person to whom a financial debt is owed. [Para 8]

In view of the facts and circumstances of the case, the present claim does not fall within the definition of a financial debt nor is it an unsecured loan repayable on demand. There is not Demand Promissory Note executed, nor is there any agreement for payment of any interest. As submitted by the corporate debtor and not denied by the operational creditor, the amount given by him along with 6 others was for promoting and setting up a business. The terms for raising the bank loan necessitated investment of the margin money. This was done by all the promoters and is reflected as unsecured loans, subordinate to the claim of the bank. The bank agreement corroborating this is on record.

Whether the amount claimed by the Financial Creditor is a Financial Debt under the IBC ?

(i) From a conjoint reading of the provisions of the Act and the documents executed between the parties, it can be safely concluded that JKSIDCO leased out 200 kanals of land to JKITPL for a period of 90 years, where JKITPL paid a premium of Rs.3 crore to JKSIDCO and further paid Rs.12 lakhs as an advance ground rent for two years. The ownership of the land vests with the JKSIDCO and the ownership of the building constructed upon that land vests with JKITPL. The industrial units were to pay annual lease rent to JKITPL for the use of the leased premises. Further, as mentioned in the Agreement dated 6-10-2015 between the Corporate Debtor and JKITPL, it is mentioned that the net cost of the project/building is Rs.3.04 crores for the construction of building and in the same project, the cost incurred by the party of the second part is Rs.3.04 crores for the component of building constructed.

(ii)

The amount of Rs.1.24 crores mentioned as cost of land to be paid by the Corporate Debtor to JKITPL is not a financial debt advanced by JKITPL to the Corporate Debtor. The annual lease rent, which the industrial units, including the Corporate Debtor were to pay to JKITPL, is not in nature financial debt, as it intends towards availing services from JKITPL by the Corporate Debtor, i.e., use of the leased premises and buildings.

(iii)

While determining, whether a debt falls within the definition of financial debt as defined under section 5(8), mere existence of the debt is not to be ascertained. In addition to the existence of the debt, the intended use of such debt is also to be seen in order to categorise it as a financial debt.

(iv)

Further, in the Petition filed under section 7, the Financial Creditor has not appended any cogent evidence of disbursal of the debt amount to the Corporate Debtor. The only evidence annexed with the section 7 petition is the balance sheet of the Corporate Debtor for the Financial Year ending as on 31-3-2022, where the alleged debt is shown in Note as ''''Unsecured Loans- From Others'''' under the head ''''Long Term Borrowings''''.

(v)

However, in the Balance Sheet of Financial Creditor, JKITPL for the year ended 31-3-2018, depicts that the amount due from member industrial units is shown as ''''Investments in Units'''' instead of ''''Long-Term Loans and Advance''''s.

(vi)

No evidence on behalf of the Financial Creditor regarding the disbursal of the said debt through transfer of monies or banking transaction is appended with the Petition evidencing the disbursal of debt to the Corporate Debtor. Moreover, no document duly signed by both parties acknowledging the disbursal of the debt amount has been placed on record.

(vii)

Mere reflection of the debt amount in the balance sheets of the Corporate Debtor and reliance on the bank statements to allege that some money in the nature of financial debt was given to the Corporate Debtor, does not hold good in the eyes of law. The financial debt and its default must be established beyond reasonable doubts.

(viii)

Moreover, it is pertinent to note that the alleged lease deed dated 22-3-2012 under which the land was leased out to JKITPL for a period of 90 years and the agreement dated 6-10-2015 executed between JKITPL and the Corporate Debtor, where it has been mentioned that JKITPL has already leased out the land to the Corporate Debtor, both the documents are not registered, otherwise compulsory registerable under section 17(d) of the Indian Registration Act of 1908.

(ix)

Thus, in the case in hand, alleged debt as claimed by JKITPL does not fall under the definition of financial debt as envisaged under section 5(8)
