4. CCD under the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016 ['IBC']

4.1 Debentures are prima facie considered to be financial debt as per the definition of financial debt given in the IBC. As per section 5(8), financial debt means a debt along with interest, if any, which is disbursed against the consideration for the time value of money and includes- (c) "any amount raised pursuant to any note purchase facility or the issue of bonds, notes, debentures, loan stock or any similar instrument";

Thus, it is interesting to know the classification of CCD under the IBC in a case where a Financial Creditor holding debentures of the Corporate Debtors.

4.2 The question was raised before the Hon'ble Supreme Court in IFCI Ltd. v. Sutanu Sinha [2023] 156 taxmann.com 681 (SC) whether CCDs can be treated in essence as a form of debt instead of an equity share. The court, having examined the definition of debt in the Code as a 'liability or obligation in respect of a claim,' concluded that the appellant can be deemed a part-owner (i.e. an equity participant) of the company. This is because (as per the subscription agreement), if the company fails to buy back the shares within a specific period, the debentures can automatically be converted into equity shares.

4.3 As a result, the company does not have the right to claim any dues or debt from the Corporate Debtor ("CD"). Therefore, in case such an instrument is treated as debt, it would go against the agreement terms. The court further went on to hold that the investment is essentially a form of debenture which must be compulsorily converted into equity shares, and thus, not specified to be considered as a financial debt under certain circumstances that means it will be part of equity.

4.4 Therefore, it has become a settled position of law that when an investment is made like debentures which are compulsory convertible into equity it will be treated as equity.

4.5 Whereas, the issue relating to Optionally Convertible Debentures [OCD] is still unclear wherein the judiciary has taken to different contradicting opinions. The Hon'ble NCLAT in MAIF Investments India PTE. Ltd. v. Bharath Energy (Utkal) Ltd. [2019] SCC Online NCLAT 825 held that OCDs are considered as financial debt in view of Section 5(8) of the code.

5. CCD under the Foreign Exchange Management Act [FEMA]

5.1 The investment by a non-resident in an Indian Company, in any form, is regulated by the Foreign Exchange Management Act, 1999 read with Foreign Exchange Management (Transfer or Issue of a Security by a Person Resident outside India) Regulations, 2017 as amended in 2019 ('FEMA Regulations').

5.2 Regulation 2(xviii) defines 'Foreign Investment' to mean any investment made by a person resident outside India on a repatriable basis in 'capital instruments' of an Indian company or to the capital of an LLP.

5.3 Regulation 2(v) 'defines Capital instruments' to mean equity shares, 'debentures', preference shares and share warrants issued by an Indian company. The Explanation further provides that the expression 'Debentures' means fully, compulsorily and mandatorily convertible debentures. Thus, the CCDs which are fully and mandatorily convertible into equity, are considered as 'capital instruments' being at par with equity shares.

5.4 As fully, compulsorily and mandatorily convertible debentures alone are regarded as capital instruments, optionally convertible or partially convertible debentures are treated as debt instruments under the FEMA Regulations. These debentures which do not fall within the ambit of 'capital instruments would have to conform to the guidelines on External Commercial Borrowings, i.e. Foreign Exchange Management (Borrowing and Lending in Foreign Exchange) Regulations, 2000.

6. CCD under Income Tax Law

CCDs are treated as equity rather than debt under FEMA regulations and IBC from the date on which the CCDs are issued. We can analyse from the viewpoint of income tax law whether till the time of conversion can the same be recharacterised as equity.

6.1 Allowability of interest deductions

6.1.1 Section 36(1)(iii) of the Income-tax Act, 1961 ('IT Act') provides for the deduction of interest paid in respect of capital borrowed by a taxpayer for its business or profession. That is, if CCDs are treated as capital 'borrowed' for the IT Act, then the interest paid thereon shall be allowable as a deduction, whereas if the same is treated as 'equity', no deduction would be permissible for return paid on equity investment. The re-characterization of CCDs as equity and the disallowance of the interest expenditure claimed thereof, has been an issue for consideration under the IT Act.

Critical Analysis of the Supreme Court's Judgment in the Orator's case.

Considering the Orator's judgment by the Supreme Court in the light of various judgments and points discussed above, the authors vehemently states that the judgment has not removed the black cloud over the issue of interest not being an essential part of financial debt. Instead, it has brought forward various ambiguous points, upon which a necessary deliberation is required. Firstly , as observed from various judgments of the Supreme Court and the NCLAT, it can be concluded that the time value of money is the most important and quintessential part of the financial debt without which an application under section 7 will not get admitted. It is also evident from the various definitions as referred above that the time value of money includes the interest component, and is the difference between the present values of payment and the payment due and payable in future discounted by compound interest. Hence, for a debt to be disbursed against the consideration for the time value of money, it needs to have an interest component in it. Further, as can be seen from the Insolvency Committee Report, 2018, the time value of money has two components, i.e., interest or factoring in discount of payment. Though, the Supreme Court has clarified that the word "interest" before the phrase "if any" under the definition of financial debt is not required to file a case under section 7 if there is no interest attached to the loan, however, a lot of clarity is required upon the component of interest which also exist in the phrase "time value of money". Thus, it can be said that the consideration for the time value of money under section 5(8) also includes interest as a major component. Hence, in the humble submission of the authors, the interest constituent is necessary for a debt to qualify as financial debt and the ratio in the case of Narendra Kumar Agarwal v. Monotrone Leasing Private Limited should be taken into consideration which provides that the interest component in a transaction is the time value of money.

Secondly , seeing the factual matrix of the present case in hand, the Appellant/FC in its application has mentioned Rs. 1.56 cr as the total default by the CD. Here, it is important to bring to the notice that the total loan amount sanctioned was Rs. 1.60 cr out of which the CD had only paid Rs. 4 lakhs, thereby making default on Rs. 1.56 cr. Although the loan disbursed was interest-free, the Supreme Court didn't take notice of the same and allowed the application to be admitted in which only the principal amount was given, the principal amount was partly paid, and application was also filed for the principal amount without any interest, thereby implying that the amount disbursed was not in consideration against the time value of money.

Thirdly , the Supreme Court has failed to deliberate upon the point basing which the NCLAT had given its judgment, i.e., the consideration for the time value of money is for the benefits of the FC and not the CD. The Supreme Court has unforeseen this aspect of the judgment by the NCLAT. In the present case, there was no consideration for the time value of money for the FC as the loan agreement was interest-free and the CD was only liable to repay the principal amount even after maturity of the contract, i.e., only Rs. 1.56 cr. Also, the Supreme Court in the case of Pioneer's case has held that the definition of financial debt under section 5(8) should be read as "means and includes" thereby providing an extensive meaning to the definition. This means that clauses (a) to (i) under section 5(8) is an extension of the definition of financial debt and is not an exhaustive list and thus, the substantial part of the definition cannot be ignored. In the present case, the Supreme Court is only putting its reliance on the clause (f) of Section 5 which provides for commercial effect of borrowing but is completing ignoring the principal/substantial part of the definition which provides for the component of time value of money in the financial debt. Hence, the Appellant should not be termed as FC by the Supreme Court and his application should have been rejected.

Conclusion

From the point of view of the authors, it is evident that the Supreme Court's decision in Orator's case can have negative implications as the Court has predominantly based its reasoning taking into consideration Section 5(8)(f) of the IBC only and have ignored the principal aspect of the definition of financial debt, i.e., the consideration for the time value of money. This obstinate view of the Court has created ambiguity and vagueness in the understanding of the substantial part of the definition of financial debt and hence, a much-needed clarification is required on interest being an essential constituent of "time value of money".

Appellants also relied on an order passed by the SEBI where it stated that "where the developer assured to pay assured returns to the buyer are not pure real estate transactions, rather they satisfy all the ingredients of a Collective Investment Scheme as defined under section 11AA of the SEBI Act." Based on this the appellants contended that the transaction was interest paid on funds. The NCLAT referred to the NCLT order which examined the classifications of "Financial Creditor and "Financial Debt". It observed the following: "The Key feature as postulated by section 5(8) is its consideration for time value for money. In other words, the legislature has included such financial transactions in the definition of 'Financial debt' which are usually for a sum of money received to be paid for over a period of time in a single series of payments in the future. It may also be a sum of money invested to be repaid over a period in a single or a series of instalments to be paid in the future."18 With this reason NCLT concluded that the current transaction was a simple sale deal and mere payment of "assured returns" was not sufficient to bring it under sections 5(8) of the IBC. Though the NCLAT accepted the NCLT order, it took a little different stand. It observed that in the MOU the appellants were denoted as 'investors', who were investing in "committed returns plan" and getting "committed returns" for it. Therefore, it concluded that the assured returns would be in the nature of "debt" under section 3(11) of the IBC. The same principle has also been followed in the case of "Anil Mahindroo v. Abstract

The Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code 2016 did away with the requirement of assessing the financial health of a company before initiating the Corporate Insolvency Resolution Process in order to further the aim of timely disposal of cases. The Hon'ble Supreme Court in Vidarbha Industries Power Ltd. v. Axis Bank Ltd [2022] 140 taxmann.com 252, however, has reinstated this requirement in case of admitting the applications filed by the financial creditors under section 7 of the Code.

This judgment may benefit certain sectors but is likely to defeat the very purpose for which the code was brought in. The Court through this judgment made it mandatory to admit the applications filed by the Operational Creditors whereas the applications filed by the Financial Creditors may or may not be admitted depending on the discretion of the Adjudicating Authority. Thus, the judgment is also likely to distort the settled order of preference of Financial Creditors over Operational Creditors under the code and is likely to result in unnecessary delays.

The Supreme Court went with the literal interpretation of the code without taking into context and purpose of the same. This judgment is likely to cause confusion due to lack of proper guidelines and may even turn the clock to pre-IBC period.

Introduction

The Financial Creditors ("FCs") and Operational Creditors ("OCs") of a corporate debtor ("CD") are empowered under S.7 and S. 9 of Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016 ("IBC"/ "Code") respectively to file an application for initiating a Corporate Insolvency Resolution Process ("CIRP") before National Company Law Tribunal ("NCLT"). The Hon'ble Supreme Court("SC") of India in its landmark ruling of Innoventive Industries Ltd. v. ICICI Bank Ltd. [2017] 84 taxmann.com 320/143 SCL 625 (SC) pronounced that according to S.7, if the Adjudicating Authority ("AA") is satisfied with the existence of a debt and a default, and no disciplinary proceedings lie against the proposed interim resolution professional, then the AA is bound to admit the application unless the application is incomplete.

However, the SC in its recent verdict of Vidarbha Industries Power Ltd. (supra) while dealing with the issue concerning the nature of S.7(5)(a) of the IBC, conferred a discretionary power on the NCLT not to admit a CIRP application filed by a FC even if it is satisfied that a debt exists and the CD is in default. The SC observed that the legislature deliberately used the expression "may admit" in S.7(5)(a), whereas the expression "shall admit" has been used in S.9(5) in order to convey a different meaning therefore intending section S.7(5)(a) to be discretionary while S.9(5) to be mandatory.

This post, therefore, seeks to examine the Vidarbha Industries judgment in the light of the objective behind the Code, which is speedy recovery and revival of financially distressed entities. Further, it tries to analyze its impact on the IBC regime and address the legal conundrum resulting therefrom.

Judgment & Analysis: A case of inconsistent precedents

Vidarbha Industries, the CD is a power generation company operating a coal-fired thermal power plant in Maharashtra. Aggrieved with the decision of the Maharashtra Electricity Regulatory Commission ("MERC") with regard to the determination of tariff, Vidarbha industries challenged the MERC's decision before the Appellate Tribunal for Electricity ("APTEL"). The APTEL allowed the appeal and consequently Vidarbha was to receive a sum of INR 1,730 crores in terms of APTEL's order.

Subsequently, Axis Bank Limited ("ABL"), the FC filed an application before the National Company Law Tribunal ("NCLT") u/s 7(2) of the Code to initiate CIRP against Vidarbha for non-payment of its debt amounting to INR 553 crore. Vidarbha challenged the admission of CIRP on the ground that its inability to repay the dues of ABL was directly attributable to the MERC's failure to pay INR 1,730 crore on account of litigation pending before the SC against the APTEL's order. Hence, Vidarbha sought a stay of the CIRP proceedings until the question in the appeal regarding the liability of MERC to pay the said amount is resolved by the SC.

The NCLT as well as the NCLAT citing previous SC judgements rejected Vidarbha's application and held that the only two things that the Adjudicating Authority is required to consider are the 'existence of debt' and 'default in servicing the debt', and the fulfillment of both these conditions will instantly trigger corporate insolvency. Further, it was emphatically held that the reason for non-payment of the debt is immaterial to the scheme of the code.

Whether written financial contract be the only material to prove the financial debt

The submission of the respondent that the written financial contract is necessary for proving debt. A financial contract supported by financial statements as evidence of the debt is one of the documents contemplated in regulation 8(2) of the IBBI (Insolvency Resolution Process for Corporate Persons) Regulation, 2016 but that is not exclusive requirement for proving existence of debt. Financial contract, thus, can very well be furnished to prove the financial debt but a plain reading of regulation 8(2) indicate that it is not mandatory that existence of financial debt has to be proved by a financial contract. For example: records available with an information utility can very well be used as proof for existence of financial debt. Further, financial statements showing that the debt has not been paid is also one of the clauses in regulation 8(2) by which existence of debt can be proved. [Para 11]

The Financial Creditor has failed to establish that the transaction in question is a Financial Debt and due and payable and the Corporate Debtor has committed default. The judgment Pawan Kumar v. Utsav Securities (P.) Ltd. [2021] 131 taxmann.com 211/168 SCL 692 (NCLAT - New Delhi), cannot be relied as laying down any preposition that unless there is Financial Contract to establish financial debt, Financial Creditor cannot prove the financial debt by any other document. [Para 15]

When one looks into the statutory scheme as reflected in the application to Adjudicating Authority Rules, 2016 and CIRP Regulations, 2016, it is clear that financial debt can be proved from other relevant documents and it is not mandatory that written financial contract can be only basis for proving the financial debt. Thus, it is not necessary that written financial contract be the only material to prove the financial debt. [Para 21]

Analyzing the Order passed by the NCLT relying upon the decision of CoC

In the instant Appeal, Rajnish Jain ('the Appellant') is seeking a declaration that 'BVN Traders' is not a 'Financial Creditors.' As per Section 5(7) of the Code, only such Creditor could be the 'Financial Creditor' of the 'Corporate Debtor' to whom a financial debt is owed by the 'Corporate Debtor,' and as per Section 5(8) of the Code, the critical requirement of the financial debt is disbursal against the 'Consideration for the time value of money'. The reliance was put on the judgments Pioneer Urban Land & Infrastructure Ltd. v. Union of India5, Swiss Ribbons Ltd.6 etc.

In the present case the record shows that the Appellant Company is a borrower, and the loan amount was directly disbursed to Appellant's Company for which the title deed was deposited with the BVN Traders. In the said transaction time value of money is unambiguously involved, and the Appellant Company's liability is regarding the debt owed by it. It is reiterated that the Appellant Company had raised the said amount from the BVN Traders to meet its working Capital Requirement. Hence the BVN Traders is a Financial Creditor within the meaning of Sections 5(7) and 5(8) of the Code. The transaction involved in the present case meets the root ingredients/basic element of 'financial debt' within the meaning of the Code.

Thus, the tribunal held that the Order of the NCLT dated 23rd Jan, 2020 is correct and needs no interference. However, it set aside the reasoning, relying on the decision of CoC for holding BVN Traders as Financial Creditor.

Blurring the Lines between Financial Creditor and Operational Creditor In order to qualify as a financial creditor under section 5(8) of the IBC, one should be owed a financial debt6 which includes two conditions, firstly, there should be a debt along with interest, if any, which is disbursed against the consideration for the time value of money,7 and secondly, it should be included in one of the specified categories.8 Moreover, a financial creditor must prove that a default has occurred, which takes place when a debt becomes due and payable as per the proof of claims submitted by the creditor.9 Since a claim/payment is flexible enough to include "recompense",10 an operational creditor who has suffered any harm or has to be compensated will become the stakeholder of the insolvencyprocess.11 With respect to the first requirement, any debt, with or without interest is covered under the scope of Section 5(7) of the code. The time value of money requirement, according to which any money we have right now is worth more than the identical sum in future, due to its potential earning capacity12 is present in any kind of transaction. The Court in the case of DF Deutsche Forfait AG v. Uttam Galva Steel Ltd.13 held that if a party fails to repay within the fixed time, then interest can be claimed over operational debt as well, and it is nowhere said that the operational creditor is barred from claiming interest. Therefore, since the premise of claim is based on whether the "X" has taken something from "Y' with an intention to pay back the value, then the law should be applied in a manner to ensure that it is repaid but not dismissed on the ground of procedural irregularities. We need not stick to the ground that procedural justice is always subservient to substantial justice.14

With respect to the second prong, the authors believe that such an operational creditor is at par with home buyers. It is submitted that since Section 5(8)(f) of the IBC uses the words 'any amount' and 'any other transaction', it means that the amounts that are "raised under transactions and not covered by any of the other clauses", would amount to a financial debt if they had the commercial effect of borrowing, making it a 'catch-all provision'.15 Section 3(33) of the IBC defines a 'transaction' as an agreement or arrangement in writing for the transfer of assets, or funds, goods or services, from or to the corporate debtor. Furthermore, the expression "borrow" means to obtain or receive something, on loan for temporary use, intending to give it, or something equivalent back to the lender.16 A perusal of these definitions shows that the expression borrow is wide enough to include an advance given by operational creditors in the form of their services, workmen/employees in the present case when the payment for the same was neglected by a company to keep its operations afloat. This implies that the same amount was borrowed for 'temporary use' i.e. for honouring their commitments and paying back other creditors as long as they intended to give 'something equivalent' back to the operational creditors. Additionally, the commercial aspect, which means transactions having profit as its main aim is present in such a situation of employees who have not been paid, since the company wants to keep its operations afloat by temporarily borrowing the requisite amount from operational creditors, and the operational creditors demanding interest due to delay in payments.17 Additionally, the proof of claim as per the IBBI (Insolvency Resolution Process for Corporate Persons) Regulations, 2016 can be proved by any contractual document indicating that the amount is due in case of employees or through muster rolls in case of workmen.18 It therefore follows that the employees/workmen in such a situation will be considered as a financial creditor at par with home buyers as per Pioneer since they qualify all the parameters based on which the home buyers have been considered as a financial creditor. Therefore, treating them differently will lead to gross violation of principles of natural justice.19

The Trial Court may be wrong in holding that the TDS certificate by itself constitutes an admission of liability. This is not so, inasmuch as the TDS can be deducted even on the expectation of estimated liability. Independently of the TDS certificate, the liability of the Defendant is quite clear. The Supreme Court in CIT v. Gujarat Fluoro Chemicals [2012] 13 SCC 731 categorically held that "both advance tax as well as TDS are based on estimation of income by the assessee." The Bombay High Court as well, in S.P. Brothers v. Biren Ramesh Kadakla [2009] 1 Bom CR 453 has held that "the issuance of TDS certificates does not amount to an acknowledgement of defendant within the meaning of section 25 of the Indian Evidence Act...... The TDS certificate is primarily to acknowledge the deduction of tax at source." The judgment dated 27th November, 2012 in Bigdot Advertising & Communications (P.) Ltd. v. Union of India [CS(OS) No. 226/2000] was dealing with the question of the person who is liable once the TDS certificate is issued. It is not a precedent on the proposition that if a TDS certificate is issued, it amounts to admission of liability. In light of this, though the deduction of TDS by itself cannot be sufficient to impose liability, but on a totality of facts it is clear that the defendant is liable."

Is interest-free loan received liable to be treated as sum of money received without consideration?

The consideration in an interest-free loan is to return the money. The detriment suffered by lender in parting with use of funds is valid consideration to support promise of repayment of the loan by the borrower. This view is supported by the following observations of the Hon'ble Delhi High Court in CIT v. Mridu Hari Dalmia [1982] 8 Taxman 138/133 ITR 550 :

'A transaction of a loan implies an agreement to repay the money that is borrowed. Shri Harihar Lal cited a definition of 'loan' from Corpus Juris Secundum (Vol. 54, p. 654). According to this passage a loan of money is defined as 'a contract by which one delivers a sum of money to another and the latter agrees to return at a future time a sum equivalent to that which he borrows'; and again as the delivery by one party and the receipt by the other party of a given sum of money on an agreement, express or implied, to repay the sum lent with or without interest. These definitions can be accepted, succinctly summarising or analysing the ingredients of a loan. They are in line with the definitions enunciated by our Supreme Court (vide K.M.S. Lakshmanier & Sons v. CIT [1953] 23 ITR 202, Badridas Daga v. CIT [1958] 34 ITR 10 and other cases). They make it clear that a loan, involves an enforceable agreement between two parties, one of whom is the lender and the other the borrower. The former lends monies to the latter. The latter receives the sum and promises to repay it by an equivalent amount at a future date with or without interest. . . .'

In Chandrakant H. Shah v. ITO [2009] 28 SOT 315 (Mum.), the Tribunal held that 'consideration for a promise may consist of either some benefit conferred on the promisor or detriment suffered by the promisee or both, hence, on this criteria the assessee has gained by way of interest-free loan and the lenders have suffered by or giving interest-free loans and such suffering has got some value and, therefore, the said transaction cannot be said to be without consideration'.

In view of the above, interest free loan cannot be said to be sum of money received without consideration and is not taxable u/s 56(2)(x)(a).

The corporate debtor, with an intention of setting up a project for the manufacture of flexible packaging material under co-extension process at an estimated cost of Rs.30 crores, had approached Canara Bank for financial assistance. While the said bank sanctioned a term loan of Rs.14.2 crores for construction of the building and purchase of plant and machinery, the promoters of corporate debtor were required to meet the condition of investing the margin money. Accordingly, all six promoters, including the financial creditor, had given interest free unsecured loan to the corporate debtor.

The financial creditor alleged that the corporate debtor failed to take any steps to liquidate or reduce the liability qua him despite various reminders. Thus, he issued demand notice under section 8. In response to the said notice, corporate debtor submitted that the amount being claimed was not a loan in terms of financial debt, nor was there any agreement to pay interest thereon. It was not to be repaid on demand as it was the basis of procuring financial assistance from their bank for establishing the corporate debtor for its working capital. The financial creditor was an equity holder and with a view to set up a plant, all shareholders had paid various amounts as the margin money to enable them to get the loan facility from Canara bank.

All Promoters including the Financial Creditor herein, have confirmed the Subordination Agreement with their Bank, for and on behalf of the Corporate Debtor, and have undertaken that the unsecured creditors had extended or continued to extend interest free unsecured loan on the express understanding that all their claims against the respondent company would be subject to the claims of Canara Bank; that all the claims of the unsecured creditors against the respondent company would at all times be subordinate and be subject to any claims of Canara Bank; that unsecured creditors agree not to sue the respondent company for recovering any money tendered to the respondent company as unsecured loan until all the claims of Canara Bank get settled; that the unsecured creditors agree not to join in any bankruptcy or any assignment.

It is therefore submitted by the respondent that since the unsecured loans were interest-free, no interest was promised. Further, it is stated that the transaction inter se the parties does not fall within the definition of financial debt nor is the financial creditor a person to whom a financial debt is owed. [Para 8]

In view of the facts and circumstances of the case, the present claim does not fall within the definition of a financial debt nor is it an unsecured loan repayable on demand. There is not Demand Promissory Note executed, nor is there any agreement for payment of any interest. As submitted by the corporate debtor and not denied by the operational creditor, the amount given by him along with 6 others was for promoting and setting up a business. The terms for raising the bank loan necessitated investment of the margin money. This was done by all the promoters and is reflected as unsecured loans, subordinate to the claim of the bank. The bank agreement corroborating this is on record.

Though it is admitted by the financial creditor that this unsecured loan would be subordinate to the claim made by the Canara Bank, it appears that notwithstanding his agreement not to seek recovery of his unsecured loan till the liability of Canara Bank stands extinguished or his undertaking not to participate in Insolvency proceedings, it is his wish and desire that the resolution process be initiated and the entire project be dumped before it comes into operation, irrespective of whether he can realise any proceeds or not in the watershed for repayment should the assets of the corporate debtor be liquidated. It is being noted that Canara Bank is not an aggrieved party. [Para 9]

The said attitude of the financial creditor is irreprehensible as the principal money lender i.e., Canara Bank has not made any claim. Insolvency Resolution Process of a corporate entity cannot be initiated on such grounds which reek of personal vendetta. The financial creditor seeks to scuttle the project even before it get into operation. Such arm twisting tactics cannot be the basis for initiation of Insolvency Process. [Para 10]

The petition is, therefore, rejected. [Para 11]

From the agreement/Memorandum of Understanding it was clear that appellants were 'investors' and had chosen 'committed return plan'. The respondent in their turn agreed upon to pay monthly committed return to investors. Thus, the amount due to the appellants came within the meaning of 'debt' as defined in section 3(11). From the 'Annual Return' of the respondent it was found that the 'Corporate Debtor' treated the appellants as 'investors' and borrowed the amount pursuant to sale purchase agreement for their commercial purpose treating at par with 'loan' in their return. Thereby, the amount invested by appellants came within the meaning of 'financial debt', as defined in section 5(8)(f) subject to satisfaction as to whether such disbursement against the consideration was for time value of money.

Thus, the Adjudicating Authority had rightly highlighted the opening word of the definition clause which indicate that a 'financial debt' is a debt along with interest which is disbursed against the consideration for the time value of money and may include any of the events enumerated in sub-clauses (a) to (i). Therefore, it was to be seen whether the amount paid by the appellants to the corporate debtor fulfilled the other condition of 'disbursement against consideration of time value and money' to come within the definition of 'financial creditor' having satisfied that the corporate debtor raised the amount through a transaction of sale and purchase of agreement having commercial effect of a borrowing [section 5(8)(f)].

The agreement showed that the respondent agreed to complete the construction of shopping mall on or before December, 2009, in all respects, and was required to complete and handover the shop in the shopping mall before the said date. It was not the case of the respondent that the construction was stopped or delayed on account of factors beyond the control of the respondent, as stipulated in the later part of the Memorandum of Understanding. It was agreed upon by the respondent that since the appellants had paid most of the amount the respondent was ready to pay 'monthly committed returns' to the appellants. However, as the appellants were not required the monthly return till December, 2008 i.e. for 9 months so the respondent-Corporate Debtor undertook to make a consolidated payment of Rs. 99,600 less TDS for every calendar month. The corporate debtor was liable to pay committed return with effect from January, 2009 till the date of handing over of the possession to the appellants. Therefore, it was clear that the amount disbursed by the appellants was 'against the consideration of time value of the money' and the respondent corporate debtor raised the amount by way of sale-purchase agreement, having a commercial effect or borrowing. This was also clear from annual returns filed by respondent and not disputed by the respondent-corporate debtor in their annual returns, wherein the amount so raised/borrowed had been shown as 'commitment charges' under the head 'financial cost'. The financial cost included 'Interest on loans' and other charges. Therefore, the 'commitment charge', which included interest on loan, shown against the head 'financial cost' having been accepted by the corporate debtor in their annual return, the appellants successfully proved that they were 'financial creditor' within the meaning of section 5(7). Therefore, the application for initiating CIRP was to be admitted.

Nikhil Mehta & Sons (HUF) (supra): The NCLAT in the present case elaborately dealt with the question as to who is an FC and consequently upheld the decision of the AA on the said point which provides that the FC is a person to whom a financial debt is owed. It further went on to elaborate the phrase "time value of money" and referred to the Black's Law Dictionary which provides that it is the "price which is associated with the length of time that an investor has to wait until an investment matures or related income is earned". Hence, the investment and outcome are separated by time and the compensation for such time is the time value of money.

IBC : Where appellant-financial creditor filed a section 7 application against corporate debtor on basis of a Deed of Assignment, where sum given to corporate debtor by IIL was transferred to appellant, however, said sum was clearly shown as a trade receivable rather than a loan and there was no contract or agreement between corporate debtor and IIL designating sum given as a loan, NCLT did not commit any error in rejecting section 7 application filed by appellant against corporate debtor

Section 5(8), read with section 7, of the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016 - Corporate insolvency resolution process - Financial debt - Appellant-financial creditor advanced loan of Rs. 1 crore to respondent, a real estate company for construction of a project 'Madina Heights' - Respondent assured to repay loan with interest @ 18 per cent per annum besides offering 15 per cent share in profit of project - However, respondent failed to repay loan - Appellant issued demand notice - Since payments were still not forthcoming from respondent, appellant filed a section 7 petition seeking admission of respondent into corporate insolvency resolution process which was rejected by Adjudicating Authority as non-maintainable - It was an admitted fact that there was no written contract or agreement between appellant and respondent governing terms and conditions by which sum was advanced by appellant and disbursed to account of respondent - Whether since appellant had failed to muster clinching proof and evidence in terms of financial records to show that sum advanced by them was indisputably interest-bearing and that interest had continued to accrue and was being realized as consideration for time value of money, sum advanced by appellant to respondent did not satisfy ingredients of financial debt of disbursal, time value of money and commercial effect of borrowing - Held, yes - Whether further said project was still in progress and compliances, both procedural and regulatory, were still pending and hence no occasion for default could be said to have occurred as debt was not due or payable - Held, yes - Whether thus, debt and default not having been clearly established, there was no infirmity in impugned order rejecting Section 7 application - Held, yes [Paras 21, 25, 26 and 27]

The plea of the appellants, that no record of default, from information utility, was filed by the financial creditor, the instant Tribunal, poignantly points out that the ingredients of section 7(3)(a), latently and patently specify that the financial creditor, is required to furnish the record of default, recorded with an information utility or such other record or evidence of default. Viewed in that perspective, the contra plea taken on behalf of the appellants, is not acceded to, by the instant Tribunal. [Para 62]

In the instant case, it transpires that the financial creditor, had issued a letter dated 17-11-2021, to all the board of directors of the corporate debtor, stating that he had infused funds, into the company, for the past few years, and these monies were brought in as unsecured loans, to save the company, from its repayment obligations, and also meet the obligations, towards one-time settlement, entered into the SBI bank, and further he had infused funds, to meet the operational losses of the company, at various times. [Para 63]

Added further, the financial creditor, had averred in the said letter dated 17-11-2021 that the company, makes arrangement to compensate him for the monies brought in at various times and suggested that the company may allot equity shares, in the corporate debtor at valuation, as per I.T. Rules, in lieu of repayment of unsecured loans, brought in by him, and the same may be converted into equity shares, within 30 days of this notice serving date, by passing the necessary resolutions, in the board. [Para 64]

In the instant case, the sum of Rs. 13.84 crores infused by the financial creditor, is to be repaid to him, and section 5(8), defines financial debt, meaning a debt, along with Interest, if any, which is disbursed against the consideration for the time value of money, and by commercial practice, any loan, long-term or otherwise, in the absence of any agreement for repayment, falls due and payable on demand, made by the creditor, in the considered opinion of the instant Tribunal. [Para 65]

As regards to notice/letter, dated 17-11-2021, issued by the financial creditor, to all the directors of the corporate debtor, there was no reply, from the appellants, and there is non-payment of debt, by the appellants, and they have committed default, coming within the purview of section 3(12), as held by the instant Tribunal. [Para 66]

There is no embargo in law, for a director of a company, to infuse the funds, into the company, with a view to rescue a company from financial distress/crisis, and the monies advanced clearly come within the umbrage of section 5(8). [Para 67]

In the instant case on hand, the financial creditor, in its application, under section 7, is to prove the existence of debt, which is due from the corporate debtor. No doubt, the corporate debtor or its directors, can point out that the debt, is not payable, by the corporate debtor, in law, and also in fact. [Para 68]

In a section 7 application an Adjudicating Authority, is not required to go into the claim or counter claim, made by the parties, except to find out, whether or not, record is complete, and whether or not, there is debt and default, committed by the corporate debtor. [Para 69]

In law, an application, under section 7, deserves to be admitted, where the sum, is more than Rs. 1 lakh (now Rs. 1 crore) and default of the corporate debtor, was established. [Para 70]

It cannot be gainsaid that a financial debt, is to be understood to include interest free loans, given to a company/entity, for its business purpose/operations, as the case may be. [Para 71]

One cannot ignore a vital fact that the auditor of the corporate debtor, had issued a certificate, dated 8-5-2022, stating that an unsecured loan, was shown, in the balance sheet of the corporate debtor, as on 31-3-2021, which was advanced, by the financial creditor. [Para 72]

It is brought to the fore on behalf of the financial creditor, that a sum of Rs. 3.97 crores, was advanced to the corporate debtor, by the financial creditor, and the same was used by the corporate debtor, to repay the loans, taken by the corporate debtor, from the SBI bank, under the one-time settlement scheme, provided by the bank, to save the corporate debtor, from distress. [Para 73]

HELD: Whether amount paid by the financial creditor to the account of the corporate debtor is a 'Financial debt'

The agreement dated 21-10-2017 which was entered between the directors of the financial creditor and the directors of the corporate debtor noted that the appellant is committed to return the principal amount of USD 1.5 million and Rs. 3.5 crores. [Para 12]

The agreement relied by both the parties unequivocally contains the acknowledgement of corporate debtor towards liability to refund the amount of Rs. 3.5 crores to the financial creditor and the agreement mentions the mechanism to return the amount. The agreement also mentions giving an IDBI cheque of Rs. 3.5 crores to the financial creditor which raise clear presumption of owing debt by the corporate debtor to the financial creditor. The agreement between the parties makes it clear that the corporate debtor has acknowledged the liability to refund aforesaid amount of Rs. 3.5 crores. The acknowledgement to refund the amount of Rs. 3.5 crores also proves that amount of Rs. 3.5 crores was a financial debt. [Para 13]

It was further noted that the e-mail dated 12-3-2018 which has been issued by the appellant - director of the corporate debtor to director of the financial creditor acknowledge payment of USD 1.5 million as well as Rs. 3.5 crores (0.5 million USD). [Para 14]

Further an e-mail dated 28-5-2018 written by the director of the corporate debtor was also part of section 7 application and was also relied by the Adjudicating Authority. [Para 15]

The e-mail also mentions that amount of Rs. 3.5 crores was a 'short term loan' given to corporate debtor by the financial creditor. In the e-mail director also conceded that maximum interest which can be considered is only 12 per cent. [Para 16]

Subsequently, financial creditor issued a legal notice and filed a section 7 application against corporate debtor before NCLT, which was rejected by NCLT on ground that debt and default did not exist - Whether since assigned amount had been clearly shown as trade receivable in Deed of Assignment, it could not be viewed as a loan particularly when there was no contract/agreement between corporate debtor and IIL recording advance of any loan - Held, yes - Whether there was nothing placed on record by appellant to substantiate that disbursement had been made for consideration for time value of money and, thus, NCLT did not commit any error in rejecting section 7 application filed by appellant - Held, yes [Paras 14, 25 and 26]IBC : Where appellant-financial creditor filed a section 7 application against corporate debtor on basis of a Deed of Assignment, where sum given to corporate debtor by IIL was transferred to appellant, however, said sum was clearly shown as a trade receivable rather than a loan and there was no contract or agreement between corporate debtor and IIL designating sum given as a loan, NCLT did not commit any error in rejecting section 7 application filed by appellant against corporate debtor

tor, since in the last audited balance sheet for the financial year ending 31.03.2017, available at the commencement of CIRP, the said amount is reflected only under the head "Other Advances" and not as a loan, as alleged. Even in the audited balance sheet of the Applicant as uploaded on the MCA portal, no loan advanced to the Corporate Debtor is reflected and, on the contrary, the same has been shown as "Trade Receivables." 34. We have already reproduced the balance sheet of the Corporate Debtor for FY 2016-17 at para 17 above. When we look at the above audited financial statement for FY 2016-2017 of the Corporate Debtor, we find that the Notes forming part of the balance sheet of the Corporate Debtor as on 31.03.2017 provides separate categories for "Long Term Borrowings" under Note 3 and "Other Long Term Liabilities" under Note 4. The audited balance sheet of the Corporate Debtor also classifies the amount claimed by the Appellant to be a loan to figure under the head of 'Other Advances' which does not denote any financial liability or loan obligation. Moreover, there being no record of TDS deduction reflected in the financial records in respect of the Corporate Debtor, there is no provision of interest. It is also clear therefrom that Rs 30,95,000/-appearing against the name of the Appellant company appears in the head of 'Other Advances' rather than as an unsecured loan as claimed by the Appellant. However, we find that the sum appears under the sub-category of "Other Advances" under the category of "Other Long Term Liabilities". It is clear from the above categorisation that the sum was provided as an advance and was treated as a liability and not a borrowing in the balance sheet and therefore does not partake the character of financial debt. Hence the transaction was not in the nature of a financial debt and could not have been claimed in Form-C. We therefore do not find any infirmity in the finding recorded by the Adjudicating Authority that the claim filed by the Appellant does not find support in the books of the Corporate Debtor as a loan.

35. We also notice that not only was the amount of Rs 30.95 lakh never treated or acknowledged as a loan in the books of the Corporate Debtor, but this amount was never ever demanded by the Appellant from the Corporate Debtor during the last 15 years since the time the amount was advanced. There is no material placed on record evidencing any communication sent to the Corporate Debtor seeking payment of interest. The records of the Corporate Debtor also do not reflect any provision for interest on the said loan having been credited to the account of the Corporate Debtor. Nor is there any proof for accrual of interest in any F.Y or any evidence of TDS deduction such as Form 26AS. While we have already held at para 22 above that it is a well settled precept that in the judgment of Hon'ble Supreme Court in Orator judgement supra, it has been clearly held that financial debt does not expressly exclude an interest free loan and also includes any sum raised under any other transaction having the commercial effect of borrowing even it does not carry an interest component. Nevertheless, we also cannot be unmindful of the fact that the Appellant in the present case has not demonstrated any efforts made by it to recover the loan amount since 2007. There is no material on record to show that any notice or any demand was raised either for repayment of the purported loan. It was equally unusual that for a loan given way back in 2007, there was no demand of repayment made by the Appellant for 15 long years until the Corporate Debtor got admitted into CIRP. To our minds, the Adjudicating Authority has also rightly taken note of the masterly inactivity on the part of the Appellant to recover their dues. The inordinate and unexplained delay in raising the demand until the Corporate Debtor was admitted into rigours of CIRP does cast doubts on the legitimacy and bonafide of the alleged transaction as a whole irrespective of the interest component.

36. In this backdrop, we find substance in the contention raised by the Respondents that the claim filed by the Appellant was not bonafide and hence the rejection of the claims filed by the Appellant company by the Adjudicating Authority is sustainable in the eyes of law.

37. In view of the foregoing discussion, we do not find any infirmity in the impugned orders dismissing I.A. Nos. 3020 of 2022 and 1950 of 2023. The impugned orders do not warrant any interference. Both Appeals being devoid of merit are dismissed. No costs.

The respondent, a money lender, advanced loans of about Rs. 2.50 crores (interest 12.75% p.a., payable half-yearly) and Rs. 2 crores (interest 3% per month, payable half-yearly) to the appellant in 2010. After cheque dishonour and a 2013 compromise, the appellant had paid about Rs. 3.53 crores by July 2014. The respondent filed a summary suit in 2016 for about Rs. 4.38 crores; a second compromise in 2016 recorded a full and final settlement figure of about Rs. 2.39 crores. On 11.01.2018, the Delhi High Court decreed about Rs. 4.38 crores with 24% p.a. interest from 01.02.2016, after deducting Rs. 25 lakhs and awarding costs of Rs. 5 lakhs. The appeal was dismissed in 2018 and the SLP was dismissed in 2021, rendering the decree final.

■

On 13.12.2021, instead of pursuing execution of the money decree, the respondent filed a Section 7 application under the IBC before the NCLT alleging default of the decretal amount as a financial debt. On 20.06.2022, the NCLT dismissed the petition, recording that a decree holder under Section 3(10) is a distinct class and does not automatically become a financial creditor, that the debt did not qualify as a financial debt under Section 5(8), that the appellant was a solvent, functioning company (revenue about Rs. 35 crores, profits about Rs. 8 crores, 95 employees), and that the IBC is not a recovery mechanism and was being misused as the claim rested on the civil decree rather than the underlying loans.

■

On 01.11.2022, the NCLAT set aside the NCLT’s order and directed admission of the Section 7 petition, holding that the loan agreements stipulated interest and repayment periods satisfying the time value of money under Section 5(8), and relying on the proposition that a money decree can furnish a fresh cause of action for a Section 7 filing; it rejected the appellant’s fraud plea against the decree. Meanwhile, the appellant moved the Delhi High Court by I.A. No. 17634 of 2022 under Section 151 CPC for redetermination of the decretal dues, asserting uncredited payments and inconsistent stands. The High Court directed the respondent to file a computation after crediting all payments and directed the appellant to deposit Rs. 3 crores plus costs; Rs. 3 crores was deposited on 02.11.2022. Separately, for AY 2012-13, the tax authorities raised a demand on interest income in the respondent’s hands premised on TDS of about Rs. 9.23 lakhs on interest of about Rs. 92.29 lakhs deposited by the appellant; the CIT(A) dismissed the respondent’s appeal in 2020. In ITAT proceedings decided on 01.09.2022, the respondent placed a computation showing only about Rs. 96.48 lakhs outstanding as on 31.03.2012 after accounting for disbursals, repayments and adjustments, which conflicted with higher claims; the I.A. remains pending.

are relevant:

(a)

The term "loan" generally refers to borrowing something, especially a sum of cash that is to be paid back along with interest decided mutually by the parties. In other terms, the debtor is under a liability to pay back the principal amount along with the agreed rate of interest within a stipulated time [CIT v. Mahindra and Mahindra Ltd. [2018] 93 taxmann.com 32/255 Taxman 305 (SC)];

(b) The expression 'loan', though not defined under the Act, has a well-settled connotation, i.e., advancing of money by one person to another under an agreement by which the recipient of the money agrees to repay the amount on such agreed terms with regard to the time of repayment and the liability to pay interest. The person advancing the money is generally called a creditor, and the person receiving the money is generally called a borrower. The most simple form of a loan transaction is a contract by which the borrower agrees to repay the amount borrowed on demand by the creditor with such interest as stipulated under the agreement. Such a loan transaction may be attended by any security arrangement, a mortgage or pledge etc., depending upon the agreement of the parties[Keshavlal Khemchand And Sons (P.) Ltd. v. UOI [2015] 53 taxmann.com 470 (SC)/4 SCC 770];

(c)

If A pays money to B, who agrees to return not the identical currency in specie but an equivalent sum subsequently, no bailment arises but simply a loan owing by B to A. The fact that it is called a "deposit" can make no difference [K.M.S. Lakshmanier and Sons v. CIT and CEPT [1953] 23 ITR 202 (SC)];

(d)

A loan imports a positive act of lending coupled with an acceptance by the other side of the money as a loan. The relationship between borrower and lender cannot ordinarily come about by mere inaction. At the bottom, this is a question of fact. Of course, money so left could, by a proper agreement between the parties, be converted into a loan, but in the absence of an agreement, mere inaction on the part of the managing agents cannot convert the money due to them, and not withdrawn, into a loan[Shree Ram Mills Ltd. v. CEPT [1953] 23 ITR 120 (SC)];

(e)

A loan can be with interest or without interest because no condition exists in law of contract that a loan can be with interest only[Chandrakant H. Shah v. ITO [2009] 28 SOT 315/[2010] 3 ITR (Trib.) 398/124 ITD 177 (Mum. - Trib.)].

The following points flow as corollaries from the above judicial decisions:

(a)

Two parties: Loan involves two parties - the lender/creditor and borrower [seepara 8.1-11a];

(b)

Money is taken with Obligation to return: Loan involves taking money from another person lender under a contract whereby the person taking the loan (borrower/debtor/loanee) promises to repay the loan [seepara 8.1-11b];

(c)

Unpaid purchase price is not a loan: Where there has been no transaction of taking a loan but purchase of goods or property, the deferring or giving more time for payment by the vendor does not convert the unpaid purchase price into a loan [seepara 8.1-11c];

(d)

Loan may be interest-free: Loan may be interest-bearing or interest-free. If ingredients in (a) and (b) above are there, the loan does not cease to be so merely because it is to be repaid without any interest.

8.1-11a Two parties essential to a loan - The following judicial decisions are noteworthy in this regard:

(a)

For a transaction to be considered as a loan, two different persons are required. A contract of loan requires two persons. There cannot be a loan by the same person to himself merely because he functions in two different capacities [Mohan Lal Shyam Lal, In re [1942] 10 ITR 219 (All.), CIT v. Mridu Hari Dalmia [1982] 8 Taxman 138/133 ITR 550/27 CTR 20 (Delhi)].

(b)

Amount invested by the proprietor in his proprietorship concern is not a loan. Under no circumstances can a person borrow from himself and transpose as 'creditor' and 'borrower' at the same time. To this extent, 'proprietor' and 'proprietorship concern' are not two different entities. Whatever is pumped in by the 'proprietor' to his proprietorship, is nothing other than investment. The proprietorship concern could have borrowed any amount to be categorised as a 'loan', only if it was procured from some other source, then himself/the proprietor [CIT v. K. V. FACT: ■

The respondent/corporate debtor had undertaken to construct a project and for this purpose had approached the appellant for advancing a sum of Rs. 1 crore. The corporate debtor had purportedly assured to repay the advance with interest at the rate of 18 per cent per annum besides offering 15 per cent share in the profit of the project. The amount of Rs. 1 crore was given by appellant to the corporate debtor.

■

Though the corporate debtor was to repay the outstanding loan on completion of the project, they did not release payments to appellant as per the terms even though the project was purportedly completed. Appellant issued a Demand Notice claiming repayment of the outstanding amount from the corporate debtor.

■

Since payments were still not forthcoming from the corporate debtor, the appellant filed a section 7 petition seeking the admission of the corporate debtor into corporate insolvency resolution proceedings which was rejected by the Adjudicating Authority as non-maintainable.

■

On appeal:

HELD: ■

The corporate debtor was a family company that struggled financially and was indebted to various banks/financial institutions and there was no access to funds.

On request of other directors and to bail out the corporate debtor, the respondent No.-1 financial creditor, had lent a sum of Rs. 9.15 crores from time to time as financial loans.

The financial creditor also issued a loan of Rs. 13.84 crores and was entitled to interest at 14 per cent per annum.

Thereafter, the corporate debtor, was requested by financial creditor, to return amount, without any success, a letter dated 17-11-2021 was issued to corporate debtor in which it was stated that he had infused funds, into the company, for the past few years, and those monies were brought in as unsecured loans, to save the company, from its repayment obligations.

However, no reply was received from the corporate debtor, on default in making payment, the petition under section 7 was filed by the financial creditor against the corporate debtor.

The corporate debtor alleged that the financial debt of Rs. 13.84 crores without any basis and, it was the duty of the financial creditor to annex all material documents along with the Form I in order to substantiate its debt.

The corporate debtor further alleged that section 7 casts an obligation on the financial creditor to furnish the record of default and, the corporate debtor had three shareholders, who were also directors of the corporate debtor and, thus it was not out of place to state that the said shareholder directors were own brothers.

The NCLT admitted said petition under section 7 and, declared moratorium under section 14.

The appellant, shareholders and suspended director of the corporate debtor filed instant appeal on ground that impugned order passed by NCLT in admitting the section 7 application was per se an illegal and an invalid one, because of the fact that there was no privity of contract, between the corporate debtor and the financial creditor appellant. The appellant further alleged that there was no agreement or document, proving loan, was taken by the corporate debtor, from the financial creditor.

5. In a recent decision dated 21st July 2017, by the National Company Law Appellate Tribunal in Nikhil Mehta & Sons v. AMR Infrastructure Ltd. [2017] 84 taxmann.com 163 (NCLT - New Delhi), the Hon'ble Appellate Tribunal noted that pursuant to the Memorandum of Understanding dated 12th April 2008, reached between the appellant and the respondent-corporate debtor, in respect of booking and payment of Rs. 36,00,000/- for a commercial shop which was being developed by the respondent-corporate debtor, the debtor had treated the appellant as an investor and had agreed to a payment of a monthly 'Committed Interest/Return Plan'. The Hon'ble Appellate Tribunal also noted that from the annual return of the corporate-debtor and Form 16A with regard to tax deducted at source from the said returns under the "Committed Interest/Return Plan", the corporate-debtor had treated the appellant as an "investor" and borrowed the amount pursuant to sale/purchase agreement for their commercial purpose, treating it at par with "loan" in their return. Thereby, the amount invested by the appellant came within the meaning of "financial debt" as defined under section 5(8)(f) of the I&B Code 2016. It was further noted by the NCLAT that the amount disbursed by the appellant was "against the consideration of the time-value of the money" and that the respondent-corporate-debtor raised the amount by way of a sale/purchase agreement having a commercial effect of borrowing. Therefore, the NCLAT held that the respondent-corporate-debtor had treated the amount so raised/borrowed as commitment charges under the head "financial cost". Thus, the NCLAT held the appellant as a "financial creditor" within the meaning of section 5(7) of the I&B Code 2016, and remitted the case back to the adjudicating authority for further proceedings under section 7 of the I&B Code 2016, provided the appellant's application was otherwise complete in all respects.

Thus, the aforesaid NCLAT decision of Nikhil Mehta & Sons case (supra) makes a distinction between flat-buyers who had booked and paid money to the builder/corporate debtor for purchasing a flat on one hand and those flat-buyers who made payments for flats under a "Committed Monthly Return Plan" agreed to by the builder/corporate-debtor on the other hand, as such latter category of flat-buyers would be classified as "financial creditors" and would be entitled to maintain insolvency proceedings against the concerned builder/corporate-debtor under section 7 of the I&B Code 2016.

8.1-11c Unpaid/deferred purchase price is not a 'loan' - The following judicial decisions are noteworthy:

(a) An agreement to pay the balance of consideration due by the purchaser does not give rise to a loan. A loan of money undoubtedly results in a debt, but every debt does not involve a loan. Liability to pay a debt may arise from diverse sources, and a loan is only one of such sources. Every creditor who is entitled to receive a debt cannot be regarded as a lender [Bombay Steam Navigation Co. (P.) Ltd. v. CIT [1965] 56 ITR 52 (SC)].

(b)

A loan is defined by the Oxford English Dictionary as 'a thing lent; something the use of which is allowed for a time, on the understanding that it shall be returned or an equivalent given; esp., a sum of money lent on these conditions and usually with interest'. The essential requirement of a loan is the advance of money (or of some article) upon the understanding that it shall be returned, and it may or may not carry interest. The debt here arose not out of an advance but out of the sale of the flat by the company to the seventh petitioner. The company gave to the seventh petitioner time to pay a part of the purchase price. The seventh petitioner was, thus, given financial accommodation by the company in the matter of payment of the debt. Such financial accommodation was not and did not amount to a loan [Dr. Fredie Ardeshir Mehta v. Union of India [1991] 70 Comp. Cas. 210 (Bom.)].

(c)

The legislative has, for reasons of policy, thought it fit not to define the term "loan" in an inelastic or rigid manner, and in every case, we have got to look to the substance or the essential nature of the transaction for the purpose of determining as to whether or not it is a "loan" within the meaning of the Act. If a vendor of property feeling unable to rely on the personal credit of the purchaser merely takes a bond or security from him in respect of unpaid purchase money the transaction by itself cannot rank as a loan because there is no element of advance involved in it [Kunja Behari Pal v. Satyendra Nath, AIR 1941 Cal 689 cited in Radha Kisen Chamria v. Keshardeo Chamria, AIR 1954 Cal 105].

(d)

The amount of the unpaid price (of plant & machinery supplied by a non-resident) cannot be said to be a loan advanced by the non-resident to the buyer, nor can be the non-resident be said to be a lender to the buyer so far as that amount was concerned [CIT v. Saurashtra Cement & Chemical Industries Ltd. [1975] 101 ITR 502 (Guj.)].

(e)

Amount payable to electricity company in respect of electricity charges is not a loan from the electricity company [Ashiana Paper Mills Pvt. Ltd. v. Punjab State Electricity Board, AIR 2008 P&H 119].

(f)

Provisions of section 68 are not attracted to amount representing purchases made on credits - Principal CIT v. Kulwinder Singh [2018] 99 taxmann.com 449 (Punj. & Har.). In CIT v. Pancham Dass Jain (2006) 156 Taxman 507 (All. HC) it was held that provisions of section 68 are not attracted to amounts representing purchases made on credit.

8.1-11d Whether renewal of loan is a loan? - Renewal of loan may be taken to be a payment by the debtor with one hand and a fresh borrowing with the other, and, in that view of the matter, a renewal amounted to a fresh loan [Pratap Singh v. Gulzari Lal, 1942 ALJ 3, AIR 1942 All 50 explained in Lachmi Lal v. Babu Narain Das, AIR 1950 All 152].

8.1-11e Whether overdraft facility is a loan? - In Bareilly Electricity Supply & Co. Ltd. v. State of U.P AIR 1977 Cal 426, it was held as under:

A loan was a matter of special agreement. In the absence of agreement, express or implied from a course of business, a banker was not bound to allow his customer to overdraw.

Whether unpaid amount claimed by financial creditor was financial debt

The corporate debtor has admitted that the amount paid by the applicant-financial creditor was towards an arrangement entered into between the parties as per the MoU. [Para 16]

On perusal of the pleadings and looking in to the terms and conditions contained in the MoU, it appears that the intentions of the parties were to give life to the corporate debtor which was facing a financial crisis. The financial creditor was under the obligation to arrange for working capital and took responsibilities of the day-to-day management of the corporate debtor. The applicant-financial creditor was also made responsible for payments of statutory dues and other administrative expenses including liabilities as on the 'effective date' given in the MoU. [Para 17]

In pursuant to the terms and conditions of the MoU, the applicant-financial creditor had started to make payments to the corporate debtor as reflects from the Certificate issued by the Bank of Maharahstra. The total amount now claimed is Rs. 2.14 crore along with further interest at the rate of 18 per cent per annum. [Para 18]

As per the terms and conditions of the MoU the financial creditor brought funds from time to time for corporate debtor's working capital, cleared its liabilities and paid other expenses. However, the corporate debtor did not perform its obligation, i.e., to proceed to negotiate the terms of definitive agreement, as was envisaged for implementation of provisions of the MoU. Therefore, money infused by the applicant-financial creditor into the corporate debtor is being demanded back by the applicant, which the corporate debtor failed to pay. The money brought by the financial creditor into the corporate debtor was part of a purchase agreement i.e., for the purchase of the corporate debtor company, including its subsidiary in terms of the MoU, which did not happen. Thus, the amount raised falls within the purview of 'any other transaction/purchase agreement, having the commercial effect of borrowing' which certainly carried the element of time value for money. Therefore, the debt claimed by the financial creditor falls within the purview of the provisions of section 5(8)(f).

The view is based on the well-established maxim of interpretation which says 'ut res magis valeat quam pereat'. This Latin maxim of interpretation when translated into English means that 'it is better for a thing to have effect than to be void'. In other words, where the provisions of a statute are plain, precise and unambiguous; it must be given the same meaning which it receives in ordinary parlance so as to give effect to same. Accordingly, the issue stands decided in favour of the financial creditor and against the corporate debtor. [Para 19]

There is no bar on relying upon the Whatsapp messages, which have been exchanged between the parties in the instant case, as the same are admissible under section 65B of the Indian Evidence Act, 1872. In this case the last transaction took place in 14-9-2014 between the financial creditor and corporate debtor and the Whatsapp messages have started to get exchanged between the parties from 7-7-2015 till 28-1-2016, by which the corporate debtor assured to make the payments to the financial creditor and the application under section 7 has been filed on 22-6-2018, which is within the period of limitation. Therefore, the issue is decided in favour of the financial creditor and against the corporate debtor. [Para 21]

Counter claim of corporate debtor

The corporate debtor has come up with defence claiming the outstanding against the financial creditor but the same is not substantiated with the documentary evidence. In short, the existence of any dispute, counter claims etc., as raised by the corporate debtor is/are irrelevant in the face of non-payment of the amount claimed. At this stage the corporate debtor is not permitted either to claim set off or to make counter claim against the financial creditor. If the corporate debtor has any genuine claim against the financial creditor, the same can be taken care of during the CIRP. It is also noted that the financial creditor controverted the contention of the corporate debtor and submitted that the financial creditor has not availed any facility from the corporate debtor. [Para 22]

Notice under section 8 being issued to corporate debtor as 'operational creditor', application under section 7 not barred

The financial creditor has submitted that the notice under section 8 was issued inadvertently, which does not operate as an estoppel against the financial creditor.

Harmonious and purposeful construction of IBC provisions by NCLAT

The NCLAT heard the appeal against the decision of the Adjudicating Authority (NCLT, Kolkata Bench) and on a harmonious and purposeful reading and reasoning, noted that as per the definition of "Corporate Person" under Section 3(7) of the IBC, insolvency resolution process under section 7 of the IBC can be initiated against the "Guarantor", who is a "Corporate Person" and who, by operation of law, ipso-facto, becomes a "Corporate Debtor" by satisfying the ingredients of the terms as defined under Section 3(8) of IBC, which means a "Corporate Person" who owes a debt to any person. The term "debt" under Section 3(11) of the IBC stipulates that "debt" means a liability or obligation in respect of a claim, which is due from any person and includes a financial and operational debt. It was argued that the term "Corporate Debtor" under Section 3(8) may also be any person. Further, as per section 3(23) of the IBC, "person" includes a company. Thus, a "Corporate Debtor" must be a "Corporate Person" who owes a "debt" to "any person". The "debt" as used in Section 3(8) has to be a "debt" as defined under Section 3(11) of IBC. It must be the "liability" or "obligation" in respect of a "claim"(section 3(6)) which is due from any person – which means even a corporate entity and shall include "financial debt" and "operational debt" as defined under Sections 5(8) and 5(21) of the IBC.

NCLAT noted that under section 3(6) of the IBC, the term "claim" means—

(a)

a right to payment, whether or not such right is reduced to judgment, fixed, disputed, undisputed, legal, equitable, secured or unsecured;

(b)

right to remedy for breach of contract under any law for the time being in force, if such breach gives rise to a right to payment, whether or not such right is reduced to judgment, fixed, matured, un-matured, disputed, undisputed, secured or unsecured;

Also, as per section 3(8) of the IBC, a "financial debt" means a "debt along with interest, if any, which is disbursed against the consideration for the time value of money and includes—

(a)

money borrowed against the payment of interest;

…(h) any counter-indemnity obligation in respect of a guarantee, indemnity, bond, documentary letter of credit or any other instrument issued by a bank or financial institution; and

(i)

the amount of any liability in respect of any of the guarantee or indemnity for any of the items referred to in sub-clauses (a) to (h) of this clause."

Salient aspects of the 14-member committee on Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016 [Code for short] 3. Regarding the report, it may be mentioned that the suggestions given by the committee cover the entire Code of 255 sections, including the changes made by the Ordinance in Nov., 2017, which was later on replaced by the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code (Amendment) Act, 2018, in January, 2018. Despite the changes brought in by Ordinance, later on replaced by an Amendment Act, 2018 (supra), the Govt. did not feel happy about the shape of the Code and, hence, appointed a 14-member committee to examine the entire legislation afresh. The committee was constituted by an Office Order dt. 16.11.2017 under the Chairmanship of Shri Injeti Srinivas, Secretary, Ministry of Corporate Affairs and comprised of 13 other members from various disciplines.

The Committee's mandate

3.1 The Committee was constituted with the mandate of making recommendations on (a) issues arising from the functioning and implementation of the Code; (b) issues that may impact the efficiency of the corporate insolvency and resolution and liquidation framework prescribed under the Code; and (c) any other relevant matters as it deems necessary.

In furtherance of its mandate, the Committee claims to have consolidated its views and recommendations from a gamut of stakeholders. It deliberated upon relevant issues and considered market practices as well as the legal principles, including international jurisprudence. Based on this detailed study, the Committee prepared a report, which recommends and provides several amendments to the Code and subordinate legislations, which are imperative for the smooth functioning of the Code.

The Committee submitted its report on 26th March, 2018.

3.2 *Analysis of the suggestions of the Committee – Part-wise and Chapter-wise of the Code

Structure of the report

3.2.1 The report deals with the recommendations of the committee and the rationale for such recommendations, in relation to the Code and the relevant subordinate legislation, viz., Insolvency and Bankruptcy (Application to Adjudicating Authority) Rules, 2016 ("CIRP Rules"), Insolvency and Bankruptcy Board of India (Insolvency Process for Corporate Persons) Regulations, 2016 ("CIRP Regulations"), Insolvency and Bankruptcy Board of India (Liquidation Process) Regulations, 2016 ("Liquidation Regulations").

It also contains three annexures: Annexure-I comprising of the notification dated 16th November 2017, constituting the Committee. Annexure-II containing comments from the World Bank Rajya Sabha Subordinate Legislation Committee and the issues raised in the Parliamentary debates when the Code and the Amendment Act were passed, along with summary responses to the same. Annexure-III contains the summary of proposed amendments to the Code and the proposed amendments to be subordinate legislation affected by the amendments to the Code.

Preamble to the Code

3.2.2 The Preamble to the Code reads thus:-

"It is an Act to 'financial debt' to mean a debt along with interest, if any, which is disbursed against the consideration for the time value of money and, inter-alia, includes money borrowed against payment of interest, etc."

The Committee has not suggested any changes in the Preamble to the Code.

3.2.3 Changes in definitions

3.2.3.1 Financial debt/financial creditor

Most of the definitions are contained in section 5 of the Code in Chapter-I of Part-II, designated as 'Preliminary'. One of these is 'financial debt' contained in section 5(8). This provision defines 'financial debt' to mean a debt along with interest, if any, which is disbursed against the consideration for the time value of money and, inter-alia, includes money borrowed against payment of interest, etc."

This definition created problems for homebuyers, who gave advances for purchase of real estate. Non-inclusion of homebuyers within either of the definition of 'financial' or 'operational' creditors became a cause for worry since it deprives them of, first, the right to initiate the Corporate Insolvency Resolution Process (CIRP), second the right to be on the CoC and third, the guarantee of receiving at least the liquidation value under the resolution plan. Recent cases like Chitra Sharma v. UOI – Writ Petitioner(s) (Civil) No.744 of 2017, Supreme Court of India – and Bikram Chatterji v. UOI - Writ Petitioner(s) (Civil) No.940 of 2017, Supreme Court of India – have evidenced the stance of the Hon'ble Supreme Court, safeguarding the rights of homebuyers under the Code due to their current disadvantageous position.

In these cases the Registrar of Companies filed a petition under section 433(e) of the Companies Act on the ground that the financial position of the company was found unsatisfactory on a scrutiny of the balance-sheet. It was held that "debt" means an amount which is due and can be claimed by the creditor, but if a debt has not yet accrued due, no demand can be made and the liability which will accrue in future did not lead to the conclusion that the company will be unable to meet its liabilities at that time. Again, the contention, in my view, has no merit. Undisputedly the parties are not related to each other nor is there a business dealing between them. No document is forthcoming in support of the plea of the respondents that the amount was advanced to it as interest free loan for a period of ten years and is not repayable before the expiry of the period. Learned counsel for the respondents submitted that the petition raises disputed questions of fact and, therefore, resort to the present proceedings in a situation like this, is not warranted. The Government of India launched the Scheme for Integrated Textile Parks in 2005, under which a special purpose vehicle (SPV), the financial creditor (a public company), was incorporated to implement a textile park at Kathua. J&K SIDCO leased 200 kanals to the SPV for 90 years; premium of about Rs. 3 crores and advance ground rent of about Rs. 12 lakhs were paid. The SPV executed a Memorandum of Agreement with the Ministry of Textiles, which sanctioned a project cost of about Rs. 39.70 crores. The SPV allotted plots to nine unit-holders (the corporate debtors) through tripartite agreements with J&K SIDCO, conferring leasehold rights of 20 kanals each.
